System Design Interview — Master Framework

Six steps. Two goals. One habit you run every time.

Every "design X" prompt — HLD or LLD — collapses into the same repeatable sequence. Steps 1–4 build the skeleton. Step 5 proves it satisfies what the system must do. Step 6 proves it survives what the system must withstand.

← scroll to see the full diagram →
1

Requirements

Foundation

What it is

The step where a vague prompt — "design X" — becomes a bounded contract: a short list of things the system must do, and a short list of qualities it must have while doing them.

Why the interviewer cares

This is the highest-leverage step in the interview. Every later decision — entities, API, architecture — gets graded against what you write here. Rush it, and even a technically strong design gets marked down for solving the wrong problem.

The micro-process

  1. Restate the prompt in one sentence, in your own words.
  2. Ask 3–5 clarifying questions that would actually change your design if answered differently — not questions for the sake of asking.
  3. Split findings into two explicit lists: Functional (the verbs — what a user can do) and Non-Functional (the adjectives — scale, latency, availability, consistency, durability, cost).
  4. Rank the functional list and draw a line under the top 3–5. Everything below the line is "acknowledged, out of scope for today."
  5. Say the scope back to the interviewer as a checkpoint before moving on.
Say this out loud

"So to confirm — we're building a system where users can [X], [Y], and [Z]. I'll treat [feature] as out of scope unless we have time at the end. On the non-functional side, I'm assuming roughly [N] users with [latency] reads — does that match what you had in mind?"

Common failure mode

Treating this as a 30-second formality before "the real design" starts. Candidates who skip to boxes-and-arrows almost always end up re-deriving requirements mid-design — which reads as disorganized and burns time you don't get back.

Mini-example — "Design a URL shortener"Functional: (1) shorten a long URL (2) redirect short → long (3) optional custom alias Non-functional: read:write ≈ 100:1 · redirect latency <100ms · codes never collide · links persist indefinitely

Where this shows up differently

  • Infrastructure-style prompts like a rate limiter: the interesting constraints are almost entirely non-functional — latency budget, correctness across instances. The functional list is short enough that debating it for five minutes wastes time you need elsewhere.
  • Consumer-product prompts: functional requirements do the deciding. A small difference like "can a link expire?" ripples all the way through the entity list and API.
  • Pipeline-shaped systems like a web crawler: often need one more non-functional requirement than you'd first guess — something about bounded resource growth (storage, crawl budget) that only becomes obvious once you picture the system running for months, not seconds.
2

Core Entities

Foundation

What it is

Naming the nouns — the handful of objects the whole system is organized around — before touching a schema or class diagram.

Why the interviewer cares

Entities are the shared vocabulary for the rest of the interview. Agree early that this system revolves around "User, Post, Follow relationship" and you can both talk in shorthand for the next 30 minutes instead of re-explaining objects every time.

The micro-process

  1. Reread the functional requirements — every verb usually implies a noun.
  2. List each entity with a 3–5 word description. No attributes yet.
  3. Sketch relationships in one line each (one-to-many, many-to-many) — enough to inform the API step, not a full schema.
  4. Stop there. Attribute-level detail belongs in Data Flow or Deep Dives, not here.
Say this out loud

"Looking at these requirements, I see three core entities: a User, a UrlMapping linking short-code to long-url, and a ClickEvent for analytics. A User has many UrlMappings, and a UrlMapping has many ClickEvents."

Common failure mode

Jumping straight to a full SQL schema with every column and index — premature detail that eats time you need later, and locks in decisions (like SQL vs NoSQL) before you've even designed the API that accesses this data.

Mini-example — URL ShortenerUser (id, plan_tier) UrlMapping (short_code, long_url, owner_id, created_at, expires_at) ClickEvent (url_id, timestamp, referrer)

Where this shows up differently

  • Pipeline-shaped systems like a web crawler: entities often represent the same piece of data at different pipeline stages rather than a fixed set of business objects — a "Frontier entry" and a "Page" both describe a URL, but they're genuinely different entities with different lifecycles. Expect one more entity than you'd first guess, roughly one per meaningful stage.
  • Internal/infrastructure systems like a rate limiter: entities skew toward configuration and live counters rather than anything a user would recognize — "RateLimitRule" and "RequestCounter" aren't nouns from the problem domain, they're nouns from the solution, and that's fine.
  • LLD problems like designing a parking lot: this is where the step goes furthest — entities become real classes with methods, not just fields, and relationships stop being "one line each" and become the actual design (composition, interfaces, inheritance). The class diagram in Step 5 is this step, finished.
3

API / Interface

Foundation

What it is

Turning each functional requirement into a concrete method signature or endpoint — the contract every later component has to honor.

Why the interviewer cares

The API is where "vague feature" becomes "testable interface." It forces decisions on inputs, outputs, and ownership, and gives you a checklist for High-Level Design later: "does my architecture serve every one of these?"

The micro-process

  1. One endpoint or method per functional requirement — no more.
  2. For each: name, inputs, outputs, and the one or two things that can realistically go wrong.
  3. Pick a style — REST, RPC, GraphQL — only if it matters for this system. Say why in one sentence; don't debate it.
  4. Keep it to 3–5 endpoints. More than that usually means Step 1's scope was too wide.
Say this out loud

"For the shorten flow: POST /urls with a long_url and optional custom alias, returns a short_code. For redirect: GET /{short_code} — a 302 to the long URL, or a 404 if it doesn't exist."

Common failure mode

Designing a full CRUD API for every entity "just in case," instead of the specific endpoints the functional requirements actually call for. This bloats the interview and signals template-matching rather than problem-solving.

Mini-example — URL ShortenerPOST /urls {long_url, custom_alias?} → {short_code} GET /{short_code} → 302 redirect | 404 GET /urls/{short_code}/stats → {click_count, created_at}

Where this shows up differently

Not every system centers on a public HTTP API.

  • An internal service like a rate limiter exposes a method signature — allow(client_id) — called by other services, not by end users.
  • A pipeline like a web crawler exposes almost nothing outward at all: an ingestion point to submit seed URLs, and a downstream query interface for whatever consumes the crawled content.

Default to REST out of habit and you'll waste time designing endpoints nobody asked for — say which kind of interface this system actually needs before picking a style.

4

Data Flow

Optional — pipeline systems only

What it is

Tracing how a single piece of data moves, stage by stage, through the system — used only when the core challenge is a pipeline (ingest → transform → store → serve), not a simple request/response system.

Why the interviewer cares

For pipeline-shaped problems (a web crawler, log analytics, video transcoding, feed ranking), the pipeline stages are the architecture — skip this and your High-Level Design becomes boxes with no real sequencing logic. For request/response systems (a URL shortener, a rate limiter), this step usually adds nothing beyond what the API already captured — say so explicitly and move on.

The micro-process

  1. Ask: does data transform across multiple async stages, or is this "request in, response out"? If the latter, skip this step out loud.
  2. If it applies: list the stages in order (e.g. Fetch → Parse → Dedupe → Store → Index).
  3. For each stage, note the trigger (sync call, queue message, schedule) and what it hands to the next stage.
  4. Flag where back-pressure or a stalled stage could block the whole pipeline — this feeds directly into Deep Dives.
Say this out loud

"This is a pipeline problem, so let me trace one page through it: a URL is pulled off the frontier queue, fetched by a worker, parsed for new links and content, deduped against a seen-set, then the content is written to storage and any new URLs go back onto the frontier."

Common failure mode

Either skipping this step for a system where it was the whole point — rushing to a High-Level Design that hides the actual hard part — or forcing it into a simple CRUD system, where it just repeats the API step with extra words.

Mini-example — Web CrawlerFrontier Queue → Fetch Worker → Parser → Dedupe Filter (bloom filter) ↓ ↓ Content Store new URLs → Frontier

Where this shows up differently

The tell for whether this step applies: can you draw the system as a straight line of transformations with no branching decision logic?

  • If yes — a crawler, a log pipeline, a video transcoding job — it's pipeline-shaped, and this step is where the real design happens. See the crawler walkthrough for a fully worked example, including the loop-back that makes a crawler's pipeline different from a simple linear one.
  • If every request is answered by a single synchronous path — a URL shortener, a rate limiter — you're not missing anything by skipping it out loud and moving straight to Step 5.
5

High-Level Design

→ Satisfies Functional Requirements

What it is

The architecture diagram — boxes and arrows from client to storage — walked through once per functional requirement, tracing an actual request through the system rather than presenting a static picture.

Why the interviewer cares

This step proves the system works at all — it's your primary evidence for satisfying Functional Requirements. Interviewers watch whether every box exists because a requirement needs it, not because it's a familiar pattern. You don't need a queue if nothing in your requirements is asynchronous.

The micro-process

  1. Draw components in a consistent order: client → load balancer / gateway → service(s) → cache → database → async workers/queue → CDN — including only what your requirements justify.
  2. Pick your first functional requirement and trace it left to right through the diagram, narrating each hop.
  3. Repeat for each remaining core functional requirement — same diagram, different path through it.
  4. Flag where you're making a default choice ("single relational DB for now, revisit sharding in the deep dive") rather than over-engineering upfront.
Say this out loud

"Let's trace the write path first: a shorten request hits the load balancer, routes to a stateless API service, which generates a code and writes the mapping to the database. Now the read path: a redirect request hits the same service, checks the cache first, falls back to the database on a miss, and issues the 302."

Common failure mode

Presenting the diagram as a finished picture without tracing data through it — "here's my architecture," full stop. This is where the thread connecting design to requirements gets lost, and it's the easiest place for an interviewer to probe and find a gap.

Mini-example — URL Shortener HLDClient → LB → API Service ─┬─ write path → DB ╰─ read path → Cache → (miss) → DB

Where this shows up differently

  • Systems with a write path and a read path that genuinely diverge — like the URL shortener — deserve a diagram that clearly separates them; don't force one static picture to represent both flows if it makes the diagram harder to follow. Trace each path in its own pass through the same boxes, ideally with its own color, the way the worked examples on this page do.
  • Systems built around a single decision point — like the rate limiter — have a simpler HLD but a sharper fork: the diagram's whole job is to make the allow/deny branch and what happens on each side unmistakable.
  • LLD problems replace the service diagram entirely with a class diagram: boxes become classes instead of services, and arrows mean implements/extends and composition instead of network calls. The walkthrough is the same — trace a park and an unpark through the classes — but what you're tracing is method calls in one process, not requests across a network.
6

Deep Dives

→ Satisfies Non-Functional Requirements

What it is

A second, deliberate pass over your Step 5 design — not new diagramming, but taking each Non-Functional Requirement from Step 1 one at a time and asking: does what I built actually survive this, and if not, what changes?

Why the interviewer cares

This is where interviews are actually won or lost. Anyone can draw a load balancer and a cache; showing you know when and why a specific piece breaks under specific conditions — and what you'd change — is the signal that's hard to fake.

The micro-process

  1. List your NFRs from Step 1 again, explicitly.
  2. For each: at the stated scale/latency/availability target, where does the current design break first?
  3. Propose the specific fix — sharding key, cache strategy, replication mode, queue, circuit breaker — and name the trade-off it introduces. Nothing is free.
  4. Go genuinely deep on only 1–2 of these, usually wherever the interviewer leans in. Breadth-first across all NFRs, depth on the one or two that matter most.
Say this out loud

"At 10K redirects/second, a single Postgres instance handling both reads and writes becomes the bottleneck. I'd add read replicas and put a cache in front — since redirects are read-heavy and short codes are immutable once created, cache invalidation isn't even a real concern here, which is a nice property of this specific problem."

Common failure mode

Listing generic scaling techniques — "we'd add a cache, we'd shard the database" — without connecting them to this system's actual numbers or access pattern. This reads as recited vocabulary rather than reasoning, and interviewers can tell the difference immediately.

Mini-exampleNFR "handle 10K redirects/sec" → bottleneck: DB read load → fix: Redis cache keyed by short_code, no TTL needed (mappings are immutable) → trade-off: extra infra + cold-start latency for brand-new links

Where this shows up differently

How many genuine deep dives a system needs varies:

  • A request/response system like the URL shortener usually has one or two (short-code generation, cache design) because there just aren't that many moving parts to stress-test.
  • A pipeline system like the web crawler often has more, because more stages means more places for something to break under scale — duplicate work, politeness, storage growth are all separate failure modes worth their own pass.
  • An algorithm-centric system like the rate limiter can have a deep dive that's almost entirely about a single data-structure choice.
  • An LLD problem like the parking lot swaps scale-shaped deep dives for correctness-shaped ones: race conditions, deadlocks, and whether a design pattern earns its complexity — the non-functional requirements are about a single process behaving correctly under concurrency, not a fleet of servers behaving correctly under load.

Match your depth to what the system actually needs, not to a fixed count you memorized.

Toolkit

Case Catalog — the Case, the Approach, the Trade-off, and How to Say It

System design is mostly recognising a case and reaching for the right approach — and then saying what it costs. Every card below has four parts: when this happens, do this, accept that — and how to say it: a first-person answer that names the choice, why it beats the obvious alternative, and the cost you accept. That last line is what an interviewer actually hears, so practise saying it.

Six tensions sit behind almost every trade-off here: consistency ↔ latency · freshness ↔ cost · exactness ↔ speed · isolation ↔ efficiency · simplicity ↔ scale · safety ↔ speed of change. When you read a card, ask which one it is buying.

143 of 143 cases
Search & discovery#01 elasticsearch opensearch full-text inverted index

A user searches products by text and filters

Millions of products. People type words, pick a category and a price range, and expect results in under 200 ms.

Say it in the interview

“I'd put a search engine — OpenSearch — beside the database and feed it from the change stream, rather than LIKE queries on the primary, because inverted indexes make text, filters and ranking fast at millions of rows. The trade-off I accept is a few seconds of lag, so checkout always reads price and stock from the source.”

Approach

A search engine (Elasticsearch or OpenSearch) fed by a change stream. Pre-built inverted indexes make text matching, filters and ranking fast; shard by product id and replicate for reads.

Trade-off

Eventual consistency. The index lags the database by seconds and is only a copy, so price and stock on a result are for display and checkout reads the source.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A price change rewrites the whole indexed document. Coalesce price and stock updates before indexing instead of indexing every change.

Not when

A few thousand rows. A database index or built-in full-text search is simpler and always consistent.

See
AXMarketplace: search to payIInvoice search⚡Caching Playbook
Search & discovery#02 typeahead trie prefix

Autocomplete as the user types

A suggestion must appear within about 100 ms of every keystroke.

Say it in the interview

“I'd precompute popular prefixes from search logs into a trie or edge n-grams and cache the top suggestions at the edge, rather than querying the main index on every keystroke, and debounce on the client. I accept that suggestions are as fresh as the last refresh — they show what's popular, not what's new.”

Approach

A prefix structure (a trie or edge n-grams) over precomputed popular queries, refreshed offline from logs; cache the top suggestions per prefix at the edge; debounce keystrokes on the client.

Trade-off

Suggestions are stale by the refresh interval and cost memory. They show what was popular, not what is new.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Never suggest private, offensive or removed items, and make sure personalised suggestions respect permissions.

Not when

When the user needs exact, live results for a specific query. That is search, not suggestion.

See
⚡Caching Playbook
Search & discovery#03 acl authorization permission filter

Search must never show what a user may not see

Private channels, restricted documents and per-tenant data all sit in one index.

Say it in the interview

“I'd put the permission filter inside the search query — public, or one of the scopes this user belongs to — rather than filtering the results afterwards, because filtering a truncated result set drops real matches and moves data the user can't see. The cost is a heavier query and a reindex when visibility changes.”

Approach

Filter inside the query: a public flag plus the few private scopes the user belongs to. Store a scope id on every document, and re-check the hits against the source before returning them.

Trade-off

The permission filter costs more than the text match itself (about 100 times an unfiltered query in the chat test), and a visibility change forces a bulk reindex.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Filtering after the search returns empty pages for users with narrow access. Filter inside the query and verify at the end.

Not when

Public data that everyone may see.

See
AYSlack-style channels
Search & discovery#04 tombstone soft delete versioning

A deleted or edited item must disappear from search

A deleted message or product still shows up in results.

Say it in the interview

“I'd treat edits and deletes as versions: a delete is a tombstone with a higher version, and every copy applies a change only if it's newer. Rather than deleting from each index directly — which a late update can resurrect — the version rule makes order irrelevant. The cost is tombstones until compaction.”

Approach

Model edits and deletes as versions. A delete is a tombstone with a higher version, and every consumer applies a change only if it is newer than what it holds.

Trade-off

Tombstones take space until compacted, and every consumer has to follow the rule.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A late edit that arrives after a delete resurrects the item if the delete removed the row. In the test, 1,244 of 1,667 deleted messages came back.

Not when

Append-only data that is never edited or deleted.

See
AYSlack-style channels
Search & discovery#05 geohash quadtree s2 proximity location nearby

Find things near me

Nearest drivers, shops or listings within a few kilometres.

Say it in the interview

“I'd index locations by spatial cell — geohash or S2 — query the user's cell and its neighbours, then sort the candidates by exact distance, rather than computing distance to every row. I'd pick the cell size from the search radius and split dense cells, accepting edge cases at cell boundaries.”

Approach

Index locations by a spatial cell (geohash, quadtree or S2), query the cell and its neighbours, then sort the candidates by exact distance.

Trade-off

Cell size is a compromise between precision and cost. Queries near a boundary need neighbouring cells, and dense areas create hot cells.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A point just across a cell boundary is missed unless neighbours are queried, and a busy downtown cell must be subdivided.

Not when

A small fixed set of places, where a linear scan is fine.

See
GUber
Search & discovery#06 reindex alias swap zero downtime

Rebuild or change a search index without downtime

A new analyzer, a new field or a bigger shard count needs a fresh index.

Say it in the interview

“I'd build a new index from a snapshot plus the change stream, let it catch up, verify counts, then swap an alias, rather than reindexing in place. The old index stays until I'm sure, so rollback is one alias swap.”

Approach

Build the new index from a snapshot plus the change stream from a saved offset, let it catch up, verify counts, then swap an alias and keep the old index until you are sure.

Trade-off

Double the storage and indexing work while both exist, and a longer build means more catching up.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Updates that arrive during the build are lost unless you replay the stream from the offset you saved when the snapshot began.

Not when

A tiny index that you can rebuild in seconds.

See
AXMarketplace: search to pay
Search & discovery#07 fuzzy synonyms stemming relevance ranking analyzer

Typos, synonyms and relevance

People misspell words, use different names for the same thing, and expect the best result first.

Say it in the interview

“I'd add stemming and synonyms, fuzzy matching with a small edit distance, and per-field boosts, then tune ranking from real clicks, rather than guessing relevance once. Each recall gain risks precision, so I'd measure it.”

Approach

Analyzers for stemming and synonyms, fuzzy matching with a small edit-distance limit, boosts per field, and ranking tuned from real clicks and conversions.

Trade-off

Better recall costs precision, and relevance tuning is continuous work that needs measurement.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Fuzzy matching on very short terms explodes the candidate set, and boosting popularity can bury new items.

Not when

Exact lookups by id or code.

See
IInvoice search
Search & discovery#08 search_after track_total_hits facets deep paging

Result counts and deep paging on huge result sets

“About 1.2 million results”, and someone jumps to page 10,000.

Say it in the interview

“I'd cap exact counts — '10,000+' — compute facets on the filtered set, and page deep with search_after, rather than exact totals and offsets, which get slower the deeper users go.”

Approach

Cap exact totals (for example stop counting at 10,000) or show an estimate, compute facet counts on the filtered set, and page deep with a cursor (search_after) rather than offsets.

Trade-off

Counts become approximate and users cannot jump to an arbitrary page.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Deep offset paging makes every shard sort and discard millions of hits.

Not when

Small result sets, where exact counts are cheap.

See
IInvoice search
Data & storage#09 relational document key-value dynamodb postgres mongodb

Choose SQL or NoSQL for a new feature

A team has to pick the store for a new service.

Say it in the interview

“I'd name the access patterns first. If the data is relational and needs transactions, PostgreSQL — with JSONB for the few flexible fields. If each entity is read and written whole as one JSON document, a document store like MongoDB; if it's key lookups at a scale one primary can't take, DynamoDB or Cassandra, with a partition key I've checked spreads load. Relational gives ACID; many NoSQL stores are BASE — and CAP is about what any distributed store does during a network partition, not SQL versus NoSQL.”

Approach

Name the access patterns first, then pick the family. Relational (PostgreSQL) when data has relationships and needs ACID transactions, constraints and ad-hoc queries — with a JSONB column for the few flexible attributes. A document store (MongoDB) when each entity is an aggregate read and written as one JSON document (a product with its variants, a profile) and its shape varies. Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB) for lookups by key at very high scale; wide-column (Cassandra) for huge write volumes read by partition and time; a graph store only for deep relationship traversal; a search engine as a copy for text.

Trade-off

ACID vs BASE: relational gives atomic, isolated transactions, constraints and joins; many NoSQL stores trade some of that for availability and soft, eventually consistent state (BASE) — though MongoDB and DynamoDB now offer transactions, at a cost. Scaling: relational scales reads with replicas and writes by sharding you plan (Citus, Vitess); NoSQL partitions by the key you choose and adds capacity by adding nodes — but only if the key spreads load evenly; a hot key still overloads one partition. CAP is a separate axis: during a network partition any distributed store either refuses some requests (consistent — Spanner, CockroachDB, a MongoDB primary) or answers with possibly stale data (available — Cassandra, DynamoDB's default reads); PACELC adds that, even without a partition, stronger consistency costs latency.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Choosing NoSQL for a model that later needs transactions across records — or a document store whose documents grow without bound: embed what is read together and bounded, reference what keeps growing.

Not when

Never choose by fashion. The access pattern decides.

See
▦Data Stores
Data & storage#10 noisy neighbour neighbor cell isolation

One tenant is most of the load

Two customers use 80% of the database, the queue and the cache.

Say it in the interview

“I'd add per-tenant limits first, then move the largest tenant to its own cell — compute, cache, and finally database — with a routing table, rather than scaling the shared stack for one customer. That buys isolation and independent scaling at the cost of more stacks and a planned migration.”

Approach

Per-tenant limits first. Then separate compute, cache and finally the database for the largest tenants — a dedicated cell — moved with a filtered replication stream and a versioned routing table.

Trade-off

More stacks to run and a migration to plan, in exchange for isolation and independent scaling.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

The cutover must pause that tenant’s writes briefly, and a router with a stale cache must not write to the old copy.

Not when

Many mid-size tenants, where fair limits are enough.

See
ATIsolating big orgsVMulti-tenant limits
Data & storage#11 partitioning retention archive time-series

A table that only grows

Messages, events or logs: billions of rows, recent ones hot, old ones rarely read.

Say it in the interview

“I'd partition by time, keep queries key-and-range shaped, and drop or tier old partitions on a retention policy, rather than deleting rows from one huge table. Dropping a partition is instant; the catch is that unique keys must include the partition column.”

Approach

Partition by time (or by a hash of a key), set a retention period, tier old data to cheaper storage, and keep queries key-and-range shaped.

Trade-off

A partitioned table’s unique keys must include the partition column, which can break idempotency, and restoring old data is slower.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A retry after a partition boundary can create a duplicate. Use a small registry table for the uniqueness.

Not when

Tables that stay small.

See
AVClock-in schemaAYSlack-style channels
Data & storage#12 blob object storage s3 presigned

Store big files and blobs

Uploads of images, documents or video.

Say it in the interview

“I'd keep the bytes in object storage, uploaded and downloaded through short-lived presigned URLs, and only metadata in the database, rather than blobs in the database, which bloats backups and replication. The trade-off is two systems that must agree, so I'd add a cleanup job for orphans.”

Approach

The bytes go to object storage through presigned URLs. Only metadata — name, owner, hash, size — lives in the database.

Trade-off

Two systems that must agree: a metadata row can point at a missing object, or an object can be left orphaned.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Commit the metadata only after the object exists, and sweep orphaned objects after a grace period.

Not when

Tiny payloads that fit comfortably in a row.

See
AZFile sync & video
Data & storage#13 migration expand contract ddl

Change the schema without downtime

Rename a column or split a table while traffic keeps running.

Say it in the interview

“I'd use expand, migrate, contract: add the new column or table, write to both, backfill, switch reads, then remove the old shape — rather than one ALTER that locks a big table. It takes a few releases, but every step can be rolled back with no downtime.”

Approach

Expand, migrate, contract: add the new shape, write to both, backfill, switch reads, then remove the old one.

Trade-off

It takes several releases and temporary duplication, in exchange for no outage and an easy rollback.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A naive ALTER that takes a long lock on a big table, or a backfill that starves production traffic.

Not when

A tiny internal table with a maintenance window.

See
⇪Schema Migrations
Data & storage#14 schema per tenant database per tenant shared tables

Multi-tenant data: shared tables, schema per tenant, or database per tenant

Many customers, very different sizes and isolation needs.

Say it in the interview

“I'd default to shared tables with the tenant id in every key, plus row-level security, and give only very large or regulated tenants their own schema or database — one database per tenant multiplies migrations and connections.”

Approach

Shared tables with the tenant id in every key by default; a separate schema or database for the few very large or regulated tenants.

Trade-off

Shared tables are efficient but rely on discipline for isolation. Separate databases isolate well but multiply migrations, connections and operations.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Running one migration across ten thousand schemas, and a connection pool that cannot serve them all.

Not when

A single-tenant product.

See
AETenant isolationATIsolating big orgs
Data & storage#15 tree folders org chart closure table materialised path

Store a hierarchy

Folders, an org chart, or nested comments.

Say it in the interview

“I'd keep parent pointers for cheap moves, plus a closure table or materialised path when I need fast 'everything under this node' queries — the choice depends on whether moves or subtree reads dominate.”

Approach

Parent pointers for cheap moves, plus a closure table or a materialised path when you need fast “everything under this node” queries.

Trade-off

Parent pointers make moves one row but subtree queries need recursion; paths make subtree queries fast but a move rewrites every descendant.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Moving a folder of 100,000 files was one row with parent pointers and 100,000 rows with stored paths in the file-platform test.

Not when

Shallow, static hierarchies.

See
AZFile sync & video
Data & storage#16 social graph followers adjacency list

Who follows whom

A social graph with followers, following and mutual connections.

Say it in the interview

“I'd store follow edges in both directions, sharded by user id, with special handling for accounts with millions of followers, rather than a graph database by default. Expensive queries like friends-of-friends are precomputed.”

Approach

Adjacency lists in both directions, sharded by user id, with special handling for accounts that have millions of followers; precompute expensive graph queries.

Trade-off

Two writes per edge that must stay consistent, and deep graph queries (friends of friends) get expensive.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A celebrity’s follower list is a hot key, and unfollow must update both directions.

Not when

Deep traversal as the main workload, where a graph database fits better.

See
JNews feed
Data & storage#17 migration dual write shadow reads cutover strangler

Migrate to a new system without downtime

Replace a legacy service or database while it serves traffic.

Say it in the interview

“I'd stream changes with CDC into the new system, compare with shadow reads, and move traffic gradually — tenant by tenant — keeping a rollback path, rather than a big-bang cutover weekend.”

Approach

Dual-write or stream changes with CDC, read from both and compare (shadow reads), move traffic gradually or tenant by tenant, and keep a rollback path until the old system is quiet.

Trade-off

A long period running two systems, and verification effort, in exchange for a reversible cutover.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

The two systems drifting apart. Compare continuously and alert on mismatches.

Not when

A small dataset you can move in a maintenance window.

See
ANLegacy migrationATIsolating big orgs
Data & storage#18

Normalise or denormalise

A page view joins five tables every time.

Say it in the interview

“I'd keep the source of truth normalised so each fact lives once, and denormalise only for the hot read — a summary table or document fed by CDC — rather than duplicating data everywhere. Writes then touch two places, so I'd name who owns the copy and how it's reconciled.”

Approach

Keep the source of truth normalised so each fact lives once; denormalise into read models — a column, a summary table, a document, a search index — only where a hot read needs it, kept in step by the same transaction, a trigger, or CDC.

Trade-off

Denormalised copies make reads fast, but every write must update them and they can drift, which needs an owner and reconciliation.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Denormalising before measuring, or copies with no owner and no repair path.

Not when

Small tables, or reads that are already fast with the right index.

See
JNews feed▦Data Stores
Data & storage#19

B-tree or LSM-tree storage

A table takes a very high, steady write rate.

Say it in the interview

“For a write-heavy workload like events or time series I'd pick an LSM-based store such as Cassandra, which turns writes into sequential appends, rather than a B-tree database that updates pages in place. The cost is compaction I/O and slower reads, which Bloom filters and a good partition key keep in check.”

Approach

B-tree engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB) update pages in place: fast point reads and range scans, more random I/O per write. LSM-tree engines (Cassandra, RocksDB, ScyllaDB) append to memory, flush sorted files and compact them: very high write throughput, while a read may check several files (Bloom filters skip most).

Trade-off

LSM is write-optimised, but compaction costs I/O and space, and reads and deletes (tombstones) cost more. B-tree is read-optimised and simple, but heavy random writes and many indexes limit write throughput.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Ignoring compaction: an LSM store that falls behind on compaction slows every read.

Not when

Ordinary transactional load that a B-tree database handles comfortably.

See
▦Data Stores
Consistency & correctness#20 double booking reservation lock hold

Two people book the last seat or room

Concurrent requests race for one slot.

Say it in the interview

“I'd let the database decide with a unique constraint or a conditional update on the slot, plus a short hold that expires, rather than checking availability in application code, which races. Under extreme demand I'd put a queue in front so the database sees an orderly line.”

Approach

Make the database decide: a unique constraint or a conditional update on the slot, with a short hold (a TTL) while the user pays.

Trade-off

Contention on popular slots, and holds that must expire; extreme demand needs a queue in front.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Expired holds that never release, and two holds racing for the same seat.

Not when

Inventory that can safely oversell, where you overbook on purpose.

See
ETicketmasterHMeeting rooms
Consistency & correctness#21 oversell inventory stock hot row

A flash sale on one product

One row that everybody wants at the same moment.

Say it in the interview

“I'd guard stock with a conditional decrement — only if stock is above zero — and put a queue in front that answers 'accepted, processing', rather than reading stock and then writing, which oversells. If one row is too hot I'd split stock into buckets, accepting a fallback when a bucket empties.”

Approach

A conditional decrement (stock greater than zero) is the guard against overselling. Split stock into buckets to spread the lock, and put a queue in front that answers “accepted, processing”.

Trade-off

Buckets need a fallback when one empties, and a queue adds delay. On one core the bucket gain was modest; it grows with more cores.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A read followed by a write oversells, and a cache can keep showing “in stock” after it is gone.

Not when

Normal-demand items.

See
PFlash saleAXMarketplace: search to pay
Consistency & correctness#22 idempotency key dedupe exactly-once

A retried request must not repeat its effect

A client retries a payment or a send after a timeout.

Say it in the interview

“I'd require an idempotency key on the request and store it with a unique constraint, so a retry returns the first result, rather than hoping clients don't retry. I'd keep keys for a window and reject the same key with a different payload.”

Approach

The client sends an idempotency key. A unique constraint on it makes the second attempt return the first result.

Trade-off

You store keys for a window and must handle a request that is still in flight; a key reused with a different payload should be rejected.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Concurrent duplicates: the loser must wait or fail cleanly, and a counter bumped inside a failed insert can leave gaps in a sequence.

Not when

Naturally idempotent operations, such as setting a value.

See
XIdempotent paymentsAVClock-in schemaAYSlack-style channels
Consistency & correctness#23 outbox cdc debezium dual write

Update the database and publish an event

A change must reach other systems without being lost or invented.

Say it in the interview

“I'd write the business change and the event in one transaction with an outbox table, and publish it with CDC reading the database log — Debezium — or a small relay, rather than writing to the database and then to Kafka, where a crash between the two loses or invents an event. Events can repeat, so consumers dedupe by event id or version.”

Approach

The outbox pattern: write the business change and the event in the same transaction, then publish at least once — from a relay that polls the outbox, or with CDC reading it from the database log (Debezium), which avoids polling — and make consumers idempotent by event id or version.

Trade-off

Events arrive late by the relay’s interval and can repeat, and the outbox needs cleanup.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Make the event id at the start, inside the transaction, never at send time. Otherwise a retry looks like a new event.

Not when

When losing an event is acceptable, as with best-effort metrics.

See
ASNotification schemaAXMarketplace: search to pay
Consistency & correctness#24 saga two-phase commit 2pc ledger transaction

Money moves across services

A payment touches several systems that each have their own database.

Say it in the interview

“I'd model the flow as a saga of local transactions with compensations, or as a double-entry ledger, rather than a distributed two-phase commit, which blocks when a participant is down. I accept that intermediate states are visible and that compensations need their own retries and reconciliation.”

Approach

A saga of local transactions with compensations (a refund), or a double-entry ledger. Avoid distributed two-phase commit.

Trade-off

Intermediate states are visible and compensations can fail. A ledger is append-only and must be reconciled.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A compensation that fails needs its own retry and alert. Never edit history: append a correction.

Not when

Everything in one database, where a single transaction does the job.

See
XIdempotent payments
Consistency & correctness#25 read-your-writes replica lag session consistency

The user must see their own write

A user saves a change and the next page load shows the old value.

Say it in the interview

“I'd route the user's next reads to the primary for a short time after they write, or pass a version token so a replica waits until it has caught up, rather than reading every request from the primary. Only the writer needs read-your-writes, so only they pay for it.”

Approach

Route their next read to the primary or a fresh replica for a short time, or pass a version token so a replica waits until it has caught up.

Trade-off

More load on the primary and extra complexity; a read may wait.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A read served by a lagging replica right after a redirect, or a cache serving the old value.

Not when

Content where a few seconds of staleness is invisible.

See
⇆Data Correctness
Consistency & correctness#26 optimistic concurrency etag if-match lost update version

Two users edit the same record

Both open it, both change it, the second save overwrites the first.

Say it in the interview

“I'd use optimistic concurrency: every update carries the version it read, and a stale one is rejected so the client reloads or merges, rather than last-write-wins, which silently loses an edit, or locks held while a user thinks.”

Approach

Optimistic concurrency: send the version (or an ETag with If-Match) with every update; reject a stale write and let the client reload or merge.

Trade-off

Clients must handle conflicts and retry, but nobody waits on a lock and no edit is lost silently.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

An update that forgets to check the version is a lost update. In the file-sync test, an unguarded update lost 200 of 400 edits.

Not when

Data that only one writer ever touches.

See
AZFile sync & videoKCollaborative editing
Consistency & correctness#27 unique username email shards reservation

A value must be unique across shards

A username or an email that no two accounts may share.

Say it in the interview

“I'd route uniqueness to the shard that owns a hash of the unique value — or a small reservation table written first — rather than checking every shard, which races.”

Approach

Route by a hash of the unique value to the one shard that owns uniqueness, or keep a small global reservation table written first.

Trade-off

A second write and an extra hop, or a central table that can become a bottleneck.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Case and Unicode variants of the same name. Normalise before hashing and comparing.

Not when

A single database, where a unique index does the job.

See
▦Data Stores
Consistency & correctness#28 reconciliation drift checksum repair

Copies drift apart

The index, the cache, the replica and the warehouse each disagree slightly with the source.

Say it in the interview

“I'd run a scheduled reconciliation that compares counts and checksums by key range against the source of truth, repairs differences and alerts on the mismatch rate, rather than assuming copies stay in sync — they always drift eventually.”

Approach

Reconciliation: compare counts and checksums by key range on a schedule, repair from the source of truth, and alert on the mismatch rate.

Trade-off

Extra load and another pipeline to run, in exchange for finding silent divergence.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Repairing from a stale copy. Always repair from the source, never from another copy.

Not when

Copies that are rebuilt from scratch often anyway.

See
AXMarketplace: search to payAZFile sync & video
Consistency & correctness#29

Pick a transaction isolation level

Two transactions read and update related rows at the same time.

Say it in the interview

“I'd stay on Read Committed for most code and guard updates with conditional writes or SELECT FOR UPDATE, and use Serializable only where an invariant spans rows — like 'at least one doctor on call' — with a retry on serialization failure. Aborts and retries are the price for no write skew.”

Approach

Know the anomalies: lost updates, non-repeatable reads, phantoms and write skew. Read Committed (PostgreSQL's default) plus conditional updates or SELECT … FOR UPDATE covers most code; use Serializable — or explicit locks — where an invariant spans several rows ('at least one doctor on call'), and retry on serialization failures.

Trade-off

Stronger isolation means more aborted transactions and retries, or more locking and lower throughput; weaker isolation is fast but lets anomalies through unless the code guards them.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Assuming the default level prevents lost updates or write skew — in PostgreSQL's Read Committed it doesn't.

Not when

Single-row updates guarded by a condition or a version — they're already safe at the default level.

See
⇆Data CorrectnessHMeeting rooms
Scaling reads & writes#30 cache ttl cdn stampede

Read-heavy hot data

The same items are read far more often than they change.

Say it in the interview

“I'd use cache-aside with a TTL plus jitter and keep the database authoritative, rather than making the cache the source of truth. Events invalidate entries, the TTL catches what events miss, and I'd protect against a cold cache stampeding the database with request coalescing.”

Approach

Cache-aside with a TTL and jitter, an eviction policy (LRU or LFU) sized to the working set, request coalescing so one miss loads once, the source of truth kept authoritative, plus a CDN for static content.

Trade-off

Stale data and invalidation logic, and a cold cache sends a burst of reads to the database.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A stampede when a hot key expires: coalesce identical requests or serve stale while refreshing.

Not when

Write-heavy data that is rarely read twice.

See
⚡Caching Playbook
Scaling reads & writes#31 hot partition celebrity skew

One key is hot

A celebrity, a viral product or a shared counter concentrates traffic on one partition.

Say it in the interview

“I'd split the hot key into N copies with a suffix, add a small in-process cache, and coalesce identical in-flight requests, rather than scaling the whole cluster for one key. Reads may see slightly different copies for a moment and writes touch all of them — acceptable for counters or popular items.”

Approach

Split the key across N copies with a suffix, put a small local cache in front, and coalesce identical in-flight requests.

Trade-off

Reads may see slightly different copies, writes must update all of them, and there is more complexity.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A hot partition looks like a healthy cluster with one melted node, so watch per-key load, not averages.

Not when

Load spread evenly across keys.

See
⚡Caching PlaybookPFlash sale
Scaling reads & writes#32 batching coalescing spike bulk import

A write burst

A bulk import or a flash sale sends far more writes than the steady rate.

Say it in the interview

“I'd queue writes, batch them, and coalesce per key so the latest wins, guarded by a version, rather than letting every write hit the database. Bulk and interactive writes get separate lanes. I accept that a write is acknowledged before it's applied.”

Approach

Batch the writes, coalesce updates per key so the latest wins, guard each write by version, and queue in front. Keep separate lanes for bulk and interactive writes.

Trade-off

Writes are acknowledged before they are applied, and latest-wins hides intermediate values.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A batched upsert cannot touch the same key twice, so coalesce first.

Not when

Steady, low write rates.

See
AXMarketplace: search to pay
Scaling reads & writes#33 sequence ordering partition key

Order within a busy conversation or account

Everyone must see one channel’s messages in the same order.

Say it in the interview

“I'd give each conversation or account its own sequence number, taken in the same transaction that stores the message, and partition streams by that key, rather than relying on timestamps, which tie and drift. One key's writes serialise on its counter, which batching relieves.”

Approach

Give each key (channel, account) a sequence number taken in the storing transaction, and partition streams by that key.

Trade-off

One key’s writes serialise on its counter. Batching per key lifts the ceiling.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A one-statement, retry-safe insert can move the counter without inserting, leaving holes in the sequence.

Not when

Data with no ordering requirement.

See
AYSlack-style channels
Scaling reads & writes#34 fan-out feed fanout timeline

One event goes to millions

A post or an announcement must reach a huge audience.

Say it in the interview

“I'd use hybrid fan-out: precompute feeds for ordinary accounts on write, and merge celebrity posts in at read time, rather than one strategy for all — writing to 50 million followers per post doesn't work. Two code paths is the price.”

Approach

Hybrid fan-out: precompute for ordinary accounts (fan-out on write), compute on read for huge ones, and keep unread state as cursors rather than rows.

Trade-off

Write amplification and storage against read latency, and the hybrid has two code paths.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A celebrity post that writes millions of rows at once.

Not when

Small audiences, where reading on demand is enough.

JNews feedAYSlack-style channelsAIAnnouncements
Scaling reads & writes#35 likes views sharded counter

Counters at scale

Views and likes arrive faster than a database can count them one by one.

Say it in the interview

“I'd count in memory or in sharded counters and flush in batches, showing an approximate number now and an exact one from the pipeline later, rather than incrementing one row per event. Exactness in real time is rarely needed and expensive.”

Approach

Count in memory or in a sharded counter and flush in batches. Show an approximate number now and an exact one later.

Trade-off

Real-time numbers are approximate, and exactness costs a pipeline.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Double counting on retries, and bots inflating the numbers.

Not when

Money or inventory, which must be exact.

See

Scaling reads & writes#36 cache penetration bloom filter negative caching

Requests for things that do not exist hit the database

Bots probe random ids and every one misses the cache.

Say it in the interview

“I'd cache 'not found' briefly and put a Bloom filter of existing ids in front, rather than letting every lookup for a missing id reach the database — a common abuse pattern. A new item may look missing for a moment.”

Approach

Cache the “not found” answer briefly (negative caching) and put a Bloom filter of existing ids in front.

Trade-off

Negative entries can go stale (a new item looks missing for a moment), and a Bloom filter has false positives and needs rebuilding.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A Bloom filter cannot delete, so rebuild it periodically.

Not when

Traffic that only asks for real ids.

See
⚡Caching Playbook
Scaling reads & writes#37 write-through write-back write-behind cache-aside

Choose a cache write strategy

Data is written and read through a cache.

Say it in the interview

“I'd default to cache-aside with LRU eviction sized to the working set, use write-through only where reads must immediately see writes, refresh-ahead for a few hot keys, and avoid write-behind unless losing recent writes is acceptable.”

Approach

Cache-aside (the application loads on a miss) for most read-heavy data; read-through when the cache library loads for you; write-through when reads must see writes immediately; write-behind only when you can tolerate losing recent writes; refresh-ahead for hot keys that must never miss. Pick an eviction policy — LRU for recency, LFU for steady popularity — and size the cache to the working set.

Trade-off

Cache-aside can serve stale data, write-through slows writes, and write-behind risks data loss on a crash.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Two writers racing to fill the cache with an older value. Use versions, or delete on write.

Not when

Data with no reuse.

See
⚡Caching Playbook⇆Data Correctness
Scaling reads & writes#38 replication lag replica

Read replicas that lag

A replica is seconds behind after a burst.

Say it in the interview

“I'd send reads that must be fresh to the primary, or wait for a version token, and drop a replica from rotation beyond a lag threshold, rather than treating replicas as always current.”

Approach

Send reads that must be fresh to the primary, or wait for a version token, and stop routing to a replica beyond a lag threshold.

Trade-off

More load on the primary, or added latency waiting for a replica.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A user reading a stale replica right after writing.

Not when

Analytics reads that tolerate lag.

See
⇆Data Correctness
Scaling reads & writes#39 connection pool pgbouncer exhaustion

Database connections run out

Many app instances each open many connections.

Say it in the interview

“I'd put a transaction pooler like PgBouncer in front, give each service a sized share of connections with timeouts, and keep transactions short, rather than raising max_connections, which costs memory and makes contention worse.”

Approach

A pooler (transaction pooling), sized limits per service, timeouts, and no long transactions holding connections.

Trade-off

Transaction pooling breaks session features (temporary tables, session settings), and queuing at the pool adds latency under load.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

One slow query holding a connection can starve everyone.

Not when

A low-traffic app.

Scaling reads & writes#40 priority queue lanes

Urgent and bulk work share a queue

A security alert waits behind a 200,000-item announcement.

Say it in the interview

“I'd give urgent and bulk work separate queues with their own workers, so a security alert never waits behind a batch job, rather than one queue with priority fields. Some reserved capacity sits idle — that's the price.”

Approach

Separate lanes by priority with their own workers, and let the urgent lane reserve or preempt capacity.

Trade-off

More queues, and capacity reserved for a lane that is often idle.

Starving the bulk lane forever. Give it a minimum share.

Not when

Uniform work.

Scaling reads & writes#41 index covering partial slow query explain

A query scans too much

A page that was fast at 10,000 rows takes seconds at 100 million.

Say it in the interview

“I'd look at the query plan, then add the right composite index in the right column order — a covering index for hot queries, a partial index for a small live subset — rather than adding indexes everywhere, since each one costs writes.”

Approach

The right composite index in the right order, covering indexes for hot queries, partial indexes for a small “live” subset, and keyset pagination.

Trade-off

Every index costs write time and space, and a partial index over a churning state bloats and needs rebuilding.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

In the notification test, a queued-rows index measured 22.08 MB after a burst and 1.31 MB rebuilt.

Tables that stay small.

Precompute expensive results

A dashboard or a leaderboard recalculates the same aggregate on every view.

Say it in the interview

“I'd precompute the expensive result into a materialised view or aggregate table, refreshed incrementally, rather than computing it on every request, and say how stale the number may be.”

Approach

Materialised views or pre-aggregated tables, refreshed incrementally or on a schedule, and served instead of the raw data.

The numbers are stale by the refresh interval, and you store the aggregate twice.

Many readers all triggering the refresh at once. Refresh in one place.

Rarely viewed reports.

Scaling reads & writes#43 cdn edge cache immutable origin shield

Serve static and popular content from the edge

Images, scripts and downloads reach users far from your servers.

Say it in the interview

“I'd serve static content from a CDN with immutable, content-hashed URLs cached forever, and an origin shield, rather than invalidating mutable URLs, which is slow and unreliable.”

Approach

A CDN with sensible cache keys and TTLs, immutable content-hash URLs that can be cached forever, and an origin shield in front of your storage.

Trade-off

Invalidation is slow and egress is billed, but latency and origin load drop sharply.

Watch for

A cache key that includes cookies or a query string nobody needs gives a hit ratio near zero.

Not when

Private, per-user responses that must not be shared.

Scaling reads & writes#44 waiting room queue flash sale launch

A million people arrive at the same second

A ticket sale or a launch far above what you can serve.

Say it in the interview

“I'd put a virtual waiting room in front, admitting users at a rate the system can take and showing their honest position, rather than letting a million requests hit the core at once. Fairness and bots become product decisions.”

Approach

A virtual waiting room: admit users at a controlled rate from a queue, protect the core system, and show honest position and time.

Trade-off

People wait, and fairness and bot resistance become product problems.

Watch for

Bots and refresh-spamming. Use signed queue tokens and rate limits on joining.

Demand you can serve directly.

Scaling reads & writes#45 kafka hot partition skew lag

One partition in a stream is hot

One key produces most of the traffic and one consumer falls behind.

Say it in the interview

“I'd pick a finer partition key, or split the hot key with a suffix, or coalesce upstream so only the latest state is published — accepting that splitting gives up ordering across the sub-keys.”

Approach

Choose a finer key, split the hot key with a suffix, or coalesce upstream so only the latest state is published.

Trade-off

Splitting a key gives up ordering across the sub-keys, and coalescing hides intermediate values.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Averages hide it: consumer lag on a single partition is the signal.

Not when

Traffic spread evenly across keys.

AYSlack-style channelsAXMarketplace: search to pay
Scaling reads & writes#46

Spread traffic across servers: load balancing

Requests must reach many identical servers.

Say it in the interview

“I'd put a redundant L7 load balancer in front for path routing, TLS and health checks, use least-connections because request costs vary, and keep servers stateless so any server can take any request — rather than sticky sessions, which lose users on a restart.”

Approach

An L7 load balancer for routing by path or header, TLS termination, retries and health checks; L4 when you only need fast TCP distribution. Least-connections (or least-latency) when request costs vary, round robin when they're uniform, consistent hashing when a key should stick to one server (a cache). Drain connections on deploy, and run the balancer redundantly.

Trade-off

L7 costs more CPU than L4 but understands requests; sticky routing helps caches but unbalances load when keys are hot; the balancer itself must not be a single point of failure.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Sticky sessions holding user state on one server — a restart logs people out. Keep servers stateless.

Not when

A single server, or a managed platform that balances for you.

SAPI gatewayAMResilient front door
Async & real-time#47 polling long polling sse websocket push

Live updates to a page

A price, a badge or a message should appear without a refresh.

Say it in the interview

“I'd choose per feature: SSE for one-way updates like a price, WebSocket when the client also sends, like chat, long polling as a fallback — rather than polling everything, which at two million pages every 5 seconds is 400,000 requests a second. Pushes carry a version, so a missed one is recovered on reconnect.”

Approach

Choose per feature: SSE for a one-way feed, WebSocket when the client also sends (chat, presence), long polling as the fallback. Treat a push as a hint that carries a version.

Trade-off

Held connections cost memory and need a reconnect protocol; polling costs requests. Two million pages polling every 5 seconds is 400,000 requests a second.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

SSE’s Last-Event-ID is a single value, but a chat needs a per-channel map of last seen sequence numbers.

Not when

Data that changes hourly. Poll it.

Async & real-time#48 reconnect storm thundering herd jitter

A deploy drops millions of connections

Async & real-time#57

Queue, pub/sub or log: SQS, RabbitMQ or Kafka

Say it in the interview

“If each message is a task for one worker, I'd use a queue like SQS — per-message acks, retries and a dead-letter queue. If many consumers need the same ordered events and replay, I'd use Kafka, partitioned by the key whose order matters. I wouldn't use Kafka as a retry queue, because one poison message blocks its partition.”

Approach

A work queue (SQS, RabbitMQ) when each message is a task for one worker: per-message acknowledgement, redelivery, delays and a dead-letter queue. A log (Kafka, Kinesis) when many consumers each read the same events in order, replay history, or need very high throughput: ordering per partition key, consumers track offsets. Pub/sub (SNS) to fan one message out to several queues.

Trade-off

Queues are simple per task but forget a message once it's acknowledged; logs keep history and per-key order, but a slow or poison message blocks its partition and consumers manage offsets.

Say it in the interview

“I'd start with roles, add relationship-based checks for sharing, and route every decision through one policy point with cached results, rather than permission checks scattered through the code.”

Approach

RBAC for simple roles, ABAC for attribute rules, and relationship-based checks for sharing (a folder, a document); one policy decision point, with results cached and invalidated by change events.

Trade-off

RBAC explodes into many roles as needs grow, while richer models cost complexity and latency.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Check on every path, including background jobs, exports and search results.

Not when

A tiny app with two roles.

Security, identity & tenancy#85 mtls zero trust internal auth token

Service-to-service calls must be authenticated

Internal traffic is not automatically trustworthy.

Say it in the interview

“I'd authenticate service calls with mutual TLS or short-lived signed tokens scoped to an audience, rather than trusting the internal network, since an attacker inside one service shouldn't reach all of them.”

Approach

Mutual TLS or short-lived signed tokens with an audience, and least-privilege scopes per service.

Trade-off

Certificate and token management, and a little latency.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Trusting the internal network: one compromised service can call everything.

Not when

A single process.

Users upload files you do not trust

Documents, images and archives from the internet.

Say it in the interview

“I'd limit size, check the real content type, quarantine until a scan passes, process images in a sandbox and serve uploads from a separate domain, rather than trusting the file extension.”

Approach

Enforce size limits, sniff the real content type, scan asynchronously and quarantine until clean, resize images in a sandbox, and serve from a separate domain as attachments.

Trade-off

Files are not available instantly, and scanning costs money.

Watch for

An SVG or HTML file served inline can run script in your origin.

Uploads only from authenticated staff of one trusted team.

Files, media & sync#87 resumable chunked multipart upload

Upload a huge file over a flaky network

A multi-gigabyte file and a connection that drops every few minutes.

Say it in the interview

“I'd split the file into chunks with hashes, ask the server which are missing, and upload those in parallel straight to object storage with presigned URLs, then commit once — rather than one long upload that restarts from zero on a dropped connection.”

Approach

Chunk it, hash each chunk, ask the server which chunks are missing, upload those in parallel straight to object storage, then commit once.

Trade-off

Metadata per chunk and a two-step commit; a small delay per file.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A file that changes mid-upload, and abandoned chunks that need garbage collection.

Not when

Small files, which fit in one request.

Files, media & sync#88 offline sync conflict journal cursor

Sync across devices that go offline

A laptop edits files on a plane and reconnects later.

Say it in the interview

“I'd keep a journal per namespace with a cursor per device, and make each commit carry the version it was based on, so a conflicting edit is detected and both versions are kept — rather than last-write-wins, which silently loses work.”

Approach

A per-namespace journal and a cursor. Each commit carries its base version, and a guarded update detects conflicts and keeps both versions.

Trade-off

Conflicted copies for users to reconcile, and a journal to compact.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Never order by modified time, and a device offline past the journal horizon must do a full reconcile.

Not when

Live co-editing, which needs operational transforms or CRDTs.

Files, media & sync#89 hls dash transcode abr cdn

Stream video

Play a large uploaded video quickly on any connection.

Say it in the interview

“I'd transcode into a bitrate ladder of short segments with a manifest and serve them from a CDN, publishing the lowest rendition first so the video is watchable early, rather than one file the player must download. It costs CPU and storage per rendition.”

Approach

Transcode in parallel into a bitrate ladder, package as short segments with a manifest, and serve from a CDN. Publish the lowest rendition first so it is watchable early.

Trade-off

Heavy CPU and storage (about 2 GB an hour for a four-rung ladder at the bitrates tested), and a trade between start-up speed and quality.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Encoding very short pieces costs about 40% more per second of video, while long pieces delay availability.

Not when

Short internal clips, where serving the original is fine.

See
AZFile sync & video
Files, media & sync#90 dedupe content addressed hash refcount

Store identical data once

Many users store the same bytes.

Say it in the interview

“I'd store content-addressed chunks keyed by hash with reference counts and a grace period before deletion, rather than storing every copy, accepting the privacy side channel and planning around it.”

Approach

Content-addressed chunks keyed by hash, with refcounts and a grace period before garbage collection.

Trade-off

Large storage savings, but a privacy side channel if the server says “already have it”, and conflicts with per-user encryption.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Deleting a live chunk is the worst failure. Keep the collector conservative and auditable.

Not when

Data that is unique or encrypted per user.

Files, media & sync#91 range request resume etag if-range

Download a huge file reliably

A multi-gigabyte file over a flaky connection.

Say it in the interview

“I'd support range requests with ETag and If-Range so downloads resume, and verify a hash per chunk, rather than restarting a 10 GB download from zero after a dropped connection.”

Approach

Range requests, resume with an ETag and If-Range, parallel ranges, and verify a hash per chunk.

Trade-off

More requests and client complexity.

Watch for

The object changing between resumed requests. Pin the version by ETag.

Not when

Small files.

Files, media & sync#92 thumbnail resize variants image processing

Turn an uploaded image into many sizes

Thumbnails, previews and responsive variants.

Say it in the interview

“I'd generate the common sizes once, asynchronously, named by content hash and size and cached at the CDN, and resize rare sizes on demand behind the cache.”

Approach

Generate variants asynchronously once, name them by content hash and size, cache at the CDN; or resize on demand behind a cache.

Trade-off

Pre-generating costs storage for variants nobody may view; on-demand costs CPU on first request.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Image bombs: cap dimensions and pixel counts before decoding.

Not when

A handful of fixed images.

AZFile sync & video
Files, media & sync#93 signed url share link expiry revoke

Share a file with a link that expires

Send a link to someone outside the organisation.

Say it in the interview

“I'd issue a share token that maps to a permission and hand out short-lived signed URLs for the bytes, rather than one long-lived public URL, so a link can be revoked by deleting the token.”

Approach

A share token that resolves to a permission, short-lived signed URLs for the bytes, optional password and expiry, and revocation by deleting the token.

Trade-off

Short expiries are safe but annoying, and revocation needs a lookup on every access.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A leaked link. Log access and make it revocable and scoped to one item.

Not when

Content that is public anyway.
