Distributed building blocks#94 consistent hashing ring virtual nodes sharding rebalancing

Spread data over many nodes and add nodes without reshuffling everything

A cache or store outgrows one machine, and machines come and go.

Say it in the interview

“I'd place keys and nodes on a hash ring with virtual nodes, rather than key mod N, because adding a node with mod N moves almost every key, while the ring moves about 1/N of them. Virtual nodes keep the load even.”

Approach

Consistent hashing with virtual nodes: keys and nodes sit on a ring, a key belongs to the next node clockwise, and each node owns many small ranges.

Trade-off

Adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys, but clients need the ring, and virtual nodes add bookkeeping. Without them the load is uneven.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A node that joins starts empty, so its keys miss until refilled. Add nodes gradually.

Not when

A small, fixed set of nodes, where a directory or a modulo is simpler.

See
▦Data Stores⚡Caching Playbook
Distributed building blocks#95 sharding range hash partition key hotspot

Choose how to split data: by range or by hash

A table or a stream needs partitioning.

Say it in the interview

“I'd hash-partition when access is by key and load must be even, and range-partition when queries scan ordered ranges like time — or combine them, hash of tenant then time range. I'd never range-partition on a timestamp alone, because every write lands on the last partition.”

Approach

Hash partitioning for even load and point lookups; range partitioning for ordered scans and time windows; a compound key (a hash of the tenant, a range of time) to get some of both.

Trade-off

Hashing spreads load but makes range scans expensive. Range keeps scans cheap, but a monotonically increasing key such as a timestamp sends every write to the last partition.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Re-sharding later is the expensive part, so pick a key with growth in mind.

Not when

Data that fits comfortably on one node.

See
▦Data Stores
Distributed building blocks#96 quorum replication raft paxos durability

Data must survive the loss of a node

A replica, or a whole node, dies while requests keep arriving.

Say it in the interview

“I'd replicate to three nodes and use quorums — write to two, read from two — so every read overlaps the latest write, rather than writing to one and hoping. Larger quorums cost latency; smaller ones risk stale reads.”

Approach

Replicate to N nodes and use quorums: write to W, read from R, with W + R greater than N so a read overlaps the latest write. Or use a leader with synchronous followers.

Trade-off

Larger W or R buys consistency at the cost of latency and availability. W + R at or below N is faster but can read stale data.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Replica lag and sloppy quorums during failures can still return old data, so repair on read.

Not when

Data you can rebuild from another source.

See
⇆Data Correctness⛨Disaster Recovery
Distributed building blocks#97 leader election lease raft zookeeper etcd fencing

Exactly one node must do the job

A scheduler, a compactor or a partition owner must never run twice at once.

Say it in the interview

“I'd elect a leader with a lease in etcd or ZooKeeper and pass a fencing token with every write, so a deposed leader's late write is rejected, rather than trusting the lease alone — a paused process can wake up still thinking it leads.”

Approach

Elect a leader with a lease in a consensus store (etcd, ZooKeeper) and use a fencing token: every write carries an increasing number and the resource rejects an older one.

Trade-off

Failover takes as long as the lease, and you depend on the consensus service being available.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A paused old leader (a long garbage-collection pause) that wakes up and acts. Only the fencing token stops it.

Not when

Work that can safely run twice. Make it idempotent instead, or claim rows with SKIP LOCKED as the announcement scheduler does.

See
AIAnnouncements
Distributed building blocks#98 distributed lock redlock mutex lease

Mutual exclusion across services

Two services must not change the same thing at the same moment.

Say it in the interview

“I'd avoid a distributed lock if a conditional update or unique constraint can make the decision, because locks expire mid-work and holders die. If I must lock, I'd use a lease with a fencing token and keep the critical section short.”

Approach

Avoid the lock: use a conditional write, a unique constraint or an optimistic version check. If you must lock, take a lease with a fencing token and keep the critical section short.

Trade-off

Locks add failure modes — expiry in the middle of work, a dead holder, clock trouble — and cap throughput.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A lock that expires while the work continues silently allows two holders.

Not when

Updates inside one database, where a transaction is the lock.

See
ETicketmaster⇆Data Correctness
Distributed building blocks#99 lamport logical clock version vector

Order events across machines with no shared clock

Two services stamp events, and their clocks differ.

Say it in the interview

“I'd give each key a sequence number from one owner, rather than ordering by wall-clock timestamps from different machines, which drift and tie. When there's no single owner, version vectors at least detect concurrent updates.”

Approach

Order by a sequence assigned by one owner per key, or use logical clocks (Lamport) and version vectors to detect concurrent updates.

Trade-off

A sequence costs a serialisation point per key. Version vectors grow with the number of writers and detect conflicts without resolving them.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Never compare wall-clock timestamps from different machines to decide who wrote last.

Not when

Events that only need approximate time.

See
AYSlack-style channelsAZFile sync & video
Distributed building blocks#100 snowflake uuid uuidv7 sequence

Generate unique ids on many machines

Millions of new rows a second across many services.

Say it in the interview

“I'd use time-ordered 64-bit ids — Snowflake-style or UUIDv7 — rather than random UUIDs, which scatter index writes, or a database sequence, which is a single bottleneck. I'd accept the dependency on clocks and unique machine ids.”

Approach

A time-ordered 64-bit id (a Snowflake-style timestamp, machine and counter) or UUIDv7 for sortable ids; a random UUID when order does not matter; a database sequence only when one writer is fine.

Trade-off

Time-ordered ids keep indexes compact but depend on clocks and machine ids. Random UUIDs are simple but scatter index writes. A sequence is a bottleneck.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A clock that moves backwards can repeat an id. Refuse to issue until it catches up.

Not when

One database with modest write rates, where a sequence is enough.

See
NUnique ID generator
Distributed building blocks#101 service discovery registry dns consul

Find other services when addresses keep changing

Instances start, stop and move all day.

Say it in the interview

“I'd use a service registry with health checks and let clients or a mesh balance across healthy instances, rather than hard-coded addresses or long-TTL DNS. Registry entries can be stale, so callers still need retries and timeouts.”

Approach

A service registry with health checks, and either client-side load balancing or a proxy or mesh that watches the registry. DNS with short TTLs for coarse discovery.

Trade-off

The registry can be stale, so callers must retry and tolerate dead entries, and client-side balancing spreads logic across every client.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Instances that fail health checks under load flap in and out, shrinking capacity exactly when you need it.

Not when

A handful of static services behind a load balancer.

RService registryAMResilient front door
Distributed building blocks#102 failure detector gossip heartbeat phi accrual

Detect a dead node without false alarms

A node stops answering. Is it dead or only slow?

Say it in the interview

“I'd use heartbeats with an adaptive timeout and require confirmation from more than one observer before declaring a node dead, rather than a fixed short timeout, which flags slow nodes as dead and triggers needless failovers.”

Approach

Heartbeats with a timeout that adapts to observed latency (phi-accrual style), confirmed by several observers or by gossip before anyone acts.

Trade-off

A short timeout detects failure fast but flags slow nodes as dead and triggers needless failovers. A long one is safe but slow.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A network partition looks exactly like a dead node from one side. Make sure both sides cannot promote a leader.

Not when

Nodes whose failure a load balancer health check already handles.

See
⛨Disaster Recovery
Distributed building blocks#103

Consistency or availability when the network splits (CAP, PACELC)

Replicas in two zones lose contact; both still receive requests.

Say it in the interview

“I'd decide per operation what happens when replicas can't talk: for money, stock and uniqueness I'd stay consistent — a single leader or majority quorum, refusing when it can't be reached; for feeds and product pages I'd stay available and reconcile later. And PACELC: even with no partition, stronger consistency costs latency on every request.”

Approach

Decide per operation. Where a wrong answer is worse than none — balances, inventory, uniqueness — stay consistent (CP): a single leader or a majority quorum, and refuse when it can't be reached. Where availability matters more — feeds, product pages, presence — stay available (AP) and reconcile later with versions or CRDTs.

Trade-off

CP rejects or delays some requests during a partition; AP stays up but may return stale or conflicting data that must be reconciled. CAP only bites during a partition — the everyday trade is latency versus consistency (PACELC).

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Calling a whole system 'CP' or 'AP' — it's a per-operation, per-configuration choice, and a single-node database isn't a CAP case at all.

Not when

One database node with no replication: there's no partition to choose about — think about durability and failover instead.

See
▦Data Stores⇆Data Correctness
Analytics & pipelines#104 hyperloglog hll cardinality distinct

Count unique users at scale

Daily active users across billions of events.

Say it in the interview

“I'd use a HyperLogLog per day — a few kilobytes that estimate distinct users within about 1% and merge across shards — rather than storing every user id in a set, as long as the business accepts an estimate.”

Approach

A HyperLogLog sketch: a fixed few kilobytes per counter that estimates distinct counts and can be merged across shards and days.

Trade-off

It is an estimate — Redis’s implementation quotes a standard error of about 0.8% — and you cannot list who was counted or remove someone.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Unions merge exactly, but intersections cannot be computed precisely from sketches.

Not when

Billing or compliance counts that must be exact.

MView countsΣMath Toolkit
Analytics & pipelines#105 heavy hitters count-min sketch trending

Find the top-K or trending items

The 100 most searched terms in the last hour.

Say it in the interview

“I'd count in sliding windows with a count-min sketch, keep a small heap of the leaders per shard, and merge the shard results, rather than exact counts on every event. Slight overcounting of rare items is acceptable for 'trending'.”

Approach

Count in sliding windows with a count-min sketch (or exact counts on a sample), keep a small heap of the leaders, and merge the per-shard results.

Trade-off

Approximate counts overestimate rare items slightly, and windows add memory and complexity.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A sudden spike can crowd out steady leaders, so decay old counts.

Not when

A short list you can count exactly.

Analytics & pipelines#106 lambda kappa architecture flink spark

Stream processing or batch

Numbers must be fresh and also right.

Say it in the interview

“I'd prefer a Kappa shape — one streaming pipeline over a replayable Kafka log, re-run from the beginning when logic changes — over Lambda, where a stream and a batch job compute the same thing twice and drift apart. If the batch is genuinely different, I'd make it the authoritative one.”

Approach

Two named shapes: Lambda — a stream for low-latency results plus a batch job that recomputes the truth — or Kappa — one streaming pipeline over a replayable log, re-run from the start to recompute. Make both idempotent; prefer Kappa when one code path can serve both.

Trade-off

Two code paths can drift apart. Replaying one log keeps a single path but needs a retained log and enough compute.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

The stream and the batch disagreeing. Decide which is authoritative.

Not when

Reports that can wait until tomorrow, where batch alone is simpler.

ZObservability
Analytics & pipelines#107 watermark windowing late data flink

Events arrive late and out of order

A mobile client uploads yesterday’s events today.

Say it in the interview

“I'd window by event time and close windows with a watermark plus a bounded allowed lateness, rather than by arrival time, which misplaces anything delayed in the pipeline. Stragglers after the lateness become corrections.”

Approach

Group by event time, not arrival time, with windows closed by a watermark, and allow a bounded lateness with corrections for stragglers.

Trade-off

A longer allowed lateness makes results more complete but later and costs state. A shorter one is fast and drops or patches late data.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A corrected window means downstream consumers must accept updates to numbers they have already read.

Not when

Processing-time metrics, where arrival time is the truth.

ZObservability

A dashboard query scans billions of rows on the primary database.

Say it in the interview

“I'd stream changes with CDC into a columnar warehouse and run analytics there, rather than heavy queries on the production database. Dashboards read pre-aggregated tables, and minutes of staleness is the accepted cost.”

Approach

Stream changes with CDC into a columnar warehouse or OLAP store and run analytics there. Serve dashboards from pre-aggregated tables.

Trade-off

The data is minutes stale, you run another pipeline, and it costs more storage.

Watch for

Source schema changes breaking the pipeline, and deletes that must propagate to the warehouse.

Not when

Small data, where a read replica is enough.

Analytics & pipelines#109 backfill reprocess replay

Reprocess or backfill history safely

A bug corrupted a column, or a new field must be filled for old rows.

Say it in the interview

“I'd backfill in a separate idempotent job that walks key ranges in small batches, throttles itself and writes to a new column, then switch reads — rather than one big UPDATE that locks the table. It's slower but production keeps serving and I can roll back.”

Approach

Write a separate, idempotent backfill that processes key ranges in small batches, throttles itself and writes to a new column or table; then switch reads and remove the old.

Trade-off

It takes time and temporary storage, but production keeps serving and you can roll back.

A backfill that competes with live traffic, holds long locks or overloads replicas. Throttle it and watch replication lag.

Analytics & pipelines#110 event sourcing cqrs audit

Keep the full history as the source of truth

Auditors want every change; teams want to rebuild views.

Say it in the interview

“I'd use event sourcing only when the history itself is the product — audits, ledgers — storing immutable events and building read models from them. Otherwise I'd keep a normal table with an outbox, because event sourcing brings schema evolution and eventual consistency.”

Approach

Event sourcing: store immutable events as the truth and build read models (CQRS) from them, taking snapshots periodically to keep rebuilds short.

Powerful history and rebuilds, but eventual consistency between the write and read sides, event schema evolution and a steeper learning curve.

Batch at the device, ingest through a partitioned log, write to a time-series store, downsample old data and set a retention period.

Some latency for efficiency, and detail is lost as data is downsampled.

Watch for

A reconnect storm sending every device’s backlog at once, and devices with wrong clocks.

Analytics & pipelines#112 dedupe stream idempotent window

Producers retry and brokers redeliver.

Deduplicate by event id in a state store with a time window, or make the sink idempotent by key and version.

State to store and a window during which duplicates are caught.

Watch for

A duplicate that arrives after the window expires.

ASNotification schema
Analytics & pipelines#113 csv bulk import staging validation

A customer uploads 200,000 rows to create or update records.

Validate and report first (matched, unknown, duplicate), stage the rows in a table, apply them in batches with idempotent keys, and allow a re-run.

Staging storage and a two-step experience, in exchange for no half-imported surprises.

A failure halfway: the batches must be repeatable, not restart from zero.

API & integration#114 pagination cursor keyset offset

Page through a list that keeps changing

A feed or an admin table gains rows while someone scrolls.

Say it in the interview

“I'd use keyset pagination — 50 rows after this sort key and id — rather than OFFSET, which gets slower with depth and skips or repeats rows when the list changes. I give up jumping to page 37.”

Approach

Keyset (cursor) pagination: “give me 50 after this (sort key, id)” rather than OFFSET.

Trade-off

No jump to page 37, and the cursor is opaque — but pages are stable and cost the same at any depth (in the chat test, a page 300,000 deep took 0.029 ms against 0.022 ms for the first).

The sort key must be unique. Add the id as a tiebreaker, or rows are skipped or repeated.

Small, static lists.

API & integration#115 dataloader batching graphql n+1

Avoid the N+1 calls

A list of 50 items triggers 50 follow-up calls for details.

“I'd collect the ids and fetch them in one batch call — a DataLoader — or join in the query, rather than one call per item, which turns one page into hundreds of round trips. The batch adds a tiny wait.”

Approach

Batch: collect the ids and fetch them in one call (a DataLoader-style batcher), or join in the query, or offer an aggregated endpoint.

Batching adds a small wait and more code, and one slow item can delay the whole batch.

Watch for

One or two calls.

API & integration#116 async job long-running export 202 polling

A request takes minutes

A user asks for a year of data as a file.

Say it in the interview

“I'd return 202 with a job id, do the work in the background and let the client poll or get a webhook, rather than holding the HTTP request open for minutes, which timeouts and proxies break. The job state needs storage and expiry.”

Return 202 with a job id, do the work asynchronously, let the client poll (or notify by webhook or SSE), and expire the result.

You store job state and results, handle expiry and cancellation, and the user waits without a live answer.

A retried request creating a second job. Give the client an idempotency key.

Work that finishes within a second or two.

Hundreds of integrations you do not control.

Prefer additive, backward-compatible changes; version the breaking ones; publish a deprecation window with usage metrics per client; run old and new side by side.

Supporting two versions costs code and tests, and some clients never migrate.

Approach

Sign the body with an HMAC and include a timestamp. The receiver rejects bad signatures and old timestamps, and dedupes by event id.

Secret distribution and rotation, tolerance for clock skew, and receivers must store recent event ids.

API & integration#119 retry storm amplification budget

Retries multiply across layers

“I'd retry at one layer only, with a retry budget and backoff with jitter, and propagate a deadline, rather than retrying at every layer, which multiplies one failure into dozens of calls and makes an outage worse.”

Approach

Retry at one layer only, with a retry budget (a fraction of recent calls), exponential backoff with jitter, and a propagated deadline so nobody works on a request the caller has abandoned.

Trade-off

Less resilience at inner layers, and budgets need tuning.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Retrying non-idempotent calls, and retrying while the dependency is already overloaded.

Not when

A single hop making a cheap, idempotent call.

See
AMResilient front door
API & integration#120 backpressure load shedding 429 503 retry-after

Overload: shed load on purpose

Demand exceeds capacity and everything gets slow.

Say it in the interview

“I'd shed load early — 429 or 503 with Retry-After — and protect critical traffic with priorities, rather than queueing everything, because an unbounded queue just converts overload into huge latency for everyone.”

Approach

Reject early and cheaply (429 or 503 with Retry-After), protect critical traffic with priorities, cap concurrency, and prefer a fast failure to a queue that grows without bound.

Trade-off

Some users see errors during the overload, but the rest stay fast. A growing queue hides the problem until latency explodes.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Shedding the wrong traffic. Health checks and payments should outrank recommendations.

Not when

Short bursts that a bounded queue absorbs.

See
AMResilient front door⚑Status Codes
API & integration#121 fair queue weighted round robin noisy neighbour

Fairness between tenants in a shared queue

One customer floods a queue and delays everyone else.

Say it in the interview

“I'd give each tenant its own lane and serve lanes in weighted turns with per-tenant quotas, rather than one FIFO queue, where the biggest tenant's backlog delays everyone. The largest tenants get a dedicated lane.”

Approach

Per-tenant lanes served by weighted round-robin (fair turns), per-tenant quotas, and a dedicated lane for the largest.

Trade-off

More queues and a scheduler to run, and a strict fair share can leave capacity idle.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A tenant starving because its lane is always behind. Measure the age of each lane.

Not when

A single-tenant system.

See
APNotificationsVMulti-tenant limits
API & integration#122 bulk api partial failure multi-status

A batch request where some items fail

A bulk endpoint receives 1,000 items and 12 are invalid.

Say it in the interview

“I'd return a per-item result and make each item idempotent, so the caller retries only the failures, with an all-or-nothing mode for callers who need it, rather than failing the whole batch for one bad item.”

Approach

Return a per-item result (a multi-status style response), make each item idempotent, and offer an all-or-nothing mode when the caller needs it.

Trade-off

Clients must handle partial results, and the server tracks item state.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Retrying the whole batch repeats items that already succeeded.

Not when

Single-item endpoints.

See
⚑Status Codes
API & integration#123 webhook polling streaming events replay

Let customers know when something changes

Integrations want to react to your events.

Say it in the interview

“I'd offer webhooks for events, with event ids and a way to replay missed ones, and polling as the simple fallback, rather than webhooks alone, because receivers go down.”

Approach

Webhooks for events, polling as the simple fallback, and streaming for high volume; give each an event id, a cursor and a way to replay missed events.

Trade-off

Webhooks push complexity to the receiver, polling wastes requests, and streaming needs long-lived connections.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A receiver that is down for hours must be able to catch up without losing events.

Not when

A single internal consumer, where a queue is enough.

See
AFWebhooksAXMarketplace: search to pay
API & integration#124 graphql depth cost limit query complexity

Clients can ask for too much

A flexible query language lets one request ask for a million rows.

Say it in the interview

“I'd limit query depth and cost, cap pagination, and prefer persisted queries for our own apps, rather than letting any client ask for everything, which turns a flexible API into a denial-of-service vector.”

Approach

Query depth and cost limits, pagination caps, persisted queries or allowlists, and timeouts.

Trade-off

It restricts the flexibility that made the API attractive.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A cheap-looking query that fans out into thousands of backend calls.

Not when

A private API with one trusted client.

See
AOGraphQL layer
API & integration#125

REST, gRPC or GraphQL

A new API for mobile apps, partners and internal services.

Say it in the interview

“I'd expose REST to partners because it's simple and cacheable, use gRPC between internal services for typed contracts and low overhead, and add GraphQL only when many clients need different shapes of the same data — with depth and cost limits, since it shifts complexity to the server.”

Approach

REST for public and partner APIs: simple, cacheable, every tool speaks it. gRPC for internal service-to-service calls: typed contracts, HTTP/2, streaming, compact payloads. GraphQL when many clients need different shapes of the same data and round trips hurt — with depth and cost limits and persisted queries.

Trade-off

REST can over- or under-fetch; gRPC is awkward from browsers and for outside partners; GraphQL moves complexity to the server — N+1 queries, caching and query cost.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

GraphQL for a simple CRUD API, or gRPC handed to partners who can't easily use it.

Not when

One client and a handful of endpoints: plain REST.

See
AOGraphQL layerSAPI gateway
Edge cases: time, money & text#126 dst timezone utc

Time zones and daylight saving

A meeting at 09:00 local time, every Monday.

Say it in the interview

“I'd store instants in UTC with the user's zone id, but store future local events as local time plus zone, rather than converting everything to UTC up front — when zone rules change, a 9 a.m. meeting must stay at 9 a.m.”

Approach

Store instants in UTC plus the zone id. For recurring events store the local time and the zone, and convert at display time.

Trade-off

Conversion code everywhere, and future local times can shift if the zone rules change.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

A time that does not exist (the spring gap) or occurs twice (the autumn overlap).

Not when

Durations and logs, which are plain UTC.

See
HMeeting rooms
Edge cases: time, money & text#127 rrule calendar recurrence

Recurring events

Every second Tuesday, except holidays, edited from one occurrence onward.

Say it in the interview

“I'd store the recurrence rule and expand it on read for the visible window, with exceptions as overrides, rather than materialising every future occurrence, which goes stale when the rule changes and never ends.”

Approach

Store the recurrence rule (an RRULE) and expand it on read for a window; store exceptions and edits as overrides.

Trade-off

Expanding on read costs CPU; materialising occurrences costs storage and must stay in step with the rule.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

“This and following” edits: split the rule at that date.

Not when

A few one-off events.

See
HMeeting rooms
Edge cases: time, money & text#128 currency cents decimal rounding float

Money

Prices, taxes, splits and refunds.

Say it in the interview

“I'd store money as integer minor units with a currency code, never floats, round with an explicit rule, and allocate leftover cents deliberately — floats lose cents, and those errors surface in reconciliation.”

Approach

Store integer minor units (cents) with a currency code, round by an explicit rule, and allocate remainders deliberately.

Trade-off

Conversions and formatting everywhere, and some currencies have no minor unit or three decimals.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Floating point, and splitting 100 three ways: the extra cent has to go somewhere.

Not when

Non-monetary measurements.

See
XIdempotent payments
Edge cases: time, money & text#129 clock skew ntp monotonic

Clocks disagree between servers

A record “from the future”, or timestamps out of order.

Say it in the interview

“I'd order events by a sequence or version from one owner, and use monotonic clocks for durations, rather than comparing wall-clock times from different servers, which can be skewed by seconds.”

Approach

Order by sequence or version, use monotonic clocks for durations, and sync time while tolerating skew.

Trade-off

Ordering is less human-readable, and you need a sequence owner.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Leap seconds, and machines whose clock jumps backwards.

Not when

Times that are only displayed.

See
AYSlack-style channels
Edge cases: time, money & text#130 unicode utf-8 collation normalisation

Text is harder than it looks

Usernames, search, sorting and length limits.

Say it in the interview

“I'd normalise text to NFC, compare usernames with a case-insensitive collation, and reject confusable characters in identifiers, rather than raw string equality, which lets two visually identical names exist.”

Approach

Normalise Unicode (NFC), compare with a case-insensitive collation, count limits in bytes or code points as storage needs, and reject confusable characters in identifiers.

Trade-off

Normalisation can surprise users (two different inputs become the same name), and collation changes affect indexes.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

An emoji or an accented letter that is several code points, and look-alike characters used to impersonate.

Not when

Opaque ids.

Edge cases: time, money & text#131 int64 bigint precision javascript

Large numbers in JSON

A 64-bit id arrives in a browser.

Say it in the interview

“I'd send 64-bit ids as strings in JSON, because JavaScript numbers lose precision above 2^53 and silently change the id — clients treat ids as opaque anyway.”

Approach

Send 64-bit ids as strings, because JavaScript numbers lose precision above 2^53.

Trade-off

Clients must treat ids as opaque strings, and sorting numerically needs care.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Ids that look fine in tests and change in production once they pass 9,007,199,254,740,992.

Not when

Small counters.

See
NUnique ID generator
Edge cases: time, money & text#132 deleted flag retention

Soft delete or hard delete

Users delete things, and want them back — or want them gone.

Say it in the interview

“I'd soft-delete recoverable data with a flag and a retention job that hard-deletes later, with partial unique indexes, rather than either alone. For erasure requests it's a real delete, everywhere.”

Approach

Soft delete with a flag and a retention job for recoverable data, hard delete for erasure, and make every query and unique constraint aware of the flag.

Trade-off

Every query must filter deleted rows, unique keys need a partial index, and a forgotten filter leaks deleted data.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Deleted rows showing up through joins, search and exports.

Not when

Data with a legal erasure duty.

See
AUAnnouncement schema
Edge cases: time, money & text#133 batch backfill throttle

A bulk operation touches millions of rows

Recalculate a column, or delete old records.

Say it in the interview

“I'd process the bulk change in small key-ordered batches with short transactions and throttling, each batch repeatable, rather than one giant transaction that locks rows and makes replicas fall behind.”

Approach

Process in small key-ordered batches with short transactions, throttle, and make each batch repeatable.

Trade-off

The whole operation is not atomic and takes longer, but locks stay short and replicas keep up.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Replication lag and lock queues. A batch that fails halfway must resume, not restart.

Not when

A table small enough for one statement.

See
⇪Schema MigrationsANLegacy migration
Edge cases: time, money & text#134 int32 overflow bigint sequence

Ids run out

A 32-bit integer key reaches 2,147,483,647.

Say it in the interview

“I'd use 64-bit ids from day one and watch the sequence as a metric, rather than 32-bit ids, because running out of ids is a hard outage and migrating a primary key late is painful.”

Approach

Use 64-bit ids from the start, or migrate before the table is half full; watch the sequence value as a metric.

Trade-off

More storage per key and index, and a migration if you started small.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Every place the id appears: foreign keys, other services, and client-side integer types.

Not when

A small table that will never approach the limit.

See
NUnique ID generator
Edge cases: time, money & text#135 spf dkim dmarc deliverability bounce unsubscribe

Send email that actually reaches the inbox

Transactional and bulk mail both land in spam.

Say it in the interview

“I'd set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC, keep transactional and bulk email on separate streams, handle bounces automatically and warm up new senders — deliverability is earned, not configured once.”

Approach

Set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC, keep transactional and bulk on separate streams, handle bounces and complaints automatically, and always include unsubscribe.

Trade-off

Operational work and warm-up time for new sending addresses.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Sending to addresses that have bounced damages your reputation for everyone.

Not when

In-app notifications only.

See
APNotificationsASNotification schema
Edge cases: time, money & text#136 histogram percentile average ratio metrics

An average or a percentage that lies

A dashboard shows “average latency” and a “conversion rate”.

Say it in the interview

“I'd store counts and sums, which merge, compute ratios at read time, and take percentiles from histograms, rather than averaging averages or percentiles, which gives confident wrong numbers.”

Approach

Store counts and sums (which merge), compute ratios at read time, and take percentiles from histograms, not averages of percentiles.

Trade-off

More stored data and slightly more complex queries.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Averaging averages across groups of different sizes gives the wrong answer.

Not when

One small population where a plain average is fine.

See
ZObservabilityΣMath Toolkit
AI & LLM systems#137 rag retrieval augmented generation embeddings vector search llm

Answer questions from your own documents

An assistant must answer from company documents, not from memory.

Say it in the interview

“I'd use retrieval-augmented generation: chunk and embed the documents, retrieve with vector plus keyword search, rerank, and answer only from the passages with citations — rather than fine-tuning, which goes stale and can't cite.”

Approach

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): chunk the documents, embed the chunks, retrieve with vector search combined with keyword search, rerank, and pass the best passages, with citations, to the model.

Trade-off

The index lags the documents, retrieval can miss the right passage, and every answer costs tokens and latency.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Permissions: retrieval must filter by what the asker may see, exactly like search.

Not when

Questions that do not depend on private documents.

See
AYSlack-style channelsAXMarketplace: search to pay
AI & LLM systems#138 streaming llm sse tokens

Show tokens as they arrive

A model takes 20 seconds to finish an answer.

Say it in the interview

“I'd stream tokens over SSE and cancel generation when the client disconnects, rather than waiting for the full answer, which makes users stare at a spinner and wastes compute after they leave.”

Approach

Stream the response over SSE or WebSocket, and cancel generation when the client disconnects.

Trade-off

Long-held connections and partial results to handle, and a retry restarts the answer.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Paying for tokens nobody reads. Stop on disconnect.

Not when

Short answers.

See
AXMarketplace: search to pay
AI & LLM systems#139 llm cost cache routing tokens

Control model cost and latency

Traffic grows and the bill grows faster.

Say it in the interview

“I'd cache repeated requests, route simple tasks to smaller models, and cap tokens per request and per tenant, rather than sending everything to the largest model. Routing mistakes cost quality, so I'd measure them.”

Approach

Cache identical and near-identical requests, route simple tasks to smaller models, batch where latency allows, and cap tokens per request and per tenant.

Trade-off

Quality drops when routing is wrong, a semantic cache can return a slightly wrong answer, and limits annoy heavy users.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Cache poisoning across tenants. Key caches by tenant and permissions.

Not when

Low volume.

See
VMulti-tenant limits
AI & LLM systems#140 llm rate limit fallback provider

The model provider is slow or rate-limited

The API returns errors or timeouts.

Say it in the interview

“I'd set timeouts, keep a fallback model or provider, queue non-interactive work, and degrade gracefully — showing search results instead of a summary — rather than letting the user wait on a slow provider.”

Approach

Timeouts, a fallback model or provider, a queue for non-interactive work, and graceful degradation (a search result instead of a summary).

Trade-off

Fallbacks can behave differently, and you carry two integrations.

Edge case · when not to use · examples
Watch for

Retrying without backoff, which makes rate limits worse.

Not when

Offline batch jobs.

AI & LLM systems#141 agent tools mcp prompt injection least privilege

An agent can call tools that change things

An assistant can send emails or move money.

Say it in the interview

“I'd give the agent least-privilege credentials per tool and per user, an allowlist of actions, human approval for irreversible ones, and an audit log of every call — rather than broad credentials, because a model can be talked into misuse.”

Approach

Least-privilege credentials per tool and per user, an allowlist of actions, human approval for irreversible ones, and an audit log of every call.

Friction from approvals and more plumbing.

Keep a model’s answers grounded and measured

Say it in the interview

“I'd keep a golden set of questions to evaluate offline, require citations from retrieved passages, add guardrails, and track feedback online, rather than judging the model on a few hand-picked examples.”

Approach

A golden set of questions for offline evaluation, citations from retrieved passages, guardrails on what it may answer, and online feedback tracked over time.

Building and maintaining evaluations costs time, and stricter guardrails refuse more.

Approach

Redact or tokenise personal data, retrieve only what the asker may see, keep tenant data separate, and log carefully.

The rule: compute a number only if the answer could change a decision. If you already know you need a cache regardless of the exact QPS, don't spend two minutes deriving it to three significant figures.

What each variable means

1 Traffic2 QPS3 Storage4 Bandwidth5–6 Advancedcolour = the calculator step each variable feeds
VariableHow to estimate it
Daily Active UsersDistinct users active in a day — given in the prompt, or inferred from the company's rough scale.
Actions / user / daySum of every core-flow call one user triggers per day (a redirect, a post, a search) — count it flow by flow, not as one guess.
Peak multiplierHow far the busiest hour exceeds the daily average. 2–3× is a safe default; go higher for anything with a sharp event-driven spike.
Read : write ratioReads per 1 write, taken straight from your NFRs — a feed or redirect service is often 10:1 to 1000:1.
Avg record sizeBytes per write, summed across the entity's fields from Step 2. A few short strings is usually 100–500 bytes.
RetentionHow long a record must be kept before it can be deleted or archived — state it as an assumption if the interviewer doesn't give one.
Replication factorCopies of each byte kept for durability. 3 is the standard default — it survives one node loss while a quorum of 2 remains.
Avg payload sizeBytes on the wire per request/response — close to record size for simple CRUD, larger for anything returning media or batches.
Requests/sec per serverLoad one stateless instance can handle. A reasonable HTTP service handles roughly 500–2,000 req/s — state it as an assumption, not a fact.
Avg request latencyEnd-to-end time to serve one request. Pull it from your latency NFR, or the latency reference table below.

When math actually changes the design

The row below lights up to match the peak QPS from the calculator above. The middle column is the one worth reading — a number only changes your design by telling you which bounded resource saturates next.

ScaleWhat saturates firstWhat that forces, and what it costs
< 1K QPS Nothing architectural. If it's slow here it's an N+1 query, a missing index, or a synchronous third-party call. One app tier, one primary database. Reaching for a cache or a queue at this rung creates problems you then have to solve.
1K – 10K QPS DB connections — instances × pool size exceeds max_connections long before CPU does. Then read IOPS start stealing from writes. Connection pooler, read replicas, cache-aside for hot keys. Costs you replication lag — read-after-write breaks visibly.
10K – 100K QPS Synchronous write throughput on one primary. A single Redis node. Cache stampedes on viral keys. Async writes behind a queue, sharded cache, partitioned tables. Costs you durability at response time — you now owe the client a way to check the outcome.
100K+ QPS Random write I/O on B-trees. Cross-region latency. Coordination between shards rather than any single node. LSM engines, regional sharding, in-process L1 cache. Costs you global strong consistency — this is where CAP stops being theoretical.

The full version — what else saturates, the arithmetic behind connection limits, Little's Law, and the cost of every common fix — is in the Scale Ladder.

Toolkit

Metrics and Percentiles — What to Measure, and Why

Every design ends with the question "and how would you know it works?" This section is the vocabulary and the checklist for that answer: what p50, p90 and p99 really mean, why averages lie, how success latency and error latency differ, and a catalog of about 60 metrics — what each one measures and what a change in it tells you.

Percentiles in one minute

A percentile answers one question: what share of requests were at least this fast? Sort 1,000 requests from fastest to slowest. The median (p50) is the 500th, p90 the 900th, p99 the 990th, p99.9 the 999th, and the max is the last one. So "p99 = 800 ms" means 1 request in 100 took 800 ms or longer. That is all p50, p90 and p99 are — they are just positions in the sorted list.

MetricReads asWho feels itUse it for
p50 (median)half of requests are faster, half slowerthe typical requestbaseline and capacity planning
p909 in 10 requests are fastermost usersan SLO for normal, non-critical paths
p9519 in 20 are fasteralmost everyonethe most common latency SLO
p9999 in 100 are faster — 1 in 100 is this slow or slowerheavy users, and any page that makes many callsSLOs and alerts on important paths
p99.9999 in 1,000 are fasterthe unluckiest 0.1%, and fan-out pagespayments and other critical paths
maxthe single slowest requestone unlucky requestdebugging; it is bounded by your timeouts — never alert on one max
averagetotal time ÷ number of requestsnobody in particularcapacity and cost arithmetic only

Why not just the average? The average adds everything up and divides, so a few very slow requests barely move it. A service can have a healthy-looking average while 1 request in 100 is awful — and that 1% is real people: at 10 million requests a day it is 100,000 slow requests.

Why the tail hurts more than it looks: users and pages make many requests. If each call has a 1% chance of being p99-slow, the chance that at least one of N is slow is 1 − 0.99N:

A user or a page makes…p99 case: chance of at least one slow callp99.9 case
1 request1.0%0.1%
5 requests4.9%0.5%
20 requests18.2%2.0%
100 requests63.4%9.5%

A page that makes 100 backend calls hits a p99-slow call 63% of the time. That is why big systems watch p99 and p99.9, not the median — and why one slow dependency can make a whole page feel slow.

Try it — a simulated service of 10,000 requests
presets

Simulated: most requests follow a bell-shaped spread around the typical time; the slow ones are that many times slower. Move the sliders and watch the average barely react while p99 and p99.9 jump.

You cannot average percentiles. The p99 of the whole fleet is not the mean of each server's p99. Record latencies in histograms (counts of requests per time bucket), add the histograms together across servers, and read the percentile from the merged histogram. In practice: Prometheus histograms with histogram_quantile, HDR histograms, or t-digest sketches; the ones that merge are the ones to use.

Latency of successes vs latency of errors

Latency means two different things depending on the outcome, and mixing them gives misleading numbers. Fast errors — a rejection, a 429, an open circuit breaker — answer in a few milliseconds. Slow errors — timeouts — answer at your timeout, often seconds. Put either into the same histogram as successes and the percentiles stop describing what users experience.

SituationError rateAll requests: avg · p50 · p99 · p99.9 (ms)Successes only: avg · p50 · p99 · p99.9 (ms)What it shows
healthy: everything succeeds0%108.2 · 99.6 · 255.3 · 345.1108.2 · 99.6 · 255.3 · 345.1the baseline
5% fail fast (rejected in about 5 ms)5%103.3 · 97.4 · 253.3 · 347.8108.5 · 100.1 · 255.8 · 349.3barely visible in the mix — yet 1 request in 20 is failing
20% fail fast (rejected in about 5 ms)20%87.8 · 88.1 · 246.1 · 341.8108.4 · 100.2 · 254.3 · 351.9the service looks faster (average and p50 fall) while it fails 1 in 5
1% time out at 30 seconds1%417.4 · 100.5 · 678.5 · 39,082.4108.3 · 100 · 253.5 · 339the average quadruples and p99.9 becomes the timeout — but successes are unchanged

Simulated with 100,000 requests per row; successes take about 100 ms (a bell-shaped spread), fast failures about 5 ms, timeouts 30 seconds. The point is the pattern, not the exact numbers.

  • Make the headline latency SLI the latency of successes — that is what a user gets when it works.
  • Plot the latency of errors separately. A cluster near 5 ms means rejections; a cluster at the timeout means a stuck dependency. The max latency of errors is normally your timeout, which is exactly why it is a useful diagnostic.
  • Count a timeout as an error (with a latency equal to the timeout), never as "no data" — a request that never completed is the worst outcome, and dropping it makes the service look better.
  • Define success by the business outcome, not only the status code: an HTTP 200 that returns "payment declined" or an empty result is not a success for the user.

The metric catalog — 62 metrics, searchable

Use the search box and the family chips. Each row says what the metric measures, what it is for (what a change in it tells you), and how to use it. Thresholds are ideas, not rules — you set real ones from the promise you made to users.

Pitfalls

  • Averaging averages, or averaging percentiles. Merge histograms instead; the mean of per-server p99s is not the fleet's p99.
  • Measuring only the successes. A service that times out most requests can show a lovely latency for the few that finish.
  • Counting only 5xx as errors. Timeouts, hung requests and "200 with an error body" are failures too.
  • Alerting on the max. One bad request will page you; alert on the p99, on the share over a threshold, or on the count of timeouts.
  • High-cardinality labels. A user id or request id on a metric creates millions of series and a huge bill; keep labels to a small fixed set.
  • Percentiles over too few samples. A p99 from 50 requests is noise; widen the window or look at the share over a threshold.
  • Coordinated omission. A load test that waits for each response before sending the next hides the tail — while one request stalls, the tool stops sending, so the slow period is under-sampled. Send at a fixed rate and record the intended send time.
  • Mixing clocks. Compare durations measured on one machine; client and server timestamps drift.
  • Dashboards without a promise. A graph with no target answers nothing; tie each key metric to an SLO or a stated expectation.

In an interview

When asked "how would you monitor this?", answer in four layers and name numbers:

LayerSay…
1 · what users feel"The success rate and p99 latency of successes for each key journey, with an SLO — say 99.9% under 300 ms — and alerts on error-budget burn."
2 · headroom"Saturation: queue depth and age, connection-pool and database-connection usage, CPU — with alerts before the limit."
3 · dependencies"Per-dependency p99 and error rate, circuit-breaker state, cache hit ratio, replication lag — so a slow call is found fast."
4 · correctness and business"Reconciliation mismatches, oversell and duplicate counts (target zero), data freshness, and the funnel or conversion for the flow."
Out loud — a 30-second answer"For checkout I'd watch the success rate and p99 of the place-order call, the payment success rate per method and provider, and the lag of the payment webhook. For headroom: the age of the webhook queue and database connections. For correctness: reconciliation mismatches and oversell, both zero — I'd page on one. I'd alert on error-budget burn, not on single spikes, and keep the causes on a dashboard. I'd report latency percentiles from histograms, separately for successes and errors — and never an average."

Three habits that sound senior: say the percentile ("p99 of successes"), separate success from error latency, and name what would page you.

Toolkit

Caching Playbook — Search & Hot Keys

Two caching problems that don't fit the simple "cache a key, return a value" shape covered elsewhere on this page: caching something as high-cardinality as free-text search, and protecting a cache from a single key that gets hit far harder than the rest. Both show up directly in the invoice search example below.

Caching free-text search

A simple key-value cache — like the URL shortener's short_code → long_url — has a small, well-defined key space and one stable answer per key. Free-text search breaks both assumptions: the space of possible queries is effectively unbounded, and the correct answer can depend on more than the query string alone.

1×Cache the query, not (user, query)

Match text once, shared. Filter for permissions after every fetch, hit or miss. Scale-dependent — see the table below.

AaNormalize before keying

Lowercase, trim, collapse whitespace, so near-identical strings share one entry instead of fragmenting.

×2Admit by frequency, not by guessing

Only cache a query once it's been seen twice in a short window (Count-Min Sketch). Governs negative results too.

∅Cache negatives, briefly

A genuine zero-match is a shared negative — short TTL, gated by the same admission policy as everything else.

msDebounce on the client

Wait for a pause in typing before sending anything — cuts backend load before it starts.

L1Two cache tiers

A small local (in-process) cache for the hottest queries per instance, backed by shared Redis for everything else.

Does this hold up at millions of searchers?

Redis's raw throughput usually isn't the bottleneck — a sharded cluster handles millions of ops/sec. The real risk is quieter: a polluted cache doesn't go down, it just stops helping — hit rate collapses and nearly the full query volume gets forwarded to the index anyway, which is what actually falls over while the cache still looks "up." Judge a cache by its hit rate at your actual traffic mix, not by whether it's technically running.

Illustration — admission by frequency, not by guessing
QueryWhat happenedSeen-countResult
"12lasdla"searched once seen-count: 1→ NOT cached yet
"12lasdla"searched again 40 seconds later seen-count: 2→ NOW admitted to cache
"inv-2024-0099"searched once, never again seen-count: 1 forever→ never cached
"inv-2024-0088"searched by 6 different people this hour seen-count: 6→ cached, stays hot

The counter itself (a Count-Min Sketch) uses fixed memory no matter how many distinct strings it's seen — so remembering "have I seen this" never becomes its own unbounded cache.

This idea has a name worth knowing: TinyLFU — frequency-based admission backed by a Count-Min Sketch. It's the admission policy inside Caffeine (Java) and Ristretto (Go), so in a Go service you'd usually reach for Ristretto rather than build it.

Illustration — why the key design decides whether this scales
Per-(user, query) keys:
≈ 100M+ keys/week5M active users × ~20 distinct searches/user/week

most never requested a second time — memory spent, nothing gained

Shared, query-only keys:
~500Ksame week, maybe ~500K genuinely distinct query strings actually searched

(many users searching the same or similar invoice numbers, customer names)

per-user100M+
shared~500K

→ roughly 200x smaller key space, and each entry now serves many users, not one

Keeping negative caching honest

"Cache the zero-results too" can quietly become its own burden if it's treated as a separate policy. It isn't one.

SignalWhat to do about it
One-off typos, most negativesThe same frequency-based admission policy from above governs negatives too — a typo nobody repeats never gets written to Redis at all. There's no separate negative-cache policy to maintain or tune.
Negative-cache hit rate is lowDon't reach for a longer TTL — that trades freshness for a hit rate that a longer window usually won't meaningfully fix. If negatives genuinely don't repeat in your traffic, the honest answer is to stop caching them and make sure the index itself resolves "no match" cheaply on its own.
A burst of repeated negative writes (bot, retry loop)That's a rate-limiting problem, not a caching one — bound it at the edge (see the Rate Limiter example), not by tuning cache parameters.

Typos that almost match something real

Prefix matching catches "inv-2024-00" typed partway through — it doesn't catch "vin-2024-0088," a genuine typo of a real invoice number with the wrong letters up front. That needs a different technique, and it comes with a real risk worth naming.

≈Fuzzy matching is the standard fix

Elasticsearch/OpenSearch's fuzzy query tolerates a small edit distance — insertions, deletions, transpositions — so "vin-2024-0088" can still find "inv-2024-0088."

!IDs aren't names — precision beats recall

Two real invoice numbers are often one digit apart. Silently fuzzy-matching an ID risks returning the wrong document, which is worse than returning nothing.

?Fuzzy only as a labeled fallback

Run exact/prefix first. Only on zero results, run a fuzzy lookup and show it as "Did you mean…" — never merged into the primary result list.

+1Same caching architecture, one more layer

The fuzzy fallback is itself a query — cached by query text, admission-gated by frequency, exactly like everything else above.

Illustration — a typo handled as a labeled suggestion, not a silent match

search "vin-2024-0088"

  1. exact/prefix match

    → 0 results

  2. fallback

    → fuzzy lookup (edit distance ≤ 2)

  3. shown to the user
    No results for "vin-2024-0088"."Did you mean: inv-2024-0088?"

    — shown separately, never merged into the result list

Both the empty exact-match and the fuzzy suggestion are cached independently, keyed by the same normalized query text, gated by the same admission policy above.

Illustration — same query, three ways in
"INV-2024-0088"/"inv-2024-0088 "/" INV-2024-0088"

normalize"inv-2024-0088"

ONE shared cache entry, not three, not per-user

"ZZZZ-NOTHING" (matches nothing, for anyone) → index returns 0 results

  • cached as a shared negative, TTL 5s
  • same string searched again by ANY user within 5s → "no results" served instantly, index untouched
Step-by-step — two different users, one cache entry

Two users, subscribed to different products, search the same invoice number nine seconds apart.

  1. User A types "INV-2024-0088." The client waits 300ms after the last keystroke before sending anything.
  2. The query is normalized to "inv-2024-0088" — this is the entire cache key. No user_id in it.
  3. First time anyone has searched this text: cache miss. The Search Service queries the index for the raw match set across all 30+ products and writes it to cache with a 30-second TTL — still unfiltered.
  4. Before returning anything, the Search Service filters that result down to User A's ever-subscribed products and tags each one's status. This step runs regardless of whether the line above was a hit or a miss.
  5. User B searches the identical text nine seconds later: cache hit on the same shared entry — then User B's own subscription filter runs against it, independently. User B may see a different subset of products than User A did, from the exact same cached data.
  6. Net effect: the expensive part (matching text against the index) happened once for both users; the cheap part (who's allowed to see what) ran separately for each of them, every time, with no exceptions.
Strategy by scale

Every card above is a real technique — but applying all of them at 50 QPS is over-engineering, and applying none of them at 5,000 QPS is how a cache quietly stops working. Match the effort to what the traffic actually demands.

~50 QPS
  • Key shape: per-(user, query) — simpler, safer by construction, nothing to get wrong.
  • Skip admission policy and negative-result caching entirely.
  • A plain TTL (30–60s) is enough either way.
100–500 QPS
  • Key shape: per-user is usually still fine — watch actual query diversity, don't assume.
  • Normalize before keying, regardless of shape.
  • Add negative-result caching if typo-heavy traffic is common.
1,000–5,000 QPS
  • Key shape: switch to shared, query-only + filter-after-fetch — the math stops forgiving per-user keys here.
  • Add a cache admission policy and a local (in-process) tier.
  • The filter must never be skipped, on any code path, forever.
5,000+ QPS
  • Everything above is load-bearing, not optional.
  • Shard the cache layer itself (Redis Cluster) if one node's throughput is the limit.
  • Size the index's replica capacity for the residual miss traffic — even 95%+ hit rate still forwards hundreds of QPS.
  • Consider admission control (rate limiting) in front of search entirely.
DecisionThe trade-off
Short TTL vs. long TTLShort keeps results fresh but lowers the hit rate; long improves the hit rate but risks serving stale results — worse here than a simple KV cache, since search results are business data people act on.
Caching negative (zero-result) queriesPrevents repeated typos from hammering the index, at the cost of a small window where a just-indexed record stays invisible until the negative entry's short TTL expires.
Shared query-only cache + filter-after-fetch vs. per-(user, query) cache keysShared keys keep the hit rate real as the user base grows — the permission filter still runs on every single request, cache hit or miss, so nothing is skipped. Per-user keys are simpler to reason about (a cached entry is exactly what was already permitted), but the key space multiplies by active users — at real scale, that's the gap between a cache that works and one that quietly doesn't.
Fuzzy fallback on zero results vs. strict prefix-only matchingCatches genuine typos on structured IDs without risking a silent wrong-document match — fuzzy results are always labeled as suggestions, never merged into exact results — at the cost of an extra, more expensive lookup on every empty search, and a second result type to design and build.

Caching hot keys

A hot key is one cache key that gets far more traffic than the rest — enough that even a well-distributed cluster can have a single node buckling under one key's load, because consistent hashing sends that key to the same place every time. Sharding the cluster doesn't fix this; it only spreads the other keys around it.

First, find them — you can only protect a key you know is hot

Three practical ways: redis-cli --hotkeys (it needs an LFU maxmemory-policy to work), sampling key accesses in the client and keeping a top-K with a heavy-hitters sketch — the same family as the Count-Min Sketch above — or per-key metrics on the handful of keys you already suspect. Detect first: every technique below should apply only to keys detection actually flags.

:NSplit the key

cache_key:0 through cache_key:N — reads and writes pick a shard at random, spreading one hot key across many nodes.

L1Local cache for known-hot keys

A small in-process cache in front of the shared one removes the network hop entirely for the traffic that matters most.

1:NRequest coalescing

When a hot key expires, one request refetches it while every other concurrent request waits on that result, instead of all of them hitting the store at once.

↻Refresh before expiry, not after

A background or probabilistic early refresh keeps a genuinely hot key from ever going fully cold — sidestepping the stampede question rather than reacting to it.

Illustration — two ways to relieve one hot key
Key splitting:

"trending:productX" (50,000 req/s) → split into 8 shards

one node, one key50,000 req/s

each request: shard = hash(request_id) % 8 → ~6,250 req/s per shard

:0~6,250:1~6,250:2~6,250:3~6,250:4~6,250:5~6,250:6~6,250:7~6,250
Local cache vs. shared cache, for a key known to run hot:
Redis round trip:~1–2 ms
In-process memory read:~0.01 ms

(100–200x faster)

Step-by-step — a real stampede, prevented

A flash-sale item's price cache expires at the exact moment 200 shoppers are refreshing the page.

Without coalescing

200 queries hit the pricing database at once

With coalescing

1 query fetches; 199 wait for its result

  1. The cached price expires at 12:00:00.000.
  2. Without coalescing: all 200 requests miss the cache within the same millisecond and independently query the pricing database — 200x duplicate load arriving at once.
  3. With coalescing: the first request to miss marks the key "in-flight" — a short-lived lock — before fetching the real value.
  4. Requests 2 through 200 see the in-flight marker and wait on that first request's result instead of querying the database themselves.
  5. The first request finishes, writes the price to cache, and clears the marker — all 199 waiting requests read the now-populated cache in the same instant.
  6. Net effect: one database query served 200 requests, instead of 200 queries landing on it simultaneously.

GoIn Go this is golang.org/x/sync/singleflight: group.Do(key, fn) runs fn once per key while a call is in flight and hands every concurrent caller that same result — the stampede fix in one call.

Strategy by scale

Hot-key protection has a cost too — splitting and local caching add real complexity. The question isn't "should I defend against hot keys," it's "at what scale does a hot key become likely enough to justify that cost."

~50 QPS
  • True hot keys are unlikely to matter — full concentration on one key is trivial load for a single node.
  • Plain TTL expiry is fine.
  • Stampede protection here solves a problem that doesn't exist yet.
100–500 QPS
  • Hot keys become theoretically possible.
  • Start with request coalescing — cheap, and covers the one scenario that's now plausible.
  • Splitting and local caching are still premature.
1,000–5,000 QPS
  • A single popular key (a dashboard, a viral query) can now account for a real share of traffic.
  • Add local (in-process) caching + proactive early refresh for keys detected as hot.
  • Key splitting only for genuine outliers — not applied universally.
5,000+ QPS
  • Full toolkit: dynamic hot-key detection, splitting, local caching, coalescing, early refresh.
  • Detection matters — apply this only to keys that are actually hot.
  • Applying it uniformly to every key is its own form of over-engineering.
DecisionThe trade-off
Key splittingSpreads load across nodes, but invalidation and writes now have to reach every shard, not one key — more moving parts for the keys that need it.
Local (in-process) caching for hot keysThe fastest possible read, but reintroduces a small consistency question across every service instance's own cache — usually accepted via a short TTL, not solved outright.
Request coalescingProtects the backing store from a burst of duplicate work, but the one request actually doing the fetch still pays full latency while everyone else queues behind it.

Applying this to Multi-Product Invoice Search

Both playbooks map directly onto decisions already made in that example — worth spelling out explicitly rather than leaving "Cache" as an unlabeled box in a diagram.

Free-text caching → the Cache in front of the Search Index
  • Normalize the query text so equivalent searches collapse into one entry.
  • Cache negative results with a short TTL, so a mistyped invoice number doesn't repeatedly hit the index.
  • Key the cache by the query alone — not (user, query). With 30+ products' worth of users typing typos, a per-user space would explode into millions of entries never requested twice.
  • The subscription filter runs after every fetch — that's what keeps the hit rate real at this scale.
Hot keys → two different places, not one
  • An automated dashboard polling the same query on a schedule is a textbook hot key on the search-result cache — worth coalescing and a short early-refresh.
  • The Subscriptions lookup is actually more likely to go hot — a smaller key space to begin with, one entry per user, not per query.
  • A local cache in front of the shared Subscriptions lookup absorbs a heavy user or shared service account without a network round-trip on every search.
Toolkit

The Scale Ladder

The single most useful reframe for scale questions: a system almost never fails because "traffic got high." It fails because one bounded resource saturated, and everything behind it queued. Scale questions are therefore not "what's the architecture at 1M RPS" — they're "which bound do I hit next, and what does hitting it look like."

First: the bounded things

Before any tier table, know what can actually saturate. In practice it's almost always one of these, and the first one is far more common than the rest combined.

What saturates, roughly in order of how often it bites first
#1
DB connections the #1 first wall

and it is pure arithmetic: app instances × pool size = connections needed

40 instances × 25 pool = 1,000 connections
↑ Postgres default max_connections = 100

you hit this at trivial traffic, and the symptom is "the database is down" when it is fine

#2
Threads / workers

per instance. A blocking call to a slow dependency holds one for its whole duration — see the API Gateway example's bulkhead dive.

#3
Single-threaded components

Redis executes commands on one core. Node has one event loop. One slow O(n) command or one CPU-bound handler stalls everything behind it.

#4
Disk IOPS

random writes on a B-tree, or unindexed reads scanning pages and stealing IOPS from writes.

#5
Lock contention

a hot row. 50k RPS against one counter row is a serialisation point no amount of hardware fixes.

#6
Partition count

Kafka consumer parallelism is capped by partitions. More consumers than partitions = idle consumers.

#7
Memory / FDs

cache working set exceeding RAM, or file-descriptor limits on a connection-heavy service.

#8
Network

bandwidth rarely; packets-per-second and NAT/conntrack table limits more often than people expect.

#9
Downstream & third-party APIs

their rate limit and their latency become yours. A partner capped at 100 req/s caps you at 100 req/s, and while it is slow it holds your threads (#2).

How to tell which one you hit the USE method — for every resource, check three things:
UUtilization

how busy it is — e.g. connections in use ÷ pool size

SSaturation

how much work is waiting for it — e.g. time spent queued for a free connection

EErrors

what it's refusing — e.g. "too many connections", pool-acquire timeouts

Saturation is the one that matters most and is least often graphed: a resource at 70% utilization with a growing wait queue is already your bottleneck. The method is Brendan Gregg's; it turns "the system is slow" into a checklist you can walk resource by resource.

The ladder — what breaks, and what it costs to fix

Numbers are deliberately rough and assume a typical read-heavy web workload on ordinary hardware. A write-heavy or fan-out-heavy system hits each rung far earlier. Use them to locate yourself, not as thresholds to quote.

How you climb — one loop, repeated at every rung
  1. MeasureUSE on every resource — utilization, saturation, errors
  2. Find the one boundthe resource whose queue is growing; there is almost always exactly one
  3. Cheapest move firstthe smallest change that relieves that bound — not the next rung's architecture
  4. Say its costevery move buys headroom with a new failure mode
  5. Re-measurethe bottleneck moves; find where it went

↺ back to Measure — you climb one bound at a time, never a whole rung at once

Cheapest first — the order to try moves in
fix the queryadd the indexpool connectionsscale upcache & replicasscale outgo asyncpartitionre-architect

Each step right is more expensive to build, to run and to undo. Skipping left-hand steps is how a team ends up sharding a database that needed one index.

< 100 RPSmost systems, forever
What actually breaks

Nothing architectural. If it's slow here it's an N+1 query, a missing index, or a synchronous third-party call — not scale.

The move
  • One app tier, one primary database, managed backups. Stop.
  • Instrument it now — request rate, errors, p50/p99 latency, per-resource saturation — so the next rung announces itself instead of arriving as an outage.
What the move costs you

Nothing. Reaching for a queue or a cache at this rung is how teams create problems they then have to solve.

Signals you've reached itslowness traces to one query or one external call, not to load; p99 stays close to p50
~1k RPS
What actually breaks

Connection exhaustion (the arithmetic above). Slow queries under concurrency that were fine in isolation. Tail latency starts diverging badly from the mean.

The move
  • Connection pooler (PgBouncer) in transaction mode.
  • Fix the top 5 slow queries. Add the indexes the query planner is asking for.
  • Make the app tier stateless (sessions in Redis or a signed token) and run 2+ instances behind a load balancer.
  • Move slow side-work — email, PDF generation, webhooks — onto a background queue so it stops holding request threads.
What the move costs you

Transaction-mode pooling breaks session state — prepared statements, SET, advisory locks, some ORMs. Real migration work, not a config flag. Background jobs need retries and idempotency from their first day.

Signals you've reached itconnection-pool wait time climbing, "too many connections" errors, p99 pulling away from p50
~10k RPS
What actually breaks

Read volume saturates the primary's IOPS and steals them from writes. One instance can no longer hold the working set.

The move
  • First, scale the primary up — a bigger instance is the cheapest rung you will ever climb.
  • Read replicas for read traffic. Cache-aside in Redis for hot keys. CDN for anything static or semi-static.
  • Autoscale the stateless tier on a leading signal (in-flight requests, queue depth), not CPU alone.
What the move costs you

Replication lag — read-after-write breaks visibly ("I saved it and it's gone"). Invalidation — now your correctness depends on cache eviction being right. Autoscaling lag — it reacts in minutes; a spike arrives in seconds (see the edge cases below).

Signals you've reached itprimary CPU and IOPS dominated by reads, the working set no longer fitting in memory, cache and replica lag alarms appearing
~100k RPS
What actually breaks

Synchronous ACID writes max out disk. Replication lag balloons under write pressure. A single Redis node caps out. Cache stampedes on viral keys melt nodes.

The move
  • Accept writes asynchronously (202 + queue + batch flush).
  • Shard the cache. Partition hot tables by tenant or entity.
  • Shed load deliberately at the edge (429/503 with Retry-After) and propagate backpressure instead of letting queues grow without bound.
  • Give hot keys and hot tenants their own treatment.
What the move costs you

The write is no longer durable when you answer. You now owe the client a way to find out if it succeeded, plus retries, duplicate delivery, and ordering concerns. And you now decide who gets degraded first — a product decision as much as an engineering one.

Signals you've reached itwrite latency and replica lag rising together, one Redis node pinned at 100% CPU, queues growing faster than they drain
~1M RPS
What actually breaks

B-tree random-write I/O stalls SSD controllers. Cross-region latency dominates. Coordination between shards becomes the bottleneck rather than any single node.

The move
  • LSM-tree engines for write-heavy tables (Cassandra, ScyllaDB), or a managed partitioned store (DynamoDB).
  • In-process L1 cache. Regional sharding with local writes.
  • Split the stack into cells — independent copies, each serving a slice of tenants — so one failure or one hot tenant has a bounded blast radius.
What the move costs you

LSM trades write speed for read amplification and compaction load. Regional writes mean giving up global strong consistency — this is where CAP stops being theoretical. Anything that spans cells (global search, admin views, cross-tenant reports) becomes a fan-out query.

Signals you've reached itcompaction and write-amplification alarms, cross-region round trips visible in p99, locks or consensus as the slowest span in traces
Reads and writes climb different ladders

Reads have cheap relief valves — cache and replicas multiply read capacity without touching the primary. Writes have none: every write still has to land somewhere durable, so the write path is almost always the one that forces the architecture to change.

Read pathWrite path < 100 RPSthe single primary serves every readthe single primary takes every write ~1k RPSindexes, fix N+1 queries, pool connectionspool connections, keep transactions short, push side-effects (email, webhooks) to a background queue ~10k RPScache-aside, read replicas, CDN — reads are the easy halfstill one primary: scale it up, batch small writes, move hot counters out of single rows ~100k RPSsharded cache, in-process L1 for hot keys, request coalescingaccept asynchronously (202 + queue + batch flush), partition by tenant or entity ~1M RPSregional caches and replicas close to usersLSM engines, regional primaries with local writes, conflict resolution across regions

Where the RPS ladder lies — ten edge cases

The ladder measures one axis: requests per second on a read-heavy workload. These are the cases where that number tells you the wrong rung — worth naming out loud in an interview, because each one is a question the interviewer may be waiting for you to ask.

WWrite-heavy workloads

Why RPS liesThe read-side relief valves — cache and replicas — do nothing for writes. Ingest, logging and IoT pipelines hit the write wall while their RPS still looks modest.

What to doReach for queue, batch and partition one or two rungs earlier than the table suggests, and size the primary for write IOPS rather than request count.

×NFan-out

Why RPS liesOne external request becomes N internal operations: a post to 1,000 followers is 1,000 inbox writes.

What to doCount internal operations, not external RPS. Bound the fan-out — fan-out on read for huge accounts — as the News Feed example does.

⚡Spikes vs. autoscaling lag

Why RPS liesScaling takes minutes — new instances, warm-up, health checks. A sale, a push notification or a news mention arrives in seconds.

What to doPre-scale for known events; for unknown ones, queue or put users in a waiting room rather than letting the spike reach the database — see the Flash Sale example.

∞Long-lived connections

Why RPS liesA million idle WebSockets is close to zero RPS — and a million sockets' worth of memory and file descriptors.

What to doSize by concurrent connections, not requests. Give connections their own tier, and watch FD limits and conntrack tables.

MBLarge payloads

Why RPS lies100 RPS × 10 MB = 1 GB/s. That is a bandwidth problem at a request rate the ladder calls trivial.

What to doMove the bytes out of the request path: presigned uploads straight to object storage, a CDN for downloads.

TBStorage growth

Why RPS lies50 writes/s × 5 KB ≈ 7.9 TB a year. Size forces partitioning long before traffic does.

What to doPartition by time, archive or tier cold data, and set retention before it becomes a migration.

1:NOne tenant dominates

Why RPS liesOne enterprise customer or one runaway script can be most of your traffic, and every other tenant inherits its bad day.

What to doPer-tenant quotas, isolate heavy tenants, and at the top rung cells — see Multi-Tenant Rate Limiting.

↘Downstream limits

Why RPS liesA partner API that allows 100 req/s caps you at 100 req/s, whatever you build in front of it.

What to doQueue and smooth to their rate, cache their responses, and circuit-break and bulkhead so their outage stays theirs.

❄Cold starts

Why RPS liesAfter a deploy, a restart or a cache flush, every request misses at once and the database takes the whole load — at normal traffic.

What to doWarm caches before cutting traffic over, roll out gradually, and coalesce misses — see the Caching Playbook.

⏰Synchronised load

Why RPS liesCron jobs at :00, apps that all sync on the hour, clients that retry together after an outage — average load is fine, the same second is not.

What to doAdd jitter to schedules and to retry backoff; stagger batch jobs instead of starting them together.

Every fix creates its next problem

This is the part that separates a rehearsed answer from a real one. Naming the move is easy; naming what it costs is the actual signal.

The trade you are making, every time
caching

→ invalidation, stampedes, and a second source of truth that can silently disagree with the first

replication

→ stale reads, and read-after-write that works in dev (one node) and breaks in prod (many)

queues

→ at-least-once delivery, so every consumer must be idempotent; plus ordering, and a backlog that can grow silently with no caller timing out

sharding
