→ rebalancing, hot partitions, and cross-shard queries that used to be one JOIN

async writes

→ the client no longer knows if it worked; you owe them a status endpoint or a webhook

read replicas

→ someone will eventually point a write at one, or route a read-after-write to a lagging node

more retries

→ amplification. Three layers × three retries = 27× load on the thing already struggling. Retry budgets, not retry counts.

denormalisation

→ multiple copies to keep in sync, and the sync itself becomes a correctness problem

A useful habit: when you propose a move, say the cost in the same breath. "Add a read replica — and I'd need to decide which reads tolerate being a few seconds stale" is a far stronger answer than "add a read replica."

Two numbers worth knowing by heart

Little's Law, and the connection arithmetic
Little's Law

concurrency = throughput × latency

It tells you how many things are in flight at once, which is what actually determines pool sizes, thread counts, and whether you are about to saturate something bounded.

2,000 RPS × 50ms= 100 concurrent requests in flight
2,000 RPS × 500ms= 1,000 concurrent

← same traffic, 10× the resources held

This is why a dependency getting SLOWER looks exactly like traffic getting HIGHER from inside your service. Latency and load are the same problem wearing different clothes.

Connection math

instances × pool_size ≤ max_connections

40 instances × 25 = 1,000 wanted
↑ Postgres max_connections = 100 (default)

900 connections refused; the app reports "database down"

With PgBouncer in transaction mode:

40 instances × 25 app-side = 1,000 client connections

multiplexed onto ~50 real server connections
↑ limit 100

the pooler is doing the arithmetic for you

The second one is worth internalising because it is the most common production incident in this entire list, it happens at embarrassingly low traffic, and the error message points at the wrong component.

How to actually use this in an interview

  • Trace one request end to end before scaling anything — client → gateway → service → cache → database → queue → worker → dependency. You cannot say what saturates first without knowing what it touches.
  • Estimate only enough to pick a rung — peak QPS, read/write ratio, payload size, and working-set size — plus storage growth and concurrent connections, the two axes where RPS misleads most. The Math Toolkit calculator places you on a rung from these numbers. At 50 writes/sec, a distributed write architecture is a wrong answer. At 500k, partitioning and backpressure deserve real discussion.
  • Peak, not average — daily traffic divided by 86,400 is only the average; the peak is the number that makes systems fall over. Real traffic concentrates; a 3–10× peak-to-mean ratio is ordinary, and event-driven spikes are far worse.
  • Design for the next rung, not the last one — building for 1M RPS at 1k is as wrong as ignoring growth entirely, and it is the more expensive mistake because you pay the complexity immediately.
  • Watch p99, not the mean — the mean hides the queueing that precedes every saturation event. When p99 rises while the mean is flat, something bounded is filling up.
Toolkit

HTTP Status Codes, Decided Properly

The reason this matters more than it looks: the status code is the contract that decides what every client, SDK, proxy and load balancer does next. It is not documentation. A 5xx tells a client library to retry; a 4xx tells it to stop and surface the error. Get it wrong and you either hammer a struggling service with retries, or silently swallow a transient failure that would have worked on the second attempt.

Nine checks, in the order that avoids leaking information — authentication before semantic validation, so an anonymous caller never learns whether their data would have been accepted. Two things the common version of this chart leaves out: 429, which is the most frequent real rejection in any public API, and 409, which is the only 4xx that means "try again later" rather than "fix your request." Colour encodes what a client should do, which is the actual job of a status code.

The decision, in order

Walk these top to bottom and stop at the first match. The order matters — checking authentication before validating the contents, for instance, avoids telling an anonymous caller whether their data would have been accepted.

One pass, first match wins
1 · Could you parse it at all?
malformed JSON, bad syntax400 Bad Request
2 · Does the route exist?
no such path404 Not Found
3 · Who is calling?
no credentials, or invalid/expired401 Unauthorized← the name is wrong; 401 means UNAUTHENTICATED
4 · Are they allowed?
authenticated, but lacks permission403 Forbidden← 403 means authenticated and still no
leaking existence is a concern?404 instead← "this repo exists but isn't yours" IS information
5 · Over their limit?
rate or quota exceeded429 Too Many Requests← ALWAYS with Retry-After
6 · Is the shape right but the meaning wrong?
valid JSON, fails validation422 Unprocessable Entity← e.g. end_date before start_date, or a negative amount
7 · Does the target resource exist?
valid request, no such record404 Not Found
8 · Does it conflict with current state?
duplicate, version mismatch, already-consumed idempotency key409 Conflict← "not now" rather than "never"
9 · Did YOUR side fail?
unhandled exception500 Internal Server Error
upstream returned garbage502 Bad Gateway
deliberately shedding load / draining503 Service Unavailable
upstream timed out504 Gateway Timeout
10 · It worked. What kind of worked?
GET with a body200 OK
POST that created something201 Created + Location
accepted, not yet done202 Accepted
succeeded, nothing to say204 No Content← DELETE and many PUTs land here

The pairs people actually get wrong

The confusionThe ruleWhy it matters operationally
401 vs 403401 = I don't know who you are. 403 = I know, and no.A client SDK should refresh the token on 401 and give up on 403. Returning 403 for an expired token means the client never refreshes and the user is stuck logged out.
400 vs 422400 = I couldn't parse it. 422 = I parsed it, and the contents are wrong.Mostly a clarity win, but it separates "the client is broken" from "the user typed something invalid" in your dashboards — two very different alerts.
403 vs 404403 admits the thing exists. 404 doesn't.A deliberate choice, not an accident. For private resources, 403 leaks existence — an attacker can enumerate what's there. Most systems return 404 for anything the caller can't see.
409 vs 422422 is wrong forever. 409 is wrong right now.409 implies retry-after-resolving; 422 implies fix-your-input. A well-behaved client treats them completely differently.
500 vs 503500 = something broke unexpectedly. 503 = I'm deliberately not serving you.503 with Retry-After is how you shed load gracefully during a deploy or overload. 500 tells a load balancer the instance may be sick; 503 tells it this is intentional.
502 vs 504502 = upstream answered with nonsense. 504 = upstream never answered.These almost always come from your gateway or proxy, not your app — so which one you see tells you where the failure is before you open a single log.

Retryability — the thing the code is really encoding

What a client library does with each class
RETRY, with backoff
408 Request Timeouttransient
429 Too Many Requestsretry AFTER the Retry-After interval, not immediately — that is the whole point
500 Internal Server Errmight be a blip
502 Bad Gatewayupstream hiccup
503 Service Unavailableexplicitly "try later"
504 Gateway Timeout← but see the warning below

Retry-After is either a number of seconds or an HTTP date — clients must handle both. For quota visibility before a 429 ever happens, many APIs also return remaining-quota headers; an IETF HTTPAPI draft (RateLimit / RateLimit-Policy) is standardising them.

DO NOT RETRY — retrying changes nothing
400the body is still malformed
401the token is still invalid (refresh it, then retry once)
403permission will not appear on its own
404it still will not exist
422the data is still semantically wrong
THE 504 TRAP, worth stating plainly

A timeout does NOT mean the work didn't happen. The upstream may have completed it and simply answered too slowly.

  • retrying a 504 on a non-idempotent write can double-charge a customer
  • this is exactly why the payment example puts an idempotency key on the request BEFORE any of this matters
Never do this
200 OK
{ "success": false, "error": "insufficient funds" }
  • every proxy, cache, load balancer, retry policy and monitoring dashboard now believes this request succeeded
  • your error rate graph is a flat line while customers fail
  • the status code is machine-readable; the body is not

If you remember one thing: choose the code by asking what you want the caller to do next, not by which one best describes your internal state. That reframing resolves most arguments about 400 versus 422 in about five seconds.

Codes worth using that most APIs never reach for

201 Created with a Location header

tells the client where the new thing lives, so it doesn't have to guess a URL or re-query to find out.

202 Accepted

the honest answer for async work. It means "I have durably recorded your request and will process it," and it obliges you to give the client a way to check the outcome. The flash sale and payment examples on this page both depend on it.

204 No Content

the right answer for most DELETEs. Returning 200 with {"deleted": true} is noise the client has to parse to learn nothing.

410 Gone

for an endpoint you retired deliberately. Unlike 404, it says "this existed and was removed," which points a confused consumer at your migration guide instead of at their own routing config. The versioning example uses this.

412 Precondition Failed

with If-Match, this is how you do optimistic concurrency over HTTP properly rather than inventing a version field in the body.

207 Multi-Status

for genuine batch endpoints where some items succeed and some fail. The alternative, a 200 containing a mixed results array, hits the same problem as the 200-with-error above.

One structural recommendation: pair the code with a machine-readable error body in a consistent shape — RFC 9457 (Problem Details) is the standard worth adopting, because it gives you a stable type field clients can branch on without parsing prose.

403 what a Problem Details response looks like
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type":     "https://api.example.com/problems/insufficient-scope",
  "title":    "Insufficient scope",
  "status":   403,
  "detail":   "This token lacks invoices:write.",
  "instance": "/v1/invoices/inv_991"
}

type is the stable identifier clients branch on; title is for humans and may change; detail explains this occurrence. RFC 9457 replaced RFC 7807 in 2023 with the same shape, so existing 7807 clients keep working.

Toolkit

Data Correctness — Transactions, Isolation & Consistency

Most data bugs aren't crashes. They are two transactions that are each correct on their own, interleaving in a way nobody pictured — and the database's default settings don't stop most of them. This toolkit is the reference for three questions interviewers ask in every design that stores money or state: what can go wrong when writes overlap, which guarantee stops it, and what that guarantee costs.

1 · Five ways overlapping transactions go wrong

Each is two transactions, T1 and T2, reading and writing the same data. Read each timeline top to bottom.

Illustration — the anomalies, as timelines
1 Dirty read
T1: set invoice total = 900
T2: reads 900, emails the customer
T1: ROLLBACK

the email quotes a total that never existed

2 Non-repeatable read
T1: reads status = draft
T2: sets status = sent, COMMIT
T1: reads again → sent

the same query gives two answers inside one transaction

3 Phantom
T1: counts overdue invoices → 12
T2: inserts an overdue invoice, COMMIT
T1: sums overdue amounts → 13 rows

a report whose count and total disagree

4 Lost update
T1: reads balance 500
T2: reads balance 500
T1: writes 500 − 100 = 400
T2: writes 500 − 200 = 300

final balance 300 — T1's debit vanished

5 Write skew — the one that gets past snapshot isolation

Rule: every business must keep at least one admin. It has two, Ana and Budi, and each tries to remove the other at the same moment.

T1 (Ana): counts admins → 2, so removing Budi is allowed
T2 (Budi): counts admins → 2, so removing Ana is allowed
T1: removes Budi, COMMIT
T2: removes Ana, COMMIT

zero admins. Each transaction checked the rule and was right about what it saw; they wrote different rows, so nothing conflicted.

This is the double-booking bug from the meeting room example in another form: a decision based on reading rows that another transaction is about to change — or to insert.

2 · What each isolation level actually prevents — in PostgreSQL

The SQL standard describes levels loosely and each database implements them differently, so it's worth knowing the one you use. This is PostgreSQL's behaviour.

Illustration — the isolation matrix
Dirty readNon-repeatablePhantomLost updateWrite skew
Read Committed defaultpreventedpossiblepossiblepossiblepossible
Repeatable Read snapshot isolationpreventedpreventedpreventedone aborts: 40001possible
Serializable SSIpreventedpreventedpreventedone aborts: 40001one aborts: 40001
  • PostgreSQL never allows dirty reads — asking for Read Uncommitted gives you Read Committed.
  • The standard permits phantoms at Repeatable Read; PostgreSQL's snapshot implementation prevents them. MySQL's InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read and implements it differently again — check your database, don't assume.
  • "Lost update: possible" at Read Committed means read-then-write in application code. An atomic UPDATE … SET balance = balance − 100 is safe even there, because the database re-reads the row under its lock.

Stronger levels don't prevent conflicts by waiting — they abort one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization failure). Choosing Repeatable Read or Serializable is a promise that every transaction can be safely retried.

3 · The enforcement ladder — how to protect an invariant

Ordered by preference. Start at the top and stop at the first rung that can express your rule: the higher rungs are enforced by the database for every writer, including the code nobody has written yet.

Illustration — six ways to stop the anomalies, in order of preference
1
Constraint

The database rejects any write that breaks the rule — UNIQUE, CHECK, EXCLUDE, foreign keys. "One active subscription per business" is a partial unique index: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX … ON subscriptions (business_id) WHERE status = 'active'.

Use when the rule can be stated about the data itself. Loser sees a constraint violation → 409.

2
Atomic conditional update

Check and change in one statement, with no read-modify-write in the application: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance − $1 WHERE id = $2 AND balance >= $1. Zero rows affected means the rule said no.

Use when the rule concerns one row. Loser sees zero rows → a clear refusal, as in the Ticketmaster seat hold.

3
Optimistic concurrency

Each row carries a version. Updates say … WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2 and increment it; zero rows means someone else changed it first. Over HTTP this is an ETag with If-Match.

Use when conflicts are rare — a person editing a record. Loser sees 409 or 412, then reloads.

4
Pessimistic lock

SELECT … FOR UPDATE locks the rows you read, so a competing transaction waits. For write skew, lock the rows you are counting — or simply lock the parent: every admin change first locks the business row, which puts them in single file.

Use when conflicts are frequent or the rule spans rows. Watch lock ordering, or two transactions deadlock.

5
Serializable + retry

Run the transaction at SERIALIZABLE and let the database detect dangerous interleavings. It aborts one side with 40001; the application retries the whole transaction.

Use when the invariant is too complex to lock precisely. Cost retries under contention, and every transaction must be retry-safe.

6
Advisory lock

A named lock with no row behind it — for when the thing to protect doesn't exist yet, like an empty time slot. See the meeting room example.

Use when there is nothing to lock or constrain. Watch it is only as good as every writer remembering to take it.

The write-skew bug above has two good fixes: lock the business row (rung 4) or run the removal at Serializable (rung 5). It can't be a simple constraint — "at least one admin" is a rule about a set of rows, not any single row, which is exactly why it slips past every isolation level below Serializable.

4 · Across services — when one transaction isn't available

Everything above assumes one database. Once a business operation spans services, each with its own database, there is no single COMMIT — and the choice is between blocking and giving up isolation.

Two-phase commit keeps all-or-nothing semantics but leaves participants locked and unable to decide if the coordinator dies between phases. A saga never blocks — each step commits locally and failures are undone by compensations — but other transactions can see the in-between states, so the design has to tolerate them.
Illustration — the dual-write problem, and the outbox

Saving an invoice and publishing invoice.paid are two writes to two systems. Any ordering of them fails somewhere.

Database, then publish

the process crashes between the two

the invoice is paid, and no one downstream ever hears

Publish, then database

the database write fails after the event went out

subscribers act on a payment that never happened

Outbox

the invoice and an outbox row commit in one transaction; a relay publishes afterwards

both or neither — delivery becomes at-least-once, so consumers deduplicate

The problemThe tool
Write to the database and publish an eventTransactional outbox — as in webhook delivery and the audit log.
Change data owned by several servicesA saga with a compensation per step, as in the payment API; 2PC only between databases you control that support it.
A client retries a request that may have succeededAn idempotency key, claimed atomically before the work — the payment API's first deep dive.
A consumer receives the same message twiceDeduplicate on the message or event id; at-least-once delivery makes duplicates normal.
Other transactions see a saga half-finishedMake the state explicit — a PENDING status others respect — and design steps to be safely re-readable.

5 · Reading your own writes when reads go to replicas

Read replicas lag the primary by milliseconds to seconds. That is invisible in aggregate and very visible to one user who has just saved something — the "I saved it and it's gone" cost on the Scale Ladder's ~10k rung.

Illustration — the save that disappears, and three fixes
  1. t = 0

    the user saves an invoice — written to the primary

  2. t = 30 ms

    the app reloads the invoice list — read from a replica 200 ms behind

  3. result

    the new invoice isn't in the list; the user saves it again, and now there are two

Read from the primary after a write

route that user's reads to the primary for a few seconds after they write. Simple, and usually enough.

Wait for the replica to catch up

remember the commit's WAL position; read from a replica only once it has replayed that far (pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()), otherwise use the primary.

Stick a user to one replica

each user always reads the same replica, so time never appears to go backwards between two reads — monotonic reads.

The duplicate save in the timeline is also why the create endpoint deserves an idempotency key: a user retrying because the UI looked wrong is a retry like any other.

How to answer "how do you stop X from happening twice?"
  1. Name the invariant in one sentence — "a seat is held by at most one booking", "a business keeps at least one admin".
  2. Name the anomaly that breaks it — lost update, or write skew — and the isolation level at which it happens. That one sentence shows you know why the default isn't enough.
  3. Pick the highest rung of the ladder that can express the rule: a constraint if possible, an atomic update if it's one row, a lock or Serializable if it spans rows.
  4. Say what the loser sees — a 409, a 412, or a transparent retry on 40001 — because "one of them fails" is only half an answer until you've said how.
Toolkit

Disaster Recovery & Multi-Region

"What happens if the region goes down?" is a standard senior follow-up, and the answer isn't "we'd fail over". It is two numbers the business has agreed to, a strategy priced to meet them, and a drill that proves it works. Every choice here trades money against how much data you can lose and how long you can be down.

1 · The two numbers — agree them before designing anything

Illustration — the two numbers every DR plan starts from
RPO recovery point objective

How much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. RPO of 5 minutes means losing the last 5 minutes of writes is acceptable.

decided by how often data leaves the region

RTO recovery time objective

How long you can be down before service is restored. RTO of 1 hour means the business survives an hour of outage.

decided by how much is already running elsewhere

Per data type, not per system

Payments and ledgers may need an RPO near zero; a search index can be rebuilt from source and tolerate hours.

tiering the answer is what keeps the cost sane

2 · Replicas are not backups

A warm standby. Asynchronous replication keeps a second region seconds behind — protection against losing the region. Continuous WAL archiving to object storage is the separate protection against losing the data: a replica applies a mistaken DROP TABLE within milliseconds, while a base backup plus the WAL archive can restore the database to the moment just before it.
  • Point-in-time recovery — restore the latest base backup, then replay archived WAL up to a chosen timestamp. It's the only thing on this page that undoes a bad migration or a deleted table.
  • Synchronous vs. asynchronous replication across regions — synchronous gives RPO zero but adds a cross-region round trip, roughly 50–150 ms, to every commit. Most systems replicate asynchronously and accept an RPO of a few seconds.
  • A backup you have never restored is a hope — schedule restore drills, time them, and treat the measured time as your real RTO.

3 · Four strategies, priced against the two numbers

Illustration — from cheapest to most available
1
Backup & restore

Backups and WAL shipped to another region; nothing running there until disaster strikes.

RPO minutes, with continuous WAL archiving RTO hours — the whole stack is rebuilt Cost lowest

2
Pilot light

Data replicates continuously; compute in the second region is defined but switched off.

RPO seconds RTO tens of minutes — start the fleet, promote the replica Cost low

3
Warm standby

A scaled-down copy of the whole system runs in the second region all the time — the diagram above.

RPO seconds RTO minutes — promote, scale up, shift traffic Cost medium

4
Active-active

Both regions serve production traffic. Losing one means the other absorbs its load.

RPO seconds or less RTO close to zero Cost highest — and writes become the hard problem

These are orders of magnitude, not guarantees — the real RTO is whatever the last drill measured.

4 · Where multi-region actually gets hard

Illustration — writes, split brain, and the failover decision
Writes in two regions

If both regions accept writes to the same row, they will conflict — and "last write wins" silently discards one of them.

give every tenant a home region that owns its writes; the other region serves its reads. The tenancy example's Business.region is exactly this.

Split brain

The link between regions fails, each side thinks the other is dead, and both promote themselves. Two primaries now accept conflicting writes.

decide with a quorum — a witness in a third location — and fence the old primary so it cannot keep writing

Automatic or human failover?

Automatic regional failover can flap on a brief network blip and cause the split brain above.

common answer: detect automatically, page a human to approve a regional failover, automate everything after the decision

  • DNS-based failover is only as fast as the record's TTL and the clients that honour it — keep TTLs short on failover records, and expect some clients to cache longer.
  • Failing back is a second failover — the original region must be rebuilt from the new primary, not simply switched on.
  • A regional failover that has never been rehearsed will fail in a new way on the day — game days are part of the design, not an extra.
Toolkit

Zero-Downtime Schema Migrations

The database equivalent of API versioning. During a rolling deploy, old and new code run against the same database at the same time, so every schema change has to work for both — and on a large table, the wrong ALTER takes a lock that stops every query behind it. The rule: never change a schema in one step that code depends on; expand, migrate, then contract.

1 · Expand and contract

Renaming a column is the classic example because the naive version — one RENAME COLUMN — breaks whichever code version is still running. Spread over five steps and four code versions, no deploy ever depends on a column that doesn't exist yet or no longer exists.
  • Additive changes ship before the code that needs them; destructive changes ship after the code that no longer uses them. That single ordering rule is most of zero-downtime migration.
  • Changing a column's type usually rewrites the whole table under a lock. Treat it as expand and contract too: add a new column of the new type and migrate into it.

2 · The lock that takes production down

Illustration — a millisecond ALTER that causes a two-minute outage
  1. 12:00:00

    a slow report is running a 2-minute query on invoices

  2. 12:00:05

    a migration runs ALTER TABLE invoices … — it needs an exclusive lock, so it waits behind the report

  3. 12:00:06

    every ordinary SELECT and INSERT on invoices now queues behind the waiting ALTER — the table is effectively down

  4. 12:02:00

    the report finishes, the ALTER runs in milliseconds, and two minutes of requests have timed out

The fix is one line
SET lock_timeout = '2s';        -- give up instead of queueing everyone behind you
ALTER TABLE invoices ADD COLUMN display_name text;   -- retry later if it timed out

The ALTER itself was never slow. The outage came from the lock queue — which is why every migration should set a short lock_timeout and retry, rather than wait.

3 · Safe versions of common changes — PostgreSQL

Illustration — the risky form, and the safe form
ChangeRiskySafe
add a column with a defaulta volatile default such as clock_timestamp() rewrites every rowa constant default is metadata-only since PostgreSQL 11
add an indexCREATE INDEX blocks writes for the whole buildCREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY — slower, can't run in a transaction, and leaves an INVALID index to drop if it fails
make a column NOT NULLSET NOT NULL scans the table under an exclusive lockadd CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT without blocking writes; since PostgreSQL 12, SET NOT NULL then skips the scan
add a foreign keyvalidates every existing row while holding locksADD CONSTRAINT … NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT separately
rename a column or tableinstant in the database, and instantly breaks running codeexpand and contract — the diagram above
change a column typeusually rewrites the table under an exclusive locknew column, dual-write, backfill, switch, drop

4 · Backfilling millions of rows without hurting anyone

Illustration — one giant UPDATE vs. small batches
One statement
UPDATE invoices SET display_name = customer_name;
  • one enormous transaction holding row locks for its whole duration
  • replicas fall far behind while it replays
  • a failure at 90% rolls back everything
Batches by key range
UPDATE invoices SET display_name = customer_name
WHERE id > $last_id AND id <= $last_id + 5000
  AND display_name IS NULL;
  • short transactions; each batch commits on its own
  • pause between batches when replica lag rises
  • safe to stop and resume — IS NULL skips finished rows

The backfill runs while the application is dual-writing, so new rows already have the new column filled — the batches only have to catch up on history.

Toolkit

Choosing a Data Store & Partitioning

Two decisions interviewers probe right after the high-level design: which store holds each kind of data, and how data is split once one machine isn't enough. Both are answered by access patterns — how the data is read and written — rather than by which technology is fashionable.

1 · Start from the access pattern

Illustration — what you need to do with the data, and what fits
You need to…Reach forBecause
keep money and state correct across related rowsrelational PostgreSQL, MySQLtransactions, constraints and joins — the data correctness toolkit depends on them
look things up by key at very high scale, with patterns known up frontwide-column / key-value DynamoDB, Cassandrapartitioned by design and predictable at scale — but you model tables around your queries, and ad-hoc queries are hard
serve hot reads in under a millisecondcache Redismemory speed; not the source of truth — see the Caching Playbook
search free text, filter and ranksearch index Elasticsearch, OpenSearchinverted indexes; fed from the database, rebuilt when it drifts
store files, exports, attachmentsobject storage S3 or equivalentcheap and durable; the database holds only the key and metadata
record metrics over timetime-series Prometheus, TimescaleDBcompression and downsampling built for append-only, time-ordered data
analyse across all customers and historycolumnar warehouse BigQuery, Snowflake, ClickHousescans billions of rows fast; never on the request path

The strongest interview default: PostgreSQL until a specific access pattern forces something else — then say which pattern, and what the new store costs you. Adding a store adds a copy of the data to keep in sync.

2 · Three ways to split data across machines

Range partitioning keeps neighbouring keys together, so range queries stay cheap — but time-based ranges send every new write to the newest partition. Hash partitioning spreads keys evenly and gives up range queries. A directory records where each key lives, so any single tenant can be moved — at the price of a lookup that must itself be fast and available.

3 · Choosing the partition key — the decision that's hardest to undo

Illustration — good keys, bad keys, and why
A good key
  • many distinct values — so it can spread across many partitions
  • even traffic per value — no single value dominates
  • groups what's queried together — so common queries hit one partition

in B2B: business_id — each business's data stays together, and businesses spread out

Keys that go wrong
  • created_at — every new write lands on the newest partition
  • country or status — a handful of values, badly skewed
  • a random id — even spread, but every query for one business now touches every partition

Even a good key has outliers: one very large business is a hot partition by itself. Split that one key (the Caching Playbook's key splitting), or move that tenant to its own database — the silo tier in the tenancy example.

4 · Growing without reshuffling everything

Illustration — why hash % N breaks, and the fix
hash(key) % number_of_nodes

Going from 4 nodes to 5 changes the answer for most keys — so most of the data has to move at once, while you're already short of capacity.

Many fixed partitions, few nodes

Hash into a fixed, large number of partitions — say 1,024 — and assign partitions to nodes. Adding a node moves whole partitions to it; no key ever changes partition.

  • consistent hashing achieves the same effect — only about 1/N of keys move when a node joins (see the glossary's ring diagram)
  • secondary indexes need a choice too: local indexes live with each partition, so a query by that field asks every partition; global indexes are partitioned by the indexed value, so reads are targeted but index updates become asynchronous
  • resharding is a migration: copy, keep in sync, switch reads, stop the old path — the same expand-and-contract shape as the schema migrations toolkit
Toolkit

Glossary

The shared vocabulary — reach for these building blocks in Steps 5 and 6, not as buzzwords, but because a specific one solves a specific problem you named.

47 terms
HLD⇄Traffic & the edge 4⚡Caching 3▦Data distribution & storage 6⧉Replication & consistency 8✉Async & messaging 5◎Resilience & capacity 4
LLD◇Design principles 3▣Creational & structural patterns 4↻Behavioural patterns 3⌗Concurrency primitives 5⚠Concurrency bugs 2

HLD — Distributed Systems Service architecture & scale

30 terms in 6 families

⇄

Traffic & the edge

Getting each request to a healthy server quickly — and turning away what shouldn't arrive at all.

4 terms
Load Balancer

Distributes incoming requests across multiple servers so no single instance is overwhelmed; enables horizontal scaling and failover.

Reverse Proxy

Sits in front of servers, forwarding client requests to the right backend; often bundles load balancing, TLS termination, and caching.

CDN

A geographically distributed network of edge servers that caches content close to users, cutting latency and origin load.

Rate Limiting

Controls requests per client per window via token bucket (allows bursts), leaky bucket (smooths bursts), or sliding-window counters.

⚡

Caching

Serving repeated reads from somewhere faster than the source of truth, without serving stale lies.

3 terms
Cache

A fast, usually in-memory store (Redis, Memcached) holding frequently accessed data to avoid repeated expensive reads.

Cache Invalidation

Keeping cache and source in sync: write-through (both together), write-back (cache first, flush later), write-around (DB only, cache fills on read).

Bloom Filter

A space-efficient probabilistic structure answering "definitely not present" or "maybe present" — cheap first-pass dedupe checks.

▦

Data distribution & storage

Deciding where each piece of data lives, and how it's found again, once one machine isn't enough.

6 terms
Sharding / Partitioning

Splitting a dataset across multiple machines by some key, so no single node holds — or serves — all the data.

Consistent Hashing

A hashing scheme that minimizes data movement when nodes join or leave, by mapping both keys and nodes onto the same ring.

Hot Partition

One shard or key receives disproportionate traffic, becoming a bottleneck even though the system is "sharded."

Database Indexing

A secondary structure (often a B-tree) trading extra storage and slower writes for much faster lookups on specific columns.

SQL vs NoSQL

SQL favors strong consistency and relational integrity at some scaling cost; NoSQL favors flexible schemas and horizontal scale, usually looser consistency.

Replication Factor

The number of copies of each piece of data kept for durability. 3 is the standard default — it survives one node loss while a quorum of 2 remains available.

⧉

Replication & consistency

Keeping copies of data in agreement — and deciding what to give up when the network won't let you.

8 terms
Leader-Follower Replication

One node accepts writes and propagates them to read-only replicas — trades replication lag for read scalability and durability.

Leaderless Replication

Any node can accept writes, resolved via quorum reads/writes — more availability, more complexity resolving conflicts.

Consensus

Getting nodes to agree on a value or leader despite failures (Raft, Paxos), usually requiring a majority quorum to proceed.

Strong vs Eventual Consistency

Strong guarantees every read reflects the latest write immediately; eventual allows a lag where reads may return stale data.

CAP Theorem

Under a network partition, a distributed system must choose between Consistency and Availability — it can't fully have both.

PACELC

Extends CAP: even without a partition, you still trade off Latency against Consistency during normal operation.

ACID

Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the guarantees classic relational transactions provide.

BASE

Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent — the looser guarantee many distributed stores favor for availability and scale.

✉

Async & messaging

Decoupling who produces work from who does it, so neither has to wait for the other.

5 terms
Message Queue

Holds messages between producers and consumers, decoupling them in time and allowing buffered, async processing.

Pub/Sub

Publishers emit events to a topic; any number of subscribers receive a copy — useful for fan-out.

Fan-out (Push vs Pull)

Push (fan-out-on-write) pre-computes each recipient's feed at write time; pull (fan-out-on-read) computes it at read time — a write-cost vs read-cost trade-off.

Idempotency

Performing the same operation multiple times has the same effect as once — critical for safely retrying over unreliable networks.

Backpressure

Lets a slower downstream component signal a faster upstream one to slow down, preventing queues from growing unbounded.

◎

Resilience & capacity

How much the system can take, and how it behaves when one part of it can't.

4 terms
Circuit Breaker

Stops calling a failing downstream service after repeated errors — failing fast instead of piling up retries and cascading failure.

Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling

Vertical adds power to one machine with a hard ceiling; horizontal adds more machines, requiring work to be distributable.

Little's Law

A queueing identity: average concurrent requests in flight = throughput × average latency (L = λW). Useful for sizing connection pools and thread pools from a QPS and latency estimate.

Availability (The Nines)

Uptime target expressed as a percentage of nines — 99.9% ("three nines") permits about 8.76 hours of downtime a year, 99.99% about 53 minutes. Each extra nine is roughly a 10× tighter budget.

LLD — Object-Oriented Design & Concurrency Class design & single-process correctness

17 terms in 5 families

◇

Design principles

Rules of thumb that keep classes easy to change without breaking what already works.

3 terms
SOLID Principles

Five OOD guidelines: Single Responsibility (one reason to change), Open/Closed (extend without modifying), Liskov Substitution (subtypes must be substitutable), Interface Segregation (many small interfaces beat one fat one), Dependency Inversion (depend on abstractions, not concretions).

Interface vs Abstract Class

An interface defines a contract with no implementation; an abstract class can share partial implementation. Favor interfaces when unrelated classes share a capability, abstract classes when they share real code.

Composition over Inheritance

Prefer building behavior by holding references to other objects ("has-a") over deep inheritance chains ("is-a") — composition can change at runtime, inheritance locks in at compile time.

▣

Creational & structural patterns

How objects get created, and how they are assembled into bigger structures.

4 terms
Factory Pattern

Centralizes object creation behind a method or class, so callers ask for "a spot for this vehicle" instead of knowing every concrete subclass that could satisfy it.

Singleton Pattern

Guarantees a class has exactly one instance with a single global access point. Useful, but a common overuse — it's effectively global mutable state, which complicates testing and concurrency.

Decorator Pattern

Wraps an object to add behavior without modifying its class or affecting other instances — adding logging or caching around a service call.

Composite Pattern

Lets individual objects and groups of objects be treated through the same interface, typically for tree structures — a File and a Folder both responding to getSize().

↻

Behavioural patterns

How objects divide up responsibility and react to one another at runtime.

3 terms
Strategy Pattern

Encapsulates an algorithm behind a common interface so it can be swapped at runtime without changing the code that uses it — a pluggable fee calculator or sorting comparator.

Observer Pattern

Objects subscribe to another object and get notified automatically when its state changes — the in-process ancestor of pub/sub.

State Pattern

Encapsulates state-dependent behavior into separate state objects, so behavior changes with internal state without a scatter of if/switch statements.

⌗

Concurrency primitives

The building blocks for letting threads share work and state safely.

5 terms
Mutex / Lock

A primitive that lets only one thread hold it at a time, protecting a critical section from concurrent access.

Semaphore

Like a mutex but allows up to N holders at once — caps concurrent access to a limited resource, e.g. a connection pool.

Thread Pool

A fixed set of reusable worker threads pulling from a task queue, avoiding the cost of spawning a new thread per task.

Producer-Consumer

Producers add work items to a shared queue; consumers pull and process them — decouples creation rate from processing rate, the single-process cousin of a message queue.

Immutability

An object that can't change after construction. Side-steps a large class of concurrency bugs, since there's nothing to race over once an object exists.

⚠

Concurrency bugs

The failures those primitives exist to prevent — and the ones they can cause.

2 terms
Race Condition

Two or more threads access shared state such that the outcome depends on timing — classic form: check-then-act, where the check and the act aren't atomic.

Deadlock

Two or more threads each hold a resource the other needs and neither can proceed — commonly caused by acquiring multiple locks in inconsistent order.

No terms match that filter.

Worked Examples

49 Systems, Run Through the Framework

Each one is collapsed by default — open the ones you want. They're roughly ordered from simplest to most specialised, and later examples reference earlier ones rather than repeating them. Toward the end they assemble the platform pieces into one architecture and work through identity, isolating huge customers, live updates, chat, file sync, a subscription membership, a scheduled savings summary and a payroll run. The six database-schema deep dives have their own group, Database Schemas, after this one.

Worked Example A — Simple

Design a URL Shortener

request/response · no pipeline
Click to expand

"Design a service that turns a long URL into a short, shareable one and redirects it back." The cleanest system to run the framework on end-to-end — nothing here distracts from the mechanics.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Shorten a long URL, with an optional custom alias.
  • Redirect a short code to its original URL.
  • Optional — per-link click analytics.
  • Optional — links can expire.
Non-functional
  • Read:write ≈ 100:1 — redirects dwarf creates.
  • Redirect latency <100ms, so it never feels like a broken link.
  • Codes must never collide.
  • Links persist indefinitely by default — people bookmark and share them for years.

Worth asking: does a custom alias need profanity/reservation checks? Is there a max URL length? We'll assume no for this walkthrough and say so out loud.

2
Core Entities
  • User (id, plan_tier) — optional, only if accounts/custom links exist.
  • UrlMapping (short_code PK, long_url, owner_id?, created_at, expires_at?) — the entity that matters most.
  • ClickEvent (url_id, timestamp, referrer) — kept separate on purpose: the hot redirect path never touches write-heavy analytics data.
3
API

POST /urls {long_url, custom_alias?, expires_at?} → {short_code} (409 if alias taken)
GET /{short_code} → 302 redirect, or 404
GET /urls/{short_code}/stats → {click_count, created_at, last_clicked_at}

4
Data Flow

Skipped — this is a plain request/response system, not a pipeline. There's no multi-stage async transformation happening between write and read; saying so explicitly is the correct move, not a gap.

5
High-Level Design

Two distinct paths through the same stateless service layer — diagrammed and walked through step by step below.

6
Deep Dives

Three below: (a) short-code generation at scale, (b) cache design under a heavy read:write ratio, and (c) recording clicks without slowing down the redirect.

High-level design — write path (amber) and read path (cyan) through the same stateless service layer
← scroll to see the full diagram →
Write path
  1. Client sends POST /urls to the Load Balancer.
  2. LB routes to any stateless API Service instance — no session affinity needed.
  3. The service calls the ID Generator to mint a short code.
  4. The service writes {short_code, long_url, owner_id} to the Primary DB.
  5. The Primary DB replicates asynchronously to the Replica DB.
  6. The service returns the new short_code to the client.
Read path
  1. Client requests GET /{short_code}.
  2. LB routes to any API Service instance.
  3. The service checks the Cache for that short_code.
  4. Cache hit: return the long_url immediately, issue a 302.
  5. Cache miss: read from a Replica DB, then backfill the cache.
  6. Because codes are immutable once created, there's no invalidation problem — only a cold-start miss for brand-new links.
Key deep dive — short-code generation
FRShorten + custom aliasNFRCodes never collide
Thought process
  1. State the actual requirement: two different long URLs must never end up with the same short code.
  2. First instinct — generate something random. But now every write has to check "has this code been used?" before it can save, an extra round-trip on every single request.
  3. Better instinct: if something already guarantees uniqueness — like an auto-incrementing counter — just encode that into a short string. Collisions become structurally impossible, not just unlikely.
  4. New problem this creates: one shared counter across many servers is a bottleneck. Fix: hand each server its own reserved block of numbers upfront.
  • Counter-based: base62-encode an auto-incrementing ID. Collision-free and simple, but needs a coordinated counter — solved by pre-allocating ID ranges per app server rather than a single global lock.
  • Random-and-check: generate a random string, check the DB for a collision, retry if needed. Trivially distributed, but adds a write-path check on every request.
Illustration — counter-based
id 125,000,000base62 encode"8M0kX"

Either is defensible — the trade-off is what you're paid to articulate. A custom alias skips generation entirely: it's the same uniqueness check as random-and-check, just against a user-supplied string instead of a random one — reject on collision rather than retry with a new one.

Key deep dive — cache design under a 100:1 read:write ratio
FRRedirectFRLinks can expireNFR100:1 read:writeNFR<100ms redirectNFRPersist indefinitely
Thought process
  1. Reads massively outnumber writes, so the cache is doing almost all the real work here — its design deserves real attention, not an afterthought.
  2. Ask the question that shapes everything else: what changes about a mapping after it's created? Nothing — a short_code points to the same long_url forever.
  3. That answer removes a whole category of caching bugs: if nothing changes, there's no "stale data" to invalidate — the only decision left is what to evict when the cache runs out of room.
  4. One thing can still break even a perfect cache: a single link going viral can flood one cache server while the rest of the cluster idles. That's a different problem (a hot key), needing its own fix.

The cache key is simply the short_code, mapping to the long_url — small values, trivially shardable across cache nodes by consistent hashing.

  • No invalidation to design: a UrlMapping never changes after creation, so this is one of the rare caches that just needs an eviction policy (LRU is fine) for memory pressure — no TTL is strictly required.
  • The one real risk — a hot key: a single link going viral can overwhelm one cache node while the rest of the cluster sits idle.
  • If link expiration is in scope, that "no TTL" claim needs qualifying: an expired mapping has to stop resolving, so either the cache entry gets a TTL matching the link's own expiry, or every cache hit checks an expires_at field before returning the redirect. The write-once immutability argument still holds — what changes is "does this row still count," not the row's content.

At that scale, the fix is a short-lived, per-instance local cache in front of the shared cache for the handful of keys receiving disproportionate traffic — so one hot key doesn't become a single point of failure.

Key deep dive — recording clicks without slowing down the redirect
FRClick analytics
Thought process
  1. State the constraint plainly first: the redirect has to be fast, no matter what else the system needs to do.
  2. Ask whether recording the click actually needs to happen before the user gets redirected. It doesn't — the user only cares that they land on the right page instantly, not when the click gets logged.
  3. So don't make the redirect wait on it. Hand the event to a queue and return the redirect immediately — the write happens somewhere else, on its own schedule.
  4. Go one step further: batch the downstream writes instead of one row per click. A few seconds of delay in a dashboard is invisible; writing one row per click at high volume isn't free.

If click analytics are in scope, they cannot sit in the redirect's critical path — every added millisecond there defeats the entire point of a URL shortener.

  • Fire-and-forget: write the click event to a lightweight queue and return the 302 immediately. The redirect never waits for that write to finish.
  • Batch downstream: a consumer drains the queue and writes clicks to the analytics store in batches, trading a few seconds of "when a click shows up in a dashboard" for far lower write amplification than one write per click.

The general habit this reflects: the path that has to be fast and correct (the redirect) never waits on a path that only has to be eventually correct (the analytics). Decouple them with a queue rather than making one request do both jobs.

At 10x scale

Once redirects push past 100K/sec, put a CDN in front of the API for anonymous redirects — the 302 response itself is cacheable at the edge, since a given short_code always redirects to the same long_url. The origin only gets hit on a genuine cache miss anywhere across the entire CDN network, not per-request.

Does it hold up?

Non-functional requirementHow this design satisfies it
Redirect <100msCache in front of the DB; CDN-level edge cache for very hot links.
High read:write ratioOptimize the read path (replicas + cache); keep the write path simple.
No collisionsCounter + pre-allocated ranges, or random generation with a unique index and retry.
Links persist indefinitelyStandard replicated storage, no TTL sweep unless expires_at is set — storage cost, not correctness, is the real constraint here.

Key trade-offs

Every "yes" above was also a "no" to something else — stating both sides is what the checklist's "trade-off articulation" row is actually asking for.

DecisionThe trade-off
Counter-based vs. random short codesCounter-based is collision-free but needs a coordinated ID range; random needs zero coordination but adds a write-path collision check.
Cache with no TTLSimpler — no invalidation logic to design — but leans entirely on LRU eviction for memory pressure. Safe only because the underlying data is immutable.
Async replication (Primary → Replica)Writes stay fast, never wait on replicas — but a just-created link can briefly 404 on a replica before it catches up.
Single relational DB, not sharded from day oneSimpler to build and reason about now, at the cost of a re-architecture later if write volume outgrows one primary.

Tools you might reach for

Named last, on purpose — reason to "I need a fast key-value cache" before you reach for "Redis." Naming tools first is how design turns into buzzword bingo.

Load BalancerNGINXAWS ALB
