Third time this exact shape has shown up on this page — a parking spot, a seat, and now a ride request are all the same problem: two actors racing to claim one thing.

Key deep dive — tracking a ride in real time
FRTrack progress in real timeFRClear ride lifecycle
Thought process
  1. Notice this splits into two different questions that get conflated easily: how does a status change reach both people, and what are the actual valid statuses to move between?
  2. For delivery, recognize this is the exact same problem WhatsApp already solved — pushing an update to a specific online user's device. Reuse that, don't re-invent it.
  3. For the states themselves, list what's actually possible: a ride can't go from Requested straight to Completed, and once Completed it can't go anywhere. That's not a free-text status field, it's a constrained set of transitions.
  4. Model that constraint directly — a state machine — so an invalid transition (marking a Requested ride as Completed) is rejected by the model itself, not caught by a scattered if-check somewhere in application code.

Rider and driver apps both need to see the ride move through its states as they happen — not by polling, and not by re-deriving delivery from scratch.

  • Delivery reuses WhatsApp's push mechanism: each status change (Matched, driver arriving, InProgress, Completed) is a small message pushed to both the rider's and driver's live connections — the same connection-registry lookup and gateway push from the WhatsApp example, aimed at ride events instead of chat messages.
  • The lifecycle is a state machine, not a status string: Requested → Matched → InProgress → Completed is an explicit set of allowed transitions. The Ride Record only accepts a write that moves it to a state reachable from its current one — the same discipline as the parking spot's status field, applied to a longer chain.

Splitting these apart matters: the state machine is about what changes are even valid; the push mechanism is about how a valid change reaches the people who need to see it. Conflating them tends to produce code where an invalid state transition and a failed notification look like the same kind of bug.

Does it hold up?

Non-functional requirementHow this design satisfies it
Fast matchingGeohash grid or quadtree turns nearby-search into a handful of cell lookups, not a full scan.
High-volume location writesLocation pings update an in-memory index, decoupled entirely from the durable Ride record store.
Real-time ride trackingSame push-delivery pattern as the messaging example — the rider's client is pushed location updates, not polling for them.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
In-memory, non-durable geospatial indexMillisecond lookups that match the "roughly current" requirement, but a node restart loses recent pings until drivers re-ping — acceptable here, wouldn't be for a system that actually needed durability.
Geohash grid vs. quadtreeGeohash is simpler to implement and good enough for most cases; a quadtree adapts to uneven driver density at the cost of extra implementation complexity.
Straight-line "nearby" vs. actual driving-time distanceFast to compute with no routing engine needed for the first match pass, but can suggest a driver who's close as the crow flies yet far by road — a river or highway between them.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Geospatial IndexRedis Geo commands, Elasticsearch geo-queries
Location ingestionKafka
Ride RecordPostgreSQL, DynamoDB
Worked Example H — Conflict Detection

Design a Meeting Room Booking System

interval-overlap queries · recurring events
Click to expand

"Design a system that lets employees book meeting rooms for a time range, without double-booking, including recurring meetings." Smaller stakes than Ticketmaster, but the same correctness question wearing a calendar costume — and a genuinely different algorithmic core: not a single point of contention, but a range that has to be checked against every other range.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Book a room for a specific time range.
  • Check a room's availability before booking.
  • Search for available rooms across a given time range — not just check one specific room, but find any room (optionally filtered by capacity or location) that's free.
  • Support recurring meetings (e.g. a weekly standup).
  • Cancel or modify a booking — including a single occurrence of a recurring series.
Non-functional
  • Never double-book a room — the same correctness bar as Ticketmaster, at far smaller scale.
  • Overlap checks stay fast even for a room with a dense calendar.
  • Searching across many rooms for a free slot stays a single query, not one check per room.
  • Recurring meetings shouldn't require pre-generating years of instances up front.

Worth asking: single building/timezone, or multi-office? Can one meeting need two rooms at once? Should room search return every free match, or just the best fit? We'll assume single timezone, one room per meeting, and return every free match sorted by capacity — smallest first.

2
Core Entities
  • Room (id, capacity, location) — the resource being booked.
  • Booking (id, room_id, start_time, end_time, organizer_id, status, recurrence_rule?) — a single reservation, or the anchor of a series. Status is Confirmed or Cancelled — record-keeping, not the conflict guard; a cancelled row stays for history instead of being deleted, and the overlap check simply excludes it.
  • RecurrenceRule (frequency, interval, end_condition) — e.g. "every Monday until Dec 31."
3
API

POST /rooms/{id}/bookings {start, end, recurrence_rule?} → booking id, or 409 with the conflicting slot
GET /rooms/{id}/availability?from&to → free/busy blocks for one room
GET /rooms/available?from&to&capacity_min?&location? → every free room matching the filters, sorted by capacity
DELETE /bookings/{id}?scope=single|series → cancels one occurrence or the whole series

4
Data Flow

Skipped — this is synchronous request/response, same reasoning as the URL shortener and rate limiter. Recurring-meeting expansion is a real design question, but it's answered as a storage strategy in the deep dive below, not a pipeline.

5
High-Level Design

Every booking attempt passes through the same overlap check before it's allowed to write — diagrammed below.

6
Deep Dives

Three below: (a) efficient overlap detection, (b) storing recurring meetings, and (c) time zones.

Check-then-write, same shape as Ticketmaster's hold — the correctness question is identical, the stakes and scale aren't
← scroll to see the full diagram →
Book a meeting
  1. Client requests a room for a time range.
  2. Booking Service asks the Availability Checker whether any existing booking in that room overlaps the range.
  3. No conflict found — Booking Service performs an atomic conditional write to the Bookings DB.
  4. Booking confirmed, returned to the client.
Handle a conflict
  1. Client requests a room for a time range.
  2. Availability Checker finds an existing overlapping booking.
  3. Booking Service returns a 409 with the conflicting slot — no write occurs.
  4. Client retries with a different time or room; nothing needed to be rolled back, since nothing was written.
Key deep dive — efficient overlap detection
FRBook a roomFRCheck availabilityFRSearch available roomsNFRNever double-bookNFRFast overlap checksNFRRoom search stays one query
Thought process
  1. Write down the overlap condition precisely: two ranges conflict when each one starts before the other ends. A simple comparison — not the hard part of this problem.
  2. Test the naive way to use that comparison: check a new booking against every existing booking in the room. Ask what happens as a room's calendar fills up — the check gets slower with every booking added.
  3. Narrow the search before comparing: an index on room and start time means only bookings anywhere near the requested window even get looked at. This is enough for almost every room.
  4. Ask what "almost every room" leaves out: a genuinely high-traffic room's calendar is still large even indexed, and every check still costs a database round trip. For that specific case, skip the database at read time entirely.
  5. Notice a fast single-room check doesn't answer a different question: "which of N rooms are free" isn't "run the single-room check N times" — it's the same predicate, expressed as one query instead of N.
  6. Realize none of the above touches correctness under concurrent writes: a fast, correct read can still race against another booking's write — a separate problem, needing its own fix.
The full journey — from search to a confirmed booking
  1. Search: the user asks for any free room matching a time and a filter (capacity, location). Read-only — no conflict is possible yet, since nothing has been claimed. Scales as one anti-join query across every room, not one check per room. Detailed below.
  2. Pick: the user selects one specific room and slot from the results and clicks "Book." This is the exact moment a race becomes possible — another user could have searched a second earlier and be about to pick the same slot. A UI action, not a mechanism — no dedicated section below.
  3. Check: the Booking Service asks "does anything on this one room overlap this range" — fast, via an index or a database constraint's own index. This step only makes the question fast; it does not, by itself, prevent anything on its own. Detailed below, together with write — they're one decision, not two.
  4. Write: the actual prevention happens here, and only here — one of two complete paths depending on what your database supports. Detailed below.
  5. Resolve: exactly one booker's write succeeds. The other needs a real answer, not a stack trace. Detailed below — and it reuses step 1's exact query, no new mechanism required.

Check makes "is this free" fast; write is the only step that actually stops two people from getting the same slot — worth keeping those two questions separate while designing this, even though the section below covers them together, since which check you use determines which write mechanism you need.

Two ranges [s1, e1) and [s2, e2) overlap exactly when s1 < e2 AND s2 < e1 — a simple comparison, the building block every step below is built on.

Illustration — the overlap condition itself
Existing: [10:00, 11:00)
New request: [10:30, 11:30)
overlap
10:0010:3011:0011:30

10:00 < 11:30 AND 10:30 < 11:00

true → conflict

Worth heading off directly: why not a status column on Room, the way Ticketmaster flags a seat Available or Held? A seat has exactly one state at a time — the column is the answer. A room is free at 9am, booked at 10, free again at 2 — one column on the room can't hold that. Booking does get a status (Confirmed/Cancelled, added to Core Entities above), but it's record-keeping, not the conflict guard: the check is never "does a row exist with this status," it's "does any row's range overlap this one" — the same range comparison above, status column or not. A cancelled booking just gets excluded from that check with one added clause, not a different mechanism.

Step 1 — search: the same predicate, as an anti-join

"Is this one room free" is a single query; "which of N rooms are free" doesn't mean running that query N times.

One query — rooms with no matching row in an overlap subquery, filtered by capacity or location — answers it in a single pass, against the exact same (room_id, start_time) index and the same materialized near-term bookings the recurring-meetings strategy below already produces.

Illustration — one query, not one check per room
SELECT room.id FROM rooms room
WHERE room.capacity >= 6 AND room.location = 'floor-3'
AND NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM bookings b
  WHERE b.room_id = room.id
    AND b.start_time < :to AND b.end_time > :from
)

every matching free room, in one round trip — not N overlap checks for N rooms

Step 2 — the user picking one room and clicking "Book" — sits between here and the next section. It's a UI action, not a mechanism, so nothing to design; the walkthrough below picks back up at check and write.

Steps 3 & 4 — check and write: one fork, not six options

These were named as separate steps above, but "how do we check fast" and "how do we prevent a conflict" aren't independent choices — which one you use for the check determines what you need for the write. It's one fork, then one complete path to follow, not a checklist of every technique.

The fork

Does your database support a native exclusion constraint for overlapping ranges (Postgres's EXCLUDE, or an equivalent)?

Yes → Path A

One constraint on the table. Done — no separate index for this query, no SERIALIZABLE, no lock. The database is the whole guarantee.

No → Path B

An index for the fast check, a conditional insert for the write, and one guard (SERIALIZABLE or a lock) wrapped around it — three pieces, working together.

Either path, optionally: layer an in-process tree on top for one genuinely hot room — that part is the same regardless of which path you're on, detailed at the end.

Path A — the EXCLUDE constraint (recommended, on Postgres)

A database-enforced rule: no two bookings for the same room may have overlapping ranges. Its own index handles the fast check too — this is the entire path, nothing else in this deep dive needs to be added on top of it.

Illustration — the constraint, and the ordinary insert it protects
CREATE TABLE bookings (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  room_id INT NOT NULL,
  during TSRANGE NOT NULL,
  EXCLUDE USING GIST (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&)
);
The write is a completely ordinary insert — no WHERE, no NOT EXISTS:
INSERT INTO bookings (room_id, during)
VALUES (:room_id, tsrange(:start, :end));

If a row already exists for this room whose "during" range overlaps — Postgres REJECTS the insert outright, atomically, at the storage engine level. No SERIALIZABLE isolation, no lock required — the guarantee is built into the schema, enforced the same way a UNIQUE constraint is.

Two bookers, same slot, same instant: one INSERT succeeds, the other fails with a constraint violation — the database decided who won, not the app.

Why this is the recommendation, not just one option among several: it protects you even if a future developer writes a careless query, since the guarantee lives in the table, not in any one statement someone has to remember to write correctly every time.

Path B — index, conditional insert, and a guard (when EXCLUDE isn't available)

Three pieces that only work together — an index makes the check fast, a conditional insert bundles the check into the write, and one guard closes the race the conditional insert alone can't.

1 — the index
Illustration — the B-tree index, and the query it speeds up
CREATE INDEX idx_bookings_room_start ON bookings (room_id, start_time);

SELECT 1 FROM bookings
WHERE room_id = :room_id
  AND start_time < :end
  AND end_time > :start;

the index narrows this to rows for the right room, near the right time — fast, but still just a SELECT.

Two concurrent transactions can both run it, both see zero rows, and both then insert. The index makes the check fast; it does nothing to prevent the race below.

2 — the conditional insert

Ticketmaster's fix doesn't transfer as-is: a seat is one row with one status flag — a single conditional UPDATE is enough. A room's calendar has no single row to flip, so the check-across-many-rows and the insert have to happen as one atomic step — the pattern commonly called a conditional insert, the insert-side counterpart to Ticketmaster's conditional update.

Illustration — INSERT … WHERE NOT EXISTS
INSERT INTO bookings (room_id, start_time, end_time, organizer_id)
SELECT :room_id, :start, :end, :organizer_id
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM bookings
  WHERE room_id = :room_id
    AND start_time < :end AND end_time > :start
);

one statement: the check and the insert happen together, not two round trips

Still not automatically safe on its own — a building block, not the complete guarantee. At the commonly-default READ COMMITTED isolation level, two concurrent transactions can both evaluate NOT EXISTS against the same pre-insert snapshot, both see "nothing conflicts," and both insert. Piece 3 is what actually closes this.

3 — the guard: pick exactly one
Illustration — the race this guard closes
Booker A: checks [10:30, 11:30) → free
Booker B: checks [10:30, 11:30) → free(both pass the check)
Booker A: writes the booking
Booker B: writes the booking
  • double-booked, same room, same slot
SERIALIZABLE isolation — optimistic

Run the conditional insert inside a transaction at SERIALIZABLE isolation. Neither booker locks anything upfront — both proceed as if uncontended, and the database catches the real conflict at commit time, aborting one.

  • No explicit locking code — the database enforces it.
  • The loser gets a serialization error and has to retry, which the app must handle.
  • Costs more under real contention.
An explicit lock — pessimistic

Acquire a lock scoped to the room before the check-and-insert, held until the transaction ends — assume contention and prevent it upfront. Two ways to take it, below.

  • Only bookers on the same room ever wait on each other.
  • Simpler to reason about — the second booker just waits its turn.
  • Must be released on every code path, including a crash, or it becomes its own outage.

Why not a Redis lock instead of either of these? Because the lock and the write it protects would live in two separate systems — if the app crashes between acquiring a Redis lock and committing to Postgres, the lock needs a TTL to self-clean, and that TTL becomes its own tuning problem. Both mechanisms above live inside the same transaction as the write — Postgres releases the lock automatically the instant that transaction ends, crash or not, with nothing to tune. Redis earns its place coordinating something that spans more than one database transaction, not for guarding one insert Postgres can already guard for free.

Two ways to take that lock
Advisory lock — an arbitrary token

pg_advisory_xact_lock(room_id) — Postgres-specific. Locks a number that means "room 101" only by convention; works against any schema, needs no existing row to lock.

SELECT ... FOR UPDATE — the actual row

Standard SQL, portable beyond Postgres. Locks a real row in the rooms table — the thing the contention is actually about, not a synthetic hash standing in for it.

Illustration — the advisory lock, traced across two bookers
BEGIN;
SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(:room_id);   -- acquire FIRST, before checking
INSERT INTO bookings (room_id, start_time, end_time, organizer_id)
SELECT :room_id, :start, :end, :organizer_id
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM bookings
  WHERE room_id = :room_id AND start_time < :end AND end_time > :start
);
COMMIT;  -- lock releases automatically, tied to the transaction
  1. Booker A

    BEGIN → lock(101) acquires instantly → check+insert → COMMIT (released)

  2. Booker B

    BEGIN → lock(101) BLOCKS, waiting — B's query hasn't even run yet

  3. ...the moment A commits...
  4. Booker B, resumed

    B's lock acquires → check+insert now correctly sees A's booking

    0 rows affected → app tells B "someone got it first"

B never raced A — B's check didn't start until A's transaction had already finished. That's the actual difference from SERIALIZABLE: the lock prevents the interleaving, rather than catching it afterward.

Caveat: pg_advisory_xact_lock takes a bigint, so a UUID/string room_id is hashed down first — a hash collision means two different rooms could occasionally, harmlessly wait on each other.

Illustration — SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, catching a deleted or mistyped room_id for free
BEGIN;
SELECT 1 FROM rooms WHERE id = :room_id FOR UPDATE;   -- lock the real row
-- if that returned 0 rows, room_id doesn't exist — caught right here,
-- in the same round trip that acquired the lock. Bail out before ever
-- attempting the insert.

INSERT INTO bookings (room_id, start_time, end_time, organizer_id)
SELECT :room_id, :start, :end, :organizer_id
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM bookings
  WHERE room_id = :room_id AND start_time < :end AND end_time > :start
);
COMMIT;
pg_advisory_xact_lock

has no such signal — it "succeeds" and grants a lock even for a room_id that was deleted or never existed, since it's locking an arbitrary number, not checking against any row.

FOR UPDATE

can't grant a lock on a row that isn't there, so the existence check comes free.

Between the two locks, concretely: FOR UPDATE if you need this to run on a non-Postgres database too, or you want a deleted/mistyped room_id caught in the same round trip that acquires the lock, instead of a silent no-op. The advisory lock if what you're protecting isn't tied to one row at all — locking a whole floor for a bulk operation, or a business rule keyed on something that spans tables — where there's no single row to lock against in the first place. A plain UNIQUE constraint on (room_id, start_time) is worth adding either way, as a cheap backstop against the exact-duplicate case — the same room, the same exact start time, submitted twice. It won't catch a genuine partial overlap (10:00–11:00 against 10:30–11:30) the way EXCLUDE does — a narrower guarantee, but one available on databases that don't support range exclusion at all.

Escalation — an in-process tree, on top of either path

Not a third path — an optional speed layer for one genuinely hot room (a popular shared space, an all-hands room), sitting in front of whichever path above is doing the actual guaranteeing.

Illustration — the tree speeds up the check; the path above still does the guaranteeing

New booking request, handled by the Booking Service instance that owns this room:

  1. Acquire an in-process lock scoped to this one room_id(a mutex inside THIS process — not a database lock, not Redis)
  2. tree.overlaps(start, end) → true/false← the fast, local check
  3. If false: INSERT into the database (still protected by Path A or Path B above, as the real backstop) AND insert into the tree
  4. Release the lock

The tree makes step 2 fast by skipping a database round trip — it doesn't, by itself, stop two requests on the SAME instance from both reaching step 2 before either finishes step 3. The in-process lock prevents that; the tree just makes the thing being guarded cheap to check.

One requirement this creates, easy to miss:

if multiple Booking Service instances sit behind a load balancer, this room's bookings must always route to the SAME instance — otherwise each instance holds a different, incomplete view of its calendar, and the in-process lock only protects against other requests on the same instance. The same partition-by-key discipline as the price alert system pinning BBCA to one Detector instance, applied here to a room.

Step 5 — resolve: what the loser actually sees

Every mechanism above produces exactly one outcome for the losing request: a failure. What happens next is a real product decision, not an afterthought — a bare 500 or a generic "booking failed" is a worse experience than the race itself.

Illustration — a specific, actionable failure, not a stack trace

Booker B's write fails (constraint violation, or a serialization error):

Bad
500 Internal Server Error
Good
409 Conflict
{ "reason": "room_already_booked", "conflicting_slot": ["10:30","11:30"] }

The response tells B exactly what happened and why — not just that "something" went wrong.

The genuinely good version doesn't stop at explaining the failure — it immediately re-runs step 1's exact anti-join query, scoped to the same time window and filters B already searched with, and returns what's still available. No new mechanism required: the same query that found B a room the first time finds B an alternative the second.

Illustration — closing the loop back to step 1

409 response, extended:

{ "reason": "room_already_booked",
  "conflicting_slot": ["10:30","11:30"],
  "alternatives": [ /* step 1's search, re-run automatically */ ] }

B never has to manually start over — the system already knows what else is free.

Key deep dive — storing recurring meetings
FRRecurring meetingsFRCancel/modify a single occurrenceNFRNo pre-generating years of instances
Thought process
  1. Consider the simplest option: generate every future occurrence the moment the series is created. Test it against "forever" — a weekly meeting with no end date means either an arbitrary cutoff or unbounded storage.
  2. Consider the opposite extreme: store only the rule, compute occurrences on the fly whenever someone asks. Test it against the common case — now every availability check does that computation, every single time.
  3. Notice neither extreme is right on its own — one wastes storage on meetings nobody will query yet, the other repeats the same computation on every read.
  4. Split the difference deliberately: materialize a bounded near-term window for fast, simple queries, and only compute on demand for anything further out.
  • Materialize on write: generate every instance of the series up front. Simple to query, but wasteful — a weekly meeting "forever" means either an arbitrary cutoff or unbounded storage, and changing the series means rewriting every future instance.
  • Expand on read: store just the rule, compute instances when a range is queried. Cheap to store, but every availability check now does more work, and modifying or canceling a single occurrence needs an "exception" record layered on top of the rule — either "this date is cancelled" or "this date is rescheduled to X" — rather than a row to simply edit or delete.

Most real systems land on a hybrid: materialize a bounded near-term window (say, the next 90 days) for fast queries, and expand on demand beyond that — the same instinct as the crawler's priority scoring, spending effort where it's actually needed.

Key deep dive — time zones
NFRNever double-book
Thought process
  1. State the requirement the way someone would actually phrase it: "book the 2pm slot." Notice that's ambiguous the moment more than one office exists.
  2. Trace what happens if a bare local time gets stored as-is — the overlap check from the earlier deep dive assumes two comparable ranges, and "2pm New York" and "2pm London" aren't comparable at all without a shared reference.
  3. Fix it at the source, not at display: store every timestamp in one absolute format, and only convert for a human to read — never before a comparison runs.
  4. Check for the sharp edge case this doesn't automatically solve: daylight saving shifts a recurring meeting's UTC time twice a year, so the recurrence expansion has to account for that explicitly, not just repeat a raw time-of-day.

"Book the 2pm slot" means something different in every office once a company has more than one, and a design that stores a bare local time will silently double-book or show the wrong availability the moment someone in a different time zone looks at the same room.

Illustration — always store UTC
"2pm Monday, New York office"→ stored as →2026-03-02T19:00:00Z
"2pm Monday, London office"→ stored as →2026-03-02T14:00:00Z
  • Store every booking's start/end in UTC, always — never let a "local time" be the source of truth. Convert to the viewer's or the room's local time only at display time, never before the overlap check runs.
  • Daylight saving is the sharpest edge case: a recurring "every Monday at 9am" meeting can shift by an hour relative to UTC twice a year, which the Recurring Expander needs to account for when generating instances — not just the raw time-of-day.

The overlap-detection math from the earlier deep dive assumes two comparable ranges — time zone bugs are almost always this assumption quietly breaking, not the comparison itself being wrong.

Does it hold up?

Non-functional requirementHow this design satisfies it
Never double-book a roomAtomic conditional write gated by the overlap check — same pattern as Ticketmaster's seat hold.
Fast overlap checksIndex on (room_id, start_time), or an in-process interval tree (inside the Booking Service, not Redis) for high-traffic rooms.
Searching many rooms stays one queryA single NOT EXISTS anti-join across rooms, filtered by capacity/location — not N separate per-room checks.
Recurring meetings don't require years of pre-generated rowsHybrid: materialize a near-term window, expand on demand beyond it.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Hybrid materialize-near-term + expand-on-readFast queries for the common case (near-term bookings) without unbounded storage, at the cost of maintaining two code paths and the boundary logic between them.
Anti-join search across all rooms vs. checking rooms one at a timeScales far better as room count grows and stays a single round trip, but needs a solid (room_id, start_time) index to keep the query planner honest — for a large multi-building portfolio, worth partitioning by location so a search doesn't scan rooms nobody's asking about.
In-process interval tree per room vs. database index aloneFaster for very hot rooms — no network call at all, not even to a cache — but requires that room's bookings always route to the same Booking Service instance, or different instances hold different, incomplete views of its calendar. Only worth it once a room's traffic justifies both the complexity and that routing constraint.
SERIALIZABLE isolation vs. an advisory lock per room_idSERIALIZABLE needs no explicit locking code but costs more under real contention and requires the app to handle retry-on-abort; an advisory lock is simpler to reason about (bookers on the same room just wait their turn) but must be released on every code path, including a crash mid-transaction, or it becomes its own outage for that room.
One room per meeting (assumed)A much simpler booking transaction — one row, one check — but doesn't support a meeting that genuinely needs two connected rooms, which would require an atomic multi-row transaction if added.

Worked Example I — Read Scalability at Scale

Search Invoices Across 30+ Products

CQRS · async indexing · federated data, unified reads
Click to expand

"A company has 30+ separate product lines, each with its own invoicing service and database. Users subscribe to a subset of these products — one user might follow 10, another 5 — and should only ever search invoices from products they're actually subscribed to. Build one search box: type something like an invoice number, and see matching invoices grouped by which subscribed product each one belongs to." A pure read-scalability problem, plus a real access-control constraint that has to be baked into the design, not bolted on after.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • One free-text search box — type something like an invoice number or customer name, no separate filter fields required to get a result.
  • Results only ever include products the querying user is subscribed to — a different user with a different subscription set sees different results for the identical query.
  • Products the user previously subscribed to still surface in results — tagged as no-longer-active — rather than disappearing from search the moment access ends.
  • Results are grouped by product — the user sees "Product A: 3 matches, Product C: 1 match," not one flat undifferentiated list.
  • Each product line keeps owning its own invoice writes independently.
Non-functional
  • Search stays fast as product count and invoice volume both grow.
  • Search must not add latency or coupling to the 30+ product services' write paths.
  • A subscription change (gaining or losing access to a product) must take effect immediately, not after some indexing delay.
  • Search results need to be reasonably fresh, not necessarily instant.

Worth asking: should the query match partial or fuzzy invoice numbers (e.g. "2024-0088" matching "INV-2024-0088-A1"), or exact only? We'll assume partial/prefix matching for typed-so-far input — a single search box is only actually useful if the user doesn't have to type the exact full string. Genuine typos (a transposed prefix like "vin-" for "inv-") are a related but separate case — see the Caching Playbook for the fuzzy-fallback approach and why it's kept out of the primary result set.

2
Core Entities
  • Invoice (id, product_id, customer_id, amount, issued_at, status) — owned and written by each product's own service; the source of truth stays scattered on purpose.
  • SearchDocument (invoice fields, denormalized, product_name) — a read-optimized copy living in the search index, carrying enough context to group results by product at display time.
  • Subscription (user_id, product_id, subscribed_at, unsubscribed_at) — the access-control source of truth. A row is closed out on unsubscribe, never deleted, so the system can tell "never subscribed" from "used to be."
  • IndexEvent (invoice_id, product_id, change_type) — emitted whenever an invoice is created or changed, the only thing connecting write side to read side.
3
API

GET /invoices/search?q=INV-2024-0088 → authenticated call, results grouped by product and pre-filtered to the caller's subscribed products. Each product's own invoice CRUD API is unchanged and out of scope — this system only adds a read path, never touches how products write.

Illustration — same query, different users
user_42 subscribes to:
Product AProduct CProduct K
user_77 subscribes to:
Product AProduct F
q = "INV-2024-0088" (for user_42)

result:

Product AINV-2024-0088-A1Acme Corp$1,240
Product CINV-2024-0088-C7Acme Corp$860
Product KINV-2024-0088-K2Beta LLC$2,010
q = "INV-2024-0088" (for user_77, same query)

result:

Product AINV-2024-0088-A1Acme Corp$1,240

(Product C and K matches exist, but user_77 never sees them)

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. Each product's invoice database emits a change event whenever an invoice is created or updated.
  2. Events from all 30+ products land on one shared Event Stream.
  3. An Indexer consumes the stream and writes a denormalized copy — including product name — into the Search Index.
  4. The read path never touches the 30+ source databases — only the one shared index — and separately consults Subscriptions to know which products a given caller may see.
5
High-Level Design

Write side and read side are fully separate systems, connected only by an async event stream — diagrammed below.

6
Deep Dives

Five below: (a) why not query all 30+ databases live, (b) keeping the index fresh without coupling to the source, (c) enforcing subscriptions on every query, (d) what to cache — and what never to, and (e) the index itself: partial matches, grouping and scale.

Write side (30+ independently-owned services) and read side (one shared index) meet only at the event stream — never at query time. Every query carries the caller's subscription filter into the index — results are never fetched first and filtered afterwards, and nothing unfiltered is cached.
← scroll to see the full diagram →
Write path (per product, unchanged)
  1. A product's invoice service creates or updates an invoice in its own database, exactly as it always has.
  2. That change reaches the shared Event Stream through an outbox row written in the same transaction (or CDC on the database log), keyed by invoice id — the only new thing each product team has to do.
  3. The product's own service never waits on search, never calls it, never knows it exists.
Read path (search)
  1. The client sends the typed text after a ~200 ms pause, once there are at least 3 characters, and cancels any earlier request still in flight.
  2. The Search Service reads the caller's product set — every product they subscribe to now, plus lapsed ones with the date access ended — from a per-user Redis entry that is deleted whenever a subscription changes, falling back to the Subscriptions table.
  3. It sends one query to the Search Index: the text as prefix tokens, and a filter of those products (for a lapsed product, only invoices issued before access ended). The engine caches each product filter and reuses it for every user.
  4. The same query groups by product: the top 3 invoices and a count per product, so one large product can't crowd out the rest.
  5. The service tags each group Active or "subscription ended", and the client shows the groups. Nothing it receives was ever outside the caller's access.
Key deep dive — why not query all 30+ databases live
FRResults grouped by productFRProducts keep owning writesNFRNo coupling to write paths
Thought process
  1. Start with the most direct-sounding idea: fan a search request out to all 30+ product databases and merge whatever comes back.
  2. Trace what happens to latency: the response can only be as fast as the slowest of 30+ independent calls — with that many in flight, something is always slow.
  3. Trace what happens to ownership: each product team now has to build and maintain search capability on their own schema, for a use case they don't actually own.
  4. Realize the fix isn't "make the fan-out faster" — it's not fanning out at query time at all. Separate the write side (30+ databases, unchanged) from a single purpose-built read copy that every search hits instead.

The naive approach — fan a search request out to all 30+ product databases and merge the results — fails for reasons that compound as the product count grows.

  • Tail latency amplification: the response is only as fast as the slowest of 30+ services on that request — with enough independent calls, something is always slow.
  • Permanent coupling: each product team now has to expose and maintain ad hoc search/filter capability on their own schema, for a use case they don't own.
  • Schema fragmentation: 30+ teams' slightly different ideas of "customer" or "amount" turn a simple query into a fragile integration problem, repeated 30+ times.
  • Grouping gets hard too: merging and grouping 30+ separate, differently-shaped result sets into one "Product A / Product B / …" view is real work, done on every single search.

The fix is CQRS: separate the write model (30+ independently-owned databases) from the read model (one denormalized, purpose-built search index). Reads never touch the write side at query time — and since every product's data already lives in the same index with the same shape, grouping by product is a trivial reshape of one result set, not a live merge of 30+.

Illustration — thirty live calls against one index
Key deep dive — keeping the index fresh without coupling to the source
NFRNo coupling to write pathsNFRReasonably fresh resultsNFRSearch stays fast at scale
Thought process
  1. Given the read side is now a separate copy, ask the obvious follow-up: how does it ever find out about a new or changed invoice?
  2. Reject the direct-call option first: if the Indexer called each product service directly, a slow or down Indexer would now be able to block someone else's invoice write — exactly the coupling CQRS was meant to remove.
  3. Decouple the two sides properly: producers publish what happened, a consumer picks it up on its own schedule — neither side waits on the other.
  4. Choose how the "what happened" gets published: either read it straight from each database's own change log (CDC), or have each service explicitly emit an event — both land on one shared stream either way.

Change Data Capture (CDC) reads each product database's write-ahead log directly, or each product service explicitly publishes an event on every invoice change — either way, changes land on one shared event stream that the Indexer consumes to keep the Search Index current.

  • Same idea as a message queue: producers (30+ product services) and the consumer (the Indexer) never call each other directly, so a slow or down Indexer doesn't block anyone's invoice writes.
  • Schema freedom: a product team can change their own internal schema freely, as long as the event contract stays the same.
  • Freshness, not caching, is this dive's job. A result cache sits in front of a copy that is already seconds behind, so it can only add staleness; deep dive (d) shows why this design caches entitlements and filters, not search results.
Illustration — from an invoice write to a searchable document
Key deep dive — enforcing subscriptions on every query
FROnly subscribed products in resultsFRLapsed subscriptions still findableNFRSubscription changes take effect immediately
Thought process
  1. Start with the real question: where does the subscription filter go — inside the search, or after it?
  2. Try it after: the index returns its top 100 across all 30 products, then the service drops what the caller can't see. Tested on 300,000 invoices where one product holds 40%, for a user on three small products: 181 of 340 queries showed nothing though matches existed, and 191 showed fewer than exist — the big product filled the top 100.
  3. The reason given for filtering afterwards was to keep one cached result per query text for everyone. That buys little and costs a lot: the full unfiltered set for "INV-2024" is 100,221 invoices, a truncated one loses matches, and either way a shared cache holds every product's invoices for every user — one filter bug and they leak.
  4. So put the filter in the query, in filter context: product ∈ the caller's products, and for a lapsed product only invoices issued before access ended. Ranking, limits and grouping then see only what the caller may see — 0 wrong in the same test, at 0.288 ms median. The engine caches each product's filter as a bitset and reuses it across users, so filtering in the query is the cheap path, not the expensive one.

Different users subscribe to different subsets of the 30+ products, a subscription change has to take effect immediately, and losing access to a product shouldn't erase the ability to find invoices from when access was active — all while the search cache itself has to stay shared, not per-user, or it collapses under real traffic (see the Caching Playbook).

  • Filter inside the query — on purpose: the subscription filter is part of the search, so the result is correct by construction, other products' invoices never leave the index, and the per-product filters are cached by the engine and shared by every user. Two users typing the same text get different results — which is exactly the requirement.
  • Tag status after filtering, not instead of it: for each product in the results, a null unsubscribed_at means "Active"; a set one means "Subscription ended [date]" — and the filter already limited that product to invoices issued before the date. The tag is a label on an already-permitted result, not a second access check.
  • The user's product set comes from a cache that is deleted on change: the Subscription service deletes the user's Redis entry when a subscription starts or ends (a short TTL is only a safety net), and a miss reads the Subscriptions table. A TTL alone would let a removed product stay visible until it expired — the requirement says immediately.
Illustration — lapsed subscription, still findable, clearly tagged
user_42's subscriptions:
Product Asubscribed 2025-11-01, unsubscribed 2026-01-15(lapsed)
Product Bsubscribed 2025-11-01active
Product Csubscribed 2026-01-01active
q = "INV-2024-0088" result:
Product B[Active]INV-2024-0088-B3Acme Corp$980
Product C[Active]INV-2024-0088-C7Acme Corp$860
Product A[Subscription ended 2026-01-15]INV-2024-0088-A1Acme Corp$1,240

This is a deliberate product decision, not a default — "unsubscribe" here means "stop seeing new activity from," not "revoke my own history." A system where that distinction matters for compliance or security should make it explicit, not inherit whichever reading was easiest to build.

Illustration — where the filter goes decides what the user sees
Illustration — what the filter tests measured
ApproachResult
post-filter a shared top 100 (340 queries, user on 3 small products)181 showed nothing though matches existed · 191 showed fewer than exist
filter inside the query0 wrong · median 0.288 ms · p99 0.644 ms
caching the whole unfiltered set for "INV-2024"100,221 invoices · 8.7 ms to fetch

tantivy (a Lucene-family engine, the same model as OpenSearch) on one core: 300,000 invoices, 30 products, one product holding 40%.

Key deep dive — what to cache, and what never to
NFRResults are always correct for the callerNFRAccess changes apply on the next search
Thought process
  1. Caching is decided per layer, by asking what is shared, what changes and what a stale copy would cost. Four layers here, and one thing that is never cached (diagram below).
  2. The client is the first cache. Search-as-you-type sends a query per keystroke — 14.2 per invoice number in a simulation of 4,000 searches. A ~200 ms debounce, a 3-character minimum and cancelling stale requests cut that to 3.0 — the biggest saving in the whole read path, and it costs nothing.
  3. Entitlements are cached, with deletion on change. Every search needs the caller's product set; it is small, read constantly and changed rarely — the ideal cache entry. The Subscription service deletes the entry when anything changes, so the next search sees it.
  4. The engine caches filters, not you. OpenSearch and Lucene keep frequently used filter clauses as bitsets; with the filter written per product, the bitset for product A serves every user who can see A. That is the sharing the old design wanted from a result cache, without its risks.
  5. A result cache is optional, and narrow if used. Key it by the normalised query and a hash of the caller's product set, store only the top hits per product, and keep its TTL at or below the index refresh. Measured on typed queries, a shared cache would hit 36.4% of debounced queries — mostly short prefixes like "INV-2024-" — and complete invoice numbers 2.0%; the index answers a filtered top 10 in about 0.288 ms, so add it only if measured traffic shows hot queries.
  6. Never cache unfiltered results keyed by the query alone: it is wrong when truncated, huge when not, stale as invoices arrive, and it puts every product's invoices in front of every user's request.
Illustration — the cache layers, top to bottom
Key deep dive — the index itself: partial matches, grouping and scale
NFRA partial invoice number finds the invoiceNFRSearch stays fast as products and invoices grow
Thought process
  1. Partial matching is an indexing decision. Split each invoice number on its separators — INV-2024-0088-A1 becomes inv, 2024, 0088, a1 — and index the prefixes of each part. A query is split the same way and every part must match a prefix, so "2024-0088" finds the invoice, and an exact full match scores higher. Customer names use a normal text field; typos are a separate, fuzzy fallback (see the Caching Playbook).
  2. Group in the query, not afterwards. An aggregation by product_id with the top 3 hits each returns "Product A · 37 matches, Product C · 1" in one request, and a large product can't crowd the small ones out of a single ranked list. "Show all 37" is a second query filtered to that one product.
  3. Scale by shards and replicas. Size primary shards at roughly 20–50 GB, add replicas for read throughput and failover, and keep old years in cheaper read-only indexes behind one alias. Routing documents by product_id can let a query visit only the shards of the caller's products — but watch skew: a product with 40% of the invoices needs its own shards.
  4. Measure the index, not just the service: query latency per shard, indexing lag (event time to searchable), rejected bulk requests, and the filter-cache hit rate.
Illustration — tokens, grouping and scale

Does it hold up?

Non-functional requirementHow this design satisfies it
Read scalability as products growNew products just emit events into the same stream — the query path and index schema don't change shape as product count grows.
Search stays fastOne denormalized, purpose-built index instead of live scatter-gather across 30+ heterogeneous databases.
No coupling to 30+ write-side schemasThe event contract is the only integration point — product teams keep full ownership of their own database internals.
Reasonable freshnessAsync indexing lag measured in seconds, matching the stated requirement rather than over-engineering real-time sync.
Aggregated, grouped resultsEvery product's invoices already share one schema in one index — grouping by product happens inside the same query (top hits and a count per product), not as a live merge of 30+.
Subscription changes take effect immediatelyThe subscription filter is part of every query, and the caller's product set comes from a cache entry deleted the moment a subscription changes — the next search sees it, with no reindex.
Historical access preserved, clearly distinguishedSubscription rows are closed out (unsubscribed_at set), never deleted — past access stays searchable and tagged separately from active access.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
CQRS (separate read/write models) vs. one shared databaseThe read side scales independently with zero coupling to 30+ write schemas, but search results are now eventually consistent — lagging real invoices by seconds — and there are two systems to operate instead of one.
CDC vs. application-level explicit eventsCDC requires no code change from product teams, but needs infrastructure access to each database's write-ahead log; explicit events are simpler to reason about, but every product team must remember to emit them correctly.
One shared search index vs. per-product indices + a federated query layerOne schema and trivial cross-product grouping, at the cost of a bigger blast radius — the whole search experience degrades if that one index has a problem, and a schema change affects every product's data at once.
Query-time subscription filtering vs. index-time ACL taggingQuery-time makes access changes effective immediately with no reindex, at the cost of an extra (cached) lookup on every search; baking permissions into each document at index time avoids that lookup, but a user who just lost access keeps seeing results until the affected documents are reindexed.
Surfacing lapsed subscriptions (tagged) vs. a hard cutoff on unsubscribePreserves a user's ability to reference their own history, at the cost of a broader exposure surface over time — "unsubscribed" no longer means "invisible," which has to be an explicit choice for any system where losing access is meant to fully revoke visibility.
Subscription filter inside the query vs. a shared result cache filtered afterwardsCorrect results, no other products' data in flight, and engine-cached filters shared by every user — at the cost of giving up one cached result per query text, which in this workload saves less than a network hop.

Indexera Kafka consumer service, or Kafka Connect
Search IndexElasticsearch, OpenSearch
CachesRedis for each user's product set (deleted on change); the search engine's own filter cache; an optional, narrow result cache only if measured
SubscriptionsPostgreSQL as source of truth, Redis for the cached user_id → product_ids lookup
Worked Example J — Fan-out at Uneven Scale

Design a News Feed

fan-out-on-write vs. fan-out-on-read · the celebrity problem
Click to expand

"Design a system where a user posts content, and anyone following them sees it in their home feed." A read-heavy, write-light system on the surface — but the follower graph is wildly uneven: most accounts have a few hundred followers, a handful have tens of millions. Any design that assumes uniform fan-out breaks on that handful.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Post content (text, optionally media) to your own timeline.
  • Follow and unfollow other users.
  • View a home feed — a merged, reverse-chronological stream of posts from everyone you follow.
  • Paginate through the feed without seeing duplicate or missing posts as new content arrives while scrolling.
Non-functional
  • Feed loads fast (low hundreds of ms) even for a user following thousands of accounts.
  • Posting must not get slower or block based on how many followers the poster has — a celebrity's post can't take minutes to "finish."
  • New posts should reach followers' feeds within seconds, not necessarily instantly.
  • Storage for materialized feeds can't grow without bound per user.

Worth asking: strictly reverse-chronological, or ranked/algorithmic? We'll design for chronological — ranking is a scoring function bolted onto the same pipeline, not a different architecture.

2
Core Entities
  • User (id, username, follower_count) — follower_count is the single number that decides which fan-out path a post takes.
  • Follow (follower_id, followee_id) — the graph edge; who follows whom.
  • Post (id, author_id, content, created_at) — the source of truth for content, written once.
  • Timeline entry (user_id, post_id, created_at) — a materialized, pre-computed row in one follower's feed; this is what fan-out-on-write actually writes.
3
API

POST /posts {content} → post id
POST /follows {followee_id} → follow relationship created
GET /feed?cursor → a page of posts for the caller's home feed, oldest-shown-first cursor for stable pagination

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. A post is written once to the Posts table — the source of truth, regardless of the author's follower count.
  2. A "new post" event is published — the write path never waits on what happens next.
  3. A Fan-out Worker consumes the event and checks the author's follower_count against a threshold.
  4. Below the threshold: write a Timeline entry into every follower's materialized feed — the normal, common case.
  5. Above the threshold: skip fan-out entirely. The post is discoverable only by the read path checking "posts from accounts I follow with a high follower count" directly, at read time.
5
High-Level Design

Two fan-out paths diverge right after the post is written, based on one number — diagrammed and walked through below.

6
Deep Dives

Three below: (a) fan-out-on-write vs. fan-out-on-read and the celebrity problem, (b) keeping the materialized timeline bounded, and (c) pagination that stays correct while new posts keep arriving.

Every post lands in Posts DB the same way — what diverges is fan-out. Below the follower threshold, the Fan-out Worker writes into every follower's Timeline Store. Above it, nothing is written; the Feed Service checks that author directly at read time instead.
Write path (post)
  1. Author posts; Post Service writes it to Posts DB and publishes a "new post" event — the write returns immediately, before any fan-out happens.
  2. The Fan-out Worker consumes the event and checks the author's follower_count against a fixed threshold (say, 10,000).
  3. Below the threshold: look up every follower from the Follow Graph and write a Timeline entry into each of their materialized feeds.
  4. Above the threshold: do nothing further — the post is discoverable only through the read path's live check.
Read path (feed)
  1. Follower opens the app; Feed Service reads that follower's materialized Timeline Store — already sorted, a fast lookup.
  2. Separately, it checks whether the follower follows any high-follower-count accounts, and if so, queries their recent posts from Posts DB directly.
  3. The two result sets are merged by timestamp into one reverse-chronological page.
  4. A cursor based on the oldest post shown is returned, so the next page picks up exactly where this one left off — even if new posts arrived in between.
Key deep dive — fan-out-on-write vs. fan-out-on-read, and the celebrity problem
FRView home feedNFRFeed loads fastNFRPosting isn't follower-count-dependent
Thought process
  1. Start with the option that makes reads trivially fast: precompute every user's feed at post time, so a read is just "fetch my already-built list."
  2. Stress-test it against the extreme case: an account with 50 million followers posts. That's 50 million writes triggered by one action — the post "hangs" while fan-out grinds through a queue, or the write path itself gets dragged into that cost.
  3. Try the opposite extreme instead: don't precompute anything, merge the feed live from everyone the reader follows at read time. Test it against the common case — a normal user following 300 accounts now does a 300-way merge on every single feed load.
  4. Notice neither extreme is right for both kinds of accounts, because the actual variable is follower count, which spans many orders of magnitude. Split the strategy by that number instead of picking one for everyone.

The two pure strategies are each right for a different, common case — the fix is choosing per-author, not picking one architecture for the whole system.

  • Fan-out-on-write (push): write a Timeline entry to every follower's feed the moment someone posts. Reads become a single fast lookup — the cost is paid once, at write time, and shared across every future read of that feed.
  • Fan-out-on-read (pull): store nothing extra; merge posts from followed accounts live, at read time. Writes stay cheap and instant regardless of follower count — the cost is paid on every single read instead.
  • The hybrid: fan-out-on-write for accounts under a follower threshold (the overwhelming majority), fan-out-on-read for the small number above it. A normal user's feed is a fast Timeline Store lookup; a celebrity's posts are picked up live by the read path, merged in only for the followers actually reading their feed right now.

This is the same instinct as Uber's location pings getting their own storage path separate from ride records — identify the one input whose scale characteristics are wildly different from everything else, and give it a different path instead of forcing one design to survive both extremes.

Key deep dive — keeping the materialized timeline bounded
NFRStorage can't grow unbounded per user
Thought process
  1. Notice fan-out-on-write has a quiet cost the read-speed win doesn't mention: every follow relationship now implies a growing set of stored rows, forever, for every active user.
  2. Ask how much of that stored history actually gets read. Almost none of it — people scroll back a few dozen or hundred posts, essentially never to the bottom of a feed that's years old.
  3. Notice the asymmetry: paying storage cost for content that's rarely if ever read is waste, not correctness.
  4. Cap it deliberately: keep only the most recent N entries materialized per user, and treat anything older as reconstructible on demand rather than permanently stored.

A Timeline Store entry exists for every (follower, post) pair from a fanned-out write — for an active user following hundreds of accounts, that's an unbounded, ever-growing list with no natural cap.

  • Cap each user's materialized timeline to the most recent N entries (a few hundred to a couple thousand) — old entries are trimmed, not kept forever.
  • Falling off the cap isn't data loss: Posts DB is still the source of truth. A user who scrolls past the materialized window falls back to a live, fan-out-on-read-style query for anything older — rare enough in practice that it doesn't need to be fast.

Same shape as the crawler's bounded storage growth — cap the common, fast path deliberately, and let the rare, slow path fall back to the source of truth instead of trying to make everything permanently fast.

Key deep dive — pagination that stays correct while new posts keep arriving
FRPaginate without duplicates/gaps
Thought process
  1. Start with the obvious pagination approach: page 1 is the first 20 rows, page 2 is the next 20, using offset and limit.
  2. Trace what happens if three new posts arrive between loading page 1 and page 2: everything shifts down by three. Page 2, requested by offset, now starts three rows earlier than the reader expects — the last three posts they already saw on page 1 repeat.
  3. Notice the real problem: an offset is a position in a list that's actively changing underneath the reader, not a stable reference to anything.
  4. Reference content instead of position: ask for "everything older than the last post I actually saw," not "whatever's at position 20 right now."

A naive offset-based page ("give me results 21–40") silently breaks the moment new posts land between two page loads — everything shifts, and the reader sees duplicates or skips posts entirely.

Illustration — offset breaks, cursor doesn't
  1. Page 1 loaded

    posts ranked 1-20 (newest first)

  2. 3 new posts arrive
Page 2 by OFFSET 20

now shows what used to be ranks 18-37

3 duplicates

Page 2 by CURSOR (oldest post_id/timestamp shown on page 1)

"give me posts older than that"

always correct, regardless of what's arrived since

  • Cursor-based pagination: the cursor is the timestamp (or id) of the last post shown, not a row count. "Older than this" is a stable reference no matter how many new posts have landed since.
  • The merged-source complication: since a page can be assembled from both the Timeline Store and a live celebrity check, the cursor has to be comparable across both — a plain timestamp works for this; an opaque per-source offset would not.

This is a narrow instance of a general rule: any paginated view over data that changes while it's being read needs a stable reference point, not a position — the same reason a database cursor scans by key, not by row number.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Fast feed loads at any follower-count scaleMaterialized Timeline Store for the common case; live merge only for the small set of high-follower accounts a reader follows.
Posting isn't slowed by follower countThe write returns immediately after publishing an event — fan-out (if any) happens asynchronously, off the critical path.
Bounded per-user storageTimeline entries capped to the most recent N; older content falls back to Posts DB on demand.
Stable pagination under concurrent writesCursor keyed on timestamp/id, not row offset — immune to new posts landing mid-scroll.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Fan-out-on-write vs. fan-out-on-readPush makes reads a single fast lookup at the cost of write amplification per follower; pull keeps writes flat at the cost of an expensive merge on every read — neither is right alone across a real follower-count distribution.
Hybrid with a fixed follower thresholdSolves the celebrity problem cleanly, but the threshold itself is a tuning knob — set it too low and too many accounts pay the read-time merge cost; too high and a large-but-not-celebrity account still causes a fan-out spike.
Capped materialized timeline vs. unbounded historyKeeps storage and fan-out cost predictable, at the cost of a slower fallback path for the rare reader who scrolls past the cap.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Event StreamKafka
Fan-out Workera Kafka consumer service, horizontally scaled
Timeline StoreRedis (sorted sets, capped per key), or Cassandra for larger retention
Posts DBPostgreSQL, DynamoDB
Follow GraphPostgreSQL for moderate scale; a graph-oriented store at very large scale
Worked Example K — Merge, Don't Reject

Design Collaborative Document Editing

operational transformation · concurrent edits, no losers
Click to expand

"Design a system where multiple people can type into the same document at the same time, and everyone converges on the same result." Every other worked example on this page solves contention the same way — one actor wins, everyone else is rejected and retries. This one is the opposite shape: two people typing in the same paragraph at the same instant both succeed, and the system's whole job is making their edits merge into something coherent, not picking a winner.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Multiple users edit the same document simultaneously; every keystroke is visible to everyone else within roughly a second.
  • Every collaborator's editor eventually shows the exact same document content — no permanent divergence.
  • A user who was offline (laptop closed, network drop) can reconnect and have their local edits merged in, not discarded.
  • Cursor position and text selection are preserved correctly for a user even while someone else's edit lands above them in the document.
Non-functional
  • Local edits feel instant — a keystroke must never wait on a round trip to the server before appearing in the typer's own editor.
  • Convergence: given the same set of edits, every client ends up with identical document content, regardless of the order edits were received in.
  • No edit is ever silently dropped, even under concurrent, conflicting edits at the same document position.
  • Reconnecting after an extended offline period doesn't require re-downloading the whole edit history.

Worth asking: rich text (bold, formatting, embedded images) or plain text? We'll design for plain text — insert/delete on a character sequence. Rich formatting is the same core algorithm with a richer operation set, not a different architecture.

2
Core Entities
  • Document (id, content, revision) — the current text and a monotonic version number; revision is what every operation is transformed against.
  • Operation (doc_id, client_id, base_revision, type, position, value) — a single insert or delete, tagged with the revision it was created against, not the revision it lands on.
  • Session (client_id, doc_id, connection_state) — one collaborator's live connection to a document.
3
API

Not a request/response API in the usual sense — a persistent connection carrying a continuous operation stream in both directions:
→ send: {type: insert|delete, position, value, base_revision} — a local edit, the moment it happens
← receive: {op, transformed_against: revision} — another collaborator's edit, already transformed to apply cleanly to this client's current state
GET /docs/{id}/snapshot → current content + revision, for a client joining or reconnecting

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. A user types; the character is applied to their local editor state immediately — before any network round trip.
  2. The edit is sent to the server as an operation tagged with the revision the client was looking at when they made it.
  3. The server transforms the incoming operation against every operation it has received since that base revision, producing a version that applies cleanly to the current server state.
  4. The transformed operation is applied to the server's document and broadcast to every other connected client, each of which transforms it again against their own local pending edits before applying it.
5
High-Level Design

Every client keeps a full local copy of the document and applies its own edits instantly; the server's job is transforming and ordering, not being the only place edits happen — diagrammed below.

6
Deep Dives

Three below: (a) why last-write-wins and locking both fail here, (b) operational transformation, the actual mechanism, and (c) offline edits and reconnection.

Every client holds a full local copy and applies its own edits instantly — the server never blocks a client's own typing. Its job is transforming each incoming operation against everything that landed since that client last synced, then broadcasting the transformed result.
A user types (the common case)
  1. Client A applies the keystroke to its own local document immediately — the character appears with zero network latency.
  2. The operation is sent to the Transform Server, tagged with the revision A's copy was at when the edit was made.
  3. The server transforms it against any operations received since that revision (from other clients), producing a version that applies cleanly to the server's current state.
  4. The server applies it, assigns the next revision number, and broadcasts the transformed operation to every other connected client.
Two people edit concurrently
  1. Client A and Client B both start from revision 41 and each make an edit at nearly the same instant, before either has heard from the server.
  2. A's operation arrives first; the server applies it as-is, revision becomes 42.
  3. B's operation, still tagged base_revision=41, gets transformed against A's now-applied edit — its position is adjusted to account for A's insertion — then applied as revision 43.
  4. Both A and B end up with identical final content: A sees B's transformed edit arrive; B's own local copy already applied its edit and now reconciles against A's, arriving in the other order but converging on the same text.
Key deep dive — why last-write-wins and locking both fail here
FREdit simultaneouslyNFRNo edit silently droppedNFRConvergence
Thought process
  1. Reach for the pattern that's worked everywhere else on this page: when two writers conflict, let one win. Try applying it here — the server keeps whichever edit arrives last.
  2. Trace what "arrives last" actually does to the loser: it doesn't get rejected and retried like a failed seat hold — it's just gone. The user who typed it sees their own words vanish.
  3. Try the other classic fix instead: lock the document, or the paragraph, while someone's editing it. Test it against how people actually use a shared doc.
  4. Notice locking doesn't solve concurrent editing, it prevents it — the whole premise of the product is that two people type in the same document at once, and a lock makes one of them wait.

Every other worked example on this page resolves contention by making one writer win and rejecting the rest — a seat hold, a parking spot, a ride acceptance. Try that same instinct here and it breaks the product's actual premise.

  • Last-write-wins silently destroys work: if the server just keeps whichever operation arrives last, the other user's edit isn't rejected-and-retried the way a failed conditional write is — it's discarded outright, with no signal to anyone that it happened.
  • Locking prevents the actual use case: a pessimistic lock on a paragraph or the whole document stops the exact behavior the product exists for — two people typing in the same place at once.
  • The reframe: this isn't a contention problem with one correct winner. It's a merge problem — both edits are valid, and the system's job is producing one document that reflects both, not picking between them.

That reframe is the whole reason this example doesn't fit the "atomic conditional write" pattern from Ticketmaster, Uber, and the parking lot — there's no single row to guard, because there's no single correct outcome to guard it toward.

Key deep dive — operational transformation, the actual mechanism
FRInstant local editsNFRConvergenceNFREdits feel instant
Thought process
  1. Restate the actual goal precisely: two edits made against the same starting document, in some order, should produce the same final document regardless of which order they're applied in.
  2. Notice naively applying both edits at their original positions doesn't do that — an insertion earlier in the text shifts every position after it, so the second edit's original position is now pointing at the wrong place.
  3. The fix has to adjust the second operation's position based on what the first operation actually did — not apply it blindly, and not discard it.
  4. Formalize that adjustment as a function: given two concurrent operations, transform one against the other so it still does what the user intended, on top of the other's result.

Operational Transformation (OT) is the algorithm Google Docs actually uses — not CRDTs, despite that being the more commonly cited answer in interviews. The core idea: don't just apply a remote operation as-is — adjust it based on what's changed locally since it was created.

Illustration — why a raw position breaks, and what transform fixes

Starting text: "HELLO WORLD" (revision 41)

Client A

inserts "X" at position 5 → "HELLOX WORLD"

(their local view)

Client B

inserts "Y" at position 8 → "HELLO WOYRLD"

(their local view)

Server applies A first: "HELLOX WORLD" is now revision 42.

B's op says "insert Y at position 8" — but position 8 in the OLD text is no longer position 8 now that A inserted a character before it.

transform(B's op, against A's applied op):
  • A inserted before B's position → shift B's position right by 1
  • insert "Y" at position 9 → "HELLOX WOYRLD" (correct, on both sides)
  • The transform function is the whole algorithm: given two operations that both started from the same revision, produce an adjusted version of one that, applied after the other, yields the same result no matter the order — this property is what convergence actually means, made concrete.
  • Every client re-derives this, not just the server: when Client A receives B's operation, A also transforms it — against A's own pending local edits — before applying it locally. The server and every client are running the same transform logic independently.
  • This is why edits feel instant: a client never waits for the server's permission to show a keystroke — it applies locally first, and reconciles with the server's transformed version afterward, in the background.

CRDTs solve the same convergence problem with a different trade-off — no central transform step, but a data structure with more per-character metadata overhead. OT keeps the document itself lightweight at the cost of needing a server (or an agreed-upon peer) to do the transforming — the right trade-off for a product where a server's already in the loop for storage and access control anyway.

Key deep dive — offline edits and reconnection
FROffline edits merge on reconnectNFRNo full re-download on reconnect
Thought process
  1. Ask what actually changes when a client goes offline for a while: nothing about the transform logic — the gap is just "how many operations happened while this client was gone."
  2. Consider making the client re-fetch the whole document on reconnect. Test it against a long meeting-room doc with hours of edit history — that's a lot of data for what might be a five-minute gap.
  3. Notice the client already has almost everything — its own last-known revision and its own queued local edits. What it's actually missing is just the delta.
  4. Treat reconnection as "catch up on what you missed," not "start over" — replay only the operations since the client's last known revision, transformed against each other the same way live concurrent edits already are.

A client that was offline is really just a client whose last-known revision is far behind — the same transform mechanism that handles two people typing a second apart handles someone reconnecting after an hour, just with more operations to transform against.

  • The client queues its own edits locally while offline — they're still applied instantly to its local copy, exactly as if the server were reachable, just not yet sent anywhere.
  • On reconnect, the client sends its queued operations tagged with its last-known revision — the server transforms the entire queued batch against everything that happened since, the same operation used for any concurrent edit, just applied more times in a row.
  • The Operation Log doesn't need to be replayed from the beginning: a periodic snapshot in Document Store means "catch up" only needs operations since the last snapshot before the client's revision, not the document's entire history.

Treating "offline for an hour" as a large version of the same problem as "offline for a millisecond between two keystrokes" is what keeps this from needing a separate reconciliation system — it's the identical transform, run more times.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Edits feel instantApplied to the local copy immediately, before any server round trip — the network is never on the typing critical path.
Convergence across clientsEvery client runs the same transform function against the same operation history, guaranteeing identical results regardless of arrival order.
No edit silently droppedConcurrent operations are transformed and merged, never discarded — the "one writer wins" pattern from elsewhere on this page doesn't apply here.
Offline edits merge on reconnectQueued local operations are transformed against everything missed, the same mechanism as live concurrent edits, just applied over a longer gap.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Operational Transformation vs. CRDTsOT keeps the document representation simple and lightweight, but every operation must pass through a central transform authority (or an agreed transform protocol between peers) — CRDTs remove that central dependency at the cost of more per-character metadata and harder-to-reason-about merge semantics.
Apply locally first vs. wait for server confirmationApplying locally makes typing feel instant, but means a client is always briefly showing content the server hasn't agreed to yet — a rare transform edge case could require a visible local correction.
Periodic snapshot vs. replaying the full operation historySnapshots keep reconnection and cold starts fast, at the cost of the extra logic and storage to generate and retain them — without one, a very old document could mean replaying thousands of operations for every new join.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Transform Servera stateful WebSocket service — ShareDB and Yjs (CRDT-based alternative) are the well-known open-source implementations
Op transportWebSocket, same connection pattern as the WhatsApp example
Operation LogPostgreSQL or DynamoDB, append-only
Document Store (snapshots)PostgreSQL, or blob storage for very large documents
Worked Example L — Real-Time State Under Real-World Lag

Design Multiplayer Game State Sync

client-side prediction · server reconciliation · lag compensation
Click to expand

"Design the system that keeps every player's view of a fast-paced multiplayer game (a shooter, a racer) in sync, despite each player having a different, constantly-changing amount of network lag to the server." Every other real-time example on this page treats the server's word as final the moment it arrives — a message is delivered, an operation is transformed and applied. This one is different: the client is deliberately allowed to be wrong for a fraction of a second, on purpose, because waiting for the truth would feel worse than briefly guessing.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • A player's own movement responds instantly to their input, regardless of their connection latency to the server.
  • Every player sees every other player's position and actions, converging on one consistent game world.
  • The server is the final authority on outcomes — did a shot land, is a player actually where they claim to be.
  • A cheating or malfunctioning client cannot force an outcome the server wouldn't otherwise allow.
Non-functional
  • Input-to-screen latency for a player's own actions must feel instant (well under 50ms) even when their real round trip to the server is 150ms or more.
  • The game must stay playable and fair for players with meaningfully different latencies to the same server, at the same time.
  • State updates for a fast-moving match (dozens of players, tens of updates per second each) can't saturate available bandwidth.
  • A brief network hiccup should degrade gracefully — a stutter, not a disconnect.

Worth asking: authoritative server, or peer-to-peer with one player's client as host? We'll assume a dedicated authoritative server — it's the only model that satisfies "a client can't force an outcome," which most competitive real-time games require.

2
Core Entities
  • PlayerState (player_id, position, velocity, tick) — the authoritative truth for one player, as of a specific server tick.
  • Input (player_id, sequence_num, keys_pressed, client_tick) — one frame of a player's raw input, tagged with a number the client can later match against the server's response.
