  • Never link on an unverified email, whatever the provider claims about itself — this is the single rule that turns a full takeover into a refused login, and it costs one conditional.
  • Notify on every link — email the account when a new provider is attached, with a one-tap "this wasn't me". Linking is exactly the kind of quiet, permanent change that should never happen silently.
  • The reverse direction needs the same care — a password reset to an email address that a social identity also asserts is the same problem wearing different clothes, and deserves the same suspicion.

Same instinct as the trusted-device example's recovery path: the dangerous route is always the convenient one that bypasses proof, and the fix is to demand proof precisely where the shortcut wanted to skip it.

Key deep dive — email is not a key
NFRSurvives a user changing their provider email
Thought process
  1. Start from why email feels like the right key: it's unique, it's human-readable, users already know it, and every provider seems to return one.
  2. Test "every provider returns one" and it fails immediately — Facebook accounts registered by phone number, or where the user declined the email permission, return nothing usable.
  3. Test "it's stable" and it fails too. People change the email on their Google account. If that's your key, the same human comes back as a stranger and gets a second account.
  4. Test "it's unique per person" and it fails in the other direction — two providers returning the same address is precisely the collision the linking dive is about.
  5. Look for something with the properties email was supposed to have. Every OIDC provider issues sub: opaque, stable for the lifetime of that account, and unique within that provider.
  6. Accept the consequence — sub is meaningless to a human, so you still store email for display and communication. It's just not what you look up by.

Email is how you talk to a user. The subject id is how you recognise them. Conflating the two is the root of most of the failures in this example.

Illustration — four ways an email key breaks
1 The user changes their Google email
keyed on email
→ budi.new@gmail.com matches nothing → a brand new account, empty. Their data is "gone" as far as they can tell.
keyed on sub
→ sub_117xyz still matches. Update the stored email, sign them in, nothing else happens.
2 Facebook returns no email
keyed on email
→ nothing to key on. The flow cannot complete.
keyed on sub
→ fb_4471 is a perfectly good identity. Ask for an email separately if you need one for comms.
3 Two providers, same address
keyed on email
→ collision. Are these the same person? Email alone cannot answer that — see the linking dive.
keyed on sub
→ two distinct identities. Whether they attach to one user is a separate, deliberate decision.
4 Email recycled by the provider

Corporate domains reassign addresses when staff leave.

keyed on email
→ the new employee inherits the old one's account.
keyed on sub
→ different person, different sub, no collision.
What this means for the schema
identities.provider_user_id
← sub. The lookup key. Never changes.
identities.email_at_provider
← last seen value. Display and change-detection only.
users.primary_email
← where you actually send mail. The user controls this directly.
  • A changed email at the provider is worth noticing, not acting on — update the stored value, and consider notifying the old address, but don't treat it as a new identity.
  • Normalise before comparing, when you do compare — case differences and Gmail's dot-and-plus handling mean the same mailbox has many spellings, which matters for the "does this email already exist" check even though it's not the key.
Key deep dive — when the provider is down
NFROne provider failing doesn't lock users out
Thought process
  1. Notice what a social login actually is operationally: a synchronous network call to a company you don't control, sitting on your login path.
  2. Ask what happens when it's slow rather than down — your login page hangs, users retry, and the retries pile more load onto a dependency that is already struggling.
  3. Apply the patterns that already exist elsewhere on this page: a tight timeout on the token exchange, and a circuit breaker so a failing provider fails fast instead of holding connections.
  4. Then ask the harder question — what does a user actually do about it? A fast failure is better than a hang, but they still can't get in.
  5. Find the real mitigation, and notice it's a product decision rather than an infrastructure one: users with a second identity are fine. So the design should actively encourage having one, before it's needed.
  6. Handle the partial-failure case that's easy to miss: the provider's authorization redirect may work while its token endpoint is failing, so the user gets bounced back to you and then hits an error. That needs a message that says what happened, not a generic failure.

A social-login-only user is, in availability terms, depending on two services being up instead of one — and only one of them is yours.

Illustration — degrading usefully rather than hanging
What failure looks like
token endpoint slow
→ your login hangs → users retry → worse
token endpoint down
→ redirect back works, exchange 500s
JWKS endpoint down
→ you cannot verify signatures← unless you CACHED the keys, which you should, exactly as the gateway does in the platform example
provider fully down
→ the button cannot work at all
Handling it
timeout on token exchange
3-5s, not the default 30
circuit breaker per provider
open → hide or grey out that button with an honest message rather than letting people click into a failure
cached JWKS
signature verification survives a JWKS outage entirely
clear messaging
"Google sign-in is unavailable right now. If you have a password, use that."
← only useful if they HAVE one
The real mitigation is upstream of the outage

After signup via a provider, prompt for a second way in:

"Add a password so you can always get in, even if Google is down."

This is a product nudge, not an infrastructure control, and it is the only thing that actually helps a user during an outage.

It is also the same reasoning as the trusted-device example requiring two trusted devices: the time to add the second way in is before you need it, and a design that waits until the user is locked out has already failed them.

  • Never let a provider outage take down password login too — shared timeouts, a shared connection pool, or a shared circuit can do exactly that. The bulkhead reasoning from the API gateway example applies here in miniature.
  • Grey out rather than hide — a button that silently disappears makes users think they never had that option; one that's visibly unavailable tells them the truth and sets expectations.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
One person, one accountUser holds no credentials; many Identity rows point at it, and adding a provider is an insert rather than a schema change.
Never grants access to someone else's accountLinking requires either a provider-verified email from a trusted provider, or proof of control via the existing sign-in method.
Survives an email change at the providerLookup is on (provider, sub); the email is stored as a display attribute and simply updated when it changes.
One provider down doesn't lock users outPer-provider circuit breakers and cached JWKS, plus an active prompt to add a second sign-in method before it's needed.
Unlinking can't orphan an accountDeleting the last remaining identity is refused outright.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Identity rows vs. a column per providerAdding providers becomes an insert and passwords stop being structurally special, at the cost of a join on every login and a schema that looks over-engineered until the second provider arrives.
Auto-link on verified email vs. always prove ownershipOne click for most real users, at the cost of your account security depending on a third party's email verification being both correct and unchanging.
Keying on sub vs. keying on emailSurvives email changes, missing emails and recycled addresses, at the cost of an opaque key that's useless for support queries and debugging by eye.
Offering social login at allRemoves password friction and outsources credential security to companies who are good at it, at the cost of taking a hard dependency on their uptime, their policies, and their definition of a verified email.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
ProtocolOpenID Connect for Google and LinkedIn; Facebook Login is OAuth 2.0 with its own userinfo shape, which is why "just OIDC" isn't quite true
Password hashingArgon2id or bcrypt — never a general-purpose hash, and stored beside the identity rather than on the user
Buy instead of buildAuth0, Clerk, Supabase Auth, Keycloak — all of them have already made the linking decision above, so check which one they made
State and link requestsRedis with short TTLs — both the OAuth state nonce and any pending LinkRequest should expire in minutes
Session issuanceidentical regardless of provider — this is where the OAuth Authorization Service example on this page picks up
Worked Example AD — The Credential That Never Expires

Design API Key Management

hash without losing lookup · rotate without downtime · keys leak
Click to expand

"Issue long-lived credentials for server-to-server integrations, where no human is present to complete an OAuth flow." Every instinct from the OAuth example inverts here. There is no user to consent, no refresh token, no short expiry doing the heavy lifting — just a string that grants access until someone takes it away. That makes three problems load-bearing that barely matter for short-lived tokens: how you store it, how you replace it without an outage, and what you do when it inevitably ends up in a public repository.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Issue a key scoped to one tenant and a specific set of permissions.
  • Verify a presented key on every request, fast enough to sit on the hot path.
  • Rotate a key without any window in which the integration is broken.
  • Revoke a key immediately, and show operators when each key was last used.
Non-functional
  • A database breach must not yield usable credentials.
  • Verification must not require scanning the key table.
  • A leaked key must be findable by automated scanners before an attacker uses it.
  • Revocation must take effect in seconds, despite verification being cached.

Worth asking first: why not just use OAuth client credentials? Often you should — but a key is operationally simpler for the integrator, and that simplicity is exactly why it gets chosen and exactly why it's dangerous. The first deep dive is about when the trade is right.

2
Core Entities
  • ApiKey (key_id, tenant_id, secret_hash, prefix, label, scopes[], status, created_by, created_at, expires_at, last_used_at) — note there is no column containing the key itself.
  • Tenant (id, name, max_active_keys) — the entity the key acts on behalf of; a key is never scoped to a person.
  • KeyEvent (key_id, type, actor, at, source) — created, rotated, revoked, leak-detected. The audit trail regulators ask for.
  • RevocationEntry (key_id, revoked_at) — small, short-lived, pushed to verifiers so a cached decision can be overridden.

key_id is the indexed lookup handle and is not secret. secret_hash is the only thing derived from the secret half. That split is what makes the next section work.

3
API

POST /tenants/{id}/keys → issue; the plaintext key is in this response and never retrievable again
GET /tenants/{id}/keys → list metadata only — label, prefix, scopes, last_used_at
POST /keys/{key_id}/rotate → issue a successor while the current key stays valid
DELETE /keys/{key_id} → revoke immediately
POST /internal/leak-report → called by a secret-scanning partner on a confirmed match

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. A request arrives carrying a key; the gateway parses its structure and rejects anything malformed without touching storage.
  2. The key_id segment is extracted and used for a single indexed lookup — no scan.
  3. The presented secret is hashed and compared in constant time against the stored hash.
  4. The result — tenant, scopes, status — is cached briefly, so the vast majority of requests never reach the database at all.
  5. Revocations are pushed to verifiers separately, so a cached allow can be overridden inside seconds.
5
High-Level Design

Structure in the key itself is what makes lookup, scanning, and revocation all tractable — diagrammed below.

6
Deep Dives

Four below: (a) when a key beats OAuth, (b) hashing without losing lookup, (c) rotation without downtime, and (d) keys leak — design for it.

The structure of the key is the design. The prefix makes it greppable by scanners, the key_id makes verification an indexed lookup instead of a table scan, and the secret half is the only part ever hashed. Get that layout wrong and every problem below becomes harder.
A verified request
  1. The key's shape is checked first — wrong prefix or wrong length is rejected without a database call.
  2. key_id is extracted and looked up on a unique index; one row or none.
  3. The presented secret is hashed and compared in constant time; status and expiry are checked.
  4. Tenant and scopes are cached for ~30 seconds and forwarded inward — the product API never sees the key.
A key appears in a public repo
  1. A scanning partner matches the mfc_live_ pattern and calls the leak endpoint with the key.
  2. It's verified as real, revoked immediately, and a KeyEvent is recorded with the source.
  3. A revocation entry is pushed to every verifier, overriding any cached allow within seconds.
  4. The owning team is notified with the key's label and last_used_at — which tells them how much is now broken.
Key deep dive — when a key beats OAuth
FRScoped to a tenant, not a person
Thought process
  1. Start from the default position, which is correct most of the time: OAuth exists, it's the standard, use it and don't invent a second credential system.
  2. Then look at what OAuth's security actually rests on — short-lived access tokens, refreshed by a long-lived refresh token, with a user present at least once to consent.
  3. Find the case where that breaks down. A nightly job syncing one company's expense records has no user at the keyboard at 3am, and no browser to redirect.
  4. Notice OAuth already has an answer: the client credentials grant. So the real question is narrower than "keys versus OAuth" — it's whether the extra round trip and token lifecycle earns its complexity for this integrator.
  5. Weigh who the integrator actually is. A partner engineering team will implement token refresh correctly. A customer's in-house script written once and left running for three years will not, and a key that simply works is the difference between an integration existing and not.
  6. Accept the trade honestly: you are choosing operational simplicity for the integrator and taking on a long-lived bearer credential in exchange. Everything else in this example is paying that debt.

The scoping difference matters as much as the lifetime one. An OAuth token says a user authorised this; a key says this tenant's systems are allowed to do this. Those answer different questions.

Illustration — the fork, and what each answer costs
OAuth(user-present)API key(server-to-server)
who authoriseda human, once, via a consent screenan admin, once, in a settings page
scoped toa user, and what THEY may accessa TENANT, and what the integration may access
lifetimeminutes; refresheduntil revoked. Possibly years.
if stolenexpires on its own, refresh reuse is detectableworks forever, silently, and nothing about it looks unusual
integrator effortredirect flow, token storage, refresh logicput a string in a header
When the key is the right answer
  • no user is present and none can be (batch jobs, webhooks, ETL)
  • the data is tenant-scoped, not user-scoped — "this company's invoices", not "what Budi personally may see"
  • the integrator is a small team or a single script, and OAuth complexity would mean the integration simply doesn't get built
When it is not
  • the action is on behalf of a specific person
  • third-party apps you do not control — they need consent and revocation per user, which is precisely what OAuth is for
  • anything where "who did this" must name a human in the audit log
  • Offering both is a deliberate product decision, not indecision — the platform serves integrators with very different capabilities, and forcing OAuth everywhere pushes the least sophisticated ones toward worse workarounds, like sharing a real user's password.
  • A key should never impersonate a user — if the audit trail needs a human name, a key is the wrong credential. Keep created_by for accountability, but the acting principal is the tenant.
Key deep dive — hashing without losing lookup
NFRA breach yields nothing usableNFRNo table scan on the hot path
Thought process
  1. Start from the non-negotiable: never store the key in plaintext. A database breach must not hand the attacker working credentials for every tenant at once.
  2. Reach for the obvious tool — hash it like a password, with bcrypt or Argon2 — and then try to verify one. You have a key and a table of salted hashes. There is nothing to look up by, so you must hash the candidate against every row.
  3. Notice how badly that fails. A deliberately slow KDF, run across every row in the table, on every single request. It is not slow — it is unusable.
  4. Find the real constraint: you need something non-secret in the key that identifies which row, so verification is one indexed read.
  5. Split the key. One segment is a public identifier stored in an indexed column; the rest is the secret, and only that half is hashed.
  6. Now revisit the hash choice, because the usual reasoning does not apply. Slow KDFs exist because human passwords are low-entropy and guessable. A key is 256 bits of randomness you generated — brute force is infeasible regardless of hash speed, so a fast hash is not a compromise here, it is correct.

This is one of the few places where "just SHA-256 it" is the right answer rather than a red flag — and being able to say why is the part that matters.

Illustration — three designs, only one of which works
Design 1 — store the key plaintext
SELECT * FROM api_keys WHERE key = $1
  • fast, trivially simple
  • one breach = every tenant's credentials, immediately usable

→ disqualified

Design 2 — bcrypt the whole key, like a password

no lookup handle exists, so:

for every row: bcrypt_verify(candidate, row.hash)
  • 100ms × 50,000 rows × every request
  • the slowness that PROTECTS a password DESTROYS you here

→ disqualified

Design 3 — structured key, hash only the secret half

mfc_live_7a2f9c1e_kR8vN2pQxW4mZ7tB9jL3

mfc_live_prefix 7a2f9c1ekey_idindexed, NOT secret kR8vN2pQxW4mZ7tB9jL3secret256 bits of CSPRNG output, never stored anywhere
verification:
  1. shape check → reject junk with zero I/O
  2. SELECT ... WHERE key_id=$1 → ONE indexed read
  3. sha256(secret) vs stored → constant-time compare
  4. check status + expiry
  • breach yields hashes of 256-bit randoms — not crackable
  • verification is O(1) and sub-millisecond
  • cacheable, so most requests never touch the database
Why SHA-256 and not Argon2 here
passwords
low entropy, human-chosen, guessable→ you WANT slowness, to make guessing expensive
api keys
256 bits from a CSPRNG→ guessing is infeasible at ANY hash speed, and you must do this on every request

a fast hash is the correct engineering choice, not a shortcut

The rule underneath: KDF slowness buys you nothing when the secret was never guessable to begin with.

  • Constant-time comparison still matters — a naive byte-by-byte compare leaks how much of the hash matched via timing. Cheap to get right, awkward to explain after an incident.
  • Show the key exactly once — at creation. If it can be retrieved later, your key store is a plaintext store with extra steps, and every support agent becomes an attack path.
  • Store a display hint, not the key — the prefix plus last four characters is enough for a human to identify which key a dashboard row refers to, and useless to an attacker.
Key deep dive — rotation without downtime
FRReplace a key with no broken windowFRShow when each key was last used
Thought process
  1. Notice why rotation is mandatory even with nothing wrong: a credential that lives for years accumulates exposure — old laptops, departed staff, CI logs, screenshots.
  2. Try the naive model, one key per tenant, and trace a rotation. Generate a new key, the old one dies, and every deployment still holding it starts failing. Rotation is now an outage, so nobody does it.
  3. Notice the second-order effect, which is worse than the first: making rotation painful means it never happens, so keys quietly live forever and the risk you were managing grows unchecked.
  4. Fix the model rather than the process — allow several keys active per tenant at once, so a new one can exist before the old one is gone.
  5. Find what makes the cutover safe rather than merely possible. You need to know the old key has genuinely stopped being used, across every deployment you may not know about.
  6. last_used_at answers exactly that, which is why it is worth the write cost. Rotation stops being a leap of faith and becomes an observation.

The design goal is not "rotation is possible" — it is "rotation is boring enough that people actually do it."

Illustration — overlap, then evidence, then revoke
The sequence
  1. t0

    POST /keys/{old}/rotate

    • new key issued, shown ONCE
    • old key still fully valid. Nothing has broken.
  2. t1

    integrator deploys the new key at their own pace

    both keys work. This window is the entire point.

  3. t2

    watch the dashboard:

    key_oldlast_used_at 4 hours agogoing quiet
    key_newlast_used_at 12 seconds agotook over
  4. t3

    old key shows no use for a full business cycle

    NOW revoke it, on evidence rather than hope

The gap between t1 and t3 is deliberate and should be generous. A weekly batch job will not touch the old key for six days — revoke on day two and you break something nobody was watching.

Why last_used_at is worth its cost

A naive implementation writes to the key row on every request, which turns a read-mostly table into a write-hot one.

Cheaper: update at most once per minute per key, asynchronously. Precision here is worthless — you need "today" versus "not for six days", not millisecond accuracy.

Max lifetime, and why it is awkward

Long-lived is why integrators chose a key. Forcing 90-day expiry gives them OAuth's operational burden with none of its security benefits.

A workable middle: an optional expiry, warnings at 30/7/1 days to the owner, and for high-privilege scopes make expiry mandatory. Tie the strictness to what the key can DO, not to a global policy.

  • Cap the number of simultaneously active keys — two or three. Unlimited keys means nobody ever cleans up, and the list becomes a set of forgotten credentials nobody dares revoke.
  • Label keys at creation and require it — "billing-sync-prod" tells you what breaks if you revoke it. An unlabelled key is one nobody will ever be confident enough to remove.
  • Rotation and revocation are different operations — conflating them in the UI is how someone kills production while trying to do routine hygiene.
Key deep dive — keys leak, so design for it
NFRFindable by scanners before useNFRRevocation beats the cache
Thought process
  1. Start from the empirical fact rather than the ideal: credentials get committed to public repositories constantly, by competent people, at every company. Treat it as a certainty, not a risk.
  2. Ask what you can do about a string that has already escaped. You cannot recall it — so the only levers are finding it fast and making it dead fast.
  3. Find what makes a key findable, and notice this is a format decision made long before any incident. A bare random string is indistinguishable from any other base64 blob. A distinctive prefix is greppable at internet scale.
  4. Follow that to the mechanism — scanning providers match registered patterns across public code and notify the issuer. Your prefix is what makes you eligible to participate at all.
  5. Then confront the awkward decision: on a confirmed match, do you revoke automatically and break the integrator's production, or notify and leave a live credential exposed while you wait?
  6. Resolve it by asymmetry of harm. A wrongly-revoked key causes a visible, fixable outage. A live leaked key on a financial API causes something you may not detect for months. Auto-revoke, and make the notification excellent.

The prefix on the key is not branding. It is the single design decision that makes automated leak detection possible at all, and it has to be made before you issue your first key.

Illustration — the leak loop, and the decision inside it
Why the prefix earns its bytes
bare random

"kR8vN2pQxW4mZ7tB9jL3"

indistinguishable from a base64 blob, a hash, an asset filename. Unsearchable.

prefixed

"mfc_live_7a2f9c1e_kR8vN2pQ…"

  • a distinctive, registrable pattern
  • scanning providers can match it across public code and tell you within minutes of the push

Also note live vs test in the prefix: a leaked TEST key is a shrug, a leaked LIVE key is an incident. Encoding that in the string means humans and scanners can both tell instantly.

The loop
  • push → scanner matches pattern → calls your leak endpoint
  • you verify it is a real, active key
  • REVOKE + KeyEvent(type=leak, source=github)
  • push revocation to all verifiers beats the 30s cache
  • notify the owning tenant with label + last_used_at
Auto-revoke or notify-first?
notify-first
  • no self-inflicted outage
  • credential is live while you wait for a human who may be asleep, on leave, or gone
auto-revoke
  • integration breaks immediately
  • exposure window is minutes, not days
  • the outage is loud, so it gets fixed now

The trade turns on asymmetry: a wrongly-revoked key produces an obvious, recoverable outage. A live leaked key on a financial API produces unauthorised access you may never notice.

revoke, and spend the effort on making the alert unmissable

The unglamorous part that prevents more leaks than any of this
  • never log the Authorization header — log key_id, never the key
  • scrub keys from error reports and crash dumps before they ship
  • the creation response is the ONLY place plaintext ever appears
  • in dashboards show mfc_live_7a2f…9jL3, never the whole thing
  • Revocation must outrank the cache — verification is cached for performance, so a revoked key stays usable for the cache TTL unless revocations are pushed separately. That list is tiny and short-lived, which is what makes pushing it cheap.
  • Record the source on every KeyEvent — "revoked because found in a public repo" and "revoked by an admin" look identical afterwards without it, and only one of them warrants investigating what else that repo contained.
  • Anomaly detection is the layer beneath — a key that has only ever called one endpoint from one IP range suddenly enumerating another tenant's data is a signal worth acting on, and it catches leaks no scanner will ever find.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
A breach yields nothing usableOnly a SHA-256 of a 256-bit random is stored; the plaintext exists in exactly one response and is never retrievable again.
No table scan on the hot pathThe non-secret key_id segment gives an indexed single-row lookup, and results are cached for seconds.
Rotation with no broken windowSeveral keys active at once, with last_used_at proving the old one has gone quiet before it's revoked.
Leaks found before they're usedA distinctive registrable prefix makes keys greppable by scanning providers, which is a format decision made at design time.
Revocation in seconds despite cachingRevocations are pushed to verifiers as a small separate list that overrides a cached allow.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Offering keys at all, alongside OAuthIntegrations get built that otherwise wouldn't, at the cost of a long-lived bearer credential — everything else in this example is the price of that convenience.
Fast hash vs. a slow KDFVerification stays viable on every request and the security argument still holds because the secret is high-entropy — but it depends entirely on generating keys from a CSPRNG, which makes that the load-bearing detail.
Caching verification vs. checking liveMost requests never touch the database, at the cost of a revocation window that must be closed by a separate push — added complexity to buy back correctness.
Auto-revoke on leak vs. notify firstCuts exposure from days to minutes, at the cost of occasionally taking down a production integration on a scanner's say-so.
Optional expiry vs. mandatory rotationRespects why integrators chose a key in the first place, at the cost of keys that genuinely live for years — which is why expiry is tied to privilege level rather than applied globally.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Key storePostgreSQL — unique index on key_id, and the ACID guarantees that make issuance and revocation trustworthy
Key generationthe platform CSPRNG — crypto/rand in Go, never math/rand. This is the detail the whole hashing argument rests on
Verification cacheRedis or in-process with a short TTL, layered under a pushed revocation list
Leak detectionGitHub Secret Scanning partner program, GitGuardian — both require a registered, distinctive pattern
Enforcement pointthe gateway's filter chain from the API Gateway example — keys and OAuth tokens resolve to the same downstream identity headers
Worked Example AE — The Invoice That Belongs to Someone Else

Design Tenant Isolation for a Multi-Product B2B API

where the tenant comes from · BOLA · pool, bridge or silo · RLS as the safety net
Click to expand

Thousands of businesses share one platform: the same services, the same databases, the same public API, across accounting, payroll and invoicing products. The single failure that ends trust in a B2B platform is one business seeing another's data. It almost never happens through a clever attack on the crypto — it happens because one query forgot one WHERE clause. This example designs isolation so that a single forgotten clause is not enough to cause a leak.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Every request acts on behalf of exactly one business — the tenant — and can only read or change that business's data.
  • One user can belong to many businesses (an accountant serving thirty clients) and switch between them.
  • Partner apps are authorised per business, never platform-wide.
  • Support staff can reach a customer's data only through a time-boxed, reasoned, audited grant.
  • A business can be exported, erased, or pinned to a region on its own.
Non-functional
  • Isolation must survive a bug in application code — one missing filter must not leak.
  • A request for another business's object must be indistinguishable from a request for an object that doesn't exist.
  • One very large or very busy business must not degrade the others.
  • Isolation checks add no meaningful latency — no extra network hop per request.
  • Hundreds of thousands of small businesses and a handful of very large ones, on the same platform.

The first NFR is the one that shapes everything. "Developers must remember to filter by tenant" is a hope, not a design — the design is whatever still holds on the day someone forgets.

2
Core Entities
  • Business (id, region, isolation_tier, plan) — the tenant. isolation_tier is pool or silo, and decides where its data lives.
  • Membership (user_id, business_id, role) — a user's role inside one business; an accountant has many rows.
  • Grant (client_id, user_id, business_id, scopes) — an OAuth grant names exactly one business.
  • Invoice (id, business_id, customer_id, amount, …) — every tenant-owned row carries business_id, with no exceptions.
  • SupportAccess (agent_id, business_id, reason, expires_at) — break-glass access, always expiring.

business_id leads every composite index — (business_id, created_at), not (created_at, business_id) — because every query filters on it first, and the database should be able to jump straight to one tenant's rows.

3
API

GET /v1/invoices/{invoice_id} → the business comes from the token, never from the request
GET /v1/businesses/{business_id}/invoices → the path business must equal the token's business, or 404
POST /oauth/token → a token is minted for exactly one business; switching business means obtaining another token
POST /internal/support-access → grant an agent time-boxed access to one business, with a reason, audited

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. A token is issued for one business; its business_id claim is signed and cannot be altered.
  2. The gateway verifies the token, strips any tenant header the client sent, and forwards the business as trusted context.
  3. The service places the business in the request context; nothing downstream reads it from anywhere else.
  4. The repository opens a transaction and sets the database's tenant context for that transaction only.
  5. Every query is scoped by business_id — and the database enforces the same rule underneath with row-level security.
  6. Anything that leaves the request — a queued job, a cache entry, a log line — carries the business_id with it.
5
High-Level Design

Defence in depth: the gateway fixes who the tenant is, the repository scopes every query, and the database enforces the same rule independently, so a bug in one layer is caught by the next. A detection layer watches for anyone probing the boundary. The paths that never touch the request pipeline — queues, caches, search, logs — each carry the tenant explicitly.

6
Deep Dives

Five below: (a) BOLA — the bug valid tokens don't catch, (b) where the tenant comes from, (c) pool, bridge or silo, (d) row-level security and the connection-pooler trap, and (e) the leaks that bypass the database — then the edge cases.

Defence in depth for one business's data. Layers 1–3 each stop a cross-tenant read on their own, so a bug has to exist in all three at once to leak; layer 4 turns quiet probing into an alert. The dashed row is where isolation most often fails in practice — outside the request pipeline, where no gateway or policy is watching.
A legitimate request
  1. A partner app holds a token for business A and asks for inv_118.
  2. The gateway verifies the token and forwards business A as trusted context.
  3. The repository reads inv_118 scoped to business A; RLS agrees.
  4. 200 OK with the invoice.
The same request, one ID changed
  1. The same token asks for inv_992, which belongs to business B.
  2. Authentication passes. The scope invoices:read passes. Nothing so far has looked at who owns the invoice.
  3. The scoped query returns zero rows — and would still return zero if that filter had been forgotten, because RLS hides B's rows.
  4. 404 Not Found: business A cannot even learn that inv_992 exists.
Key deep dive — BOLA, the bug a valid token doesn't catch
FROnly this business's dataNFRIndistinguishable from not-found
Thought process
  1. Broken Object Level Authorization is the first entry in the OWASP API Security Top 10 (API1:2023) — the most common serious API flaw, not an exotic one.
  2. It is invisible to the checks people trust: the token is valid and the scope is correct. Authentication answers who is calling and scopes answer what kind of action; neither asks whether this specific object belongs to them.
  3. The bug is a lookup by ID alone. Any endpoint that takes an ID from the caller and fetches by that ID without the tenant is vulnerable — reads, updates, deletes, and exports alike.
  4. The fix is structural: the tenant is part of every lookup, so an object from another business simply isn't found.
  5. Answer 404, not 403. A 403 confirms the invoice exists — itself a leak, and an invitation to enumerate. The status codes toolkit makes the same call.
  6. Unguessable IDs help as a second layer, but they are not the fix: IDs leak through emails, URLs, screenshots and logs.

The sentence to say in an interview: authentication tells me who you are; object-level authorization tells me whether this particular thing is yours — and it has to happen on every request that takes an ID.

Illustration — every check passes, and it still leaks
✓ token valid✓ scope invoices:read✗ owner of inv_992 never checked
Vulnerable — fetch by ID alone
SELECT * FROM invoices
WHERE id = $1
  • business A's token + inv_992 → business B's invoice
  • 200 OK — and the logs look perfectly normal
Fixed — the tenant is part of the lookup
SELECT * FROM invoices
WHERE id = $1 AND business_id = $2
  • same request → zero rows
  • 404 Not Found — identical to an ID that never existed

The repository takes business_id from the request context as a required argument on every method. A lookup that omits it doesn't compile — which is far stronger than a code-review checklist item.

  • Writes are the same bug — UPDATE … WHERE id = $1 lets business A edit business B's invoice. Scope updates and deletes exactly like reads.
  • Watch references inside bodies too — a request that creates an invoice for customer_id must check that customer belongs to the same business, or A can attach B's customer to its own invoice.
  • Test it mechanically — for every endpoint that takes an ID, CI requests business B's object with business A's token and expects 404. New endpoints inherit the test automatically.
Key deep dive — where the tenant comes from
FRExactly one business per requestFRMany businesses per user
Thought process
  1. Every isolation mechanism below depends on one value being right: which business this request acts for. If a caller can choose that value freely, every layer faithfully protects the wrong tenant.
  2. The only trustworthy source is something the caller cannot alter — a claim inside a signed token, minted by the authorization server for one business.
  3. A tenant in the URL is fine as addressing, but it must be checked against the token, never used instead of it.
  4. A tenant header sent by the client is the classic mistake: it looks like context but is just user input. The gateway strips it on the way in, then sets its own trusted version on the way to services.
  5. An accountant with thirty clients doesn't get one token for all thirty. Each token names one business; switching clients means obtaining a token for the next one. That keeps "one request, one tenant" true even for users who belong to many.
Illustration — every place a tenant could come from
SourceVerdictWhy
claim in the signed tokenauthoritativeminted by the authorization server for one business; the caller cannot change it
business_id in the URL pathmust match the tokenuseful for addressing; a mismatch returns 404, never a silent switch
X-Business-Id header from the clientnever trustedit's user input wearing a header's clothes — stripped at the gateway
business_id in the request bodynever trustedsame problem, easier to miss in review
header set by the gateway, inside the meshtrustedonly because the gateway stripped the client's version and mTLS proves who sent it — see the microservices platform example
  • API keys carry a tenant too — a key belongs to one business, so key verification yields the business_id exactly as a token does (see API Key Management).
  • A token for a removed membership must stop working — when a user leaves a business, their grants for it are revoked, and short token lifetimes bound how long an already-issued token survives.
Key deep dive — pool, bridge or silo
NFRHuge and tiny tenants on one platformNFRNo noisy neighbours
Thought process
  1. There are three ways to separate tenants' data, and they trade isolation strength against cost and operational load.
  2. Pool: shared tables, every row tagged with business_id. Cheapest per tenant and one schema to migrate — but isolation depends entirely on the scoping and RLS above.
  3. Bridge: a schema per tenant inside a shared database. Stronger separation, but every migration runs once per schema, and tens of thousands of schemas strain the catalog and the deploy pipeline.
  4. Silo: a database per tenant. The strongest isolation, per-tenant restore and residency for free — and the highest cost, which small tenants can't justify.
  5. With hundreds of thousands of small businesses and a few very large ones, no single model fits. The answer is tiered: pool by default, silo for the handful of large or regulated tenants — recorded as isolation_tier and routed on every request.
Illustration — three isolation models, side by side
Poolshared tablesBridgeschema per tenantSilodatabase per tenant
isolationlogical — code + RLSnamespacephysical
cost per tenantlowestmediumhighest — a floor per database
migrationsonceonce per schemaonce per database, orchestrated
noisy neighbourreal risk — needs quotasstill shares the servercontained
restore one tenanthard — extract its rowsrestore one schemarestore one database
residency & erasureper-row workper-schemaplace or drop the database
fitsthe long tail of small businessesa few hundred mid-size tenantslarge or regulated customers

Tiered is the usual answer, and it has a cost worth naming: two code paths for data placement, and a migration path for a tenant that grows from pool to silo — copy its rows, catch up, then flip isolation_tier at a quiet moment.

  • Sharding follows the tenant — when the pool outgrows one database, shard by business_id so each business's rows stay together and its joins stay local. A single very busy business then becomes a hot shard, which is exactly when it graduates to a silo.
  • Noisy neighbours are a quota problem as much as a data problem — per-business rate limits and connection limits come from the multi-tenant rate limiting example.
Key deep dive — row-level security, and the connection-pooler trap
NFRSurvives a bug in application codeNFRNo extra network hop
Thought process
  1. Scoping in the repository is necessary but lives in application code, where a new query can simply forget it. The database should enforce the same rule underneath, independently.
  2. Postgres row-level security attaches a policy to the table: the database adds the tenant condition to every query itself, and a row that doesn't match is invisible — even to a query that forgot its WHERE clause.
  3. The policy compares each row against a per-transaction setting holding the current business, set by the repository at the start of every transaction.
  4. The setting must be transaction-scoped. The platform runs PgBouncer in transaction mode, and a session-level setting stays on the server connection after the transaction ends — where the next tenant's transaction can pick it up.
  5. Three details decide whether RLS actually protects anything: the app must connect as a role that is neither the table owner (or the table must use FORCE) nor a superuser nor granted BYPASSRLS; a missing setting must fail closed; and business_id must lead the indexes so the added condition is cheap.
Illustration — the policy, and the connection-pooler bug that defeats it
ALTER TABLE invoices ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE invoices FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;      -- applies to the table owner too

CREATE POLICY business_isolation ON invoices
  USING      (business_id = nullif(current_setting('app.business_id', true), '')::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (business_id = nullif(current_setting('app.business_id', true), '')::uuid);

-- per transaction, from the repository:
BEGIN;
SELECT set_config('app.business_id', $1, true);   -- true = this transaction only
SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $2;             -- RLS adds the tenant condition
COMMIT;
Session-level — SET app.business_id = …
  1. txn 1

    business A's request sets A on server connection #7

  2. commit

    PgBouncer returns connection #7 to the pool — the setting stays

  3. txn 2

    business B's request lands on #7; if its code path skips the set, it runs as business A

Transaction-level — set_config(…, true)
  1. txn 1

    business A's request sets A for this transaction

  2. commit

    the setting ends with the transaction

  3. txn 2

    business B's request that forgot to set it sees no rows — the missing setting fails closed

set_config(…, true) rather than SET LOCAL for one practical reason: it takes the business as a bind parameter, so the tenant ID is never concatenated into SQL. And the policy reads the setting defensively: current_setting(…, true) returns NULL if the setting was never defined, but an empty string on a pooled connection where an earlier transaction set it — so nullif(…, '') turns both into NULL, which matches no rows. Silence instead of a leak.

  • RLS is the safety net, not the design — keep the explicit business_id filter in queries too. It makes intent readable, it helps the planner, and it means a mistake in a policy is caught by the code, and vice versa.
  • Migrations and admin jobs run as a separate role — the only role allowed to bypass RLS, never used by request-serving code, and audited when it is used.
Key deep dive — the leaks that bypass the database
FROnly this business's dataFRExport, erase, pin on its own
Thought process
  1. Row-level security protects one thing: the primary database. Tenant data is also copied into caches, queues, search indexes, warehouses, logs and files — none of which have a policy watching them.
  2. Each copy needs the tenant carried with it explicitly, and each reader needs to re-apply it. The rule is simple: tenant data never travels without its business_id.
  3. Background work is the most common gap: a worker picking up a message has no request, no token and no gateway — only what the message says. So the message carries the business, and the worker sets the database context before its first read.
Illustration — every copy of tenant data, and how each one leaks
Where the data goesHow it leaksThe fix
cachekey invoice:992 without the tenant — whoever asks first fills it, anyone can read itkey b:{business_id}:invoice:992, or re-check ownership on every read
queue / async jobthe worker has no request context and queries unscopedbusiness_id in every message; the worker sets context before any read
search indexone shared index, no row-level securitya mandatory business_id filter added by the search client, not by each caller
analytics warehousecross-tenant tables feed customer-facing reportskeep business_id in every table; customer-facing views filter by it
logs & error trackerspayloads with invoice data readable by anyone with log accesslog business_id and IDs, never payloads
exports & filesa guessable object path serves B's export to Aobject keys prefixed by business, served only through short-lived presigned URLs issued after the ownership check

The caching row connects to the Caching Playbook: a shared cache entry is safe only when every read is filtered for the caller afterwards. Tenant data that is cached should either be keyed by tenant or filtered on the way out — never neither.

Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • The accountant with thirty clients — one person, thirty memberships, one token per business at a time. The UI's business switcher obtains a new token; it never flips a header.
  • A document two businesses both need — an invoice sent from business A to business B belongs to both. Model it as two tenant-owned records (A's sent invoice, B's received bill) linked by an ID, not one row visible to two tenants; each side then has its own lifecycle, permissions and erasure.
  • Support access — a support agent never gets platform-wide read access. A SupportAccess grant names one business, a reason and an expiry, every read under it goes to the audit log, and the customer can see that access happened.
  • Offboarding and erasure — in a silo, drop the database. In the pool, delete by business_id across every table, and destroy the business's encryption key so backups and archives become unreadable — the crypto-shredding technique from the audit log example.
  • Data residency — Business.region pins where its data lives. A business that must stay in one country is served by that region's database, cache and queue — a residency requirement quietly turns into a routing requirement.
  • A tenant outgrows the pool — copy its rows to a new silo, keep them in sync while it catches up, then flip isolation_tier in a brief write pause. Plan this path before the first large customer signs, not after.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Survives a bug in application codeThree independent layers — token-derived tenant, repository scoping, and row-level security — so a leak needs the same mistake in all three at once.
Indistinguishable from not-foundAnother business's object is filtered out before it is ever loaded, so the response is a genuine 404, not a 403 that confirms it exists.
One business per request, many per userTokens name exactly one business; switching business means a new token, so the rule holds even for an accountant with thirty clients.
No noisy neighboursPer-business quotas in the pool; large tenants graduate to a silo where their load is physically separate.
No meaningful added latencyThe tenant comes from the token already being verified; RLS is a predicate on an index that already leads with business_id.
Export, erase or pin one businessEvery row, message, cache key and file carries business_id; silos make it a single database operation.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Pool vs. siloThe pool is cheap and simple to operate but isolation is logical; silos are strong and give per-tenant restore, at a cost small businesses can't justify. Tiering buys both, at the price of two placement paths.
RLS on top of query scopingSome policy complexity and a role discipline to maintain, in exchange for isolation that survives a forgotten filter.
404 instead of 403Harder debugging for the caller — "is it missing or forbidden?" — in exchange for never confirming that another business's object exists.
One token per businessAn extra token exchange when an accountant switches clients, in exchange for "one request, one tenant" holding without exception.
Tenant-keyed cachesLower hit rates for data several businesses could have shared, in exchange for caches that cannot serve one business's data to another.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Enforcement in the databasePostgreSQL row-level security with FORCE, and a non-owner application role without BYPASSRLS
Connection poolingPgBouncer in transaction mode — which is exactly why tenant context must be transaction-scoped
Sharding by tenantCitus distributes Postgres tables by a tenant column so each business's rows and joins stay on one node
Tenant propagation in Gocontext.Context carrying the business from middleware to repository, with repository methods that require it as an argument
Authorization policyOPA or Cedar when rules outgrow "same business and has this role"
ChecklistOWASP API Security Top 10 — BOLA is API1:2023; test every ID-taking endpoint against it
Worked Example AF — The Customer Whose Server Is Down

Design a Webhook Delivery System

at-least-once · signing & replay · retries that don't stampede · one dead endpoint can't stall the rest
Click to expand

When an invoice is paid or a payroll run completes, partner apps want to know immediately — so the platform calls their HTTPS endpoint with the event. The hard part isn't sending an HTTP request. It is that thousands of servers you don't control will be slow, down, misconfigured, or lying about success, and your delivery system has to stay correct and fair through all of it.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Partners subscribe an HTTPS endpoint to event types for one business.
  • Every event reaches every matching endpoint — even one that is down for a day.
  • Receivers can prove an event came from the platform, unaltered, and wasn't replayed.
  • Partners can see each delivery attempt and replay any event.
  • Endpoints that keep failing are disabled, and their owners told.
Non-functional
  • Emitting an event never slows or fails the business transaction that produced it.
  • No event is lost across crashes, deploys or outages.
  • One slow or dead endpoint must not delay deliveries to anyone else.
  • A large endpoint recovering from an outage must not be flattened by its own backlog.
  • Delivery calls must never reach the platform's own internal network.

The third NFR is the one teams miss. A delivery system with one shared queue works perfectly in testing, where every endpoint is healthy — and falls over the first time one customer's server starts dropping packets.

2
Core Entities
  • Event (id, business_id, type, resource_id, created_at) — immutable; its id is what receivers deduplicate on.
  • Endpoint (id, business_id, url, event_types, secrets, status) — status is active, failing or disabled; more than one secret during rotation.
  • Delivery (event_id, endpoint_id, state, attempts, next_attempt_at) — one per event per endpoint; pending, succeeded or dead.
  • Attempt (delivery_id, at, status_code, latency_ms, error) — the history partners see in their dashboard.

business_id is on the endpoint for the same reason it is everywhere in the tenant isolation example: fan-out must never deliver business B's event to business A's endpoint. A misrouted webhook is a cross-tenant leak that arrives by POST.

3
API

POST /v1/webhook-endpoints → register a URL and event types; the signing secret is returned once
GET /v1/webhook-endpoints/{id}/deliveries → every attempt, with status code and latency
POST /v1/events/{id}/redeliver → replay one event to one endpoint
POST /v1/webhook-endpoints/{id}/rotate-secret → add a new secret while the old one keeps working
GET /v1/events?since=… → a pull-based backstop: a partner that was down can list what it missed

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. The invoice service writes the paid invoice and an outbox row in one transaction.
  2. A relay publishes outbox rows to a durable event log and marks them sent.
  3. Fan-out matches each event against subscriptions for the same business, creating one delivery per endpoint.
  4. Workers sign and POST each delivery, one lane per endpoint, with a hard timeout.
  5. A 2xx completes the delivery; anything else schedules a retry with backoff and jitter.
  6. After the final attempt the delivery is dead-lettered, the owner is notified, and it stays replayable.
5
High-Level Design

Three stages with different jobs. Recording the event is transactional and never waits on the network. Delivery is isolated per endpoint, so the slowest customer only slows themselves. Failure handling moves retries out of the live path entirely, into a scheduler that brings each one back when it is due.

6
Deep Dives

Five below: (a) why delivery can only be at-least-once, (b) signing and replay protection, (c) retries that don't stampede, (d) one dead endpoint must not stall the rest, and (e) thin events and ordering — then the edge cases, including the one that turns webhooks into an attack on your own network.

Record, deliver, fail safely. The outbox makes emitting an event part of the business transaction without making the transaction wait on anyone's server. Per-endpoint lanes keep a slow or dead endpoint from consuming the shared worker pool, and retries return through the scheduler rather than blocking the head of a live queue.
A healthy delivery
  1. Invoice inv_118 is paid; the event is recorded with the payment itself.
  2. Fan-out finds one matching endpoint for that business.
  3. A worker signs and POSTs it; the partner verifies the signature and replies 200 in 80 ms.
  4. The delivery is marked succeeded, with the attempt visible in the partner's dashboard.
The partner's server is down for six hours
  1. The first attempt fails; the delivery is scheduled for 10 seconds later, then a minute, then five.
  2. Meanwhile every other partner's events flow normally — this endpoint's lane is the only one waiting.
  3. The server comes back; the next scheduled retry succeeds, and its backlog drains at a capped rate rather than all at once.
  4. Nothing was lost, nothing was delayed for anyone else, and the partner can see exactly what happened.
Key deep dive — why delivery can only be at-least-once
FREvery event reaches every endpointNFRNo event lost
Thought process
  1. The sender only knows a delivery succeeded when it receives a 2xx. Silence means nothing either way.
  2. A receiver can process the event and then fail to answer — its response times out, the connection drops, or it crashes after committing.
  3. From the sender's side that is indistinguishable from never having received it. The only safe choice is to send it again.
  4. So duplicates are not a bug to eliminate; they are the price of never losing an event. Exactly-once delivery across a network you don't control isn't on offer.
  5. What makes duplicates harmless is on the receiving side: every event carries a stable id, and receivers record the ids they've processed — the same idempotency idea as the payment API.
Illustration — the duplicate no sender can prevent
  1. attempt 1

    platform POSTs event evt_7f3

  2. receiver

    processes it — marks the invoice paid in its own system

  3. response

    the connection drops before the 200 arrives; the platform sees a timeout

  4. attempt 2

    platform correctly retries evt_7f3 — the receiver now has it twice

Receiver without dedupe

records the payment twice — a customer's books are now wrong

Receiver with dedupe

evt_7f3 already seen → reply 200, do nothing

The platform's documentation should say this in the first paragraph: events may arrive more than once; deduplicate on the event id. A receiver that isn't told will assume exactly-once and be wrong on its first bad network day.

Key deep dive — signing, and replay protection
FRProve it came from the platform
Thought process
  1. A webhook endpoint is a public URL. Anyone who finds it can POST a convincing fake "invoice paid" event to it.
  2. So each delivery is signed with a secret shared only between the platform and that endpoint: an HMAC-SHA256 over the event id, a timestamp and the raw body.
  3. The receiver recomputes the HMAC and compares it in constant time. A match proves who sent it and that nothing was altered.
  4. A valid signature can still be captured and resent later. Including the timestamp in the signed content — and rejecting anything older than a few minutes — closes that replay window.
  5. Rotating a secret must not break delivery: during the overlap the platform signs with both secrets, and the receiver accepts either.
Illustration — what is signed, and what the receiver checks
POST /webhooks/mfc  HTTP/1.1
webhook-id:        evt_7f3
webhook-timestamp: 1759059600
webhook-signature: v1,K5oZfzN95Z9UVu1EsfQmfVNQhnkZ2pj9o9NDN/H/pI4=

signed content = "evt_7f3" + "." + "1759059600" + "." + raw_body
signature      = base64( HMAC-SHA256(endpoint_secret, signed content) )
  1. read the raw body bytes — before any JSON parsing
  2. recompute the HMAC over id · timestamp · raw body
  3. compare in constant time (hmac.Equal in Go) — never ==
  4. reject if the timestamp is more than ~5 minutes old or in the future
  5. deduplicate on webhook-id, reply 2xx quickly, process asynchronously
The bug nearly every receiver hits once

Parsing the JSON and re-serialising it before verifying. Key order, whitespace and number formatting change, the bytes differ, and every valid signature fails. Verify first, against exactly the bytes that arrived.

These header names follow the Standard Webhooks specification. Using an existing spec means partners can verify with published libraries instead of reverse-engineering yours.

  • Why not only an IP allowlist or mTLS — publishing stable egress IPs is a useful extra, and some partners will want it, but it proves where a request came from, not that its body is intact. Signatures do both, and work behind any proxy.
  • Asymmetric signatures are an option — signing with a private key (for example Ed25519) lets receivers verify with a public key, so there is no shared secret for either side to leak.
Key deep dive — retries that don't stampede
FRReach an endpoint that is down for a dayNFRDon't flatten a recovering endpoint
Thought process
  1. Most failures are brief — a deploy, a restart, a blip — so the first retries should come quickly.
  2. Some outages last hours. Retrying every few seconds for hours wastes effort and hammers a server that is trying to recover, so the gaps grow: exponential backoff.
  3. If thousands of deliveries failed at the same moment, identical backoff brings them all back at the same moment too. Adding random jitter to each gap spreads them out.
  4. The response decides what happens next: 5xx, timeouts and refused connections are retried; 429 waits for Retry-After; 410 Gone means the endpoint was deliberately removed, so stop and disable it.
  5. Retries have to end somewhere. After the last attempt the delivery is dead-lettered, not dropped: the owner is told, and it can be replayed once the endpoint is fixed.
Illustration — ten attempts over about three days
AttemptWait before itTime since the event
1—immediately
210 s10 s
31 min1 min 10 s
45 min6 min 10 s
530 min36 min 10 s
62 h2 h 36 min
76 h8 h 36 min
812 h20 h 36 min
924 h1 day 20 h 36 min
1024 h2 days 20 h 36 min then dead letter

Each wait gets ±20% random jitter. Without it, the thousands of deliveries that failed during the same outage would all retry in the same second — and the endpoint that just came back up would go straight back down.

  • Schedule retries by time, not by sleeping — a worker that sleeps between attempts is a worker doing nothing. Store next_attempt_at and let a scheduler release deliveries when they're due.
  • Drain a backlog at a capped rate — an endpoint that was down for six hours may have thousands of events waiting. Deliver them at a limited rate that backs off on 429, not all at once.
Key deep dive — one dead endpoint must not stall the rest
NFRA slow endpoint only slows itself
Thought process
  1. The obvious design is one queue and a pool of workers. It fails in a specific, predictable way.
  2. Not all failures cost the same. A refused connection fails in milliseconds. A server that silently drops packets makes every attempt wait for the full timeout — and that is the dangerous one.
  3. Little's Law gives the cost: workers held = arrival rate × time each is held. An endpoint receiving 50 events a second, each waiting 10 seconds, holds 500 workers — more than the entire pool of 200.
  4. With one shared queue, every other partner's events now wait behind that one customer. Their webhooks go late because someone else's server is broken.
  5. The fix is a per-endpoint concurrency limit — each endpoint gets its own lane with at most a few requests in flight. A broken endpoint then backs up only its own lane.
Illustration — the same broken endpoint, two designs
One shared queue
workers the dead endpoint wants500
workers that exist200
  • 50 events/s × 10 s timeout = 500 workers held
  • the whole pool is waiting on one customer — everyone's webhooks go late
A lane per endpoint, 5 in flight
workers the dead endpoint can hold5
workers left for everyone else195
  • that endpoint's throughput drops to 0.5 deliveries/s — only its own backlog grows
  • every other partner is unaffected

This is the bulkhead pattern from the API gateway and the arithmetic from the Scale Ladder, applied to outbound calls. Latency is load: a slow dependency consumes capacity exactly as extra traffic would.

  • Keep timeouts short — receivers are asked to acknowledge quickly and process asynchronously, so a 10-second timeout is generous. A 60-second one would multiply the damage above by six.
  • Consistently failing endpoints move to a slow lane — after a run of failures an endpoint is probed at a low rate instead of receiving full traffic, until it recovers.
Key deep dive — thin events, and why order isn't guaranteed
FREvery event reaches every endpoint
Thought process
  1. Retries reorder events. If invoice.updated fails once and invoice.paid succeeds first, the receiver sees them backwards.
  2. Guaranteeing order would mean holding every later event for an endpoint until an earlier one succeeds — so one failing event would block that endpoint's entire stream. Most platforms don't promise order, and say so.
  3. The receiver needs a way to act correctly on events that arrive out of order and late.
  4. One answer is to put a version or timestamp on each resource, so the receiver ignores anything older than what it has.
  5. A simpler one is a thin event: say what happened and to which resource, and let the receiver fetch the current state. Whatever order events arrive in, the fetch always returns the truth.
Illustration — a fat event vs. a thin one
Fat — the whole resource in the payload
{ "type": "invoice.updated",
  "data": { "id": "inv_118", "status": "sent",
            "customer": {…}, "lines": [ … ] } }
  • no extra call for the receiver
  • stale by the time a retry lands
  • full customer data leaves the platform in every delivery and every retry
Thin — what happened, to what
{ "id": "evt_7f3", "type": "invoice.updated",
  "resource": "inv_118",
  "created_at": "2026-09-27T14:03:11Z" }
  • order stops mattering — the fetch returns current state
  • the fetch goes through normal authorization and scopes
  • one extra API call per event

A thin event that is replayed three days late still leads the receiver to the right answer, because it asks for the current invoice rather than trusting a three-day-old copy.

Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • A webhook URL pointed at your own network (SSRF) — a partner registers http://169.254.169.254/… (a cloud metadata service) or an internal hostname, and your delivery workers dutifully call it from inside your network. Allow HTTPS only, refuse private, loopback and link-local addresses, and check the resolved IP at connection time, not just when the URL is registered — otherwise a hostname that resolves to a public IP at registration can resolve to an internal one later. Don't follow redirects, which are another route inside.
  • An endpoint that replies 200 and then fails — the platform can only trust the status code. Delivery history and replay are what let the partner recover from their own bug.
  • A secret rotation — sign with both the old and new secrets during the overlap; the receiver accepts either, and the old one is removed once the partner confirms.
  • A business closes its account — pending deliveries for its endpoints are cancelled and its events purged on the same schedule as the rest of its data.
  • An event that matches no subscription — it is still recorded in the event log, so a partner that subscribes later, or lists events with GET /v1/events, can still find it.
  • A huge endpoint returns from a long outage — its backlog is drained at a capped, 429-aware rate, so recovery doesn't become a second outage.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Never slows the business transactionThe event is an outbox row written in the same transaction; publishing and delivery happen afterwards, off the request path.
No event lostOutbox, durable event log, and deliveries that end in a dead letter rather than being dropped — plus a pull-based events API as a backstop.
One slow endpoint only slows itselfA lane per endpoint with a small in-flight cap, so a blackholed server holds 5 workers instead of 500.
Recovering endpoints aren't flattenedExponential backoff with jitter, and backlogs drained at a capped rate that honours 429.
Receivers can trust what arrivesHMAC over id, timestamp and raw body; a short timestamp tolerance against replay; dedupe on the event id.
Never reaches the internal networkHTTPS only, resolved IPs checked at connect time against private ranges, and redirects refused.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
At-least-once deliveryReceivers must deduplicate, in exchange for never losing an event. Exactly-once isn't available across a network you don't control.
No ordering guaranteeReceivers must tolerate reordering, in exchange for one failing event never blocking an endpoint's whole stream.
Thin vs. fat eventsAn extra API call per event, in exchange for current data, normal authorization, and less data leaving the platform.
Per-endpoint lanesMore scheduling machinery than one queue, in exchange for fairness: a broken customer can't slow the rest.
A finite retry windowEvents can end in a dead letter after about three days, in exchange for bounded work — with replay so nothing is actually gone.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Recording eventsPostgreSQL transactional outbox, relayed to Kafka as the durable, replayable event log
Retry schedulingRedis sorted set scored by next_attempt_at, or a delayed queue such as SQS delay seconds
Per-endpoint concurrencya semaphore per endpoint in Redis, or partitioning deliveries by endpoint so each lane has its own consumer
HTTP client in Gonet/http with a client Timeout, CheckRedirect returning http.ErrUseLastResponse, and a net.Dialer Control hook that rejects private IPs at connect time
Signingcrypto/hmac with hmac.Equal; the Standard Webhooks spec for header names and format
Buy instead of buildSvix — webhook sending as a service, with an open-source server
Worked Example AG — Five Products, One To-Do List

Design a Unified Task Inbox Across Independent Products

push vs. pull · events that arrive twice, late, or never · counts that stay right · one product down, inbox still up
Click to expand

A company uses several separate business products — HR, attendance, expenses, payables, contracts — and each one asks employees to do things: approve a request, fix a submission that was sent back, submit a form. Without a shared view, employees log in to each product to find out what's waiting and get notifications from all of them. The goal is one home screen listing every open task from every product, while each product stays the owner of its own workflow.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • One list of the user's open tasks from every product, in the organization they're currently using.
  • Two tabs: tasks awaiting my approval, and my own items that were sent back to me — each with a count badge.
  • Clicking a task opens it in the product that owns it, where the action happens.
  • A task disappears soon after it's handled — wherever it was handled.
  • A user who belongs to several organizations sees only the selected organization's tasks.
Non-functional
  • The home screen loads quickly, however many products feed it.
  • One product being down must not blank the inbox.
  • Never show a task the user isn't allowed to see.
  • A new task appears within seconds; slightly stale beats unavailable.
  • Month-end approval rushes arrive as bursts of thousands of tasks.

The second NFR decides the architecture. An aggregator is a front door: if it depends on every product being up at the same moment, it is less reliable than any one of them.

2
Core Entities
  • Task (product, source_id, org_id, kind, title, deep_link, status, source_version, due_at) — a pointer to work that lives in a product. (product, source_id) is its identity.
  • TaskAssignee (product, source_id, user_id) — who can act on it. One task, possibly several candidate approvers.
  • ProductFeed (product, last_event_at, schema_version) — how fresh each product's data is, and which event format it sends.

kind is approval, sent_back or to_submit. status is open or done — done tasks are kept as tombstones, for a reason explained in deep dive (b).

3
API

query inbox(orgId, tab, first, after) → a page of tasks, newest or most urgent first
query inboxCounts(orgId) → the badge numbers for each tab
topic task-events → products publish created, updated and done events
GET /internal/tasks?changed_since=T → each product's reconciliation endpoint

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. An expense report is submitted; the expenses product saves it and an outbox row in one transaction.
  2. The outbox relay publishes task.created for the manager who must approve it.
  3. The inbox ingester upserts the task and its assignee, keyed by (product, source_id).
  4. The manager's home screen reads tasks and counts from the inbox store in one indexed query.
  5. The manager clicks through, approves inside the expenses product, and a task.done event closes it in the inbox.
5
High-Level Design

Products push task changes as events into a stream; the inbox keeps its own read model and serves the home screen from it. Reading never touches the products, so their outages and slow responses stay out of the page load. Actions always happen in the owning product, reached by a deep link — the inbox is an index of work, not a second copy of each workflow. Every key and index leads with the organization, events are taken in turns across organizations, and the largest organization runs in a cell of its own — so one company's month-end never sits in front of another's.

6
Deep Dives

Six below: (a) push vs. pull, (b) events that arrive twice, late, or never, (c) counts and group approvals, (d) permissions and organizations, (e) degrading when a product is down, and (f) many organizations of very different sizes — then the edge cases.

Products publish task changes through their own outboxes; the ingester takes turns across organizations and applies each event idempotently to a read model the home screen queries directly. The largest organization's events are routed to a cell of its own, so its month-end burst never sits in front of anyone else's. Two dashed loops keep it honest: deep links send every action back to the product that owns it, and a reconciliation sweep repairs anything the event path missed. The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them. The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them.
Illustration — from a product's change to the home screen, step by step
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
1a product saves its change and an outbox row in one transaction; the relay publishes task.created to the event stream, keyed by organizationproduct DB · Kafkanothing lost; at least once
2the largest organization's events are routed to its own cell's topic; everyone else's stay on the shared oneKafkaisolation its month-end burst stays in its own lane
3the ingester consumes in turns across organizations, within an ingest quota per organizationKafka · ingesterfairness a small company's task never waits behind a big burst
4it upserts the task and its assignees, applying an event only if its version is newer; done stays as a tombstoneInbox storeidempotent duplicates and late events change nothing
5a manager opens the home screen; the GraphQL API takes organization and user from the tokenGraphQL APIno way to ask for another organization
6one indexed read returns both tabs and their countsInbox storethe list and the badge come from the same rows
7clicking a task follows a deep link into the owning product, where the action happens; its task.done event then travels steps 1–4 and closes the taskthe producteach workflow lives in exactly one place
8meanwhile the reconciler asks each product what changed since T — per organization, rate-capped — and repairs any event that was lostproducts · Inbox storea lost event is repaired, not permanent

The numbers match the ones on the diagram above. Dashed red lines are the route to a dedicated cell, and are described in the step where the choice is made.

A normal morning
  1. A manager opens the home screen: 7 to approve, 1 sent back.
  2. One indexed query returns both tabs and their counts.
  3. She clicks an expense report, approves it in the expenses product, and returns.
  4. Within seconds the task is gone and the count reads 6.
The expenses product is down
  1. The home screen still loads, from the inbox's own store.
  2. No expenses events have arrived for 12 minutes, so its tasks are marked as possibly out of date.
  3. Tasks from the other four products are fully current.
  4. When expenses recovers, its backlog of events drains and the banner clears.
Key deep dive — push vs. pull
NFROne product down, inbox still upNFRLoads quickly
Thought process
  1. The obvious design is to pull: when the page loads, ask every product for this user's tasks, in parallel, and merge the answers.
  2. Pulling makes the page as slow as the slowest product and as fragile as all of them combined — every page view depends on every product at once.
  3. It also puts a new query on every product: "all open tasks for this user in this organization", served on every home-screen load.
  4. Pushing turns it around: each product publishes task changes as they happen, and the inbox keeps its own copy — a read model built for exactly this screen.
  5. The price is eventual consistency and a reliable event path from every product. Both are manageable, and deep dive (b) is how.
Illustration — the same home screen, both designs
Pull — call five products on every load
downtime / month, one product at 99.9%43 min
downtime / month, page needing all five~3.6 h
  • availability multiplies: 0.9995 ≈ 99.5%
  • latency is the slowest of five — about 1 load in 20 hits at least one call in its slowest 1%
  • every page view is five queries on five products
Push — products publish, the inbox keeps a read model
  • one indexed query, on one store the inbox controls
  • a product outage makes its tasks stale, not the page unavailable
  • products pay per task change, not per page view
  • eventual consistency — a handled task may linger for a few seconds
  • every product must publish events reliably

The common hybrid: push for the list and counts, pull only for the one task the user opens — at that point the product is asked directly, so the action is always taken against the source of truth.

Key deep dive — events that arrive twice, late, or never
FRHandled tasks disappearNFRNever lose a task
Thought process
  1. Products publish at least once, so the inbox will see duplicates. Every event is applied as an upsert keyed by (product, source_id), so seeing it twice changes nothing.
  2. Events can arrive out of order. Each carries the task's source_version; the ingester applies an event only if it is newer than what it already stored.
  3. A "done" event must not be undone by a late "created". Done tasks are kept as tombstones rather than deleted, so a late event finds a newer version and is ignored.
  4. Some events will simply be lost — a bug, a misconfigured product. A periodic sweep asks each product for open tasks changed since the last sweep and repairs any difference.
  5. The click is the final safety net: the product decides. If the task was already handled, the product says so and the inbox closes it.
Illustration — why "done" must be a tombstone, not a delete
  1. event 1

    task.created v1 arrives → stored, open

  2. event 3

    task.done v3 arrives → marked done at v3

  3. event 2

    task.updated v2 arrives late — retried after a network error

Delete on done

v2 finds no row, is treated as new, and resurrects a task that was already approved

Tombstone on done

v2 finds the row at v3, is older, and is ignored

INSERT INTO tasks (product, source_id, status, source_version, …)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, …)
