  • Some permissions come from relationships: a manager approves expenses for their own team; everyone can see their own payslip.
  • Pre-hire, active and departed members get different access; departed members see only their own documents.
  • The interface shows only what the person can do, and denials say why.
Non-functional
  • Every product enforces the same rules — no product quietly more permissive than another.
  • A page making dozens of checks stays fast; checks add microseconds, not a network call each.
  • A removal, or a plan expiring, takes effect within minutes.
  • Deny by default: a rule that fails to load denies, it doesn't allow.
  • Sensitive decisions are audited: who was allowed or denied what, and why.

The first NFR is what goes wrong in practice. When each product writes its own permission code, they drift — and the most permissive one becomes the real policy.

2
Core Entities
  • Entitlement (org_id, product, plan, status, seats, valid_until) — what the organization has paid for; status is trial, active or expired.
  • RoleGrant (membership_id, role, scope?) — a role within one organization, optionally limited to an office or department.
  • Policy (action, rule, version) — the rule for an action, written once and shared by every product.
  • Relationship (subject, relation, object) — facts like "Nadia manages the Sales team" that some rules depend on.

Membership status — pre-hire, active, departed — comes from the multi-organization identity design. Access control reads it; it doesn't own it.

3
API

authorize(subject, action, resource) → allow | deny(reason) → a library call inside each service, not a network hop
GET /me/capabilities?product=… → the actions this person can take, for the interface to show or hide
PUT /members/{id}/roles → grant or revoke a role, with an optional scope
event entitlement.changed → pushed to every service when a plan starts, changes or expires

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. Nadia, a manager in Org B, tries to approve Ravi's expense report.
  2. The expenses service calls authorize in-process, with Nadia's token claims and the report.
  3. Entitled: Org B's expenses plan is active. Allowed: Nadia has the manager role, and manages Ravi's team. State: Nadia's membership is active.
  4. All three say yes — the approval goes ahead, and the decision is recorded in the audit log.
  5. If Org B's plan had expired, the answer would be "deny: plan expired", and the button would already have been greyed out with that reason.
5
High-Level Design

Rules are written once, as policy, and evaluated by an engine that runs inside every service. The engine answers three questions from three sources — entitlements, roles and relationships, membership state — plus facts about the resource itself. Its data is synced ahead of time, so a check costs microseconds; changes that must take effect at once are pushed. The engine's data, its change events and its audit trail are all organized by organization, with a separate lane for changes that can't wait — and the largest organizations run in a cell of their own.

6
Deep Dives

Six below: (a) three questions, three owners, (b) roles, scopes and relationships, (c) where the decision runs, (d) plans that change under you, (e) filtering lists, not just items, and (f) thousands of organizations, one policy engine — then the edge cases.

A decision is the combination of three independent answers, each from the system that owns it, evaluated by the same engine in every service. The engine's data is organized by organization and synced over two lanes — critical changes that can't wait, and bulk ones that can — and the resource-level question is answered inside the query, so a list never shows what a single check would have denied. Decisions are logged per organization, and the largest organization runs in a cell of its own. The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them. The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them.
Illustration — from a change to a decision, step by step
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
1an owner system changes something — a plan, a role, a membership — and publishes an event keyed by organization, on the critical lane if it can't wait (removal, plan expiry), otherwise on the bulk lane; the largest organization's events go to its cell's own topicowner stores · Kafkaisolation an import never delays a dismissal
2the engine in each service applies the events for the organizations it is serving to its local dataLocal dataa check never needs the network
3a starting service loads the versioned snapshot for its organizations, then catches up from eventsSnapshots · Local dataa new instance starts already correct
4a request arrives: the engine asks its three questions from local data — entitled, allowed, active — and allows, or denies with a reasonProduct servicesscale microseconds per check; deny if data is missing
5the rule also becomes part of the query — organization and scope in the WHERE clause — so pages, counts and order cover only permitted rowsProduct DBlists never leak
6after the reply, the decision — who, what, which resource, result, reason — is appended to the decision log, keyed by organizationNoSQLauditing never slows a decision

The numbers match the ones on the diagram above. Dashed red lines are the route to a dedicated cell, and are described in the step where the choice is made.

Allowed
  1. Nadia opens Ravi's expense report and clicks approve.
  2. Entitled, allowed, active — all yes, evaluated in microseconds.
  3. The approval runs; the decision and its reasons are audited.
  4. The same rule, in the same engine, would give the same answer in any other product.
The trial ends at midnight
  1. Org C's trial of the expenses product expires at 00:00.
  2. The subscription service pushes entitlement.changed; every engine updates within seconds.
  3. Submitting new expenses is denied: "plan expired". Existing data stays readable for a grace period.
  4. Nothing was deleted — paying restores everything as it was.
Key deep dive — three questions, three owners
FRPlan, role and status all matterNFRSame rules everywhere
Thought process
  1. "Can this person do this?" is really three separate questions, and each has a different owner.
  2. Is the organization entitled? The subscription system knows which products and plans a company has, and whether a trial is running or has expired.
  3. Is the person allowed? Roles, their scopes, and relationships like "manages this team" — owned by the membership and organization data.
  4. Is the membership in a state that allows it? Pre-hire, active or departed — owned by the membership lifecycle.
  5. The answer is yes only if all three are yes. Keeping them separate means each can change on its own — a plan expiring shouldn't require touching anyone's roles.
Illustration — "publish a company announcement", five people
WhoEntitled?Allowed?State?Result
full admin, plan activeyesyesactiveallow
full admin, trial expirednoyesactivedeny: plan expired
employee, plan activeyesnoactivedeny: needs admin
full admin who has leftyesyesdeparteddeny: not active
admin hired, not startedyesyespre-hiredeny: not active

Each "no" names its own reason. That's what lets the interface grey out a button with the right explanation — "your company's plan has expired" is a very different message from "only admins can do this".

Key deep dive — roles, scopes and relationships
FRScoped rolesFROwn team, own payslip
Thought process
  1. Plain roles — admin, manager, employee — can't express most real rules. A manager can approve expenses, but only for their own team.
  2. Adding a role for every case ("manager of Sales", "manager of Finance", …) explodes into hundreds of roles nobody can reason about.
  3. Three building blocks cover it instead. A role says what kind of thing someone may do. A scope limits where — one office, one department. A relationship ties them to a specific resource — their team, their own record.
  4. A rule combines them: "a manager may approve an expense if they manage the submitter's team". The rule is written once; the facts it needs are data.
Illustration — which building block each rule needs
RuleRoleScopeRelationship
admins can change company settingsadmin——
HR admins can edit employees in their officeHR adminoffice = Lisbon—
managers approve their own team's expensesmanager—manages submitter's team
everyone sees their own payslip——is the payslip's owner
payroll admins see everyone's salarypayroll admin——

In the vocabulary interviewers use: roles alone are RBAC, adding attributes like office is ABAC, and rules about who is connected to what are relationship-based access control. Most real systems need all three, used for what each is good at.

Key deep dive — where the decision runs
NFRMicroseconds, not a network callNFRRemoval within minutes
Thought process
  1. One obvious design: a central authorization service that every product calls for every check. One place for the rules, always current.
  2. But a single page can make dozens of checks — which buttons to show, which rows to include — and each call adds network time. Forty checks at 5 ms each is 200 ms, before any real work. And if that service is down, every product is down.
  3. The other option: the same engine as a library inside each service, evaluating shared policy against data synced to it ahead of time. Forty checks take under a millisecond, and there is no extra dependency at request time.
  4. The price is freshness — the local copy can lag. Ordinary changes arrive as events within seconds; the few that can't wait, like removing someone or a plan expiring, are pushed immediately.
  5. Deny by default applies here too: an engine that hasn't loaded its policy or data refuses, rather than allowing everything.
Illustration — forty checks on one page
central service, 5 ms per call200 ms
in-process engine, ~20 µs per check0.8 ms
A network call per check
  • always the latest data
  • latency grows with every check on the page
  • its outage is every product's outage
Evaluate locally, sync the data
  • microseconds per check, no extra dependency
  • the same policy, so the same answer, everywhere
  • data may lag by seconds — so critical changes are pushed

The numbers are illustrative; measure your own. The argument doesn't depend on them — a check that needs the network costs orders of magnitude more than one that doesn't, and it adds a dependency. It is the same trade as the gateway's cached keys in the API gateway example.

Key deep dive — plans that change under you
FRTrial, paid, expired, seatsNFRTakes effect within minutes
Thought process
  1. Entitlements change on their own schedule: a trial ends at midnight, a payment fails, a company upgrades mid-month.
  2. An expired plan must not destroy anything. The common answer is a grace period: data stays readable, creating new work stops, and paying again restores everything.
  3. Seat limits are a shared counter under concurrency. Two admins adding the 50th and 51st employee at the same moment must not both succeed on a 50-seat plan — the data correctness toolkit's lost-update problem.
  4. So seats are taken with a conditional update that succeeds only while seats remain. The loser gets a clear "no seats left", not a silent 51st seat.
Illustration — one plan's life, and a seat taken safely
  1. trial

    everything available for 30 days

  2. active

    paid; features match the plan, up to its seat count

  3. expired

    read-only grace period: existing data visible, nothing new created

  4. restored

    payment resumes; nothing was lost

UPDATE entitlements SET seats_used = seats_used + 1
WHERE org_id = $1 AND product = $2 AND seats_used < seats;
-- 1 row: a seat is yours · 0 rows: no seats left — say so
Key deep dive — filtering lists, not just items
NFRNever show what a check would deny
Thought process
  1. Checking one item — "may Nadia see this expense?" — is straightforward. Lists are where access control quietly breaks.
  2. The tempting approach fetches a page of 20 and removes what the user can't see. Pages then come back ragged — 3 items, then none, then 7 — and an empty page no longer means there is nothing more.
  3. Worse, counts and totals computed before the filter reveal things — "20 results" when you can see 3 tells you 17 exist.
  4. So the rule becomes part of the query: an HR admin scoped to Lisbon gets a query that already filters to Lisbon. Pagination, counts and sorting are all correct, because they run on rows the user may see.
  5. Fields need the same care. Salary is visible to payroll admins and to the employee themselves; for anyone else the field is left out of the response, not sent and hidden by the interface.
Illustration — filter after fetching, or filter in the query
Fetch 20, then filter
  • each page shows whatever survived the filter — 3 rows, then 0, then 7 — so the user can't tell whether more exist
  • "20 results" reveals 17 the user can't see
  • one permission check per row
The rule is part of the query
SELECT … FROM employees
WHERE org_id = $1
  AND office = ANY($2)      -- from the admin's scope
ORDER BY name LIMIT 20;
  • full pages, correct counts, correct order

In a GraphQL API, field rules can live in the schema itself — a directive on salary that resolves to null unless the caller may see it — so no resolver can forget.

Key deep dive — thousands of organizations, one policy engine
NFROne organization's changes never delay another'sNFRData and rules stay per organization
Thought process
  1. The engine runs inside every service and decides from data it holds locally. With thousands of organizations that data has to be organized by org_id: each engine keeps only the organizations its service is currently serving, loads an organization on first use and drops it when idle. Memory follows active organizations, not the whole customer list.
  2. Sync events are keyed by org_id, so one organization's changes stay in order. They travel in two lanes: critical — removals, suspensions, plan expiry — and bulk — role edits, imports, re-organizations. An organization changing 50,000 roles at once fills only the bulk lane, and even there organizations take turns; a dismissal in the critical lane still lands in seconds.
  3. Relationship data is partitioned per organization too. "Who manages whom" lives in a store per organization — one store per tenant in the terms OpenFGA and SpiceDB use — so a huge org chart never slows checks for a small company, and one company's relationships can never be traversed from another's.
  4. Policy is shared code, so a bad policy is the one thing that could hit everyone. Rollout is therefore per organization: a new version goes to a few small organizations first, is widened in steps, and can be rolled back per cell.
  5. Sensitive decisions write an audit record, which at this scale is a high-volume stream. It goes to a store keyed by organization and time, written after the decision is returned and expired by each organization's retention — a busy organization's audit writes can lag, but they never delay a decision.
  6. The largest or regulated organizations run in a cell — their own change topic, snapshots and decision log, with the product instances that serve them loading only their data (what a cell contains) — so a bulk import in the largest can never queue behind, or in front of, anyone else's changes.
Illustration — a dismissal during someone else's import

One company changes 50,000 roles at once. Another company removes a dismissed employee a moment later. Sync handles 1,000 events a second.

dismissal · one shared lanewaits ~50 s
dismissal · critical laneunder a second

and the import barely notices: it takes 50.001 s instead of 50.0 s

The rate is an assumption. What matters is that the events that must be fast never share a line with the events that are merely many.

Illustration — what is organized by organization
PieceOrganized byWhy
sync eventsorg_id, in two lanesorder per organization; critical never waits behind bulk
engine dataan organization slice, loaded on demandmemory follows active organizations
relationshipsa store per organizationa large org chart can't slow others, and can't be traversed across
decision logorg_id and time, with expirya busy organization's writes lag alone
policy rollouta few small organizations first, then widera bad policy touches few before it is caught

The same pool-and-silo idea as the tenant isolation example, applied to the data the engine decides from.

  • An organization with a very deep org chart — its relationship store is its own; deep "manages" chains slow only its own checks, and the depth is capped.
  • A cell that falls behind on sync — its engines keep deciding from the last good data, and the critical lane is monitored separately — a stale plan is a warning, a stale removal is an alarm.
Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • Outside advisors — an accounting firm working for many client companies gets a limited advisor role in each, granted by the client, and time-limited.
  • A role removed mid-session — roles are read from synced membership data at decision time, not frozen into a long-lived token, so the change applies within minutes.
  • The interface hides a button, but the API is called anyway — hiding is a courtesy; every request is authorized on the server regardless.
  • Custom roles that multiply — companies want their own roles; they're built from the same permissions, capped in number, and still evaluated by the same engine.
  • Support staff helping a customer — never a standing super-role; a time-limited, reasoned, audited grant, as in the tenant isolation example.
  • A policy change that locks everyone out — policies are versioned and tested against recorded decisions before rollout, and can be rolled back.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Same rules in every productPolicy written once and evaluated by the same engine inside every service.
Fast pages with many checksLocal evaluation against synced data — microseconds per check, no network call.
Changes within minutesEvents for ordinary changes; immediate pushes for removals and plan expiry.
Deny by defaultMissing policy or data refuses; every "no" carries its reason.
Lists never leakRules become query filters, so pages, counts and ordering only ever cover permitted rows.
AuditedSensitive decisions logged with the subject, action, resource, result and reason.
One organization's changes never delay another'sSync keyed by organization in a critical and a bulk lane, engine data loaded per organization, a relationship store per organization, and a cell for the largest.
A bad policy can't hit everyone at oncePolicies are versioned and rolled out to a few small organizations first, with rollback per cell.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Local evaluation over a central serviceData can lag by seconds, in exchange for microsecond checks and no request-time dependency.
Three separate questionsMore concepts to explain, in exchange for plans, roles and status each changing independently.
Relationships instead of more rolesRules that need facts about the resource, in exchange for not inventing a role for every team.
Grace period on expirySome read access after payment stops, in exchange for never destroying a customer's data.
Filtering in the queryRules must translate into query conditions, in exchange for correct lists, pages and counts.
Data organized per organizationMore stores and lanes to run, in exchange for a large organization's import, org chart or audit volume never slowing a small one's checks.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Policy engineOPA (Rego, embeddable in Go) or Cedar, evaluated in-process
Relationship checksOpenFGA or SpiceDB, Zanzibar-style services for "who is related to what"
Field rules in GraphQLschema directives in gqlgen that resolve restricted fields to null
Entitlement changesevents from the subscription system over Kafka or SNS, cached with a short lifetime in each service
Isolation per organizationone store per tenant in OpenFGA or SpiceDB; a critical and a bulk topic in Kafka keyed by organization; the decision log in a NoSQL store keyed by organization and time with a TTL
Worked Example AL — Fifty Thousand Payslips at 9 a.m.

Design Payslip and Tax Document Distribution

render ahead, not on view · publish all at once · nobody else's payslip, ever · corrections as new versions, kept for years
Click to expand

Once payroll is confirmed, every employee gets a payslip, and once a year a tax withholding slip. They are the most sensitive documents most people receive, they are legal records companies must keep for years, and they are all released at the same moment on payday — when a large share of employees open them within minutes. A mistake here isn't a slow page; it's one person reading another person's salary.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • When payroll is confirmed, produce a document for every employee in the run.
  • Release them at a chosen time — for example 9:00 on payday — and notify each employee.
  • Employees view them on a phone or browser and download a PDF.
  • A mistake is fixed by issuing a corrected version; the employee is told, and the original stays on record.
  • Departed employees can still retrieve their own documents for a set period.
Non-functional
  • No one can ever retrieve another person's document.
  • Everything is generated and checked before the release time — employees never see a half-finished run.
  • The payday rush is fast, however many open at once.
  • A document shows exactly what was issued, years later, even after the layout changes.
  • Documents are kept for the legally required period, encrypted, and then deleted.

The fourth NFR quietly rules out the design most people start with — rendering the payslip from current data whenever someone opens it.

2
Core Entities
  • PayrollRun (run_id, org_id, period, status, publish_at) — status is draft, confirmed, generating, ready, or published.
  • Document (doc_id, run_id, membership_id, type, version, status, storage_key, template_version) — one per employee per run; status is current or superseded.
  • Snapshot (doc_id, data) — the exact figures the document was made from, frozen at confirmation.

Documents belong to a membership, not an email or a name — the explicit link from the multi-organization identity example, which is what keeps two people named Carter from seeing each other's pay.

3
API

POST /runs/{id}/confirm → freeze the data and start generating
GET /runs/{id}/progress → generated, failed, remaining — for the admin
POST /runs/{id}/publish {publish_at} → allowed only once every document is ready
GET /me/documents → the employee's own documents
GET /documents/{id}/download → a short-lived download link, after checking ownership
POST /documents/{id}/reissue → a corrected version

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. On the 20th, HR confirms the October run for 50,000 employees; the figures are frozen as snapshots.
  2. Render workers produce one PDF per employee into private storage — a few minutes of work across the fleet.
  3. The admin sees "50,000 of 50,000 ready" and schedules release for the 25th at 09:00.
  4. At 09:00 the documents become visible and every employee is notified — once.
  5. Maya opens hers; the API checks it is hers and returns a link valid for 60 seconds; the PDF comes straight from storage.
5
High-Level Design

Two phases. Before payday, everything is generated from frozen data and stored privately, but nothing is visible. On payday, release is a single scheduled switch, and the only work per view is an ownership check and a short-lived download link — the file itself is served by storage. Corrections add versions; nothing issued is ever overwritten. Rendering, storage keys, index and release are all per organization, with fair turns on the render queue — and the largest organization runs in a cell of its own.

6
Deep Dives

Five below: (a) render ahead or on view, (b) releasing everything at once, (c) nobody else's payslip, ever, (d) corrections and keeping documents for years, and (e) forty companies, one payday — then the edge cases.

Before payday the pipeline renders every document from frozen data into private storage, taking turns across companies, but nothing is visible. On payday the scheduler makes each company's run visible at once and notifies each employee; opening a document costs one ownership check, and the file itself is fetched straight from storage with a link that expires in a minute. Storage keys, encryption keys and the index are all per organization, and the largest company's whole pipeline runs in a cell of its own. The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them. The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them.
Illustration — from a confirmed run to an opened payslip, step by step
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
1HR confirms the run; payroll creates one render job per employee, in the organization's lane — the largest organization's run goes to its cellPayroll · render queuefairness a small company isn't behind a large run
2the frozen figures are stored as snapshotsDocument indexwhat was issued is what anyone sees, forever
3workers take jobs in turns across organizations and render each from its snapshot and template versionRender workersscale scaled on backlog, days before payday
4each PDF is written once to storage, under the organization's prefix and encrypted with its keyObject storageisolation one prefix, one key per organization
5the document is recorded in the index with owner and version; nothing is visible yetDocument indexnever half a run
6at the publish time the scheduler flips the run to published — one transitionScheduler · indexidempotent visible and notified once
7in the same transaction it queues the "ready" notifications — no amounts, no attachment — through fair lanesNotification systemsalaries never sit in an email
8on payday an employee opens their payslip; the API takes organization and membership from the tokenDocument APIthe request can only ever be theirs
9it checks the organization's request budget, then that the document belongs to the requester in the replica — or answers 404Redis · replicanobody else's payslip, ever
10it returns a signed link valid for 60 seconds, and the PDF comes straight from storageObject storagethe service never streams the files

The numbers match the ones on the diagram above. Dashed red lines are the route to a dedicated cell, and are described in the step where the choice is made.

Payday morning
  1. At 09:00 the run becomes visible; notifications go out.
  2. In the first five minutes, tens of thousands of employees open their payslip.
  3. Each open is one indexed lookup and a signed link — no rendering, no file streaming through the service.
  4. Storage serves the PDFs; the service barely notices.
A mistake is found on the 26th
  1. An allowance was missed for 12 employees.
  2. HR reissues their payslips: each gets version 2, generated from corrected data.
  3. Version 1 is marked superseded but kept; the employees are told a corrected payslip is available.
  4. Years later, both versions — and who issued the correction — are still on record.
Key deep dive — render ahead, or render on view?
NFRExactly what was issued, years laterNFRA fast payday rush
Thought process
  1. Rendering on view looks efficient: no storage, always up to date. For a payslip, "always up to date" is exactly the problem.
  2. A payslip is a record of what was paid. If it's rebuilt from current data and the current template, a later change to an allowance rule or the layout silently changes what a 2023 payslip says.
  3. So the figures are frozen as a snapshot at confirmation, the template version is recorded, and the PDF is rendered once and stored. What was issued is what anyone sees, forever.
  4. Rendering ahead also moves the heavy work off payday: 50,000 documents at about 0.2 seconds each is under three CPU-hours — a few minutes across 50 workers, days before anyone looks.
  5. The in-app view can still be pleasant on a phone: it's drawn from the same frozen snapshot, so it always matches the PDF.
Illustration — the same payslip, three years later
Rendered on every view
  • an allowance rule changed in 2025 → the 2023 payslip now shows a different figure
  • the layout was redesigned → the same payslip looks different each year
  • rendering load lands exactly at 09:00 on payday
Snapshot + render once
  • figures frozen at confirmation; template version recorded
  • the PDF and the in-app view both come from that snapshot
  • rendering happens days earlier — payday only serves files
50,000 × 0.2 s on one worker~2.8 h
the same work on 50 workers~3.3 min

The 0.2 seconds per document is an assumption — measure your own renderer. The conclusion holds across a wide range: generation is a batch job measured in minutes, not something to do while an employee waits.

Key deep dive — releasing everything at once
FRRelease at a chosen timeNFRNever half a run
Thought process
  1. Everyone in a company should get their payslip at the same moment. Releasing each document as it finishes rendering would let some employees see pay while colleagues are still waiting — and questions start.
  2. So generation and release are separate. Documents are created invisible; the run can be scheduled for release only once every document is ready, and any failures are listed for the admin to fix first.
  3. Visibility doesn't need a mass update at 09:00. A document is visible when its run is published and the publish time has passed — checked when documents are listed.
  4. Notifications do need to happen exactly once, at release. That is the same single-transition pattern as the announcement system: one state change from scheduled to published that enqueues the notifications in the same transaction.
Illustration — a run's life, from confirmed to published
  1. confirmed · 20th

    figures frozen; generation starts; nothing visible

  2. generating

    49,988 ready · 12 failed — a new allowance type the template doesn't know yet; fixed and retried

  3. ready

    50,000 of 50,000 — only now can the run be scheduled

  4. published · 25th 09:00

    visible to everyone at once; one notification each

Key deep dive — nobody else's payslip, ever
NFRNo one retrieves another's documentNFRA fast payday rush
Thought process
  1. The classic failure: GET /documents/doc_512 with someone else's ID returns their payslip, because the lookup checked the document exists but not who owns it — BOLA, from the tenant isolation example.
  2. So every lookup includes the owner: the document must belong to the requesting membership, or the answer is 404 — the same response as a document that doesn't exist.
  3. The files live in private storage that nothing can read directly. After the ownership check, the API returns a signed link valid for about a minute. The link works once it's issued, then expires; forwarding it later gets nothing.
  4. That split is also what makes payday cheap: the service does an indexed lookup and signs a link, and the storage service does the heavy lifting of sending the file.
  5. Notifications never carry the payslip. An email says a payslip is ready and links to sign in — no amounts, no attachment — because email gets forwarded, shared and read over shoulders.
Illustration — four layers between a person and someone else's salary
LayerWhat it stops
ownership in every lookupchanging a document ID in the URL — answered with 404, not someone's payslip
private storage + 60-second signed linksa leaked or forwarded link working tomorrow, or anyone reading the storage bucket directly
storage keys prefixed by organization, not guessableone company's files being reachable through another's paths
notifications without contentsa salary sitting in a forwarded email or a shared inbox

Across a platform of 1,000,000 employees, 10% opening in the first five minutes is 100,000 opens — about 333 ownership checks and signed links a second. That is light work for a service, as long as it isn't also rendering documents or streaming the files itself. The assumptions behind the number are stated: 1,000,000 employees, and 10% opening in the first five minutes.

Key deep dive — corrections, and keeping documents for years
FRCorrected versionsNFRKept for the required period, then deleted
Thought process
  1. Payroll mistakes happen after release. Overwriting the PDF would erase what the employee was told and when — exactly what matters if pay is ever disputed.
  2. So a correction is a new version generated from corrected data. The old version is marked superseded, kept, and still visible in the employee's history, labelled as replaced.
  3. The employee is told a corrected document exists, so nobody relies on the old figures without knowing.
  4. Retention is set per document type — payslips and tax slips each have a required keeping period. When it ends, documents are deleted on schedule, unless a legal hold applies to that employee.
  5. Documents are encrypted with a key per organization. Deleting that key makes every copy unreadable, including backups — the crypto-shredding technique from the audit log example, useful when a company leaves.
Illustration — one payslip, corrected once
VersionIssuedStatusWhat the employee sees
v125 Oct, 09:00supersededin history, marked "replaced by a corrected version"
v226 Oct, 15:30currentshown by default, with a note explaining the correction

Both versions keep their own snapshot and template version, so each still shows exactly what it said the day it was issued.

Key deep dive — forty companies, one payday
NFROne company's payday never slows another'sNFRScales with the largest run
Thought process
  1. Payday is shared. Many companies pay on the 25th, and many release at 09:00. A 200,000-employee company and a 40-person one run on the same platform — and the small company's owner still expects the payslips at 09:00.
  2. Rendering is the heavy step, so it gets fairness first. Render jobs go into a lane per company and workers take from the lanes in turn, so a small company's 40 payslips are done in the first turn instead of after 200,000. Workers scale on total backlog days before payday — the scheduled-peak idea from the notification system.
  3. Storage is isolated by construction. Object keys are prefixed by organization, and request-rate limits in object storage apply per prefix, so one company's payday can't use up another's request rate; a very large company's prefix is split further (organization, run, shard) to spread its own load. Each organization also has its own encryption key, so a key problem has a blast radius of one company.
  4. Release is per run, not global. Forty companies at 09:00 are forty independent single transitions, each enqueueing its own notifications through the notification system's fair dispatcher, so one company's 200,000 "ready" messages don't delay another's.
  5. The payday open rush is another per-company hot spot. The Document API is stateless and scales out; ownership lookups lead with org_id and the owner; and each company has a request budget, so a scraper or a bug in one company's integration can't take API capacity from the rest — the multi-tenant rate limiting idea once more.
  6. The largest company gets a cell: its own render queue and workers, bucket and key, index shard and API pool (what a cell contains). Its payday can't affect anyone, and no one else's can affect it.
Illustration — the same render window, one queue vs. fair turns

A company confirms 200,000 payslips while a 40-person company confirms 40. Rendering takes 0.2 s each on 100 workers.

small company · one shared queuewaits ~6.7 min
small company · fair turnsunder a second

and the large run barely notices: 6 min 40.2 s instead of 6 min 40 s

200,000 × 0.2 s is about 11 CPU-hours — roughly 6.7 minutes across 100 workers. The 0.2 s is an assumption; measure your own renderer. The conclusion is about order, and holds across a wide range.

Illustration — what is isolated per organization
PieceIsolated byWhat it prevents
render queuea lane per company, fair turnsa small company waiting behind a large run
object storagea prefix per organization (large ones split further), a key per organizationsharing a request rate; one key exposing everyone
document indexorg_id leads every keyscans that cross companies
Document APIa request budget per companya scraper or bug starving everyone else
releaseone transition per runhalf-published runs, and coupling between companies

The pool-and-silo pattern from the tenant isolation example: share the machinery, never the data, the keys or the queue.

  • A company's run is bigger than expected — its lane simply takes longer to drain, while every other lane is served in turn; workers scale on the backlog.
  • Moving a company into a cell — new runs go to the cell; documents already issued are copied to its bucket and re-keyed, and the old copies are deleted only after the copy is verified.
Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • A departed employee needs last year's tax slip — their membership is departed with access to their own documents until a set date, as in the multi-organization identity example; nothing else in the company is visible.
  • Someone employed by two companies — documents belong to a membership, so each company's payslips appear only while working in that company.
  • A bonus paid mid-month — a separate run with its own document type and release time, never mixed into the monthly one.
  • The template changes in April — new documents use the new version; every earlier document keeps the version it was issued with.
  • Employees without email — the notification is in-app only; the document is the same.
  • Release time across time zones — 09:00 is the company's local time, stored as an instant, like scheduled announcements.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
No one sees another's documentOwnership in every lookup, private storage, short-lived signed links, and notifications without contents.
Never half a runDocuments are created invisible; release is allowed only when all are ready, and happens as one scheduled switch.
A fast paydayRendering happens days earlier; payday is a lookup and a signed link per open, with storage serving the files.
Exactly what was issued, years laterFrozen snapshots, recorded template versions, and PDFs rendered once.
Corrections without losing historyNew versions; the old one kept and marked superseded; the employee told.
Kept, then deletedRetention per document type, legal holds, encryption per organization with key deletion for full erasure.
One company's payday never slows another'sA render lane per company with fair turns, storage prefixes and encryption keys per organization, a request budget per company, and a cell for the largest.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Render aheadStorage for every document, in exchange for records that never change and a payday that only serves files.
All-or-nothing releaseOne failed document can delay a whole run, in exchange for everyone getting their payslip at the same moment.
Short-lived signed linksA link must be requested each time, in exchange for links that are useless once forwarded.
Versions instead of overwritesMore documents to keep, in exchange for a history that stands up in a dispute.
Notifications without contentsOne more tap to see the figures, in exchange for salaries never sitting in email.
Per-organization lanes, prefixes and keysMore queues and keys to manage, and a cell for the largest customer, in exchange for a large payday never delaying a small company's payslips and a problem with one key touching one company.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Document storageAmazon S3 private buckets with presigned URLs, server-side encryption with a key per organization in AWS KMS
Renderinga queue of render jobs (SQS) worked by a pool of PDF renderers — an HTML-to-PDF engine or a PDF library
Index and schedulingPostgreSQL for documents and runs, with the single-transition publish from the announcement example
Retentionstorage lifecycle rules for deletion on schedule, with legal holds taking precedence
Isolation per organizationa lane per company on SQS; S3 prefixes per organization with a KMS key per organization; per-company request budgets as token buckets in Redis
Worked Example AM — Seven Dependencies, One Page

Design a Front-Door Service That Survives Downstream Failures

critical vs. optional · timeouts from a deadline · bulkheads and circuit breakers · stale beats blank · retries that don't pile on
Click to expand

A portal's home page is assembled by one front-door service — often a GraphQL layer — from many services behind it: who the user is, what their company has paid for, their tasks, announcements, documents, attendance, leave balance. Each dependency will be slow or down at some point, and several at once on a bad day. The front door's job is to be more reliable than any combination of them: to show what it can, say plainly what it can't, and never let one sick service take the whole page down with it.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Assemble each page from several services in one request.
  • When a part isn't available, show the rest of the page, with a clear message for that part.
  • Where a slightly old answer is acceptable, show it — labelled with its age.
  • During a service's planned maintenance, say "under maintenance until 05:00" rather than showing an error.
Non-functional
  • The page responds within a fixed deadline — say 400 ms — however slow any one service is.
  • The front door stays up when services behind it don't.
  • A slow service can't use up the front door's own capacity.
  • Failures don't multiply: no retry storms against a service that is already struggling.
  • Security never degrades: when permissions can't be checked, the answer is no.

The last NFR is the boundary on everything else. "Degrade gracefully" applies to showing data — never to deciding who may see it.

2
Core Entities
  • Dependency (name, criticality, timeout, max_in_flight, fallback) — each downstream service and how the front door treats it; criticality is critical or optional.
  • BreakerState (dependency, state, failure_rate, opened_at) — closed, open or half-open, per dependency, per front-door instance.
  • LastGood (dependency, key, value, fetched_at) — the most recent successful answer, for a stale fallback.
  • MaintenanceWindow (dependency, starts_at, ends_at, message) — planned downtime, published in advance by each service.
3
API

query home → one GraphQL query; each optional part is a nullable field, so one failure nulls one field
"errors": [{ "path": ["documents"], "extensions": { "reason": "stale" } }] → partial results say which part degraded and why
GET /dependencies/health → breaker states and maintenance windows, for dashboards and on-call

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. A request arrives with a 400 ms deadline.
  2. The critical calls — identity and entitlements — go first, in parallel; if either fails, the page returns an error, because nothing can be shown safely without them.
  3. The optional calls go out in parallel, each with a timeout taken from what remains of the deadline.
  4. Documents is slow and times out; its last good answer, from 08:42, is shown with that label. Attendance's breaker is open, so it isn't called at all.
  5. The page returns at 400 ms: five parts answered live, one stale, one unavailable.
5
High-Level Design

Every dependency is wrapped in the same four protections: a timeout taken from the page's deadline, a cap on concurrent calls, a circuit breaker, and a fallback. Dependencies are classed as critical or optional; only critical failures fail the page. Retries are limited to idempotent calls within a budget, and planned maintenance is known in advance and shown as such.

6
Deep Dives

Five below: (a) critical vs. optional, (b) timeouts from a deadline, (c) bulkheads and circuit breakers, (d) what may be stale and what must fail closed, and (e) retries and maintenance windows — then the edge cases.

One page, seven dependencies, each behind the same protections. Two are critical — without them the page can't be shown safely. The other five are optional: a slow one times out and falls back to its last good answer, a failing one is skipped by its open breaker, and the page still returns within its deadline.
An ordinary bad morning
  1. The documents service is slow after a deploy.
  2. Its calls time out at their share of the deadline; the page shows documents "as of 08:42".
  3. Nothing else is affected, and no one sees an error page.
  4. When the service recovers, live answers resume on the next request.
Identity is down
  1. The front door can't establish who the user is.
  2. This is not degraded gracefully: the page returns an error and asks the user to try again shortly.
  3. No stale data is shown, because without identity there's no way to know whose data it would be.
  4. This is why the set of critical dependencies is kept as small as possible.
Key deep dive — critical vs. optional
NFRStays up when services don'tNFRSecurity never degrades
Thought process
  1. A page that needs every dependency to succeed is as fragile as all of them combined — availability multiplies, exactly as in the task inbox example.
  2. So the first design decision is a list: which dependencies the page genuinely cannot do without. Usually that is only identity and entitlements — who you are, and what your company is allowed to use.
  3. Everything else is optional. A missing leave balance is an inconvenience; a missing home page is an outage.
  4. Shrinking the critical list is the biggest single reliability improvement available, and it costs nothing but a decision.
Illustration — the same seven services, two ways to depend on them
page needs all 7 (each 99.9%)~5.0 h / month down
page needs only 2 critical~1.4 h / month down
DependencyClassIf it fails
identitycriticalthe page fails — there is no safe way to show anything
entitlementscriticalthe page fails — can't tell which features the company may use
tasks, announcementsoptionalstale if recent enough, otherwise "unavailable right now"
documents, attendance, leaveoptionalthat part shows a message; the rest of the page works

Arithmetic: 0.9997 ≈ 99.3% ≈ 5.0 hours down a month; 0.9992 ≈ 99.8% ≈ 1.4 hours. The optional failures still happen — they just stop being outages.

Key deep dive — timeouts from a deadline
NFRResponds within 400 ms
Thought process
  1. Fixed per-call timeouts don't add up to a page deadline. Seven calls with 2-second timeouts can still make the page wait 2 seconds, or longer if anything runs in sequence.
  2. So the page has one deadline, and every call's timeout is taken from what remains of it — the deadline propagation from the API gateway example.
  3. Calls run in parallel wherever they don't depend on each other. Critical calls go first; optional calls get what's left, minus a margin to assemble and send the response.
  4. The deadline is passed down to each service too, so a service can stop working on a request whose caller has already given up.
  5. For the slowest few percent of requests, a hedged request — sending a second copy of a read when the first hasn't answered by its usual 95th-percentile time — trims the tail for about 5% more load. Only for reads that are safe to repeat.
Illustration — one 400 ms deadline, shared out
  1. 0 ms

    request arrives · deadline = now + 400 ms

  2. 0 – 60 ms

    identity and entitlements, in parallel — both critical

  3. 60 – 310 ms

    five optional calls in parallel, each capped at 250 ms (what remains, minus a 90 ms margin)

  4. 310 ms

    anything still pending uses its fallback — stale, default, or hidden

  5. ≤ 400 ms

    the page is assembled and sent

The 250 ms and 90 ms are example values — choose them from your own services' latency measurements, not from this page.

Key deep dive — bulkheads and circuit breakers
NFRA slow service can't use up the front door
Thought process
  1. A service that hangs is worse than one that fails, because every call to it holds a connection and a worker until the timeout.
  2. Little's Law gives the damage: at 2,000 requests a second, a dependency that hangs for 2 seconds holds 4,000 calls in flight — enough to exhaust the front door's connections and workers, and then every page fails, not just that part.
  3. A bulkhead caps how many calls can be waiting on one dependency. When the cap is reached, further calls fail at once and use their fallback; the rest of the front door keeps its capacity.
  4. A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that keeps failing. After, say, half of the last 20 calls fail, it opens: calls skip straight to the fallback, and the struggling service gets room to recover.
  5. After a pause it goes half-open, lets a few trial calls through, and closes again only if they succeed — so recovery doesn't bring the full load back at once.
Illustration — what one hanging dependency does, with and without a bulkhead
calls held: 2,000/s × 2 s hang4,000
calls held with a bulkhead of 5050
No bulkhead, no breaker
  • every page waits on the hanging service until its timeout
  • connections and workers run out
  • the whole front door stops answering — one service took everything down
Bulkhead + breaker
  • at most 50 calls wait on that service; the rest fail fast to their fallback
  • the breaker opens and stops calling it entirely
  • every other part of the page, and every other page, is unaffected

The cap of 50 and the "half of the last 20 calls" threshold are examples. The shape is what matters: a limit per dependency, and a switch that stops calling what keeps failing — see the circuit breaker in the glossary.

Key deep dive — what may be stale, and what must fail closed
FRStale answers, labelledNFRSecurity never degrades
Thought process
  1. Every fallback is one of three things: an older answer, a safe default, or hiding that part of the page.
  2. An older answer is often the best — the list of announcements from ten minutes ago is still useful. It is kept per user and per dependency, and shown with its age.
  3. It needs a limit. A leave balance from last week is misleading; past a certain age, "unavailable right now" is more honest than a stale number.
  4. And one category must never fall back to an older answer: anything that decides permission. A cached "yes, this person may see payroll" from before they were removed is exactly the answer that must not be reused. When permissions can't be checked, the answer is no.
Illustration — fallbacks by kind of data
DataFallbackWhy
announcements, task liststale, labelled up to ~15 minstill useful, and the label says how old
leave balance, attendancehide after a short agean old number is misleading — worse than none
product tiles, help linksdefaulta generic version is fine for everyone
permissions, entitlementsfail closedan old "yes" could let a removed person in

The stale copies are themselves tenant data, so they are kept per user and organization like any other cache — the rule from the tenant isolation example applies to fallbacks too.

Key deep dive — retries, and planned maintenance
NFRNo retry stormsFRMaintenance shown as maintenance
Thought process
  1. A retry is load. If the browser, the front door and the service each retry three times, one click can become 27 calls to a service that is already struggling — the amplification from the Scale Ladder.
  2. So retries happen in one layer only, only for calls that are safe to repeat, and within a budget — for example, retries may add at most 10% to normal traffic. When the budget is spent, calls fail to their fallback instead.
  3. Retries wait with backoff and jitter, so a brief failure doesn't bring every client back at the same instant.
  4. Planned maintenance is different from failure. Each service publishes its window in advance; during it, the front door doesn't call that service at all, shows "under maintenance until 05:00", and the service's alerts are silenced for the window.
Illustration — retrying at every layer vs. once, within a budget
outage · 3 layers × 3 attempts each27 calls per click
outage · one layer, 10% retry budget≤ 1.1 calls per click

Both rows describe the same outage, when every call fails: without limits every click uses every attempt at every layer — 27 calls; with a budget, retries are capped at 10% of traffic, so the average stays at about 1.1. That is 1.1 ÷ 27 ≈ 4% of the load, and the struggling service gets room to recover.

Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • The front door itself is overloaded — it sheds load deliberately, rejecting lower-priority requests first with 503 and a Retry-After, rather than slowing down for everyone.
  • A service answers quickly with nonsense — a 200 with a malformed body. Responses are validated against the expected shape, and a malformed one counts as a failure for the breaker.
  • Recovery after an outage — half-open breakers and jittered retries bring traffic back gradually, so the recovering service isn't flattened by the backlog.
  • Only some requests are slow — breakers watch failure rates, not averages, and the deadline catches the slow tail on every request.
  • Every front-door instance has its own breaker — they can disagree briefly; that's acceptable, and simpler than sharing breaker state across instances.
  • A dependency is removed from a page — the field stays nullable in the schema for a while, so older clients don't break.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Responds within its deadlineOne page deadline; every call's timeout taken from what remains; parallel calls; fallbacks for anything late.
Stays up when services don'tOnly identity and entitlements are critical; every other failure degrades one part of the page.
A slow service can't use up the front doorA bulkhead per dependency caps waiting calls; breakers stop calling what keeps failing.
No retry stormsRetries in one layer, for repeatable calls only, within a budget, with backoff and jitter.
Maintenance shown as maintenancePublished windows; the front door skips the service and says when it returns.
Security never degradesPermissions and entitlements fail closed — never served from an older answer.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
A small critical listSome parts of the page can be missing, in exchange for the page itself almost never being down.
Stale fallbacksUsers sometimes see older data, labelled, in exchange for a page instead of an error.
Circuit breakersA recovered service may be skipped for a few extra seconds, in exchange for not hammering it while it's down.
Hedged requestsAbout 5% more read traffic, in exchange for a much shorter slow tail.
Failing closed on permissionsUsers are sometimes refused when they should have been allowed, in exchange for never allowing someone who shouldn't be.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Front door in Gogqlgen with nullable optional fields, and context.WithDeadline carried into every downstream call
Breakers and limitsfailsafe-go for circuit breakers; a semaphore per dependency (golang.org/x/sync/semaphore) as the bulkhead
In the meshEnvoy outlier detection, connection limits and retry budgets, when the platform runs a service mesh
Watching itDatadog dashboards of breaker state, fallback rates and deadline misses per dependency
Worked Example AN — Changing the Engine in Flight

Design a Zero-Downtime Migration from a Legacy Service

strangler fig, one route at a time · prove it before users see it · cut over by organization · one writer per piece of data · behaviour that doesn't translate
Click to expand

A feature set lives in an older service — say a JVM monolith with its own database — and the team is moving it to a new service in a different language, such as Go. The product can't stop while this happens, customers must notice nothing, and every step has to be reversible. The risk isn't the new code; it's the moment real traffic and real data move, and the dozens of small behaviours the old system had that nobody wrote down.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Move functionality one operation at a time — not in one big switch.
  • Old and new run side by side for as long as it takes.
  • Data owned by the old service ends up owned by the new one.
  • At the end, the old service and its database are switched off and removed.
Non-functional
  • No downtime, and no change visible to customers or API clients.
  • Every step can be undone quickly — ideally by flipping a flag.
  • The new service is shown to behave the same before customers depend on it.
  • Data never diverges between old and new, and is never lost.
  • The migration has an end: it doesn't leave two systems running indefinitely.

The last NFR is the one most migrations miss. The dangerous state isn't the old system or the new one — it's both at once, forever, with every change made twice.

2
Core Entities
  • Route (operation, target, rollout, shadow) — where each operation goes: old, new, or new for some organizations, and whether it's mirrored.
  • Comparison (operation, request_ref, match, diff_category) — the result of comparing old and new answers for the same request.
  • DataOwnership (dataset, writer, sync_direction) — which service writes each dataset right now, and which way changes are copied.
3
API

Clients' API stays exactly the same — that is the point.
PUT /routes/{operation} {target, rollout_pct, shadow} → move an operation, or roll it back
GET /comparisons?operation=… → match rate and mismatch categories
PUT /datasets/{name}/writer → hand write ownership from old to new, with reverse sync switched on

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. The new service's database is filled from the old one — a backfill, then a continuous stream of changes.
  2. getProfile is mirrored: the old service answers users, the new one answers in the background, and the answers are compared.
  3. Once every category of mismatch is explained and the bugs in it are fixed, getProfile routes to the new service for 1% of organizations, then 10%, then everyone.
  4. When every operation that writes profiles is on the new service, profile writes move to it, and changes flow back to the old database so a rollback is still possible.
  5. After a quiet period, the reverse flow stops and the old code and tables are removed.
5
High-Level Design

A routing layer in front of both services decides, operation by operation, which one answers — the strangler fig pattern. Reads are mirrored and compared before any user sees the new service. Cutover is by organization, behind a flag. Data moves by change-data-capture, with exactly one service writing each dataset at any moment and a reverse sync kept open until rollback is no longer needed.

6
Deep Dives

Five below: (a) the strangler fig, (b) proving it before users see it, (c) cutting over gradually, (d) moving the data, and (e) behaviour that doesn't translate — then the edge cases.

The front door's route table is the migration's control panel: each operation points at the old service, the new one, or the new one for some organizations, and can be mirrored for comparison. Underneath, change-data-capture keeps the new database in step with the old one, and only one of them is ever the writer for a given dataset.
Moving one operation
  1. Mirror it: old answers, new answers in the background, compare.
  2. Explain every category of mismatch; fix the new service or document the difference.
  3. Route 1% of organizations to the new service, watch errors and latency, then 10%, 50%, 100%.
  4. Leave the old path in place, unused, until the next step is safe.
Something is wrong at 10%
  1. Error rate for the organizations on the new service rises.
  2. One flag change sends them back to the old service — within seconds, with no deploy.
  3. Because the old service still owns writes for that data, nothing needs repairing.
  4. The team fixes the cause, and the rollout starts again from 1%.
Key deep dive — the strangler fig, one route at a time
FROne operation at a timeNFRNo visible change
Thought process
  1. A big-bang rewrite switches everything at once, so every difference between old and new hits customers on the same day, and rolling back means rolling back everything.
  2. The strangler fig does the opposite: put a routing layer in front of the old service, then move operations behind it one at a time. The old service shrinks until nothing routes to it.
  3. The routing layer often already exists — an API gateway or a GraphQL layer. Clients keep calling the same API and never learn which service answered.
  4. Order matters: read-only, low-risk operations first, to prove the new service and the tooling; writes last, once the data has a plan (deep dive d).
  5. From the first day, new features are built only in the new service. Otherwise the old service keeps growing while you migrate away from it.
Illustration — big bang vs. strangler fig
Big bang
  • months of rewrite with no real traffic on the new code
  • one cutover night; every difference surfaces at once
  • rollback means undoing everything, including data
Strangler fig
  • real traffic reaches new code within weeks
  • each difference surfaces alone, on one operation
  • rollback is one flag for one operation
  1. week 2

    getProfile — read-only — mirrored, then moved

  2. week 5

    listTasks, getSettings — more reads

  3. week 9

    profile writes move, with reverse sync open

  4. week 14

    last operation moved; old service switched off after a quiet period

The weeks are illustrative; the order is the point — reads before writes, low risk before high.

Key deep dive — proving it before users see it
NFRShown to behave the same first
Thought process
  1. Tests cover what someone thought to write down. Production traffic covers what customers actually do — including requests nobody would have predicted.
  2. So reads are mirrored: the old service answers the user, the same request goes to the new service in the background, and the two answers are compared. Users only ever see the old answer.
  3. Writes can't simply be mirrored — sending the same "create invoice" to both would create it twice. The new service runs them in a dry-run mode that computes the result without committing, or its answer is compared with what the old service actually stored.
  4. Raw comparisons are noisy: timestamps, list order, generated IDs. Those are normalised first, so what remains is real differences.
  5. Every remaining mismatch is put in a category and explained — a bug to fix in the new service, or a deliberate difference to document. Cutover waits until the unexplained count is zero.
Illustration — a week of mirrored getProfile calls
1,000,000requests compared
99.7%identical after normalising
3,000mismatches, in three categories
MismatchCountVerdict
display name trimmed differently2,100bug in new — fixed
empty list vs. null for no phone numbers850client depends on it — match the old behaviour
old service returns a stale cached avatar URL50old was wrong — documented, accepted

The middle row is the classic surprise: the old behaviour was arguably wrong, but a client relies on it. The decision — match it, or change it with notice to the client — is made deliberately, not discovered in production.

Key deep dive — cutting over gradually, with a way back
NFREvery step undoable
Thought process
  1. Matching in comparison isn't the same as being ready for real traffic — latency, load and failure handling only show up when the new service is really answering.
  2. So traffic moves in steps behind a flag: 1% of organizations, then 10%, 50%, 100%, with the error rate and latency of each group watched against the old service.
  3. The flag is per organization, not per request. Choosing randomly per request would send one user's page loads to both services alternately — confusing if they differ, and hard to debug.
  4. Rolling back is changing the flag, not deploying. That only works while the old service still owns the writes, which is why data ownership moves last (deep dive d).
Illustration — a rollout, and a rollback that takes seconds
day 1 · 1% of organizations1%
day 3 · 10%10%
day 4 · errors rise → flag back0%
day 8 · fixed, resumed50%
day 12 · everyone100%

Day 4 is the point of the whole design: a problem at 10% was reversed in seconds, affected a tenth of customers briefly, and needed no data repair.

Key deep dive — moving the data
NFRNever diverges, never lostNFREvery step undoable
Thought process
  1. Code is easy to route. Data is the hard part, because two services must agree on it throughout.
  2. The tempting shortcut is dual writes: the application writes every change to both databases. When one write succeeds and the other fails, they disagree, with nothing to reconcile them — the dual-write problem from the data correctness toolkit.
  3. Instead, exactly one service writes each dataset at any moment. The new database is filled by change-data-capture: a backfill of existing rows, then a stream of every change read from the old database's log.
  4. When every operation that writes a dataset has moved, write ownership flips to the new service — and the stream reverses, copying changes back to the old database so a rollback remains possible.
  5. After a quiet period with no rollback, the reverse stream stops, and the old tables can finally go.
Illustration — three ways to share data during a migration
ApproachHowThe catch
new service reads the old databaseno copy at alltied to the old schema — fine briefly, never as the end state
dual writes from the applicationwrite every change to bothsilent divergence when one write fails
change-data-capture, one writerbackfill + stream from the writer's logsafe — the copy lags by seconds
  1. phase 1

    old service writes · changes stream old → new · reads compared

  2. phase 2

    new service writes · changes stream new → old · rollback still possible

  3. phase 3

    reverse stream stopped · old tables archived, then dropped

Key deep dive — behaviour that doesn't translate
NFRNo visible change
Thought process
  1. A port to a new language changes behaviour in places no one thinks of as behaviour — the defaults of the language and its libraries.
  2. Money is the sharpest example. In a float, 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. The old service may use an exact decimal type; the new one must too — integers in the smallest currency unit, or a decimal library — and round the same way.
  3. Others are quieter: which time zone a date is interpreted in, how text is sorted (byte order is not dictionary order, especially for accented or non-Latin text), null versus an empty list, how numbers are formatted.
  4. Mirrored comparison (deep dive b) is what finds these — which is why it runs on real traffic, and why every mismatch gets a verdict.
Illustration — differences that come from the language, not the code
AreaHow it goes wrongDo this
moneyfloats drift: 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3integers in the smallest unit, or a decimal type; same rounding mode as before
timea different default time zone moves dates across midnightstore instants in UTC; convert with an explicit zone
sorting textbyte-order sort ≠ the database's collationsort in the database, or with the same collation rules
empty valuesnull in one, [] in the other; a client breaksmatch the old output where clients depend on it
scheduled jobsthe old and new services both run the nightly job — emails sent twicemove each job explicitly; exactly one owner, like data
Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • Clients relying on bugs — decide deliberately whether to reproduce old behaviour or change it with notice, as in the API versioning example.
  • A migration that never finishes — keep a list of every operation, job and dataset with an owner and a status; freeze new features on the old service; measure the share of traffic on the new one every week.
  • Sessions and caches — tokens issued by the old service must be accepted by the new one, and caches keyed by old formats are cleared or converted when routes move.
  • Long-running work in flight — a report started on the old service finishes there; only new requests follow the new route.
  • Shared tables touched by other services — find every reader and writer of the old tables before moving ownership, not after.
  • Switching off — the old service is removed only after traffic is zero for a full business cycle, the same rule as retiring an API version.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
No downtime, no visible changeA routing layer in front of both services; clients' API never changes.
Every step undoablePer-organization flags; old service keeps write ownership until the end; reverse sync after the flip.
Proven before customers depend on itMirrored reads, dry-run writes, normalised comparison, and a verdict for every mismatch.
Data never divergesOne writer per dataset at any moment; change-data-capture instead of dual writes.
The migration endsAn inventory with owners, a feature freeze on the old service, and removal after a quiet period.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Strangler fig over big bangWeeks or months of running two systems, in exchange for small, reversible steps.
Mirrored comparisonExtra load on the new service and effort to explain mismatches, in exchange for finding differences before customers do.
Change-data-captureMore infrastructure than dual writes, in exchange for data that can't silently diverge.
Per-organization rolloutSlower than flipping everyone, in exchange for small, visible blast radius.
Feature freeze on the old serviceSome requests wait, in exchange for a migration that actually finishes.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Routingthe existing API gateway or GraphQL layer, with per-operation routes behind feature flags
Change-data-captureDebezium reading the database log into Kafka, or AWS DMS
Money in Gointegers in the smallest currency unit, or shopspring/decimal
Comparison and rollouta comparison service logging normalised diffs to Datadog; a feature-flag service for per-organization rollout
Worked Example AO — One Schema, Many Owners

Design a GraphQL Layer over Many Microservices

N+1 and batching · field-level authorization · query-cost limits · schema ownership · evolving without breaking clients
Click to expand

A portal's web and mobile apps talk to one GraphQL API, which sits in front of many services owned by different teams — people and organizations, tasks, documents, attendance. GraphQL lets clients ask for exactly the fields they need in one request. The same flexibility is its danger: a single innocent-looking query can fan out into hundreds of backend calls, reach fields the caller shouldn't see, or cost more than the whole server can give it.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • One schema for all clients; a screen's data comes back in one request.
  • Each type and field is owned by one team, and served by that team's service.
  • Sensitive fields — salary, bank details — are visible only to people allowed to see them.
  • Mutations go to the service that owns the data.
  • Clients keep working while the schema evolves.
Non-functional
  • The number of backend calls doesn't grow with the number of rows in a list.
  • No single query can consume unbounded work.
  • A field someone isn't allowed to see is never sent — not sent and hidden by the app.
  • One team's change can't break another team's part of the schema.
  • One slow service degrades only its own fields.

The first NFR is where GraphQL surprises people. REST endpoints are designed one at a time; a GraphQL schema lets clients combine fields in ways no one designed for, and the naive way of resolving those combinations multiplies calls.

2
Core Entities
  • Subgraph (name, owning_team, types, service_url) — one team's part of the schema, served by its own service.
  • Entity (type, key) — a type several subgraphs can add fields to, such as Employee keyed by id.
  • TrustedQuery (hash, text, client, cost) — a query the first-party apps are allowed to run, registered at build time.
  • FieldUsage (field, client, last_seen) — who still uses each field, for safe removal.
3
API

POST /graphql {id: "sha256:…", variables} → first-party apps send only the hash of a registered query
POST /graphql {query, variables} → partners send full queries, which are cost-checked before running
query { employee(id) { name tasks { title } } } → one request; the router plans which subgraph serves each field

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. The web app sends the hash of its registered "home screen" query; the router authenticates the user and takes the organization from the token.
  2. The router plans the query: name from People, tasks from Tasks, payslips from Documents.
  3. Within each subgraph, batch loaders collect every ID the query needs and fetch them in one call per type.
  4. Documents checks the caller may see net pay — their own payslip, yes; someone else's, the field comes back null.
  5. The router assembles one response; if Attendance timed out, its field is null with an error, and the rest is intact.
5
High-Level Design

A router in front of team-owned subgraphs, composed into one schema. Every request is authenticated, checked against a list of known queries or a cost limit, planned across subgraphs, and resolved with per-request batching. Field rules live in the schema, so no resolver can forget them. Changes are checked against the composed schema and real usage before they ship.

6
Deep Dives

Five below: (a) the N+1 problem and batching, (b) field-level authorization, (c) query-cost limits, (d) who owns which part of the schema, and (e) evolving without breaking clients — then the edge cases.

Clients see one schema; behind the router, each team owns a subgraph and its data. The router's six steps are where the risks of GraphQL are handled: which queries may run at all, how much they may cost, how calls are batched, and which fields a caller may see.
The home screen
  1. One request with a registered query hash.
  2. The router plans it across four subgraphs, in parallel where it can.
  3. Each subgraph makes one batched call per type, however many rows.
  4. The screen renders from one response.
A partner sends a huge query
  1. It nests 100 users, 50 documents each, 10 versions each.
  2. Before running anything, the router estimates 55,100 nodes against a limit of 10,000.
  3. The query is rejected with an error explaining the cost, and nothing is fetched.
  4. The partner pages through the data instead — within its budget.
Key deep dive — the N+1 problem, and batching
NFRCalls don't grow with list size
Thought process
  1. GraphQL resolves fields one at a time. Ask for 50 employees and each one's manager, and the obvious resolver fetches the list once, then each manager separately — 1 + 50 calls. Add documents, and it's 1 + 50 + 50.
  2. That's the N+1 problem: calls grow with the size of the list, and a screen that was fast with 5 rows is slow with 50.
  3. The fix is a batch loader. Instead of fetching immediately, each resolver asks the loader for an ID; the loader waits a moment, collects every ID requested in that pass, and makes one call for all of them.
  4. Loaders are created fresh for every request. Their cache must never be shared between requests — it would hand one user's permitted data to another.
Illustration — 50 employees, their managers and documents
query {
  employees(first: 50) {
    name
    manager   { name }        # one call per employee — unless batched
    documents { title }       # and another one per employee
  }
}
naive: 1 + 50 + 50 calls101 calls · ~505 ms
batched: one call per type3 calls · ~15 ms

Times assume 5 ms per call, made one after another. Running calls in parallel narrows the gap, but 101 calls still load the services 34 times more than 3.

Key deep dive — field-level authorization
FRSensitive fields only for those allowedNFRNever sent, not just hidden
Thought process
  1. In REST, a sensitive value lives behind a particular endpoint, which is easy to protect. In GraphQL, salary is a field any query can reach through any path — directly, through a manager, through a team list.
  2. So the rule has to be attached to the field itself, not to whichever query happens to ask for it. A directive in the schema — "only payroll admins, or the employee themselves" — is checked every time the field is resolved, by every path.
  3. A denied field comes back null, with an error naming it. The schema makes such fields nullable for exactly this reason, so one denial doesn't fail the whole response.
  4. Row-level rules — which employees you may see at all — still belong in the query that loads them, as in the access control example; field rules are the second layer.
Illustration — the rule lives on the field, so every path is covered
type Employee {
  name:   String!
  salary: Int  @requires(any: ["payroll_admin", "self"])   # checked on every path
}
Path to salaryCallerResult
me { salary }the employeevalue
team { members { salary } }a managernull + error
employee(id) { salary }a payroll adminvalue

@requires is an illustrative directive name. The point is where the rule lives — on the field, enforced by the server — so a new query written next year can't reach salary by a path nobody thought to protect.

Key deep dive — query-cost limits
NFRNo query consumes unbounded work
Thought process
  1. A REST endpoint does a fixed amount of work. A GraphQL query does as much as the caller writes — nested lists multiply, and a request that looks small can ask for millions of objects.
  2. For the first-party apps, the strongest control is to allow only known queries. Each query is registered when the app is built, and at runtime the app sends just its hash; anything else is refused. Arbitrary expensive queries simply can't run.
  3. Partners need to write their own queries, so their queries are costed before running: each list multiplies by its first argument, and queries over the limit are rejected with the estimate. Lists without a page size aren't allowed.
  4. Rate limits then count cost, not requests. One query for 10,000 objects uses the same budget as 100 queries for 100 — the rate limiter with a weight on each request.
  5. A depth limit and a server-side timeout catch whatever the estimate misses.
Illustration — costing a query before running it
users(first: 100) {             # 100
  documents(first: 50) {        # 100 × 50       =  5,000
    versions(first: 10) { … }   # 100 × 50 × 10  = 50,000
  }
}                               # total             55,100 nodes
this query55,100 nodes
limit per query10,000

rejected before anything is fetched, with the estimate in the error — the partner pages through instead

The limit of 10,000 is an example; set it from what your services can serve within the response deadline.

Key deep dive — who owns which part of the schema
FREach type owned by one teamNFROne team can't break another
Thought process
  1. A single schema maintained by one gateway team becomes a bottleneck: every change from every product waits on them.
  2. Federation splits it. Each team publishes a subgraph for the types it owns; a router composes them into the one schema clients see.
