  3. Some types matter to everyone, like Employee. The People team owns it and its key; other teams add their own fields to it — Tasks adds Employee.tasks — without touching People's code.
  4. Every change is checked in CI against the composed schema: does it still compose, and does it break any query clients actually send? A breaking change fails the build of the team that made it.
Illustration — one type, extended by three teams
# People subgraph — owns Employee and its key
type Employee @key(fields: "id") { id: ID!  name: String!  org: Organization! }

# Tasks subgraph — adds a field it owns
type Employee @key(fields: "id") { id: ID!  tasks(first: Int!): [Task!]! }

# Documents subgraph — adds a restricted field it owns
type Employee @key(fields: "id") { id: ID!  payslips(first: Int!): [Payslip!]! }
One schema, one team
  • every product change queues behind the gateway team
  • no clear owner when a field breaks
Subgraphs, composed
  • each team ships its own fields
  • composition checks catch conflicts before deploy
Key deep dive — evolving without breaking clients
FRClients keep working as the schema changes
Thought process
  1. GraphQL APIs usually aren't versioned like REST. The schema evolves continuously, so every change must be safe for clients already in the field — including mobile apps nobody has updated.
  2. Adding fields and types is safe. Removing, renaming or changing a field's type is not.
  3. So a replacement is added first, the old field is marked @deprecated with a reason, and the router records which clients still ask for it.
  4. The field is removed only when usage has been zero for a full release cycle of the mobile apps — the same evidence-before-removal rule as the API versioning example.
Illustration — renaming a field safely
  1. add

    displayName added alongside fullName

  2. deprecate

    fullName: String @deprecated(reason: "use displayName")

  3. watch

    usage by client: web 0 · Android 12% · iOS 3% — wait for the app updates

  4. remove

    zero usage across a full mobile release cycle → field removed

Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • A mutation that touches two subgraphs — the router is not a place for distributed transactions. One service owns the operation and coordinates the rest with a saga, as in the data correctness toolkit.
  • A slow subgraph — its fields time out to null with an error while the rest returns, the partial-result behaviour of the resilient front door.
  • Caching — GraphQL requests are usually POSTs, so HTTP caches don't help by default. Registered queries can be sent as GETs by hash for shared, public data; anything per-user is never cached at the edge.
  • File uploads and downloads — kept out of GraphQL; the schema returns a short-lived signed URL, as for payslips in the document distribution example.
  • Seeing the whole schema — introspection is useful internally; for a public API, decide deliberately whether outsiders may list every type and field.
  • Debugging a slow query — trace each resolver and each subgraph call, so "the page is slow" becomes "Documents' payslip resolver is slow".

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Calls don't grow with list sizePer-request batch loaders: one call per type per query, never shared between requests.
No unbounded workRegistered queries for first-party apps; cost estimates, page sizes, depth limits and timeouts for everyone else; rate limits by cost.
Sensitive fields never sentRules on the field in the schema, enforced on every path; denied fields null with an error.
One team can't break anotherSubgraphs with single owners, composed in CI, with breaking-change checks against real usage.
Clients keep workingAdditive changes; deprecation with usage tracking; removal only after usage reaches zero.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
FederationA router and composition tooling to run, in exchange for teams shipping their own parts independently.
Registered queries only, for first-party appsA build step to register queries, in exchange for no arbitrary queries in production.
Nullable sensitive fieldsClients must handle null, in exchange for a denial affecting one field, not the whole response.
Per-request loader cachesLess reuse between requests, in exchange for never leaking one user's data to another.
Continuous evolution instead of versionsDiscipline and usage tracking, in exchange for clients never having to migrate between versions.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Subgraphs in Gogqlgen with its federation support, and a batching loader such as dataloadgen
Router and compositionApollo Router or Cosmo Router, with a schema registry and composition checks in CI
Query controltrusted (persisted) documents for first-party apps; cost analysis and depth limits in the router
Tracingresolver-level spans sent to Datadog APM
Worked Example AP — Two Million Messages, and One That Can't Wait

Design a Notification System for a Multi-Product Employee Portal

events, not messages · preferences, quiet hours, digests · priority lanes for payday · providers that fail · one inbox across organizations · fair and isolated for organizations of any size · dedupe vs. idempotency
Click to expand

Every product in the suite needs to tell people things: a payslip is ready, an approval is waiting, a tax form is due, a password was just changed. Employees can be reached in the app, by push on their phone, by email, and in their company's chat tool. Built product by product, this becomes a flood of uncoordinated messages that people learn to ignore. Built as one shared service, it can respect everyone's preferences, stay quiet at night, collapse repeats, and still deliver two million payday messages in minutes — without a security alert waiting behind them.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Any product can notify employees through one service, in the app, by push, email or chat.
  • People choose which kinds of notification they receive on which channel; some kinds — security alerts — can't be turned off.
  • No push at night: non-urgent messages wait for the person's morning; many similar ones arrive as one digest.
  • An in-app inbox with an unread count, per organization, read state shared across devices.
  • Messages are in the person's language, and each product can see whether its notifications were delivered.
  • Organizations can connect chat tools — Slack, Telegram, Microsoft Teams — so people receive notifications there and can act on them (approve, reject) from the chat.
Non-functional
  • Payday — about two million messages — is delivered within minutes.
  • A security alert goes out in seconds, whatever else is queued.
  • No duplicate sends from our side, and nothing lost when a worker or a provider fails.
  • One email provider failing doesn't stop email.
  • A chat provider's rate limits or outage slow only chat delivery — never push, email or the inbox — and a revoked connection never causes a retry storm.
  • Messages never carry sensitive details that could leak through a forwarded email or a lock screen.
  • Organizations range from 50 people to 100,000: no organization's volume — or runaway bug — delays or throttles another's.

The first two NFRs pull against each other, and that tension is the heart of this design: the biggest burst of the month must not delay the smallest, most urgent message.

2
Core Entities
  • Event (event_id, type, org_id, subject_ids, data, occurred_at) — what happened, sent by a product. Its id is what deduplicates.
  • Category (type, priority, default_channels, can_opt_out, digestable) — how each kind of event is treated.
  • Preference (membership_id, category, channel, enabled, quiet_hours) — what the person has chosen.
  • Delivery (notification_id, channel, status, attempts, provider, last_error) — one row per notification per channel, from queued to delivered or failed.
  • InboxItem (membership_id, notification_id, read_at?) — the in-app copy, per organization.
  • Contact (account_id, channel, address, status) — email addresses and push tokens, marked invalid when they bounce.
3
API

POST /events {event_id, type: "payslip.published", org_id, subject_ids, data} → products report what happened
GET /me/notifications?org=… → the in-app inbox for one organization
POST /me/notifications/read {ids | all} → mark read, on every device
PUT /me/preferences → choose categories and channels, and quiet hours
GET /deliveries?event_id=… → for products: what happened to their notification

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. Payroll reports payslip.published for 1,000,000 employees at 09:00.
  2. The service expands it to one notification per person, and checks each person's preferences and quiet hours.
  3. In-app items are written for everyone; push and email jobs join the transactional lane.
  4. Meanwhile someone's password is changed. That alert enters the security lane and is sent within seconds.
  5. Senders work through the lanes at each provider's pace; bounces and dead push tokens feed back into contacts.
5
High-Level Design

Products send events describing what happened; one service decides who is told, how and when. It applies preferences, quiet hours and digests, renders templates in each person's language, and puts one job per channel onto a queue for that priority. Senders deliver at each provider's rate, retry with backoff, fail over between email providers, and feed bounces back so dead addresses stop being used. Two diagrams below: the flow in eight stages, then the services, queues and stores inside it, from write to read.

6
Deep Dives

Nine below: (a) events, not messages, (b) preferences, quiet hours and digests, (c) priority lanes and the payday burst, (d) delivery when providers fail, (e) one inbox across organizations, (f) many organizations of very different sizes, (g) inside a dedicated cell, and scaling one very large organization, (h) dedupe vs. idempotency: sending each notification once, and (i) chat integrations: Slack, Telegram and Teams — then the edge cases.

The whole flow in eight stages. An event enters once (②, deduplicated by its id), becomes exactly one delivery per person and channel (③, idempotent by a derived key), waits in its organization's own queue within its priority lane (④), is picked up by one worker on that organization's shards (⑤–⑥), and is sent, with failures fed back (⑦–⑧). The coloured tags show which concern each stage is responsible for.
Illustration — the flow, stage by stage
StageWhat happensWhat it guarantees
① productswrite the business change and an event with an event_id in one transaction; a relay publishes it, at least onceno event is lost — but it may arrive twice
② intakestores the event keyed by event_id; a repeat is acknowledged and ignored; the organization comes from the caller's tokendedupe one event, however many times it's sent
③ fan-outresolves recipients within that organization, applies preferences, quiet hours and digests, and writes one delivery row per person and channelidempotent a re-run creates nothing new — ids are derived, not random
④ priority lanesputs each delivery in its priority lane, in its organization's own queue, within that organization's quotaisolation security first; no organization waits behind another
⑤ workerstake turns across organizations on their two of eight shards; scale on backlog, and ahead of paydays; the largest organization has its own cellscale capacity follows volume
⑥ senderclaims a delivery by moving it from queued to sending; calls the provider with a collapse id; records sent with the provider's message ididempotent one worker per delivery; sent is never claimed again
⑦ channelsin-app written to our own table; push through APNs and FCM; email through two providers; chat to the company channeleach channel at its provider's allowed rate
⑧ feedbackbounces and dead push tokens mark contacts invalid; temporary failures return the delivery to the queue with backoffnothing retried blindly; nothing sent to addresses that no longer exist
The same flow, opened up: the services that do the work, the queues between them, and the three stores. Each numbered arrow is one step, described in the table below. PostgreSQL holds everything that must be correct; Redis holds the fast, shared coordination state; the NoSQL store takes the high-volume history. The read path serves the inbox from a replica and the unread badge from a cache.
Illustration — from write to read, step by step
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
W1the product saves its change and an outbox row in one transaction; a relay publishes the event to Kafka, keyed by organization — the largest by organization and recipient, so their payday spreads across partitionsproduct DB · Kafkanothing lost; at least once
W2the intake service consumes it and inserts it into events with ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHINGPostgreSQLdedupe repeats stop here
W3fan-out workers resolve recipients in that organization, read preferences and quiet hours from the Redis cache (PostgreSQL on a miss), and write deliveries and inbox_items in one transactionPostgreSQL · Redisidempotent derived ids; in-app is done at this step
W4the fair dispatcher keeps, per priority lane, a rotation of organizations with work waiting; each turn takes tokens from that organization's bucket and claims a batch for itRedis · PostgreSQLisolation turns and quotas per organization
W5batches go to SQS lane queues, one per shard — each organization's only to its two shards; the largest organization's to its own cellSQSscale workers scale on queue depth, and ahead of paydays
W6a sender claims each delivery (queued → sending), calls the provider with a collapse id, records sent and the provider's message id, and appends the attempt to the logPostgreSQL · providers · NoSQLidempotent one worker per delivery
W7a temporary failure, or quiet hours, puts the delivery in a Redis sorted set scored by when it's due; a poller moves due deliveries back to their lane queueRedis · SQSretry later without any worker waiting
W8providers report bounces and dead push tokens; the feedback service marks contacts invalid, clears their cached copies, and records the event in the logPostgreSQL · Redis · NoSQLnever send to what no longer exists
R1the web or mobile app calls the GraphQL API; the organization comes from the tokenAPImulti-org
R2the inbox list is read from a PostgreSQL replica, by membership, newest first; right after a user marks something read, their own reads go to the primary so they see the changePostgreSQL replicareads off the primary; read-your-writes
R3the unread badge comes from a Redis cache that lives a few seconds and is cleared whenever an item is added or read; on a miss it's counted from PostgreSQL's indexRedis · PostgreSQLa cheap badge that is never wrong for long
R4a product checking what happened to its event reads delivery status from PostgreSQL and attempts from the NoSQL logPostgreSQL · NoSQLstatus and history, each from its own store

R2's rule — send a user's reads to the primary just after they write — is the read-your-writes fix from the data correctness toolkit.

Illustration — why each piece is where it is
PieceHoldsWhy this and not anotherIf it's lost
PostgreSQLevents, deliveries, inbox, preferences, contactsunique keys, transactions and conditional updates — the dedupe and idempotency guarantees need all threethe source of truth — replicated, backed up, restorable to a point in time
Redistoken buckets, organization turns, the delayed set, cachesatomic counters and sorted sets in memory, shared by every worker, in microsecondsnothing is lost — every delivery's state is in PostgreSQL; a sweeper re-queues anything still queued or stuck in sending past its claim timeout
NoSQL (e.g. DynamoDB)attempt log, provider feedbackmillions of appends per payday, read by key, expiring on their own — no joins or transactions neededhistory only — sending is unaffected
Kafkaevents from productsdurable, replayable, ordered per key, read by several consumersreplicated across brokers; products' outboxes hold anything not yet published
SQSbatches waiting for a sender, per lane and shardsimple work queues whose depth drives autoscalingjobs can be rebuilt from deliveries still queued in PostgreSQL

The rule behind the table: anything that must be correct lives in PostgreSQL; anything that must be fast and shared lives in Redis and can be rebuilt; anything that is large and append-only lives in the NoSQL store. Moving the in-app inbox to a wide-column store is the natural next step if a single PostgreSQL cluster ever becomes the limit.

Payday at 09:00
  1. 1,000,000 in-app items appear together — the payslip is findable at once.
  2. 600,000 push and 400,000 email messages drain through the transactional lane over a few minutes.
  3. People who set quiet hours until 09:30 get their push at 09:30.
  4. A password-change alert sent at 09:02 goes out in seconds, in its own lane.
The main email provider goes down
  1. Sends start failing; the circuit breaker for that provider opens.
  2. New email jobs go to the second provider; the failed ones are retried there.
  3. Each job keeps its delivery row, so nothing is sent twice by our side.
  4. When the first provider recovers, traffic returns to it gradually.
Key deep dive — events, not messages
FRAny product, one serviceFRPreferences respected
Thought process
  1. If each product sends its own emails and pushes, each one reimplements preferences, quiet hours and templates — differently — and employees get a flood from six products with no coordination.
  2. So products don't ask to "send an email". They report what happened — "payslip published for these employees" — and the notification service decides who is told, how and when.
  3. That puts every person's preferences in one place, applied identically to every product, and lets the service combine and throttle across products.
  4. Each event carries an id. A product that retries after a timeout sends the same id, and the service drops the duplicate — the idempotency rule from the payment API.

"Send this message"

  subject: "Your payslip",
  body: "Net pay: $3,124.00 …")

  • salary sitting in an email
  • every product reinventing templates
"This happened"
POST /events
{ "event_id": "evt_9f3",
  "type": "payslip.published",
  "subject_ids": ["m_4c1", …] }
  • the service applies preferences and quiet hours
  • the message says "ready", links to the app — no figures
  • one template per type, in every language
Illustration — every product sending its own, against one service deciding
Key deep dive — preferences, quiet hours and digests
FRChoose what and whereFRNo push at night · digests
Thought process
  1. People stop reading notifications that are too many or at the wrong time — and then miss the ones that matter. Restraint is a feature.
  2. Each kind of notification belongs to a category with a priority and defaults. People can change channels for most categories, but not for security alerts, which always go out.
  3. Quiet hours hold non-urgent push until the person's morning, in their own time zone. Security alerts ignore quiet hours.
  4. Many similar notifications in a short time — thirty approval requests during month-end — become one digest: "30 approvals are waiting for you". The inbox still lists all thirty.

Illustration — the decision order, and one person's day
Key deep dive — priority lanes and the payday burst
NFRPayday within minutesNFRSecurity alerts in seconds
Thought process
  1. Work out the burst first. On payday, 1,000,000 employees get an in-app notification; say 60% also get a push and 40% an email — 2,000,000 messages in all.
  2. With one queue in arrival order, anything that arrives after the burst waits behind it. At 2,000 pushes a second, a password-change alert behind 600,000 pushes waits about five minutes — long enough for an attacker to act.
  3. So there are separate lanes per priority, each with its own workers: security, transactional, reminders. Lower lanes never slow higher ones; idle capacity may be lent to a lower lane, but the security lane always keeps its own workers. The lanes must reach all the way to the provider: a push project or an email account has one send quota shared by every lane, and if the payday senders push past it, the provider rejects requests at random — it can't tell a security alert from a payslip. So our own rate limiter stays under the quota and serves security first. Simulated with a 2,000-a-second quota: lanes whose senders pushed past it left a security alert waiting up to 7.18–60.45 s; lanes plus a priority limiter, 0.1 s.
  4. In-app items for the whole company are written at 09:00 in batches, so the payslip is findable within seconds: measured on PostgreSQL, a million items took 2.3 s as one set-based insert and 4.2 s in batches of 5,000 — but 2.5 minutes one insert per person. Push and email follow over minutes, at each provider's allowed rate.
Illustration — how long a security alert waits
one queue, behind 600,000 payday pushes~5 min
its own lane~1 s
Payday channelMessagesAssumed rateTime to drain
in-app1,000,000batched writesvisible at 09:00
push600,0002,000 / s~5 min
email400,0001,000 / s~6.7 min

The rates are assumptions — use your providers' real limits. The conclusion doesn't depend on them: a big burst in a shared queue delays everything behind it, so urgent messages need their own lane.

Key deep dive — delivery when providers fail
NFRNo duplicates, nothing lostNFROne provider failing doesn't stop email
Thought process
  1. Every notification and channel has one delivery row. A worker that crashes and restarts finds the row and continues it, so our side never creates a second send.
  2. Failures are retried with backoff and jitter. A provider's "try later" is honoured; a permanent failure stops retries and marks the delivery failed.
  3. Email goes through two providers. When the main one starts failing, its circuit breaker opens and new email goes to the second — the front door's breaker, used for outbound traffic. The second provider must be warm: the sending domain authenticated with it (SPF, DKIM) and a steady share of email going through it every day — a sudden flood from a cold provider looks like spam to mailbox providers.
  4. Providers also report that an address or device no longer exists: an email bounces, or a push service answers that a token is unregistered. These reports arrive later, through the providers' webhooks (and complaints when someone marks a message as spam). Those contacts are marked invalid, so the system stops sending to them — repeated sends to dead addresses damage a sender's reputation with mail providers.
Illustration — what each kind of failure means
What happenedKindWhat the system does
provider timeout, 5xxtemporaryretry with backoff; open the breaker if it keeps happening
provider rate limittemporarywait as told, then retry
email hard bouncepermanentmark the address invalid; stop emailing it
push token unregisteredpermanentdelete the token; the app registers a new one next time it opens
main email provider downproviderfail over to the second provider; drift back when it recovers

Apple's push service answers 410 with "Unregistered" for a token that's no longer valid; Firebase Cloud Messaging answers UNREGISTERED. Both mean the same thing: stop sending to that device.

Illustration — retries, failover and the feedback loop
Key deep dive — one inbox across organizations
FRInbox and unread count per organizationFRRead on every device
Thought process
  1. The in-app inbox is the channel that never fails: it's the record of every notification, whatever happened to the push or email.
  2. Items belong to a membership, not an account — someone who works for two companies sees each company's inbox while working in it, and the organization switcher can show an unread count for each. The same rule as the multi-organization identity example.
  3. Read state lives on the server, so reading on the phone clears the badge on the laptop.
  4. The unread count comes from an index on (membership_id, read_at), so it always matches the list — the reasoning from the task inbox example. "Mark all read" is one update, not one per item.
  5. Items older than a retention period, such as 90 days, are removed; the product that sent them still keeps its own records.
Illustration — one account, one inbox per organization, read state everywhere
Key deep dive — many organizations of very different sizes
NFROne organization never delays anotherNFRScales with each organization's volume
Thought process
  1. One notification service serves thousands of organizations, from 50 people to 100,000 — a 2,000× difference in volume — and many of them run payday at the same 09:00.
  2. With one shared queue, whoever arrives first is served first. A small company's payday messages wait behind a large company's, and an organization with a bug — the same reminder sent in a loop — can use up the email provider's quota and sender reputation for everyone. This is the noisy-neighbour problem from the multi-tenant rate limiting example, applied to outgoing messages.
  3. Three layers solve it. Fairness: within each priority lane, every organization gets its own queue, and workers take from them in turn, so a small company's messages go out alongside a large one's instead of after it. Limits: each organization has a quota per channel, sized to its plan and headcount, so a runaway organization only exhausts its own. Isolation: workers are split into shards and each organization is placed on a few of them; the very largest organizations get a cell of their own.
  4. Scaling follows the backlog. Workers scale on queue depth per lane, and because paydays and tax deadlines are scheduled, capacity is added before 09:00 rather than after the queues fill.
  5. Everything is measured per organization — volume, backlog, bounce rate — so a sudden spike from one organization is visible, and its quota trips automatically before anyone else notices.
Most organizations share one pool, with a queue each and a fair turn at the workers; each is placed on two of eight worker shards, so a misbehaving organization touches few others. The very largest organization runs in its own cell — its own queues, workers, database and email sending identity — so its payday can't affect anyone, and no one else's can affect it.
Illustration — the same 09:00, one queue vs. fair turns

A company sending 200,000 payday messages and a 50-person company sending 100 both start at 09:00, sharing 2,000 sends a second.

small company · one shared queuewaits ~100 s
small company · fair turnsdone in ~0.1 s

and the large company barely notices: its run takes 100.05 s instead of 100.0 s

Fair scheduling isn't slower overall — the same messages go out at the same total rate. It only changes the order, so nobody's few messages wait behind somebody else's many. And when only one organization has work, it gets every worker.

Illustration — why each organization gets two of eight shards
12.5%one shard each: chance another organization shares a noisy one's only shard — and is fully affected
3.6%two of eight: chance another organization shares both — 1 of 28 combinations
halfcapacity kept by an organization sharing just one of the noisy one's shards — its other shard is untouched

This is shuffle sharding. The noisy organization is slowed only on its own two shards; almost every other organization has at least one clean shard, and none loses everything. Assignments are fixed per organization, so its queues stay in the same place.

Illustration — tiers: where each size of organization runs
TierRuns onLimitsEmail sending
small · under ~1,000 peopleshared pool, fair turns, 2 of 8 shardsdefault quota per channelshared sending pool
medium · ~1,000–10,000shared pool, fair turns, 2 of 8 shardshigher quota and burstshared sending pool
large · 10,000+shared pool; its messages keyed by recipient so they spread across partitionsquota sized to its paydayits own sending subdomain
largest or regulateddedicated cell — own queues, workers, database and cacheagreed per contractdedicated sending IPs and identity

The size thresholds are illustrative. The pattern is the same as the pool-and-silo tiers in the tenant isolation example: share by default, isolate the few that are big enough to hurt others — or that pay to never be affected by them.

Illustration — scaling for a peak you can see coming
  1. 08:30

    the schedule shows 40 organizations releasing payslips at 09:00 — 1.2 million messages

  2. 08:40

    workers for the transactional lane scaled from 20 to 200, ahead of the burst

  3. 09:00

    the burst arrives; every organization's queue is served in turn

  4. 09:12

    backlog drained; workers scale back down

Scaling on queue depth still runs underneath as the safety net for peaks nobody scheduled. Scheduled peaks are the easy case — the system knows about them in advance, so it shouldn't wait to be surprised by them.

  • A runaway organization — an integration bug sends the same reminder 50,000 times in ten minutes. Its per-organization quota caps it, an alert fires for that organization, and every other organization's messages keep flowing.
  • Partition keys — keying the shared queue only by organization would put a large company's whole payday on one partition. Large organizations are keyed by organization and recipient, spreading their messages across partitions while keeping each person's messages in order.
  • Moving an organization between tiers — a company that grows is moved to a bigger tier at a quiet time: new messages go to the new queues while the old ones drain.
Illustration — what the fair dispatcher is, and how it works

A dispatcher, in general, is the component that decides which work goes next, and to whom: it pulls from a backlog and hands work to workers or queues by a policy — first come first served, priority, round robin, or fair share. An operating-system scheduler, a taxi dispatcher and a load balancer are all dispatchers.

Here it sits between the deliveries that fan-out wrote and the lane queues the senders read. Its policy has two parts: strict priority between lanes — anything in the security lane goes first — and fair turns between organizations inside a lane, each turn capped by that organization's token bucket. That is what stops one company's payday from starving everyone else.

It holds no work itself: the turn order and the buckets live in Redis, the deliveries in PostgreSQL. Two copies run for availability, and claiming with SKIP LOCKED means they never take the same rows.

Illustration — the dispatcher loop, in outline
loop:
    lane = "P0" if has_work("P0") else next_lane("P1", "P2")      # security first, always
    org  = LMOVE {lane}:active → back of the list                    # whose turn is it?
    n    = take_tokens(org, up_to=200)                                # Lua token bucket in Redis; 0 → skip this turn
    rows = UPDATE deliveries SET status = 'dispatched'
           WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM deliveries
                        WHERE org = $org AND lane = $lane AND status = 'queued'
                        ORDER BY created_at LIMIT $n FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
           RETURNING id                                               # claimed once, even with two dispatchers
    push_batch(lane_queue(lane, shard_of(org)), rows)                 # senders take it from here
    if nothing_left(org, lane): LREM {lane}:active org                # drops out of the rotation
Key deep dive — inside a dedicated cell, and scaling one very large organization
NFROne organization's volume never bottlenecks another'sNFRA very large organization can keep growing
Thought process
  1. Start by asking what is actually running out. A queue is rarely the limit. What runs out is the consumers, a downstream limit — the email provider's send rate, the database's write capacity — or a single hot partition. Scaling a big organization begins with finding out which of those it is hitting.
  2. Per-organization queues are the right default, and they have a cost. Consumers must poll many queues and something has to take turns between them — the fair dispatcher here — and thousands of mostly empty queues still cost polling, monitoring and autoscaling rules. So the design is tiered: the long tail shares each lane, with a queue or sub-queue per organization and fair turns; only the very largest get queues of their own. Managed options can replace the hand-built version for that tail: SQS fair queues take a tenant ID on each message and, when one tenant builds a backlog, deliver the others' messages first — without dropping or throttling the noisy one — and Temporal has fairness keys in the same spirit. Neither is hard isolation. When one organization must never share a queue, dedicated queues remain the answer.
  3. Scaling one organization's queue goes in this order, each step only if the last wasn't enough. (1) Scale its consumers on backlog and on the age of its oldest message, and ahead of known peaks such as payday. (2) Split its lane: give the organization N sub-lanes keyed by a secondary key such as a hash of the recipient — org-42-00 … org-42-15 — so throughput grows about N times while each person's messages stay in order. In Kafka that is the key organization + recipient spread over partitions; on SQS it is N queues, or FIFO message groups by recipient. It is the same trick as adding a suffix to a tenant key to spread a hot tenant across partitions in a pooled database. (3) Separate urgent from bulk inside the organization with priority lanes, so a security alert never waits behind a 200,000-message announcement. (4) Check the real limit. If the email provider allows 2,000 sends a second in total, sixteen sub-lanes only build a longer line in front of the provider; the answers are per-organization rate limits, batching, and more sending identities. (5) Cap it: a quota per organization, so a bug in its integration can only exhaust its own share. (6) Promote it to a cell of its own when its lanes, workers and database are a meaningful share of the shared pool, or when a contract asks for isolation.
  4. A cell is a complete, independent copy of the stack for one organization (or a few), with only a thin router in front that maps organization → cell. The rule of thumb: anything on the organization's hot path that could be shared, isn't. That makes "own shard, own partitions, own IPs" concrete. Shard — its own database (an instance or cluster) rather than a slice of the shared one, so its writes, vacuuming and connection limits are its own. Partitions — its own topic and table partitions, so its key distribution, retention and consumer lag belong to it and a hot partition can only hurt itself. IPs — only for traffic that leaves your system: dedicated sending addresses and a domain, so its email reputation is its own, or fixed egress addresses a customer can allow-list. Internal services need none.
  5. Inside the cell, the same code runs with different numbers. The same images and migrations go through the same pipeline — in waves, with cells for small customers first — but on larger instances, with their own autoscaling rules and their own service quotas. Monitoring carries a cell label, so an alert names the cell. Data lives only in the cell; anything that spans cells — an admin view of all organizations, a cross-customer report — is a fan-out query, or a read model fed by each cell's events. Failures stay inside: an outage in the cell touches one organization, and the other cells never notice.
  6. Moving in and out is a procedure, not a heroic act. Copy the organization's data from a snapshot, replay its events since then — idempotent upserts make repeating safe — then flip the routing at a quiet time, let the old lanes drain, and delete the old copy only after the new one is verified. That tooling has to exist before the first customer needs it. A cell is also a running cost: a full stack to deploy, watch and pay for. It is earned by volume or by contract, never the default — and the router, the one shared piece, stays as thin as it can, a lookup and nothing more.
Illustration — what is inside a dedicated cell, and what stays shared
PieceIn the shared poolIn a dedicated cell
Fair dispatcherone dispatcher, a turn per organizationits own dispatcher
Queuesa lane per organization on the shared lane queuesits own queues, with sub-lanes per priority
Sender workersshared pool — 2 of 8 shards per organizationits own pool, sized for its payday
PostgreSQL — deliveries, inboxone shared primary; every key leads with org_idits own primary and replica
Redis — quotas, retry setssharedits own
Attempt log — NoSQLone shared tableits own table
Inbox reads — API and cacheshared GraphQL API and cacherouted to the cell's API, replica and cache
Email sendingshared pool, or an organization subdomaindedicated IPs and domain
Deploys and dashboardsone pipeline, one set of dashboardsthe same pipeline (small cells first); dashboards with a cell label

Only the router and the deploy pipeline are shared with the rest of the platform. That is why a cell can be overloaded, or fail, without anyone else noticing.

Illustration — splitting a lane, and the limit that decides whether it helps

An organization sends 200,000 messages at 09:00. The workers on each lane manage 2,000 sends a second.

one lane100 s
4 sub-lanes · provider allows 8,000 / s25 s
4 sub-lanes · provider allows 2,000 / s100 s — no gain

four times the lanes, and no faster — the provider is the limit

The rates are illustrative. It is the reason to look at the downstream limit before adding lanes: more lanes only help while something behind them can absorb the traffic.

Illustration — scaling one organization: symptom, first move, next move
SymptomFirst moveIf that isn't enough
backlog grows and every worker is busyscale consumers on backlog and on the age of the oldest messagesub-lanes keyed by recipient
urgent messages wait behind bulkpriority lanes inside the organizationreserved capacity for the urgent lane
