Each row is a decision made from a measurement — backlog age, worker utilization, provider errors — not a guess.

  • Many mid-size organizations, none huge — a hundred organizations at 5% each is not a cell problem; fair lanes and quotas handle it.
  • A cell that sits mostly idle — it still costs a baseline; scale its workers down to a small floor between paydays, and up ahead of them.
  • Two very large organizations — each gets its own cell, or they share one when isolation between them isn't needed — a cell can serve several organizations.
Illustration — the cell router, a shared cell and a dedicated one, and moving between them
Key deep dive — dedupe vs. idempotency: sending each notification once
NFRNo duplicate sends, nothing lost
Thought process
  1. Duplicates can enter in two different places, and they need two different fixes. Mixing them up is the most common mistake in this design.
  2. Dedupe is about input: the same event arriving twice — a product retried after a timeout, or its outbox published twice. The event's own id is the key: the first copy is stored, every later copy is acknowledged and ignored. Without it, one payslip would become two notifications before any sending starts.
  3. Where does the event id come from? It is made at the start: by the product, in the same transaction as the business change, and stored in the outbox row beside it. The relay, Kafka and the intake only carry it. If the relay made a fresh id on every send, a crash and retry would look like two events; if the intake made it, it could not recognise a repeat. A random id covers retries of sending; an id derived from the business fact — organization, type, the thing that changed, and its version — also covers the same fact being emitted twice. The full schema, with the tests behind these claims, is in the notification database example.
  4. Idempotency is about work: the same step being done twice — the fan-out re-run after a crash, the queue delivering a job again, two workers picking up the same job. Each delivery gets a key derived from what it is — this event, this person, this channel — so repeating the work finds the existing row instead of creating another.
  5. Workers claim a delivery by changing it from queued to sending in one conditional update. Only one worker can win that change, and a delivery already marked sent can never be claimed again.
  6. One gap can't be closed by any design: the provider accepts the message, and the worker dies before recording "sent". Nobody knows if it went out, so after a timeout it is sent again. The design keeps that window small, and each channel limits the damage: in-app is our own table, so it's exactly once; push uses the notification id as a collapse id, so the phone shows one; email may, rarely, arrive twice. That is the same at-least-once limit as the webhook example.
Illustration — three keys, three kinds of duplicate
KeyWhereStops
event_idintake — primary key of eventsdedupe the same event from a product arriving twice
(notification_id, channel)
notification_id = hash(event_id, member)		fan-out — primary key of deliveriesidempotent a re-run fan-out, or a redelivered job, creating a second delivery
status queued → sending → sentsender — conditional updateidempotent two workers sending the same delivery; re-sending one already sent
Illustration — where the event id is made
Where the id is madeWhat happens on a retryVerdict
by the product, at the start, in its transactionthe same outbox row is sent again with the same id; the intake ignores the copysafe 1 event, 5 notifications
by the relay, at send timeevery attempt carries a new id; the intake sees two eventsduplicates 2 events, 10 notifications
by the intake, on arrivalit cannot tell a repeat from a new event; its own ids can never matchno dedupe
derived from the business facta re-emitted fact gets the same id, so it collapsessafe 1 event, 5 notifications (random ids gave 2 and 10)

The key in the schema example is (org_id, event_id), not event_id alone: with the bare key, one organization's id made another's event look like a repeat, and it was silently dropped. The rows for the product, the relay and the derived id were run; the row for the intake is reasoning — an id made on arrival is new every time, so it behaves like the relay's.

Illustration — every way it can fail, and what the user sees
What goes wrongWhat happensThe user gets
product sends the event twicesecond copy hits the event_id key and is ignoredone
fan-out crashes halfway, then re-runsrows already written are found by their derived ids; only the missing ones are addedone
the queue delivers a job twicethe second copy finds the delivery already sending or sent, and is droppedone
two workers reach the same deliveryonly one wins queued → sending; the other skips itone
worker dies before calling the providerthe claim times out; the delivery is sent onceone
worker dies after the provider accepted, before "sent" is recordedthe claim times out and the delivery is sent again — there's no way to know the first went outin-app: one · push: one on screen · email: maybe two
Illustration — the SQL, tested on PostgreSQL 16
CREATE TABLE events (
  event_id     text PRIMARY KEY,                 -- set by the product: the dedupe key
  org_id       uuid NOT NULL,
  type         text NOT NULL,
  received_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE deliveries (
  notification_id  uuid NOT NULL,                -- derived: same event + same person → same id
  channel          text NOT NULL CHECK (channel IN ('in_app','push','email','chat')),
  org_id           uuid NOT NULL,
  status           text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'queued'
                   CHECK (status IN ('queued','sending','sent','failed')),
  attempts         int  NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  claimed_at       timestamptz,
  provider_msg_id  text,
  PRIMARY KEY (notification_id, channel)         -- the idempotency key
);

-- ② intake: a repeat returns no row, and creates nothing
INSERT INTO events (event_id, org_id, type) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING
RETURNING event_id;

-- ③ fan-out: deterministic ids, so a re-run adds nothing
INSERT INTO deliveries (notification_id, channel, org_id)
SELECT md5($1 || ':' || r.membership_id)::uuid, r.channel, $2
FROM recipients r                                 -- resolved for this event and organization
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

-- ⑥ sender: claim a batch; rows another worker holds are skipped
UPDATE deliveries SET status = 'sending', claimed_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1
WHERE (notification_id, channel) IN (
    SELECT notification_id, channel FROM deliveries
    WHERE status = 'queued' AND org_id = $1
    ORDER BY notification_id, channel
    LIMIT 100
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
RETURNING notification_id, channel;

-- ⑥ after the provider accepts
UPDATE deliveries SET status = 'sent', provider_msg_id = $3
WHERE notification_id = $1 AND channel = $2 AND status = 'sending';
0new rows when the same event was sent a second time
15 → 15deliveries after running the fan-out twice for 5 people × 3 channels
10 + 5, 0 sharedtwo workers claiming at the same moment got disjoint rows

Those three results come from running this SQL. Claiming by organization (org_id = $1) is also what lets workers take turns between organizations. When a real queue such as SQS or Kafka carries the jobs, this table stays the source of truth: a worker receiving a job first makes the queued → sending change, and if that changes 0 rows, the job was already handled and is simply acknowledged.

Illustration — three keys along the path, and the one gap no design closes
Key deep dive — chat integrations: Slack, Telegram and Teams
NFRChat messages respect each provider's limitsNFRA chat problem never delays other channels
Thought process
  1. Chat is not just another provider like an email service. An organization connects its own workspace, so we hold its tokens; each person must be linked to their chat identity; and people act from the chat — approving or rejecting with a button — so messages flow both ways.
  2. Connecting. The admin installs our Slack app (OAuth, a bot token with the fewest scopes that work), adds our Telegram bot, or consents to the Teams app. The integration service stores the connection — organization, provider, workspace, the token encrypted with envelope encryption, its scopes and status. People are linked once: in Slack by matching their email in the workspace; in Telegram the person must open the bot with a one-time link code, because a Telegram bot can't message anyone first.
  3. Sending. Chat is one more channel in the same pipeline: fan-out writes a chat delivery row, the fair dispatcher and the lanes treat it like any other, and the sender hands it to a channel adapter per provider. One template is rendered into each format — Slack Block Kit, Telegram HTML, a Teams Adaptive Card — and each adapter paces itself by its provider's published limits: Slack about one message per second per channel plus a workspace-wide limit; Telegram about 30 messages a second per bot, one a second per chat and 20 a minute per group. It honours 429 and Retry-After instead of retrying blindly.
  4. Payday arithmetic. 100,000 employees linked to a Telegram bot, at about 30 messages a second, take roughly 56 minutes to reach — so chat is never the urgent path: the in-app inbox and push carry the payslip at 09:00, and chat follows. Telegram's paid broadcasts raise the bot's limit to up to 1,000 a second if an organization needs it; for Slack, a single post to a #payroll channel replaces thousands of direct messages when the content isn't personal.
  5. Hearing back. A tapped button calls our interaction endpoint. It verifies the provider's signature (Slack's signing secret with a timestamp, Telegram's secret token), maps the chat user to the person, applies the same permission check as the app, and calls the workflow API with the callback id as the idempotency key — so a repeated callback approves once — then updates the chat message to "Approved".
  6. The connection's life. App uninstalled, token revoked, or a person blocking the bot arrive as events (or as errors): the connection or link is marked inactive, that person's chat deliveries fall back to push and email, the admin is told — and no worker keeps retrying a dead token.
Illustration — chat integrations: connect, send, act and hear back
Illustration — what each provider allows, and what the adapter keys its limiter by
ProviderPublished limitsThe adapter limits per
Slackabout 1 message per second per channel (short bursts allowed), plus a workspace-wide limitchannel, and workspace
Telegramabout 30 messages a second per bot overall; 1 per second to one chat; 20 a minute to one group (paid broadcasts: up to 1,000 a second)bot, chat and group
Microsoft TeamsGraph API throttling per app and per tenant, returned as 429 with Retry-Aftertenant

Limits from Slack's rate-limit documentation and Telegram's Bots FAQ; Teams is governed by Microsoft Graph throttling. Providers change these — the adapter reads Retry-After rather than trusting a constant.

Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • What a message may say — never figures or personal details; "your payslip is ready" with a link. Lock screens and forwarded emails are read by other people.
  • A person with no email and no app — they still have the in-app inbox, and see it when they next sign in.
  • A departed employee — only notifications about their own documents; nothing else from the company.
  • Language — messages are rendered in the person's chosen language, with a fallback when a template hasn't been translated yet.
  • A template error — a broken template fails that notification type's rendering, alerts its owning team, and is caught by preview tests before release.
  • A reminder about a task that's already done — reminders are checked against the current state just before sending, and dropped if they no longer apply.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Payday within minutesIn-app written at once; push and email drained at each provider's rate in the transactional lane.
Security alerts in secondsA separate priority lane with its own workers; nothing queued elsewhere can delay it.
No duplicates, nothing lostDedupe by event_id at intake; deliveries keyed by (notification_id, channel) with derived ids; a conditional queued → sending claim. In-app exactly once; push collapsed on the device; email duplicates only in the provider-accepted-but-unrecorded window.
Email survives a provider outageTwo providers with a circuit breaker and failover.
Respectful of people's attentionCategories, preferences, quiet hours and digests applied in one place for every product.
Nothing sensitive leaksMessages carry no figures; the details are behind sign-in.
No organization delays anotherA queue per organization with fair turns, a quota per organization, shuffle-sharded workers, and dedicated cells for the largest.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Events instead of "send" callsProducts give up control of wording and timing, in exchange for consistent behaviour and one place for preferences.
Priority lanesMore queues and workers to run, in exchange for urgent messages never waiting behind bulk.
Digests and quiet hoursSome messages arrive later, in exchange for people continuing to read them.
Two email providersTwo integrations and costs, in exchange for email that survives one provider failing.
No details in messagesOne more tap to see the figures, in exchange for nothing sensitive on a lock screen.
Fair turns and tiersMore queues, and cells to run for the largest customers, in exchange for small organizations never waiting behind big ones and a runaway organization never taking others down.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Event intake and lanesKafka or SQS, one queue per priority and channel
PushAPNs for iOS and Firebase Cloud Messaging for Android
Emailtwo providers, such as Amazon SES and SendGrid, with bounce notifications fed back
Inbox and preferencesPostgreSQL with an index on (membership_id, read_at)
Fairness and scalingper-organization queues or partition keys in Kafka; per-organization token buckets in Redis; workers autoscaled on backlog with KEDA; separate sending identities and dedicated IPs from the email provider; for the long tail, SQS fair queues (a tenant ID on each message) or Temporal fairness keys instead of a queue per organization
Worked Example AT — Two Customers Are 80% of the Load

Design Isolation and Scaling for the Organizations That Dominate a Multi-Tenant System

finding the noisy few · limits before moves · an isolation ladder · moving an organization without losing a write · scaling inside its own cell · routing and running many cells
Click to expand

Teamline is one software product serving about 2,000 companies from one shared stack: one database, one Redis, one queue, one fleet of app servers. Two of those companies, Org X and Org Y, have grown until together they take about 80% of the database volume, the queue messages, the app-server CPU and Redis CPU and memory. Everyone else — small and medium — feels slow pages and late jobs whenever one of the two has a busy hour. The two big ones are not happy either: the shared stack cannot be scaled for them without paying to scale it for everyone. The answer is judged on the reasons: how you know who it is, what you do this afternoon, what you separate first, how you move an organization without losing a write, and how you run the result. The database steps below were run on PostgreSQL 16; the Redis, queue and app-server parts are reasoning, not run.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Show which organizations use how much of each resource — database, queue, app servers, Redis CPU and memory.
  • Contain any one organization's load quickly, before anything moves.
  • Give the largest organizations their own app servers, queue, cache and database, and let them scale on their own.
  • Route every request, job and query to where its organization lives, with the same code everywhere.
  • Move an organization into its own capacity — and back — without losing a write.
  • Let the small and medium organizations keep sharing one pool.
Non-functional
  • The small and medium organizations' latency stays flat when Org X or Org Y peaks.
  • A move pauses the moving organization's writes for seconds at most, loses none and applies none twice; reads never stop.
  • One organization's load or failure never crosses into another organization's capacity.
  • Decisions come from measurement, and the third big organization is handled by the same playbook.
  • Cost is visible: dedicated capacity is attributable to the organization that uses it.

The second requirement is the one that makes this hard. App servers and queues are easy to move because they hold no data; the database holds all of it, and it is changing while you move it.

2
Core Entities
  • Organization (org_id, tier) — the tenant that the placement is about.
  • Cell (cell_id, kind, endpoints, capacity) — a stack: app, queue, cache, database. kind is pool or dedicated.
  • Placement (org_id → cell_id, state, version) — the routing table; state is active or frozen, and the version increases on every change.
  • UsageSample (org_id, resource, window, amount) — per-organization counters for every resource.
  • Limit (org_id, resource, soft, hard) — the caps.
  • Migration (migration_id, org_id, from, to, phase) — one organization's move, resumable at any phase.
3
API

route(org_id) → the cell's endpoints, cached, with the placement version
GET /usage?resource=…&window=… → organizations ranked by share
PUT /orgs/{id}/limits → per-organization caps
POST /migrations {org_id, to_cell} → start a move; each phase is idempotent and resumable
POST /migrations/{id}/cutover and /rollback → freeze, flip, or go back

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. Monday: the dashboard ranks organizations per resource. Org X and Org Y hold 41% and 39% of the database rows; no other organization is above 0.02%.
  2. That afternoon: per-organization caps at every layer contain the two, so the others stop feeling their bad hours.
  3. This week: the team picks the level — compute first, then cache, then the database — from the resource that was measured as the bottleneck.
  4. Org X's cell is built from the same infrastructure code; its rows are copied with a filtered stream while X keeps running in the pool.
  5. At a quiet minute: X's writes are frozen, the stream catches up, the placement flips from version 2 to 3, and X's traffic goes to its cell.
  6. After a rollback window the stream is stopped and X's rows are deleted from the pool. Org Y follows by the same steps, and the pool ends up holding about a fifth of what it did.
5
High-Level Design

Three ideas. Route by organization: a thin router looks up each organization's placement and forwards it to its cell — the shared pool for the many, a dedicated cell for the two that dominate. A cell is a complete stack of its own: app servers, database, cache, queue and workers. Measure by organization: every cell reports per-organization usage, and a ranking finds the noisy few. Move by procedure: an orchestrator provisions the cell, copies the data with a filtered stream, and flips the placement under a version — so an organization moves once, safely, and the same steps serve the third one.

6
Deep Dives

Six below: (a) finding the noisy few, (b) first aid: limits before moves, (c) the isolation ladder — what to separate first, (d) moving an organization without losing a write, (e) scaling inside the dedicated cell, and (f) routing and running many cells — then the edge cases.

Requests go through a thin router to the organization's cell. Most organizations share the pool; Org X and Org Y each have a dedicated cell — the same stack, on their own. Every cell reports per-organization usage; a ranking and a rule decide who moves, and an orchestrator moves them and flips the placement. A dedicated cell starts as this simple stack; how it grows — sub-lanes on the queue, shards and partitions in the database — is drawn in deep dive (e). The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them.
Illustration — from a request to a move, step by step
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
1a request arrives from a user of any organization; the organization comes from the tokenCell routernever from a header the client can change
2the router looks up the organization's placement — organization → cell, with a state and a version; the answer is cachedPlacementthin routing is a lookup, never a query into the cells
3the router forwards the request to that organization's cell: the shared pool for most, Org X's or Org Y's dedicated cell for the two big onespool · dedicated cellsisolation a dedicated cell shares no app, queue, cache or database with the pool
4inside a cell, the app servers use that cell's own database, cache and queue, and its workers take jobs from that queuethe cellevery cell is the same stack; only the size differs
5every cell reports per-organization usage: database time, queue messages, CPU-seconds, Redis operations and memoryUsage meteringattribution in every cell, or the ranking is blind
6metering ranks organizations per resource; a rule or a person spots one that stays above its share for daysDecide who movesscale decisions come from measurement
7the decision starts a move: the orchestrator provisions a cell, copies the data and walks the phases in the migration diagramMove orchestratorthe move is a resumable procedure, not a project
8at cutover the orchestrator freezes the organization's writes, waits for the copy to catch up and flips the placement, whose version increasesPlacementone writer never two copies accepting writes

The numbers match the ones on the diagram above. The move itself — steps 7 and 8 — is opened up in deep dive (d), with its own diagram.

A normal Tuesday
  1. A user at a small company opens a page; the token names their organization.
  2. The router finds it in the pool and forwards the request.
  3. The pool serves it from its own database, cache and queue — none of them shared with X or Y.
  4. Org X has a heavy hour in its own cell; nobody in the pool notices.
The day Org X moves
  1. Its rows have been copied and are being followed; the pool still serves X.
  2. At the quiet minute X's writes are held for a fraction of a second while the stream catches up.
  3. The placement flips; the held writes go to X's cell.
  4. X's users notice nothing; the pool's load drops by about 41%.
Key deep dive — finding the noisy few
NFRDecisions come from measurementNFREvery resource, not just one
Thought process
  1. Everyone feels the slowdown, and nobody knows who causes it. A graph of the whole system — the database at 85% CPU, Redis nearly out of memory — says that something is wrong, not who. The first job is to attribute each resource to an organization.
  2. Each resource needs its own handle. Database: org_id on every table and key, so rows and bytes per organization is one GROUP BY; for time, measure query time per organization in the app, or run the biggest organizations under their own database role, so statement statistics separate by role. Queue: count messages and processing time per organization where they are produced and consumed. App servers: CPU-seconds or request time per organization, measured in middleware. Redis: it does not attribute memory or commands to tenants by itself, so prefix every key with the organization, sample memory per key with MEMORY USAGE, and count commands in the client.
  3. Look at shares, and look at the tail. Tenant sizes usually follow a steep curve — a few very large, many small — so an "average organization" does not exist. In the lab pool, 2 of 2,000 organizations held 80% of the rows; the biggest of the other 1,998 held 149 rows — 0.015%. That gap is what averages hide.
  4. Rank per resource, not overall. One organization can dominate the database and be invisible in Redis; another the reverse. Track the number that rations each resource: database time, queue messages and processing time, CPU-seconds, Redis operations and bytes.
  5. Write the trigger down so the third big organization is not a surprise: above its share of any resource for a week, or growing faster than the pool can follow, makes it a candidate. The thresholds are yours to choose; what matters is that the rule exists and runs on its own.
Illustration — what to measure, per resource, per organization
ResourceHow to attribute it to an organizationWhat to watch
Database volumeorg_id in every key — rows and bytes are a GROUP BYshare of rows and bytes; growth per week
Database timeper-organization query time in the app, or a database role per big organizationshare of total query time; the slowest queries per org
Queueorganization on every message; count and time at produce and consumeshare of messages and of worker seconds; backlog age per org
App serversCPU-seconds or request time per organization, in middlewareshare of CPU; concurrent requests per org
Redisorganization prefix on every key; sample MEMORY USAGE; count commands in the clientshare of memory and of operations; the biggest keys

Redis is the awkward one: it does not account for tenants itself, so the prefix and the client-side counters are the only way to see who is using it.

Illustration — the shape of the tail, measured on 998,807 records in 2,000 organizations

Share of all rows, by organization group.

Org X41.0%
Org Y39.0%
the other 1,998 together19.9%
the biggest of those 1,998149 rows · 0.015%

two organizations, 80% of the volume — and no other organization above 0.02%

The same ranking, run for queue messages, CPU-seconds and Redis memory, is what decides who moves. The rows and bytes here are measured; the other resources will differ in your system, and the method is the same. By bytes the split is 40.1%, 38.1% and 19.4%.

Key deep dive — first aid: limits before moves
NFRThe small and medium organizations' latency stays flatNFRContain quickly
Thought process
  1. A move takes days to prepare, and the slowdown is today. So contain first: cap what each organization may take, at every layer, so the two big ones cannot crowd out the rest while the move is built. This is the noisy-neighbour work of the multi-tenant rate limiting example, applied to every resource.
  2. Every layer has its own cap. Edge: a request rate per organization. App servers: a limit on concurrent requests per organization, so one cannot hold every worker thread. Database: a role per organization (at least for the biggest) with a connection limit and a statement timeout, and a pooler that caps connections per user and per database. Queue: a lane per organization and a cap on its share of consumers. Redis: nothing built in — its memory limit and eviction policy are for the whole instance, so a per-organization memory cap is not possible in a shared one.
  3. Try the database caps rather than assume them. On the lab pool, the role for Org X was capped at 5 connections and 2 seconds per statement, and a second role had no limits.
  4. Limits contain; they do not scale. An organization at its cap gets slower or rejected requests — the price of protecting the others. That is why limits buy time for the move instead of replacing it. Set them so a big organization keeps its normal load, and alert when they bite: a cap that trips often is the argument for the move.
Illustration — three limits on Org X's database role, run for real
CREATE ROLE org_x_app LOGIN CONNECTION LIMIT 5;
ALTER ROLE org_x_app SET statement_timeout = '2s';
ALTER ROLE org_x_app SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '5s';
AttemptResult
open a 6th connection as Org X's rolerefused FATAL: too many connections for role "org_x_app" — 5 opened
the small organizations' role, 8 connectionsaccepted no limit set
a runaway self-join over Org X's datacancelled at 2.01 s — canceling statement due to statement timeout
pg_sleep(5) as Org X vs as the small rolecancelled at 2.0 s vs completed in 5.01 s
a transaction left idle for 6 sclosed terminating connection due to idle-in-transaction timeout

Limits belong to the role, so they cost nothing when nobody trips them, and they only touch the organization they were set for.

Illustration — a cap at every layer, and what it can't do
LayerMechanismIts limit
Edgea request rate per organization at the gatewayprotects everything behind it
App serversa cap on in-flight requests per organizationa slow dependency can still hold threads
Databaserole limits, plus a pooler capping connections per user and databasecaps connections and time, not I/O or CPU shares
Queuea lane per organization; a cap on its consumers; Kafka client quotas where you use Kafkamanaged shared queues do not rate-limit a tenant
Rediskey prefix and TTLs on everythingno per-organization memory cap in a shared instance — a reason to move
Deep dive (c) — the isolation ladder. Shared resources are dimmed, dedicated ones are red. L1 is a holding position, not a destination: caps protect the neighbours, but they cap the customer too.
Key deep dive — the isolation ladder: what to separate first
NFRThe cheapest fix firstNFRThe small and medium organizations stay pooled
Thought process
  1. Not every resource needs a cell to fix. Separate in order of cost, because stateless things are cheap to move and stateful things are not. The resource you measured as the bottleneck decides how far up the ladder you go.
  2. L2 — own compute. Dedicated app servers, queue and workers for the organization. The router sends its requests to its own deployment and its producers to its own queue. No data moves: app servers are stateless, and a queue holds only in-flight work, which drains. It takes the organization's CPU and queue share out of the pool at once.
  3. L3 — own cache. A dedicated Redis. A cache can be rebuilt, so this is a warm-up, not a migration — with one caveat: a cold cache sends a burst of reads to the database, so warm it first or switch at a quiet hour. If Redis also holds anything durable (locks, counters, sessions), that has to be copied. This is the fix for Redis CPU and memory, which a shared instance cannot cap per organization.
  4. L4 — own database, the full cell. The hard step, and usually the one that matters, because the database is the one resource every organization writes to and the one that is hardest to scale out. It needs the data move in the next dive. Do it when the measured problem is database time, volume or I/O.
  5. One cell for both, or one each? Org X and Org Y are each about 40% of the pool today. If they shared a cell they would be each other's noisy neighbour at a smaller scale, so each gets its own. A shared "large" cell suits several organizations that are each 5–10% — and even then it needs the same fairness and limits the pool has.
Illustration — where do the two big organizations go?
OptionFits whenCostRisk
One cell eacheach is a large share of the pool (here, 41% and 39%), or contracts ask for separationthe most to run: two full stacksnone between them; two cells to deploy to
One shared large cellseveral organizations are each 5–10% of the poolone stack, sized for the sum of their peaksthey can crowd each other out unless limits and fair turns apply inside
Stay pooled, with limitsthe organization is growing but not dominantnothing extrathe neighbours still share its bad days

This example uses one cell each, then moves Org Y by the same steps as Org X.

Deep dive (d) — the seven phases of a move, and the cutover drawn to scale from the lab run. The placement is active in the pool through phase 4, frozen for the cutover, and active in the cell afterwards; the numbers match the table below.
Illustration — a move, phase by phase
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
1Provision the cell from the same infrastructure code: empty database with the identical schema, app, queue and cache; the placement still says poolnew cellDDL is not replicated, so the schema must match and stay frozen for the move
2Copy: a publication with a row filter for the organization, a replication slot and a subscription copy only its rowspool → cell database410,000 records and 82,000 comments in 2.4 s; 0 rows of other organizations
3Follow: the stream carries every later change while the organization keeps running in the poolpool → cell databaselag: median 1,416 bytes, at most 8,184
4Verify: counts, checksums and shadow reads — on the copy, not the primaryboth databases407,157 untouched rows identical; my count on the primary slowed neighbours' writes
5Cutover: freeze, drain, wait for the stream to reach the freeze point, check cheaply, flip the placement, unfreezeplacement · router247 ms; 8 ms of it was the mechanics; neighbours never blocked
6Watch: keep the old copy through a rollback window; the pool refuses writes for the moved organizationpool · cellrollback needs a route back, not a restore
7Clean up: drop the subscription first, then delete the old rows in batches, then vacuumpoola delete on the source with the stream alive emptied the copy (5 → 0); 51 batches in 1.0 s

Every phase is idempotent and resumable: the orchestrator records the phase, so a crash in phase 3 resumes phase 3.

Key deep dive — moving an organization without losing a write
NFRNo write lost or applied twiceNFRWrites pause for seconds, not hoursNFRReads never stop
Thought process
  1. The shape of the problem: the data keeps changing while you copy it. So copy first, then follow the changes until the copy is nearly caught up, then hold new writes for a moment, let the last changes land, and switch. Only the last step pauses anything.
  2. Something has to carry the changes. PostgreSQL's logical replication can filter by row from version 15: CREATE PUBLICATION … WHERE (org_id = …) publishes only that organization's rows, and the initial copy honours the filter, so the move costs only what the organization owns. The alternatives are a change-data-capture pipeline (Debezium into Kafka), a managed migration service, dump-and-restore for a small organization that can accept downtime, or — on a sharded database — Citus, which can isolate a tenant into its own shard and then move that shard to its own node.
  3. The rule from every schema example pays off here: org_id leads every primary key. For updates and deletes to be published, the filter column has to be part of the replica identity. In the lab, with PRIMARY KEY (id) and a filter on org_id, an UPDATE failed — "Column used in the publication WHERE expression is not part of the replica identity" — and with PRIMARY KEY (org_id, id) it was accepted. Retrofitting keys later is the expensive way to learn this.
  4. The cutover is a small state machine with a version: active in the pool (v1) → frozen (v2) → active in the cell (v3). While frozen, the router holds the organization's writes; the orchestrator drains what is in flight, waits until the stream has reached the freeze point, checks cheaply, and flips. One writer at a time: nobody writes during the freeze, and after the flip only the cell does. The pool should also refuse writes for a moved organization, so a router with a stale cache cannot write to the old copy — that is what the version is for (a design rule; it was not run here).
  5. The measured cutover took 247 ms. The mechanics — drain, wait for the stream, flip — took 8 ms; the other 238 ms was a row count I ran on both sides during the freeze. Lesson: do the heavy checks before the freeze, and on the copy. The count also slowed the neighbours' writes on the shared primary, from a median of 1.05 ms to 4.03 ms: verification is load too.
  6. Clean up in the right order. Drop the subscription first, then delete the old rows. In the lab, a delete on the source while the stream was live emptied the copy (5 rows to 0); with the subscription dropped first, it kept its 5. Then delete in batches, and vacuum. Keep the old copy through the rollback window before any of this.
  7. The other resources move by the same idea, with less ceremony. App servers: nothing to move. Queue: producers switch by placement, the old lane drains under its old consumers, and ordered work drains before the switch. Redis: flip, then warm. Three limits of logical replication to plan for: schema changes are not replicated, so freeze them for the move; sequence values are not replicated in PostgreSQL 16, so set them past the source's maximum before the flip (or assign ids in the app); and an abandoned replication slot makes the source keep its WAL until the disk fills, so watch slot lag and drop failed attempts.
Illustration — the commands, and the cutover as pseudo-code
-- on the pool (the source)
CREATE PUBLICATION org_x_pub FOR TABLE
  records  WHERE (org_id = '11111111-…'),
  comments WHERE (org_id = '11111111-…');
SELECT pg_create_logical_replication_slot('org_x_slot', 'pgoutput');

-- on Org X's new database (the target)
CREATE SUBSCRIPTION org_x_sub
  CONNECTION 'host=… dbname=pool user=…' PUBLICATION org_x_pub
  WITH (create_slot = false, slot_name = 'org_x_slot', copy_data = true);
freeze:   placement(Org X) = frozen, version 2      -- the router holds X's writes
drain:    wait until X's in-flight writes finish     --   4 ms
target  = pg_current_wal_lsn()                       -- the freeze point on the source
wait:     until slot.confirmed_flush_lsn >= target   --   3 ms
check:    cheap comparison of both sides
flip:     placement(Org X) = cell X, active, v3      --   1 ms
unfreeze: held writes are released to the new cell

The lab was one PostgreSQL 16 server with two databases, so the slot was created ahead of time to keep the subscription from waiting on itself; between two servers, create_slot = true (the default) works.

Illustration — the lab run, in numbers
MeasureResult
initial copy410,000 records and 82,000 comments in 2.4 s — and 0 rows of the other 1,998 organizations
replication lag while followingmedian 1,416 bytes, at most 8,184 — with two writers and 4,130 writes in 3 s
cutover247 ms in all: 4 ms drain + 3 ms stream + 238 ms row count + 1 ms flip
writes held2 — the longest waited 243 ms; 3,509 later writes went to the new cell
the neighbourswrites were never blocked: median 1.05 ms before, 4.03 ms during the freeze, at most 15.2 ms
verification407,157 untouched rows identical on both sides by checksum; 10,482 rows changed after the flip, excluded; 0 rows of other organizations in the cell
clean up51 batches of 10,000 rows in 1.0 s; the cell stayed at 417,639 rows; 0 replication slots left

One machine and about a million rows: the shape is real, the absolute times are small. At terabytes the initial copy takes hours to days — the stream is what does the real work — and the freeze is still measured in the mechanics, not in the size of the data.

Deep dive (e) — Org X's cell after it has outgrown one queue and one primary: four sub-lanes on the queue, three database shards each with monthly partitions and replicas, and a Redis cluster. The numbers show the order; the table below walks through them.
Illustration — inside the grown cell, step by step
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
1a request reaches the app servers; the router already sent it to this cellApp serverssame as any cell
2the app asks the shard map which shard owns the entity: a hash of a second key, such as the entity id, modulo 3Shard mapscale writes are spread over three primaries
3writes go to that shard's primary, reads to its replicasshards A · B · Creplicas add read capacity, at the price of replica lag
4inside a shard, big tables are partitioned by month; queries carry the key, so only the recent partitions are readpartitionssmall tables, small indexes, cheap vacuum
5a background job picks its lane: a hash of the recipient, modulo 44 sub-lanesone recipient always lands in one lane, so their order is kept
6each sub-lane has its own workers, so the four lanes drain in parallelWorkersscale the same 8 workers as before, now 2 per lane
7workers write their results through the same shard map, to the shard that owns the entityShard map · shardsone routing rule for requests and for jobs
8cache reads and writes go to the Redis cluster, with keys prefixed by organization and entityRedis clusterkeys spread over 3 nodes; one very hot key still sits on one node

The queue and the database are split by different keys — the recipient for the lanes, the entity for the shards — because they are protecting different things: per-person order on one side, write capacity on the other.

Deep dive (e) — the four steps for the database inside a dedicated cell: bigger primary, read replicas, partitions, and shards inside the organization. Each step waits for its own signal.
Key deep dive — scaling inside the dedicated cell
NFRA big organization can keep growingNFRIndependent of everyone else
Thought process
  1. Moving the organization fixes the noisy-neighbour problem; it doesn't make its own growth free. Inside its cell it scales by its own signals, without asking the pool — or anyone else's workload — for permission.
  2. Each resource has its own levers. App servers: more instances on CPU or queue depth, and ahead of known peaks such as month-end. Queue: more consumers, scaled on the age of the oldest message; and when one queue still can't be drained fast enough, split it into sub-lanes — several parallel queues for the same organization, the lane chosen by a hash of a second key, such as the user the job is for (worked example below). Redis: a bigger node, then cluster mode — and watch for a hot key, which adding nodes cannot split. Database: the four steps in the strip below.
  3. The database steps go in order of cost. A bigger primary first, because it changes nothing in the app. Read replicas next, moving reads off the primary at the price of replica lag. Partitioning big tables by time or hash keeps table size, indexes and vacuum manageable, as long as queries carry the partition key. Sharding inside the organization — by a second key such as a hash of the entity, a department or a region — comes last, because it changes the app: cross-shard queries fan out. It is the same idea as sub-lanes on a queue: the organization becomes the outer key, and a second key spreads its load.
  4. Partitioning and sharding are different tools, and they combine. Partitioning splits one table into pieces inside one database, by month or by hash: tables, indexes and vacuum stay small, and old months are cheap to drop, but there is still one primary, so it adds no write capacity. Sharding splits the data across several databases, each with its own primary: that is what adds write capacity and storage, at the price of routing in the app and fan-out for queries that span shards. In the drawing, each of the three shards holds partitioned tables. One point is specific to a dedicated cell: every row in it belongs to the same organization, so org_id can no longer spread anything — the shard key has to be a second column, such as the entity id, a department or a region.
  5. Every step has a signal that says it is time, and pre-scaling covers the peaks you can see coming. Decide the signals before the peak: primary CPU and I/O, replica lag, vacuum time and table sizes, write throughput.
  6. The pool benefits too. Without Org X and Org Y it holds about a fifth of the rows it did (998,807 records, of which 19.9% belong to the other organizations), so the shared cluster can be resized down — and it has room for years of small-organization growth before it needs attention.
Illustration — replica, partition, shard: what each one splits
TechniqueWhat it splitsWhat it fixesWhat it costs
Read replicanothing — a full copy of the databaseread capacityreplica lag: reads may be seconds stale; writes still go to one primary
Partitionone table into pieces inside one database, by month or hashtable, index and vacuum size; old data is cheap to drop or archiveno extra write capacity; queries must carry the partition key to skip pieces
Shardthe data across several databases, each with its own primary, by a key such as a hash of the entitywrite capacity and total storagethe app must route; queries across shards fan out; moving data between shards is work
Partition + shardeach shard holds partitioned tableseach shard stays manageable while writes are spreadthe costs of both
Illustration — signal, then action, for each resource
ResourceSignal that says scaleAction
App serversCPU, or requests waiting for a workermore instances; pre-scale before a known peak
Queue and workersbacklog age of the oldest message; workers all busymore consumers; then split the organization's queue into sub-lanes, the lane picked by a hash of a second key (see below)
Redismemory near its limit; CPU on one thread; one very hot keya bigger node, then cluster mode; split or replicate the hot key
Database, readsread latency; the primary busy with readsread replicas
Database, sizevacuum time; index and table sizepartition by time or hash
Database, writesthe write ceiling of one primaryshard inside the organization on a second key
Illustration — what "sub-lanes by organization + recipient" means

Org 42 sends one stream of messages, and a single consumer cannot keep up. Split its queue into 4 sub-lanes, each with its own consumer. A message goes to lane = hash(recipient) mod 4, where the recipient is the person the message is for.

Arrives asFor (recipient)hash mod 4Goes to
1user_1013org-42 · sub-lane 3
2user_1021org-42 · sub-lane 1
3user_1013org-42 · sub-lane 3
4user_1040org-42 · sub-lane 0
5user_1033org-42 · sub-lane 3
6user_1052org-42 · sub-lane 2
7user_1040org-42 · sub-lane 0
8user_1060org-42 · sub-lane 0
9user_1072org-42 · sub-lane 2
10user_1083org-42 · sub-lane 3

The hash here is CRC32 of the recipient ID; every lane number is computed, not picked. Different recipients spread across the lanes — lane 0 got 3 messages, lane 1 got 1, lane 2 got 2, lane 3 got 4 — so four consumers work at once. The same recipient always lands in the same lane: user_101's messages 1 and 3 are both in lane 3, in that order, and so are user_104's 4 and 7 in lane 0. So each person's messages stay in order; order between different people is not kept, which is usually fine.

The second key should be something whose messages must stay in order, or whose work is naturally separate — the recipient, the user, the account, the document. A random key spreads the load but loses order; a very lopsided key (one recipient with most of the traffic) leaves one lane hot. In Kafka this is the message key spread over partitions; on SQS it is N queues, or FIFO message groups by recipient. "Organization + recipient" just means the pair: the organization picks the family of queues, the recipient's hash picks the lane inside it.

Key deep dive — routing and running many cells
NFRThe one shared thing stays thin and upNFRCells stay operable as their number grows
Thought process
  1. The router is the only shared component on the request path, so it stays as thin as it can: look up the placement, forward, nothing else. It keeps the placement in memory with its version, and if the placement store is unreachable it carries on with the last known answer — static stability — sending unknown organizations to the pool.
  2. Requests, jobs and events all carry the organization and use the same lookup: the router for requests, the producer for queue messages, the scheduler for batch jobs, which run per cell. Every request also carries the placement version it was routed with, so a cell can refuse one that is older than the organization's current version (a design rule; not run here).
  3. Operating cells is mostly making them boring. The same code and migrations go through one pipeline, in waves — a small cell first, then the pool, then the big cells — with a rollback per cell. Every metric, log and trace carries the cell and the organization, so an alert names its cell. Capacity and service quotas are planned per cell; separate cloud accounts per cell keep one cell's quota from being another's.
  4. Some things stay global, and they are still shared resources: the accounts (one person can belong to organizations in different cells, as in the multi-organization identity example), billing, the placement store and the control plane. They get per-organization limits like any shared resource, and no heavy per-request work.
  5. What crosses cells — an admin view of all organizations, a cross-customer report, global search — becomes a bounded fan-out to the cells, or a read model fed by each cell's events.
  6. Cost stays visible: every cell is tagged, so its spend is attributable to the organization that uses it, and dedicated capacity belongs in that customer's plan. An idle cell still costs a baseline, so give it an autoscaling floor rather than a fixed size.
Illustration — who owns what
PieceWhere it livesWhy
Routershared — the only shared piece on the request paththin, stateless, several copies; last known placement if the store is down
Placement storeshared — small, replicatedone row per organization; read on change, not on every request
Usage metering, decision, orchestratorshared control planenot on the request path; can be down without users noticing
App, queue, cache, databaseper cellthe things that must not be shared
Accounts, billingglobala person or a customer spans cells
Deploy pipeline and dashboardsone pipeline; a cell label on everythingsame code everywhere, different capacity
Illustration — a release, cell by cell
  1. wave 1

    a small cell, or one canary organization in each cell — the smallest blast radius first

  2. wave 2

    the shared pool, where most organizations live

  3. wave 3

    Org X's cell — its own rollback, its own window

  4. wave 4

    Org Y's cell — never at the same time as X, so at most one large customer is exposed at once

The order is a policy, not a law: the point is that the largest customers are never the first to see a change, and never two at once.

Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • A third organization grows — the same playbook, started by the same rule. The point of the metering and the orchestrator is that cell number three is a configuration change, not a project.
  • Both big organizations peak together — they are in different cells, so they don't interfere; capacity is planned per cell, not as shared headroom.
  • An organization shrinks, or leaves — move it back by the same procedure in reverse, or retire the cell; a cell that is barely used is a cost with no benefit.
  • Long transactions during the freeze — draining waits for them; statement and idle timeouts (the first-aid limits) are what stop one straggler from stretching the freeze.
  • A router with a stale cache — the version travels with the request, and the pool refuses writes for an organization that has moved, so the worst case is a rejected request, never a write to the wrong copy.
  • Schema changes during a move — DDL is not replicated, so freeze schema changes for the length of the move, then apply them everywhere in the release waves.
  • Reads that depend on data in another cell — anything spanning cells is a fan-out or a read model; a feature that quietly needs both sides is a sign the boundary was drawn in the wrong place.
  • Data-residency requirements — a cell can also be per region; the same placement row says which.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
The small and medium organizations stay fastAfter the moves the pool has no dominant tenant; per-organization limits stay as the safety net for the next one.
Contain the two quicklyCaps at every layer within hours — measured on the database role: 5-connection cap, 2-second statements, idle transactions closed.
The big organizations scale on their ownEach has its own app servers, queue, cache and database, scaled by its own signals — replicas, partitions and shards inside the cell.
Move without losing a writeFiltered logical replication, a freeze, and a versioned placement flip: 247 ms in the lab, 407,157 untouched rows identical, 0 rows of other organizations copied.
Decisions come from measurementPer-organization usage for every resource, ranked; a written rule starts a move, so the third big organization follows the same steps.
Cost is attributableEvery cell is tagged, so dedicated capacity is a line on the organization that uses it.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Limits first, then a moveLimits are cheap and quick but cap the customer; a move takes effort and removes the cap.
A cell per large organizationMore stacks to deploy, watch and pay for, in exchange for no crosstalk and independent scaling.
Row-filtered logical replicationOnly the organization's rows travel, with the schema rules it needs (org_id in every key), in exchange for a stream to watch and slots to clean up — instead of downtime.
Freezing the organization's writesA pause of tens to hundreds of milliseconds in the lab, in exchange for never having two writers.
Keeping the old copy for a windowStorage and a delayed cleanup, in exchange for a rollback that needs no restore.
A thin shared routerOne more thing that must be up, in exchange for every cell staying independent behind it.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Attribution and meteringan OpenTelemetry attribute for the organization on every span and metric; Prometheus or Datadog tags; pg_stat_statements with a role per big organization
Limitsthe gateway's rate limits (for example Envoy); PgBouncer caps per user and database; role settings in PostgreSQL; Kafka client quotas; KEDA on queue depth
Routinga small router (Envoy with a lookup, or a small Go service) reading a placement table in PostgreSQL, DynamoDB or etcd
Moving the dataPostgreSQL logical replication with row filters (15+); Debezium with Kafka Connect; AWS DMS; Citus isolate_tenant_to_new_shard and shard moves; pg_dump for a small organization that can pause
Cells as codea Terraform or Pulumi module per cell; Kubernetes namespaces, node pools and quotas for the app tier; a cloud account per cell for quota isolation
Worked Example AX — Marketplace — Search to Payment

Design a Marketplace: Search, Live Updates, Cart, Checkout and Payment

search · live prices · watchlists · cart · checkout · payment methods · resuming an unpaid order · the change stream · scaling writes
Click to expand

A marketplace where sellers change products all day and buyers search, watch products, add them to a cart, check out several items at once and pay — by virtual account, bank transfer, card or wallet — and where a buyer who started paying and closed the app lands straight back on the payment page. The first half is the read-heavy, live side: polling against SSE against WebSocket, a deploy that drops 2 million connections, watchlists where one product has 2 million watchers, a change stream built from the database log with Debezium and Kafka, search that stays fresh, and scaling the writes. The second half is the transactional side: the cart, checkout, the order, payment and the order's state machine, and resuming an unpaid order. They meet at one rule — the database is the only place a price is true — which is why the cart stores references, the quote re-reads the source, and checkout never trusts a page. Every measurement came from one small machine (one core, 4 GB): PostgreSQL 16 for the writes, CDC behaviour, watchlists, the cart, checkout concurrency, the payment state machine and the pending-order lookup; tantivy standing in for OpenSearch; openssl and a Node server for TLS; and a simulation for the reconnect storm. Kafka, Debezium, OpenSearch, payment providers, banks and shipping services were not run, and the text says which numbers are measured, assumed or extrapolated.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Sellers create and change products, one at a time or in bulk imports of hundreds of thousands.
  • Buyers search with filters and get fresh results.
  • Buyers watch products — any change, a price at or below a threshold, back in stock — and are notified.
  • A product page shows its price and stock live while it is open.
  • Buyers see and edit their watchlist.
  • Buyers add products to a cart after searching, see the current price and stock in it, and have it follow them across devices.
  • Buyers select items from the cart and check out: choose a delivery address and shipping, apply promos, and review one total.
  • One checkout can span several sellers; it becomes one order per seller under a single payment.
  • Buyers pay by virtual account, bank transfer, card or wallet, and are told when the payment is confirmed.
  • A buyer who chose a payment method and left — closed the app, or switched to a bank app — returns directly to the payment page for that unpaid order.
Non-functional
  • Bursts of 50,000 product updates a second (a bulk import, a flash sale) never slow reads or lose an update.
  • Search p95 under 200 ms, and a change is searchable within about 5 seconds.
  • A price drop on a product with 2 million watchers reaches the matching ones within a minute — once each, not once per update.
  • 2 million connected clients, and a deploy must not turn into an outage.
  • The price a buyer pays is always the authoritative one, whatever a page or the index showed.
  • The price shown at checkout is read from the authoritative source, and a change since the cart is shown before the buyer pays.
  • An order is never created twice by a double tap or a retry, and a payment is never applied twice.
  • Stock and vouchers are held while the buyer pays, never oversold or over-redeemed, and released exactly once if the buyer does not.
  • A payment confirmation is never lost, and a paid order is never cancelled by an expiry timer.
  • Reopening the app within the payment window opens the payment page with the same account number and a countdown from the server's clock.

Five requirements, one pattern: the database is the only place a price is true, and everything else — the index, the watch matcher, the browser — is a copy that is allowed to be a few seconds late.

2
Core Entities
  • Product content — (product_id, seller_id, title, description, category) — heavy, changes rarely.
  • Product live — (product_id, price, stock, version) — small, changes constantly. A separate table, on purpose.
  • Watch — (user_id, product_id, rule, threshold) — the rule is any change, price at or below, or back in stock.
  • Change event — (product_id, version, the hot columns) — one record from the database log.
  • Search document — a denormalised copy of a product in the index.
  • Connection and interest set — which gateway holds which user, and which products each viewer is looking at — soft state in Redis.
  • Cart item — (user_id, product_id, qty, seen_price) — a reference and the price the buyer saw, never the price as truth.
  • Checkout session — the selected items, address, shipping per seller, promos and total — a quote with an expiry, and the idempotency key for placing the order.
  • Order — one per seller: status, payment deadline; grouped under a payment. Status moves only along allowed transitions.
  • Payment attempt — (order group, method, provider reference such as an account number, amount, expiry, status) — one live attempt per order.
  • Voucher and redemption — a budget, a per-buyer limit, validity; one row per redemption.
  • Stock hold — the reservation the Inventory service keeps per (order, product), with an expiry — the only binding promise that stock exists.
  • Live read model — a Redis hash per product: price, price version, stock signal and as-of time, fed from the change stream — a display copy, never the authority.
  • Quote — a server-side snapshot of the lines with their price and price version, the totals and an expiry; the client holds only its id.

The version on every row and every event is what lets each copy ignore anything older than what it already has. In the transactional half, the order's status plays the same role: it moves only forward along allowed steps.

3
API

What the clients call:

PUT /products/{id} and POST /products:bulk → seller writes, idempotent by version
GET /search?q=…&category=…&price_max=… → results, with prices for display
PUT /me/watches/{product_id} {rule, threshold} · DELETE · GET /me/watches
GET /products/{id}/live → an SSE stream (text/event-stream), resumable with Last-Event-ID
POST /checkout → reads the authoritative price
PUT /cart/items/{product} {qty} · GET /cart → items with live price and stock, and a notice where either changed
POST /checkout/sessions {items} → a quote; PATCH to change address, shipping or promo
POST /orders {session_id} → places the order (idempotent by session); POST /orders/{id}/payment {method} → payment instructions
GET /orders/pending → the unpaid order to resume; GET /orders/{id}/payment → the existing attempt and the server's time
POST /webhooks/payment → the provider's signed callback
between services: POST /products:live {ids} → price, version and stock signal for many products; POST /prices:validate; POST /reservations and DELETE /reservations/{order}, idempotent by an Idempotency-Key

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. At 09:00 a seller uploads 500,000 price changes for a flash sale; the API coalesces them and writes batched, versioned upserts.
  2. The database log is read by the CDC connector and published to Kafka, keyed by product, hot columns only.
  3. The search indexer, the watch matcher and the live-push router each read the same stream at their own pace.
  4. One product falls below 3,900: 755,294 of its 2,000,000 watchers match, and are handed to the notification system once — not once per update.
  5. Buyers with that page open see the new price within a second, through the gateway that holds their connection.
  6. At 11:00 the gateways are deployed. Connections drain in waves instead of all at once, and clients reconnect with jitter and are sent the current state.
  7. Maya adds the product to her cart. Later she opens it: each item shows today's price, and one carries "cheaper than when you added it".
  8. She selects three items from two shops and taps Buy. The checkout session re-prices them at the source, quotes shipping per shop, applies a voucher, and shows one total.
  9. She picks a virtual account and places the order: two orders (one per shop), stock and the voucher held, one payment attempt with a 24-hour deadline.
  10. She closes the app. An hour later she reopens it: one lookup finds her unpaid order and the app opens the payment page — the same account number, with the remaining time from the server.
  11. She pays from her bank app. The provider's signed callback reaches the payment service, which marks both orders paid, once. Had she not paid, the expiry worker would have cancelled them and released the stock and the voucher.
5
High-Level Design

One spine: the database log. Writes go to a sharded store; a CDC connector turns its log into a Kafka stream keyed by product; three independent consumers build three read models — a search index, a watcher notifier and a live channel to browsers — so a slow search cluster can never slow a seller, and a deploy of the gateways can never lose an update. The database stays the only source of truth; every copy carries a version, so every consumer can be idempotent, and the price that is paid is always read from the source. The transactional half adds a cart of references that reads its live data from a Redis read model fed by the change stream, a checkout that re-reads the owning services and returns a quote, an order service that places an order as a saga across the pricing, inventory, promo and payment services — holding stock and vouchers until a payment deadline — a payment service that hides several providers behind one interface and trusts only verified callbacks, and an expiry worker — with every order status moving only along allowed steps, so a late callback and a timer can never undo each other.

6
Deep Dives

Fourteen below. The first eight are the live, read-heavy half: (a) polling, long polling, SSE or WebSocket, (b) the gateway tier and the reconnect storm, (c) scaling the writes, (d) the change stream: Debezium and Kafka, (e) fast search that stays fresh, (f) watchlists at scale, (g) pushing to the browser, and (h) what fails and what to watch. The last six are the transactional half: (i) the cart when price, stock and the cart are separate services, (j) checkout across services — no zero-stock orders, no surprise prices, (k) paying — pages, redirects, callbacks and webhooks, (l) the order's state machine, (m) resuming an unpaid order, and (n) what fails in checkout and payment — then the edge cases.

Writes go to the product shards; a CDC connector reads the database log into a Kafka stream keyed by product; three consumers — search indexer, watch matcher, live-push router — each build their own copy; buyers read through a page API, and checkout reads the shard. The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them.

One price change
  1. The seller's batch is coalesced and upserted to the shard, with a new version.
  2. The connector publishes it, keyed by product, so it stays in order.
  3. The indexer, the matcher and the router each apply it once, however many times it is delivered.
  4. A viewer sees it in about a second; a watcher is notified once; a search finds it within seconds.
One gateway deploy
  1. The old gateways stop accepting and drain a few percent of their clients at a time.
  2. Each client waits a random moment, then reconnects and is sent the current state.
  3. The new gateways admit connections at the rate they can afford and refuse the rest early.
  4. Nobody is offline for more than about a second, and the connect rate never exceeds capacity.
Key deep dive — polling, long polling, SSE or WebSocket: choose per feature
NFRLive pages without melting the serversNFRLive price and stock while a page is open
Thought process
  1. There are four ways for a page to learn that something changed. Polling: ask every few seconds. Long polling: ask, and the server holds the request until something changes or a timeout passes. SSE (server-sent events): one long-lived HTTP response that the server keeps writing to; the browser reconnects by itself and resumes from the last event id it saw. WebSocket: an upgrade to a two-way channel.
  2. The arithmetic decides it. Two million open pages polling every 5 seconds is 400,000 requests a second, nearly all answering "nothing changed"; at about 1.5 KB of headers and body per round trip (an assumption) that is roughly 600 MB a second. With push, only changes travel. If 50,000 updates a second are spread evenly over 10 million products, an average product changes once every 200 seconds, so 2 million viewers on different products receive about 10,000 pushes a second. Polling scales with viewers × frequency; push scales with changes.
  3. Push isn't free: every open connection costs memory and keep-alives. Measured on a Node server, an idle TLS connection held 39.9 KB (10,000 connections took 390 MB), so 2 million connections need roughly 77 GB across the fleet — about 2 GB on each of 40 servers. That is cheap next to 400,000 requests a second. The cost that really hurts is different: how fast connections arrive — the next dive.
  4. Pick per feature, not per app. A product page's price and stock: SSE — one direction, plain HTTP that passes through proxies and CDNs without an upgrade, reconnect and resume built into the browser, and the server can tell clients how long to wait before retrying. Watch two limits: about six SSE connections per browser and domain on HTTP/1.1 (about 100 streams on HTTP/2), so open one stream per page, never one per product. A notification badge: SSE too, or a slow poll. Anything that needs the client to talk back on the same channel — typing, presence, collaborative editing: WebSocket, where you write the reconnect and resume yourself. A seller's import-progress bar: polling is fine — few users, slow changes.
  5. Keep polling as the fallback for all of them. The client library tries SSE, and where a proxy or a network breaks streaming it falls back to long polling or to conditional polling with an ETag (a 304 with no body), using an interval the server chooses and jitters. The design goal is one code path for "what is the current state?" and several ways to be told it changed.
  6. Two rules keep it honest. A push is a hint, never the truth: the payload carries the new value and its version, and the page ignores anything older than what it shows. And a background mobile app can't hold an SSE stream — for a buyer who left the app, the same change becomes a push notification through the notification system.

OptionDirectionHow it reconnectsCost at 2M viewersBest for

Key deep dive — the gateway tier, and the reconnect storm
NFRA deploy must not become an outageNFRTwo million live connections
Thought process
  1. The scenario: 2 million WebSocket connections run happily. A deploy drops them; almost immediately a huge share of clients reconnect; the new servers, sized for 2 million connections, are overwhelmed — by connections arriving. A server that holds 100,000 idle sockets can be crushed by tens of thousands of simultaneous handshakes because the two costs are different: holding a connection is memory, arriving is CPU and state.
  2. Measure both. Holding: 39.9 KB per idle TLS connection on a Node server. Arriving: a full TLS 1.3 handshake cost 0.56 ms of server CPU with an ECDSA P-256 certificate and 0.959 ms with RSA-2048 (openssl, one core: about 1,784 and 1,043 handshakes per core-second) — before the application's own work: check the token, load which products this person is viewing, replay what they missed. Assume 3 ms for that (an assumption), so each connect costs 3.56 ms.
  3. Now the arithmetic. Reconnecting 2,000,000 clients costs 7.1 million CPU-milliseconds. A fleet of 320 cores (40 servers of 8, an assumption) does 320,000 CPU-milliseconds a second, so it can accept about 89,887 connections a second at best — and reconnecting everyone takes at least 22.2 seconds even when perfectly spread. The fleet was sized for 2 million idle connections; it was never sized for 2 million arrivals in a second.
  4. A fluid simulation of six policies, with a client that gives up after 10 seconds, makes the point (table and chart below). If everyone retries at once (A, B, C), all 2 million attempts land in the first second — 2,000,496 a second — everyone is back after 23.8–24.8 s, and about 9.3% of the CPU is spent on attempts the client had already abandoned. Backoff and jitter on the retries barely changed anything, because the first wave is the problem. Jitter on the first reconnect (a random 0–30 s wait, C2) kept the peak at 67,556 a second — under capacity — with one attempt per client and no waste. Refusing early and cheaply when the queue is over 3 seconds (D) cut waste to 0.5%. And draining the deploy in waves over five minutes (E) cut the peak to 6,996 a second and each client's time offline to a median of 0.3 s.
  5. So the fixes, in the order that matters. (1) Don't drop everyone at once: drain gradually, a few percent at a time — the only fix that removes the first wave. (2) Jitter the first reconnect, not only the retries, and let the server say how long to wait (SSE's retry field, or Retry-After). (3) Refuse early and cheaply when over capacity, so a failure costs microseconds instead of a handshake. (4) Make a reconnect cheap: TLS terminated at the edge, ECDSA certificates, a resume token or Last-Event-ID so the client doesn't re-download the world (TLS session resumption should help too, but the test here showed no saving, so it is not claimed). (5) Size and alert on the connect rate — new connections a second, handshake CPU, accept-queue depth — not only on concurrent connections. (6) Deploy a canary first and watch the connect rate before the rest.
  6. What the model leaves out matters: overloaded gateways fail their health checks and are removed, which shrinks capacity and deepens the storm — a real cascade. The simulation shows the arithmetic floor and the waste, not the collapse; the collapse is what the health checks and a canary are for.
Illustration — attempts per second after a deploy, three policies (simulation)

A 2-second average, on a log scale. The dashed line is what the fleet can accept. Policy A's spikes at about 0, 11 and 22 seconds are the retries arriving in waves.

Key deep dive — scaling the writes
NFR50,000 updates a second never slow reads or lose oneNFRA flash-sale row everyone wants
Thought process
  1. Fix the shape of the write before the hardware. On one connection, one update per transaction ran at 4,165 a second; 1,000 updates in one transaction at 19,250; one batched upsert of 1,000 rows at 78,263. Batching removes round trips and commits, not work.
  2. Then coalesce. A bulk import or a flash sale changes the same product many times in a window. With 20,000 events over 2,000 products, applying every event took 0.96 s and 20,000 row writes; keeping only the latest per product took 0.05 s and 2,000 writes. It is also required, not only faster: PostgreSQL refuses a batch that touches the same key twice — "ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time".
  3. Guard every write with a version: WHERE excluded.version > product_live.version. An older batch can then never overwrite a newer row, and a retried batch is harmless — the same idea as the idempotent consumer in the next dive.
  4. Split the hot from the heavy. A price changes constantly; a description almost never. Updating only the price of a row that carries a 1,000-byte description wrote 1,272 bytes of WAL per update; the same update on a narrow table of price, stock and version wrote 244 bytes — 5.2 times less (measured with full-page writes off, to isolate the change itself). A description over about 2 KB is stored out of line and cost 430 bytes; the trap is the medium-sized row. This is also less for the CDC connector to read and for the replicas to replay.
  5. A hot row is a different problem: one product's stock, wanted by everyone at once. Eight workers made 4,800 attempts against 4,000 in stock. One row sold exactly 4,000 — no oversell — at 1,795 attempts a second; sixteen bucket rows also sold exactly 4,000 at 2,216 a second (+23%). The gain was modest here because this machine has one core and CPU was the limit; the correctness comes from the conditional update (stock > 0), not from a read followed by a write, and buckets spread the lock — a benefit that grows with cores and slower commits, which was not shown.
  6. Then scale out. Shard by product_id (a hash), so one update touches one shard and a product's content and live rows stay together; a seller's bulk import fans out across shards by product. Avoid sharding by seller — one huge seller becomes one hot shard. Put a queue in front if writes must be accepted faster than the database applies them, and answer the seller "accepted, applying" rather than making them wait. Give bulk imports their own lane and quota so they cannot starve a small seller's single edit.
Illustration — the write, and the flash-sale guard
-- one batched, coalesced, version-guarded upsert: 1,000 products in one statement
INSERT INTO product_live (product_id, price_cents, stock, version)
SELECT p, pr, 0, v                                   -- a new row starts with no stock; an existing row's stock is left alone
FROM unnest($1::bigint[], $2::int[], $3::bigint[]) AS t(p, pr, v)
ON CONFLICT (product_id) DO UPDATE
   SET price_cents = excluded.price_cents, version = excluded.version, updated_at = now()
 WHERE excluded.version > product_live.version;      -- an older or repeated batch changes nothing

-- a flash sale: the condition is the guard against overselling, not a read followed by a write
UPDATE stock_buckets SET stock = stock - 1
WHERE product_id = $1 AND bucket = $2 AND stock > 0
RETURNING 1;                                         -- no row: this bucket is empty, try the next one

Illustration — the write path, and the numbers behind it
Key deep dive — the change stream: Debezium and Kafka
NFRSearch, watchers and live pages all stay currentNFRA slow consumer never slows a seller
Thought process
  1. Why a log and not "write the database, then publish to Kafka"? Because the two steps can fail in between, and a dual write loses or reorders events. Reading the database's own log — Debezium reading PostgreSQL's write-ahead log through a logical replication slot — makes the database the single writer and the stream a faithful, ordered copy of it. (When an event isn't just a row change, the outbox in the notification schema is the alternative.)
  2. Order: Kafka orders within a partition. Key every record by product_id and all changes to one product land in one partition, in commit order. Across products there is no order and none is needed. One hot product is one partition's traffic, and that is fine — its consumers need exactly that order.
  3. It is still at-least-once: connector restarts, consumer rebalances and retries all redeliver. So every consumer must be idempotent — apply a change only if its version is newer. Tested: 30,000 distinct changes for 5,000 products, delivered as 52,718 messages (duplicates included) in random order. The version-guarded upsert ended with 0 wrong rows; a blind overwrite ended with 4,179 of 5,000 products wrong.
  4. The stream's size follows the row. A change record carries the whole new row, so a price update on a table with a 1,000-byte description produced 1,060 bytes per update on the stream; publishing only the hot columns with a column list (PostgreSQL 15+) produced 40 bytes — 26 times smaller. With the default replica identity an update record carries the new row and only the old key, so a consumer that needs the previous price keeps it itself.
  5. The operational trap is the slot. While a connector is down the database keeps the WAL it hasn't read. With a stalled consumer, 100,000, 300,000 and 600,000 updates left 24.7, 79.3 and 156.5 MB of WAL pinned — about 260 bytes per update, growing until the disk fills. The safety valve is a cap (max_slot_wal_keep_size): with 32 MB, the slot was invalidated (lost) after about 50 MB of changes. The disk is safe, but the connector must take a fresh snapshot. So alert on the slot's retained bytes, choose the cap on purpose, and keep the snapshot path rehearsed — a snapshot is the same bulk copy measured in isolating the massive organizations.
  6. Schema changes travel through the stream too. Adding a column is harmless to tolerant consumers; a rename or a type change needs a versioned contract (a schema registry) and a plan for consumers that lag. A quiet table in a busy database also needs a heartbeat, or its slot's position goes stale and pins WAL that nobody needs.
Illustration — the publication, the idempotent consumer, and the slot to watch
-- what the change stream carries: only the hot columns (PostgreSQL 15+)
CREATE PUBLICATION product_changes FOR TABLE products (product_id, price_cents, stock, version);

-- a consumer applies a change only if it is newer: duplicates and disorder become harmless
INSERT INTO search_state (product_id, price_cents, version) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT (product_id) DO UPDATE
   SET price_cents = excluded.price_cents, version = excluded.version
 WHERE excluded.version > search_state.version;

-- watch the slot, or a stalled connector fills the disk
SELECT slot_name, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained, wal_status
FROM pg_replication_slots;
