Illustration — the change stream and its consumers
Key deep dive — fast search that stays fresh
NFRSearch p95 under 200 msNFRA change searchable within seconds
Thought process
  1. Search is a copy: a denormalised index built from the change stream — title, description, brand, category, and the few numbers you filter by — never the source of truth. It can lag by seconds. That is the deal, and it is why the write path never waits for it.
  2. Freshness and throughput are one knob: how often you commit (Elasticsearch and OpenSearch call it the refresh interval). Indexing 250,000 documents with tantivy, a Lucene-family engine, on one core: committing every 500 documents ran at 16,508 documents a second; every 5,000 at 49,632 (worst-case wait 0.16 s); every 50,000 at 77,399 (wait 0.83 s) — 4.7 times the throughput for a wait that stayed under a second. Bulk loads want a long interval; the live stream wants a short one.
  3. Queries are the cheap part. On the 250,000-document index, median latency was 0.06 ms for one title term, 1.01 ms (p95 3.24 ms) for two terms across title and description, 0.08 ms for a phrase, and 0.15 ms for a term with a price range and a category. That is a small index on one core; a production index of tens of millions of documents is slower, and the p95 target is met by sharding, not by hoping.
  4. A price change is a whole-document rewrite. Lucene-family indexes are made of immutable segments: an update marks the old document deleted and indexes a new full one. Tested: 50,000 price changes ran at 46,361 a second, against 65,079 for brand-new documents (71% of the speed), and the index grew from 22.3 to 28.0 MB (+26%) with the dead copies waiting for a merge. At a flash sale's 50,000 price changes a second that is a core's worth of indexing — repeated on replicas — for a field nobody searches by text.
  5. So decide which fields belong in the index. Keep title, description, brand and category — they change rarely and they are what people search. Treat price and stock as live: coalesce their updates per product over a window of 5–30 seconds before indexing; filter and sort by price using the indexed (slightly stale) value; overwrite the displayed price and stock from the live store when the results are rendered; and never let checkout use either. The trade-off is stated: a price filter can be a few seconds out of date.
  6. Scale search by sharding. The index is split into N primary shards, each with replicas; a query goes to every shard and the top results are merged, so latency is the slowest shard's — keep shards the same size and cap replicas. The number of primary shards is hard to change later, so leave headroom or plan a rebuild.
  7. Reindex without downtime: build a new index from a snapshot of the source plus the stream from a saved offset, let it catch up, then swap an alias and keep the old one until it is verified. Because the stream that feeds live updates is the same one, "reindex" is just another consumer that starts from the beginning.

Illustration — search finds the products; the cache shows the price
Key deep dive — watchlists at scale: one product, 2 million watchers
NFRA price drop reaches the right people within a minuteNFROnce each, not once per update
Thought process
  1. A watch is a row: (product_id, user_id) with a rule — any change, price at or below a threshold, back in stock. It is read in two directions: "who watches this product?" (the fan-out, keyed by product) and "what do I watch?" (the user's page, keyed by user), so it has two indexes.
  2. Tested with 6,000,000 watches, one product holding 2,000,000 of them. The price falls from 5,000 to 3,900: everyone who asked about any change matches, plus every price threshold in the range that was crossed — 755,294 of 2,000,000. Finding them took 0.85 s scanning that product's watchers with the primary key alone, and 0.47 s with an index on (product_id, rule, threshold_cents) that touches only matches — at a price of 252.9 MB of index against a 344.7 MB table. Build it only for the hot products. Paging through the matches in keyset batches of 10,000 took 0.59 s on one worker; four workers took 0.89 s here, because there is one core — on separate machines the work divides.
  3. Finding watchers is cheap; telling them is the cost. In the notification schema, a fan-out that wrote 100,000 notifications, 300,000 deliveries and 100,000 inbox items took 41.2 s on this machine — about 12,000 rows a second. Even at only a notification and a delivery per watcher, 755,294 watchers is about 1.5 million rows: on the order of two minutes on one machine at that rate, and the email and push providers behind it are slower still. That is why the matcher hands one job per watcher to the notification system — which paces, dedupes and respects each person's preferences — instead of sending anything itself.
  4. Coalesce per product, or the number multiplies. If a price is changed 100 times in a minute — a flash sale, a repricing bot — a matcher that reacts to every event makes 100 × 755,294 = 75,529,400 notification jobs. A matcher that waits a short window per product and evaluates the final state makes at most 755,294: a hundred times fewer, and the last price is the only one anyone cares about.
  5. "At or below" should mean crossing, not being below. Notify when the old price was above the threshold and the new one is at or below it — otherwise every update on a discounted product re-notifies everyone. That needs the previous price: the matcher keeps the last price it saw per product (or the table uses full replica identity, which costs more WAL). A back-in-stock rule needs hysteresis for the same reason: stock that flaps between 0 and 3 must not notify twice an hour.
  6. Watching and unwatching are cheap writes: 2,000 inserts in 0.09 s (21,345 a second, with three indexes) and 2,000 deletes in 0.08 s; a person's watchlist read in 0.01 ms. Cap the number of watches per person, and let the notification system apply per-person hourly limits and digests.
Illustration — the table, the indexes, and the fan-out query
CREATE TABLE watches (
  product_id      bigint NOT NULL,
  user_id         bigint NOT NULL,
  rule            smallint NOT NULL,           -- 0 any change · 1 price at or below · 2 back in stock
  threshold_cents int,
  created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (product_id, user_id));          -- "who watches this product?"
CREATE INDEX watches_by_user ON watches (user_id, product_id);                              -- "what do I watch?"
CREATE INDEX watches_match   ON watches (product_id, rule, threshold_cents) INCLUDE (user_id);   -- only worth it for hot products

-- the price fell from 5,000 to 3,900: anyone who asked about any change, plus every threshold that was crossed
SELECT user_id FROM watches WHERE product_id = $1 AND rule = 0
UNION ALL
SELECT user_id FROM watches WHERE product_id = $1 AND rule = 1
                              AND threshold_cents >= $new AND threshold_cents < $old;

Illustration — one price drop, 755,294 watchers
Key deep dive — pushing to the browser: interest routing and resume
NFROnly the people looking at a product hear about itNFRReconnecting is cheap
Thought process
  1. A price change should reach only the people looking at that product. When a page opens it tells its gateway which product it is viewing (and again when it navigates). The gateway keeps a local map from product to connections, and registers its interest in Redis: product → the set of gateways with viewers. The live-push router reads the change stream, looks up those gateways, and sends each one message; the gateway fans out locally.
  2. The arithmetic (assumptions, not measurements): broadcasting every update to all 40 gateways at 50,000 updates a second is 2,000,000 messages a second, nearly all thrown away. Interest routing sends a change only if someone is viewing the product: if 2 million viewers sit on 2 million of the 10 million products, about a fifth of changes matter — around 10,000 messages a second, roughly 200 times fewer. A flash-sale product with 200,000 viewers costs 40 gateway messages and 200,000 local writes per update.
  3. A hot product's local fan-out is the next limit, so coalesce there too: send each viewer at most one update per product every half second or so, and let the latest win. The payload is tiny — price, stock and version — and the page ignores anything older than what it shows.
  4. Resume is where SSE earns its keep, and where a prices feed can be simpler than a chat feed. Each event carries an id — the product's version — and a reconnecting browser sends it back in Last-Event-ID. For prices, the gateway doesn't replay what was missed; it sends the current state, because the missed values no longer matter. A reconnect then costs one lookup, not a replay — which is exactly what keeps the connect cost low in the storm.
  5. Slow clients need a bounded queue per connection: drop older updates when it fills (latest wins) and disconnect a client that stays behind. Send an SSE comment every 15–30 seconds so proxies don't close an idle stream.
  6. Interest entries in Redis are soft state. Each gateway refreshes its entries with a short TTL, so a crashed gateway's entries expire by themselves; the client is the real source of what page it is on, and it resubscribes after every reconnect. Losing Redis degrades live updates, not correctness — clients fall back to polling until it returns.
Illustration — how many messages, with and without interest routing

50,000 product updates a second, 40 gateways, 2 million viewers on 2 million of 10 million products (assumptions).

broadcast to every gateway2,000,000 / s
send only to gateways with viewersabout 10,000 / s

the same viewers see the same changes, with two hundred times fewer messages between the router and the gateways

A flash-sale product with 200,000 viewers is 40 gateway messages plus 200,000 local writes per update — coalesced to about two updates a second per viewer at most.

Illustration — what a reconnecting page does
StepWhat happens
1the browser waits the server-suggested retry time, plus its own jitter
2it reconnects with Last-Event-ID and the product it is viewing
3the gateway registers interest in Redis and sends the current price, stock and version
4the page keeps whichever is newer; later changes arrive as events

For prices there is no replay: the current state is the whole truth. A feed that needs every missed event — a chat — would keep a per-channel buffer and replay from the id.

Illustration — routing a change only to the gateways that need it
Key deep dive — what fails in the live half, and what to watch
NFREvery consumer fails on its ownNFRKnow before the users do
Thought process
  1. Each consumer reads the stream at its own pace, so each fails on its own. A slow search cluster falls behind and catches up; a stalled watch matcher delays notifications and nothing else; a crashed gateway causes a small reconnect wave. The seller's write path waits for none of them — that is what the log is for.
  2. The failures that deserve a sentence each are in the table below. The pre-mortem to say aloud: the search cluster degrading, a connector stalling and pinning WAL, and a gateway deploy causing a reconnect storm — each with what the dashboard shows and what the system does by itself.
  3. Metrics: alert on symptoms (a price drop that takes minutes to reach a watcher; search results that are stale; a wave of connect failures) and keep causes (slot bytes, consumer lag, handshake CPU) on a dashboard. The age of the oldest unprocessed change matters more than the depth of any queue.

Illustration — the live half: what still works when one part fails
Key deep dive — the cart when price, stock and the cart are separate services
NFRThe cart shows today's price and stockNFRThe cart never waits on a slow serviceNFRMoney is never decided from a cached copy
Thought process
  1. First, the honest limit of the query in this dive's baseline: cart_items JOIN product_live works only when the cart and the product data share one database. In a real marketplace they usually don't — the cart service owns carts, and Pricing, Inventory and Catalog are other services with their own databases — so there is no join to run, and sharing one database just to allow it would tie every team's schema together. The single-database numbers below stay as the baseline: what a cart read costs when it is one query.
  2. What makes the separated version solvable is a distinction of purpose. A cart needs a display copy of live data, and a display copy is allowed to be seconds old. Money decisions are not made from it — they are made later, at checkout and when the order is placed, from the owning services. So the cart doesn't need the strictest guarantee; it needs to be fast, to survive a dependency being slow, and to tell the buyer when something may have changed. (The freshness ladder below shows the four stages side by side.)
  3. There are four ways to get live price and stock into a cart read (compared in the table below). (A) Share the database and join — only a monolith. (B) API composition: the cart service calls the Pricing, Inventory and Catalog batch endpoints on every read — always fresh, but the cart is only as fast and as available as its slowest dependency (if two calls are each fast 99% of the time, about 2% of cart reads include a slow one — arithmetic on an assumed 99%). (C) A read model fed by events: a copy of the live fields, kept current from the change stream, read in one round trip. (D) The client calls each service itself — more round trips from a phone, and the composition logic duplicated in every app. The production answer is (C) for the normal path, with (B) as the fallback for anything the read model doesn't have.
  4. The read model is Redis: one hash per product, live:{product_id}, holding the price, its version, a stock signal, and a timestamp. It is fed by the owning services' change streams: Debezium reads their database logs into a Kafka topic that is log-compacted (it keeps the latest value per product), and a small live-cache updater applies each change with a Lua script that updates only if the version is newer. Tested on real Redis 7.0.15: 20,000 products, 120,000 changes delivered 210,090 times in random order. The version-guarded updates ended with 0 wrong products; a blind overwrite ended with 16,587 of 20,000 wrong (83%). The guarded updater applied 71,286 events a second on one shared core, and because it ignores repeats, Kafka redelivery and consumer rebalances are harmless.
  5. Reading is cheap and the read is one round trip. Reading 70 products from Redis on a local socket took 3.682 ms as 70 separate calls, 1.068 ms as one pipeline, and 0.189 ms as one MGET (p99 0.352 ms). Across a real network at an assumed 0.5 ms a hop, 70 sequential calls would cost about 35 ms and a single round trip about 0.5 ms. Each product hash took 104 bytes, so ten million products fit in about 995 MB (arithmetic). In Redis Cluster a multi-key command only works for keys in one slot, so clients pipeline per node rather than relying on one MGET across the cluster.
  6. Is every product in Redis? Not necessarily — and at 100 million products, usually not. The cache is keyed by product and shared by every cart. Carts differ per user, but a product's price is the same for everyone, so a cart read is the user's own rows from the Cart DB plus one MGET of their product ids. Caching whole carts per user would be wrong: every price change would have to invalidate every cart holding that product.
  7. How much of the catalogue. A full copy is possible: at 104 bytes a product, 100 million products are about 9.7 GB per copy (19.5 GB with one replica), loaded in about 20 minutes from one client. But most of a long-tail catalogue is never in anyone's cart, and the stream would spend its writes keeping those entries fresh. A working-set cache holds the products people view or carry: in a popularity model of 100 million products, caching the top 10 million (about 1 GB) serves roughly 75.6–87.5% of reads, and a miss costs one batch call to the owners. Choose the full copy only when the active catalogue fits comfortably and nearly all of it is read.
  8. Fresh by events, not by TTL. The updater refreshes an entry only if it is cached and the version is newer; misses are filled from the product batch API. The TTL — about 30 minutes, with ±20% jitter so entries don't all expire together — is only a safety net for a missed event. Products that don't exist get a 2-minute negative entry so junk ids don't hammer the owners.
  9. The subtle race. A fill reads the owner, and an update lands before the fill writes: the update found nothing cached and skipped, so the fill caches the old price, which stays wrong until the next change or the TTL. Tested on real Redis: a plain write cached an already-old price in 12 fills and an only-if-newer write in 14 — the version check can't help when nothing was cached. Leaving a 60-second version floor when an update finds the product uncached refused those fills (8 were re-read) and left 0.
  10. When a hot entry expires, everyone misses at once: 200 readers made 200 fetches to the owners. A single-flight lock per product (SET NX) made 1; the others waited a few milliseconds and read the filled entry.
  11. Stock in the cart is a signal, not a count: "in stock", "only 3 left", "out of stock". The Inventory service publishes an event only when the signal changes — crossing a threshold — not on every decrement, so a product selling 50 units a second doesn't send 50 events a second to every cart. The exact number is needed only when stock is reserved, and that call goes to Inventory itself.
  12. Price carries a version. Pricing stamps every price with a monotonically increasing price_version (and the sale window it applies to). The cart stores the version it showed; a read compares versions, and a mismatch becomes the notice "price changed from X to Y". Scheduled changes — a sale starting at noon — are published when they take effect, and the read model also keeps the window's end so it can flip on time.
  13. Degrade; never block the cart. A Redis miss triggers one batch call to a product API with a ~150 ms timeout and a circuit breaker; if Redis is down the cart uses the batch API alone; if both are down the cart still loads with the last price the buyer saw, marked "can't confirm prices right now", and checkout is blocked (it needs authoritative data). Every item carries an as_of time and a fresh flag, so the app can say "updated 12 s ago" if lag grows. Alert on the age of the oldest unapplied change, not only on errors, and add a short TTL as a safety net with read-through on a miss.
  14. Starting and checking it. A working-set cache needs no rebuild — it warms on demand (pre-warm the best sellers before a big sale if you like). A full copy is rebuilt by replaying the compacted topic. Either way, a periodic sample comparison against the owning services counts mismatches — the copies-drift-apart case in the Case Catalog.

-- Live-cache updater: apply a change only if it is newer. Runs atomically inside Redis (EVAL).
local cur = redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'v')                       -- the version we already hold
if (not cur) or tonumber(cur) < tonumber(ARGV[1]) then
  redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'v', ARGV[1], 'p', ARGV[2], 's', ARGV[3])   -- version, price, stock signal
  return 1
end
return 0                                                           -- a duplicate or an older change: ignore it

Key deep dive — checkout across services: no zero-stock orders, no surprise prices
NFRThe price paid is authoritativeNFRNever oversold, even with retriesNFRAn order is never created twiceNFRA voucher is never over-redeemed
Thought process
  1. With price, stock, vouchers, orders and payment in different services there is no single transaction to wrap around checkout, so the guarantees have to be built. Three are needed: the buyer pays only a price they have seen and confirmed; no order is accepted for stock that does not exist; and nothing is reserved or charged twice. Each is built the same way: one owning service for the fact, a version or key that makes repeats harmless, a conditional operation at the owner, and a saga with compensations across them.
  2. The quote is a non-binding snapshot. The checkout service calls Pricing for each price and its version, Inventory for availability, the Promo service for discounts and the carriers for shipping, and stores the result server-side with an id, its lines (product, quantity, price, price version), totals and an expires_at. The client holds only the quote id — it never sends prices, so it cannot tamper with them. The expiry is the sooner of a fixed window and the next scheduled price change among the items, so a sale ending at 12:00 cannot be honoured at 12:05. Anything that differs from the cart is shown before the buyer proceeds.
  3. Price changes: validate, and ask the buyer to confirm. When the order is placed, Pricing validates every (product, price version). All unchanged: continue. Any changed: refuse with a new quote and the changed lines highlighted, and let the buyer confirm. Measured with prices changing 4,575 times a second across 2,000 hot products and about 20 ms between quote and order: if the order trusted the quote, 622 of 12,000 orders (5.2%) were placed at a stale price; with a version check 0 were, and 627 buyers were asked to confirm instead. The stale share grows with changes per product per second × the wait, which is why quotes expire. A caveat for separate services: validating and committing are not one atomic step, so the order stores the validated price and version — a change after validation doesn't alter an order the buyer has already confirmed. The alternative policy is a price lock (Pricing issues a token that holds the price for N minutes), which is fairer to buyers in a flash sale and costs the seller margin.
  4. Stock has three layers — keep them apart. A display signal (cart, product page): eventual, a hint. An availability check (the quote): non-binding — true when asked, possibly false a moment later. A reservation (placing the order): the only binding one. The reservation is an operation in the Inventory service: a conditional decrement (qty >= n) in its own database plus a hold row keyed by (order_id, product_id) with an expiry. Nothing else — not the cache, not the quote — may be treated as a guarantee that stock exists.
  5. Calls between services get retried, so every step must be idempotent. Tested on PostgreSQL: with each of 1,000 orders' reserve calls sent three times, a service that decremented on every call held 3,000 units for 1,000 orders; a unique reservation key held exactly 1,000. Releasing twice made it worse: after the naive path the stock total was 4,999,000 instead of 5,000,000 — 1,000 units of real stock lost — while the keyed path came back to exactly 5,000,000. Every call between services carries an Idempotency-Key (the order id plus the line), and the status guard on release makes it happen once.
  6. A hot SKU needs a gate in front of the database. For a flash sale, put a Redis stock gate in front of the Inventory DB: an atomic Lua script that decrements a counter if it is large enough, so "sold out" is answered without touching the database. Measured on real Redis, 16 workers on one shared core, when every attempt succeeds: a conditional update on one PostgreSQL row did 3,087 a second; the Redis Lua gate 20,597 a second (6.7×). With 1,000 in stock and 16,000 attempts the gate alone admitted exactly 1,000, oversold 0.
  7. The gate is never the authority. Redis can lose recent writes on a crash (with a once-a-second flush, up to about a second), which makes its counter too high or too low. The Inventory DB's conditional update stays the final guard. Tested: DB stock 1,000 but the Redis counter wrongly set to 1,300, as after a restart that lost writes. The gate admitted, the database refused only 16 attempts — about one per worker in flight — and then the gate closed itself when the database said no; 1,000 sold, 0 oversold, and 5,384 attempts were turned away at the gate. The rule: on a database refusal, close the gate (do not give the unit back), reseed it from the database (available minus outstanding holds); after a Redis restart, reseed before reopening; if Redis is down, go straight to the database — slower, still correct.
  8. Placing the order is a saga (diagram below) run by the Order service. It first creates the order as pending, idempotent by the quote id; then calls, in this order, price validation (read-only), stock reservation (the contended resource), voucher reservation (a budget), and finally the payment attempt (external and costly) — cheapest and likeliest to fail first. If a step fails, the Order service releases what earlier steps held. The saga's state lives in the Order DB, so a crashed Order service resumes; a workflow engine such as Temporal or AWS Step Functions can hold that state instead. Two-phase commit across these services would couple their availability; compensations work because every step has an idempotent undo. The final commit — the order becomes pending payment — happens in one local transaction with an outbox event.
  9. Partial stock is a product decision, not an error. If 2 of 3 items can be reserved, don't fail the whole checkout: return what was reserved and what wasn't, and let the buyer continue with 2. Create the order only after they confirm. Holds last until the payment deadline; the Inventory sweeper releases expired holds once (status guard), and a confirmed payment turns the hold into a committed decrement the sweeper can no longer touch (see the payment dive).

PolicyHowTrade-off

validate, then ask to confirmPricing re-checks each version; a changed line returns a new quotea confirmation step, but nobody pays a price they have not seen
price lockPricing issues a token that holds the price for N minutesfair to buyers, costs seller margin, Pricing must store locks
Illustration — who guarantees what, and with which tool
GuaranteeOwnerMechanismTool
the price paid was seen and confirmedPricing servicea version on every price; validate at the order; the order stores price and versionPostgreSQL, an Idempotency-Key
no order for stock that does not existInventory serviceconditional decrement plus a hold row with an expiryPostgreSQL; a Redis Lua gate for hot SKUs

a voucher is not over-redeemedPromo serviceone row per redemption plus a budget counter, in one transactionPostgreSQL

Illustration — the Inventory service's reservation, and the Redis gate
-- Inventory service: reserve stock. One transaction; idempotent by (order, product).
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO reservations (order_id, product_id, qty, status, expires_at)
VALUES ($order, $product, $n, 'held', $payment_deadline)
ON CONFLICT (order_id, product_id) DO NOTHING RETURNING 1;
--   no row back: this call is a repeat. Return the existing reservation and change nothing.
UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - $n WHERE product_id = $product AND qty >= $n RETURNING qty;
--   no row back: not enough stock. ROLLBACK (the reservation row goes with it) and answer
--   "insufficient, available = …".
COMMIT;

-- Release (the sweeper, or a failed saga step): the status guard makes it happen once.
UPDATE reservations SET status = 'released'
WHERE order_id = $order AND product_id = $product AND status = 'held' RETURNING qty;   -- then add qty back to stock
-- Redis stock gate (EVAL): refuse early when the counter says it is gone; never the final authority.
local q = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]))
if q and q >= tonumber(ARGV[1]) then
  redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
  return 1                                   -- admitted: now ask the Inventory DB, which decides
end
return 0                                     -- the gate is shut: answer "sold out" without touching the database
-- If the Inventory DB then refuses, SET the gate to 0 and reseed it later from the database
-- (available quantity minus outstanding holds). After a Redis restart, reseed before reopening.

TestResult
reserve called 3 times for each of 1,000 orders — decrement on every call3,000 units held
the same, with a unique (order, product) key1,000 units held
reserve ×3 then release ×2 per order, naive4,999,000 of 5,000,000 — 1,000 units lost
the same, keyed and status-guarded5,000,000 — exact
price changes 4,575/s, ~20 ms between quote and order — trust the quote622 of 12,000 placed at a stale price
the same, with a version check0 stale · 627 asked to confirm
a hot row, every attempt succeeds, 16 workersPostgreSQL 3,087/s · Redis Lua gate 20,597/s
stock 1,000, gate counter wrongly 1,300database refused 16, then the gate closed · 1,000 sold · 0 oversold

Real Redis 7.0 and PostgreSQL 16 on one shared core; client threads share that core, so absolute rates are low and the ratios matter. Pricing, Promo, Payment and the saga engine were not run: these are the owning-service rules, tested in one database, and the price test checks and inserts in one statement — across services the order stores the validated version instead.

Key deep dive — paying: pages, redirects, callbacks and webhooks
NFRPay by virtual account, transfer, card or walletNFRWe always learn about a payment, even if the buyer never returns
Thought process
  1. Two questions come first, and they have separate answers. Where does the buyer pay? That depends on the method (table below). How do we find out they paid? That is always the same: a webhook — a server-to-server call from the payment provider — and never the buyer's browser coming back to our page.
  2. Keep three words apart. The return URL (a redirect) is the buyer's browser or app coming back to us after paying: a convenience, which may never happen — the tab is closed, the app is killed, the bank app took over. The webhook (also called a callback or a notification) is the provider's server making an HTTP POST to an endpoint we expose, carrying a signed event: this is the proof. A status query is our server asking the provider "what is this payment's state?": the fallback when a webhook is late. Only the last two may mark an order paid.
  3. Card, through the provider's hosted page (first diagram). We create a payment with the provider — amount, order id, a return URL, a webhook URL, an idempotency key — and get a hosted-page URL, and the buyer is redirected there. The card is typed on the provider's page, so it never touches our systems (the smallest compliance scope). The issuer may challenge with 3-D Secure — a one-time code or an approval in the bank's app. The buyer is then redirected back to our return URL; at that moment our page can only say "checking your payment…" and ask our own server for the status. The webhook arrives on its own schedule: before the buyer returns, after, or twice.
  4. Virtual account (second diagram). There is no redirect. We create a virtual account for this order — an account number that expects exactly this amount, with an expiry — and show it on our own payment page with a countdown and "how to pay". The buyer pays outside our app, in their bank's app or at an ATM, possibly hours later with our app closed. The bank notifies the provider, the provider calls our webhook, we mark the order paid and send a push notification. The buyer never comes back through us, so for virtual accounts and manual transfers the webhook is the only way we learn — which is why webhook reliability and the resume path from the previous dive matter most here. A "check payment status" button gives the buyer a fallback.
  5. Card with embedded fields, and e-wallets. With the provider's embedded fields (a secure frame or SDK inside our page) the buyer stays on our page and we receive a token, not a card number: better conversion, a little more compliance work than a full redirect. An e-wallet redirects or deep-links to the wallet app, the buyer approves there and returns. In every case, confirmation is by webhook.
  6. The webhook endpoint (third diagram) does four small things and decides nothing. Verify the signature over the raw bytes as received, with the shared secret and a constant-time comparison; check the timestamp; store the event under a unique key of (provider, event id); answer 200 immediately. Tested with 2,000 signed events: verifying the raw bytes passed 2,000; parsing the JSON and re-serialising it first failed all 2,000 with default settings, and even a compact re-serialisation failed 286 — the events with non-ASCII text. So verify before parsing. For replays: valid signatures replayed 2 seconds and 4 minutes old were accepted and those 10 minutes and a day old were refused with a 5-minute timestamp check, whereas checking the signature alone accepted all 4,000.
  7. Store first, process later, because the provider times out slow endpoints and retries — for hours, with backoff — so a slow handler causes duplicates, and a payday burst arrives all at once. Tested: 20,000 deliveries of 14,000 distinct events (30% repeats) from 8 workers stored all 14,000 and ignored 6,000 repeats through the unique key, at 9,368 deliveries a second on one shared core. Two workers claiming with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED then applied them at 7,573 events a second, marked 14,000 orders paid, and 0 more than once. Events that fail go to a dead-letter table and can be replayed by hand.
  8. Do not trust the webhook alone. Back it with a status query — when the buyer taps "check status", and on a schedule for orders still pending near their deadline — and a daily reconciliation against the provider's settlement report, where any paid order we don't know about, or any we marked paid that the provider doesn't have, is an alert. Also alert on events sitting in the new state too long.
  9. Small rules that prevent real incidents. The return URL carries only our order or payment id — never "status=paid" or an amount — and the return page asks our backend. No secret goes in a URL. The webhook endpoint accepts HTTPS only, authenticates by signature (optionally also an IP allowlist), and secrets are rotated with an overlap, so old and new both verify for a while. An order in pending payment has one live payment attempt (a partial unique index); switching method cancels the old attempt and creates a new one.

Illustration — card, through the provider's hosted page

Read the two coloured bands as the lesson: the return path (steps 9–12) can be missing; the webhook path (13–14) cannot be. Both end in the same guarded change to the order.

Illustration — virtual account: no redirect, and the buyer may never come back

The "check status" path (10–12) asks our server, which asks the provider — it never trusts anything the app says about payment.

Illustration — the webhook endpoint: store first, process later
StepWhat happensTool or technique
1the provider POSTs a signed event to our endpointHTTPS; HMAC signature over the raw body; a timestamp
2verify, check the timestamp, store under a unique key, answer 200PostgreSQL unique key on (provider, event id)
3workers claim new events at their own paceFOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, or a queue such as Kafka
4a guarded transition marks the order paid; an outbox event leavesguarded UPDATE; transactional outbox
retryif we do not answer 200 in time, the provider tries againprovider retries with backoff; our handler must be idempotent
Illustration — the endpoint, in outline
POST /webhooks/payment                              (the shape is common; each provider's exact scheme differs)
 1. raw = the request body, as bytes, exactly as received
 2. expected = HMAC_SHA256(secret, timestamp + "." + raw)    compare in constant time; reject on mismatch (401)
 3. reject if |now − timestamp| > 5 minutes                  (a replay of an old captured event)
 4. INSERT INTO webhook_events (provider, event_id, raw, status)
    VALUES ('psp', $event_id, $raw, 'new') ON CONFLICT (provider, event_id) DO NOTHING        -- a repeat is ignored
 5. return 200 immediately                                   (the provider retries anything slower or non-2xx)

-- worker, later and at its own pace:
SELECT … FROM webhook_events WHERE status = 'new' ORDER BY received_at LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
-- parse the stored raw body → apply the guarded order transition (see the next dive) → mark the event processed
Illustration — the three ways to learn a payment happened
WayWho calls whomCan it be trusted?What can go wrong
return URL (redirect)the buyer's browser or app arrives at our pageno — it carries no proof; ask the servernever happens: tab closed, app killed, bank app took over
webhook (callback)the provider's server calls our endpointyes — if the signature verifies and the event is newarrives late, twice, out of order, or not at all
status queryour server asks the provideryes — as of the callcosts a call; use it as the fallback, not the main path

TestResult

Standard-library HMAC and PostgreSQL 16 on one shared core. The providers, banks and the 3-D Secure flow were not run, and each provider's real signature scheme differs in detail: the shape — raw bytes, timestamp, unique event id, answer fast — is the common part.

Key deep dive — the order's state machine: a payment racing the expiry timer
NFRNever paid twice, never cancelled after payingNFRMoney rules are stated, not improvised
Thought process
  1. The dangerous bug is a race between the payment webhook and the expiry timer, because the timer doesn't know who has paid. Tested on 5,000 orders with 13,641 events delivered in random order — duplicate payment callbacks, and an expiry event for every order — 3,517 paid on time, 465 paid late, 1,018 never paid. With guarded transitions, 0 orders ended wrong: 3,517 paid, 465 paid-late, 1,018 expired. With last write wins, 2,051 ended wrong, including 1,586 orders that had been paid and were cancelled — customers who paid and lost their order.
  2. The rules make the outcome independent of arrival order: the timer only ever moves pending → expired; a payment made at or before the deadline moves pending or expired to paid (with the stock checked again); a payment after the deadline becomes paid late, which needs a decision — reinstate the order if stock remains, otherwise refund. The deadline is compared with the time of the payment, not the time the webhook arrived.
  3. Money rules need stating. A virtual account normally enforces the exact amount; a manual transfer can be short or over, so an underpayment stays pending with a request to top up or a refund, and an overpayment is refunded or credited. A buyer who pays by two methods at once is refunded the duplicate.
  4. Reconcile every day: compare the provider's settlement report with the orders marked paid, find callbacks that never arrived (verify, then mark paid) and any mismatch (alert; the target is zero). The "check payment status" button on the payment screen should make the server ask the provider directly, not wait for a webhook that may be late.
  5. When an order becomes paid, an event leaves through the outbox (see the notification schema) for fulfilment, notifications and the search and stock updates in the first half of this example. Whether the marketplace holds the money until delivery and pays the seller afterwards is a separate ledger decision.
Illustration — the order's state machine
FromEventTo
pending paymenta verified payment, at or before the deadlinepaid
pending paymentthe deadline passes with no paymentexpired — stock and voucher released
expireda verified payment made at or before the deadline (the webhook arrived late)paid — stock checked again
pending or expireda verified payment made after the deadlinepaid late — reinstate if stock remains, else refund
paidthe expiry timer firesno change — the timer cannot touch a paid order
pending paymentthe buyer cancelscancelled — holds released
 
-- the provider says it was paid at $paid_at; the timer says the deadline passed. Neither may overwrite the other.
UPDATE orders SET status = CASE WHEN $paid_at <= payment_expires_at THEN 'paid' ELSE 'paid_late' END
WHERE order_id = $1 AND status IN ('pending_payment', 'expired');

UPDATE orders SET status = 'expired'
WHERE order_id = $1 AND status = 'pending_payment' AND payment_expires_at <= now();      -- the timer only ever moves pending → expired
Illustration — the payment race, measured
StrategyOrders ending in the wrong statePaid orders cancelled
guarded transitions, decided by payment time against the deadline0 of 5,0000
last write wins2,051 of 5,0001,586

13,641 events in random order, with duplicates. The providers and banks were not run: this is the state machine's rule, tested on PostgreSQL.

Illustration — the order's state machine
Key deep dive — leaving and coming back: resuming an unpaid order
NFRReopening the app lands on the payment pageNFRThe countdown is the server's, not the phone's
Thought process
  1. The scenario: the buyer chose a method, got an account number, switched to their bank app — or closed everything — and later comes back. They must land on the payment page, not on the cart and not at a fresh checkout. The way to guarantee it is that the server knows, not the app: everything the payment page shows — amount, bank, account number, deadline — is stored on the order and its payment attempt, and the app keeps nothing but an order id. Killing the app, signing in on another phone or opening the website all behave the same.
  2. On start-up the app asks one cheap question, as part of its first request: does this buyer have an order in pending payment whose deadline is in the future? If yes, it opens that order's payment page (or shows a "complete your payment" banner if the buyer arrived by a deep link elsewhere). Tested on 3,000,000 orders, 1.5% of them unpaid (45,165): the lookup took 0.015 ms with a full index on (buyer, status, date) of 139 MB and 0.012 ms with a partial index on unpaid orders of 1.4 MB — about 99 times smaller, the same speed. The partial index is the better design because it stays in memory and only unpaid orders ever touch it. At an assumed 5 million app opens in the busiest hour (about 1,400 a second) the check costs a rounding error.
  3. The payment page is idempotent: opening it reads the existing attempt and never creates a new account number by itself. A new attempt is created only when the buyer deliberately changes method. And the countdown comes from the server's clock: the response carries the deadline and the server's current time, and the app counts down the difference — a phone with a wrong clock would otherwise show 23 hours left on an expired order.
  4. A buyer can have several unpaid orders. Show the one with the nearest deadline first and a list of the rest, and when a new checkout would contain items already in an unpaid order, say so before creating another.
  5. The expiry worker that cancels unpaid orders also sends reminders at fractions of the window — say half-way and near the end — through the notification system, and each notification deep-links to the same payment page, so the reminder and the app start use one path.
  6. If the deadline passes while the app is closed, the worker cancels the order and releases the stock and voucher; on the next start the lookup finds nothing pending, and the order history says the payment wasn't received. A buyer who pays after that produces a late callback, which the state machine turns into "paid late" and handles by reinstating or refunding — see the previous dive.
  7. Changing method while an order is pending cancels the old attempt and creates a new one. Whether the deadline restarts is a policy: keep the original deadline for scarce items, so a buyer cannot hold stock indefinitely by switching methods; allow a fresh window where stock is plentiful.
Illustration — the lookup, the partial index and the payment page
CREATE INDEX pending_by_buyer ON orders (buyer_id, payment_expires_at) WHERE status = 'pending_payment';   -- 1.4 MB for 3,000,000 orders

-- on every app start: does this buyer have an unpaid order?
SELECT order_id, payment_expires_at FROM orders
WHERE buyer_id = $1 AND status = 'pending_payment' AND payment_expires_at > now()
ORDER BY payment_expires_at LIMIT 5;

-- the payment page reads what exists; it never creates a new account number by itself
SELECT method, provider_ref, amount_cents, expires_at, now() AS server_now
FROM payment_attempts WHERE order_id = $1 AND status = 'pending';

Key deep dive — what fails in checkout and payment, and what to watch
NFRNothing is charged twice or lostNFRKnow before buyers do
Thought process
  1. The failures here cost real money, so each has a deliberate answer. The ones that matter most are in the first table: a double tap, a payment callback that never arrives, an expiry that races a payment, a price that changed after the quote, and an app that dies mid-payment.
  2. Watch the funnel as closely as the servers. A drop between cart and checkout, between checkout and a placed order, or between a placed order and a paid one points at different problems — price surprises, address and shipping friction, or a payment method failing — and the payment success rate should be tracked per method and per provider, because one provider degrading looks like "payments are down" in an average.
Illustration — what fails, and what the design does
FailureWhat happensThe design answer
the buyer double-taps Place ordertwo orders could be createda unique key on (buyer, checkout session): one order, the same answer to both taps
stock runs out between the quote and the orderthe order cannot be placed as quoteda conditional decrement refuses it; say which item, and keep the rest
the price changed after the quotethe total is no longer the one shownrevalidate on placing; ask the buyer to confirm a changed total
the payment callback never arrivesa paid order stays pendinga status query when the buyer asks, and daily reconciliation against the provider's report
the expiry timer races a paymenta paid order could be cancelledguarded transitions decided by payment time against the deadline
the buyer pays after the deadlinemoney with no live order"paid late": reinstate if stock remains, otherwise refund
the app dies mid-paymentthe buyer is lostthe server holds the order and attempt; the start-up check reopens the payment page
the payment provider is downnew payments failoffer another method; keep orders pending; do not create attempts that cannot be completed
the promo service is downno discount can be computedsay so; let the buyer retry or continue without; never drop an applied promo silently
shipping rates are unavailableno delivery pricefall back to cached zone rates, or disable that carrier for now
the live read model lags or Redis is downthe cart shows an older pricea notice and an as-of time; fall back to the batch API; checkout re-reads the owning services, never the cache
the Redis stock gate is wrong or lostit may admit too many, or turn buyers awaythe Inventory DB's conditional update is the authority; close the gate on a refusal, reseed from the database
a call inside the saga times outthe outcome is unknownretry with the same Idempotency-Key — validation, reservation and release are all safe to repeat
a webhook storm at paydaycallbacks arrive in burstsacknowledge fast, queue, process idempotently

Illustration — checkout and payment: what still works when one part fails
Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • The price on the page differs from the price at checkout — checkout always reads the shard; a page price is display only. If they differ, show "the price changed" and ask for confirmation.
  • A seller changes one product 1,000 times in a minute — updates are coalesced per product; the version increases per applied write, not per event; the matcher notifies on the final state.
  • A product is unlisted or deleted — a tombstone event removes it from the index and the live channel; its watches are cleaned up lazily and never notify.
  • Stock flaps between 0 and 3 — a back-in-stock rule needs a cooldown per person and product, or it notifies again and again.
  • A buyer has the app in the background — SSE can't run there; the same change becomes a push notification through the notification system.
  • Ten tabs open on HTTP/1.1 — browsers allow about six SSE connections per domain; share one stream across tabs (a shared worker or a broadcast channel) or use HTTP/2.
  • A reindex during a flash sale — build a new index from a snapshot plus the stream, catch up, and swap the alias; the live index keeps serving throughout.
  • One product is bigger than a Kafka partition can carry — don't spread it across partitions — that breaks its order; coalesce upstream so only the latest state is published.
  • An item sells out between the cart and the order — the conditional decrement refuses it; tell the buyer which item, and keep the rest of the order.
  • The price changes between the quote and the payment — the order is revalidated when placed; if the total moved beyond a tolerance, the buyer confirms it first.
  • The buyer changes the address after the quote — shipping is re-quoted per seller; the old quote is discarded.
  • Two devices check out the same cart — each creates a session; the unique key and the stock guard mean at most the available quantity is sold, and the second sees the first's unpaid order.
  • A seller cancels after payment — the order becomes cancelled and the buyer is refunded; the bonus is not credited.
  • A partial payment — a virtual account normally rejects a wrong amount; a manual transfer that is short stays pending with a request to top up, or is refunded.
  • A buyer has unavailable items in the cart — they are shown as such and cannot be selected; the cart still loads.
  • Several unpaid orders at once — the nearest deadline first, and a warning before another checkout repeats the same items.
  • Redis restarts and loses recent stock counters — the gate is reseeded from the Inventory DB (available minus holds) before it reopens; until then requests go straight to the database.
  • A product's price changes while it sits in many carts — nothing is rewritten: carts show the notice when read, and every order re-validates the version.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
50,000 updates a second never slow readsBatched, coalesced, version-guarded upserts: 78,263 rows a second on one core against 4,165 one at a time; the hot columns live in a narrow table (1,272 to 244 bytes of WAL per update).
No update lost or applied out of orderLog-based CDC keyed by product; version-guarded consumers ended with 0 wrong rows out of 5,000 despite 52,718 deliveries in random order.
Search fresh within secondsA commit cadence trades throughput for a wait under a second (16,508 to 77,399 docs/s); price and stock are coalesced before indexing.
A price drop reaches 755,294 watchers, once eachRule index finds them in 0.47 s; coalescing cuts 75,529,400 jobs to 755,294; the notification system paces the sends.
A deploy is not an outageDrain in waves, jitter the first reconnect, refuse early: peak 6,996 attempts a second and 0.3 s offline, against 2,000,496 a second when everyone returns at once.
The price paid is always authoritativeCheckout reads the shard; the index, cache and browser are copies that may be seconds late.
The price paid is authoritativeThe cart shows live prices as notices; the quote re-reads the source; the order revalidates when placed.
An order is never created twiceA unique key on (buyer, session): 1,000 submissions of 200 orders created exactly 200 (check-then-insert created 982).
Stock and vouchers are never oversoldConditional updates: 0 oversold of 2,000 attempts; 1,000 vouchers redeemed against a budget of 1,000, none twice.
A paid order is never cancelled by a timerGuarded transitions decided by payment time: 0 wrong of 5,000, against 1,586 paid orders cancelled by last-write-wins.
Reopening the app lands on the payment pageThe server holds the order and attempt; a partial index of 1.4 MB answers the start-up check in 0.012 ms.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
SSE instead of WebSocket for live pricesOne direction, plain HTTP, resume built in — in exchange for no client-to-server channel and a six-connection limit per domain on HTTP/1.1.
A log-based connector instead of dual writesOrdered, complete copies with no lost events — in exchange for a replication slot that pins WAL when the connector stalls.
Coalescing updates before indexing and matchingA hundred times less work and no stale notifications — in exchange for prices that can lag by the window (5–30 s).
Price and stock kept out of the searchable textCheap flash sales — in exchange for a price filter that can be a few seconds out of date.
Interest routing to gatewaysTwo hundred times fewer messages — in exchange for interest sets in Redis and a soft-state protocol.
Draining a deploy over minutesAlmost no reconnect wave — in exchange for a slower rollout and two versions running side by side.
A cart of references, not pricesThe cart is always honest and cheap to keep — in exchange for a join with the live store on every read.
A quote with a short expiryThe buyer sees a stable total while choosing — in exchange for revalidating and sometimes asking them to confirm a changed price.
One payment for several sellers' ordersOne account number and one confirmation for the buyer — in exchange for reconciling one payment against several orders.
Holding stock while the buyer paysNo one is told "paid" and then "out of stock" — in exchange for stock tied up for the payment window.
Trusting only verified callbacksNo fake "payment successful" — in exchange for handling late and missing callbacks with status queries and reconciliation.
Resume decided by the serverAny device lands on the payment page — in exchange for one lookup on every app start.
A Redis read model for the cartA fast cart that survives a slow service — in exchange for a few seconds of staleness and a pipeline to keep it current.
A Redis gate in front of the stockA flash sale that does not melt the database — in exchange for a counter that can drift and must be reseeded from the database.
A saga instead of one transactionServices stay independent — in exchange for compensations and idempotent steps in every call.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Change data captureDebezium on PostgreSQL logical replication (column lists, heartbeats); the outbox pattern where events aren't row changes
The streamKafka (or Redpanda), one topic keyed by product id; a schema registry for the contract
SearchOpenSearch or Elasticsearch: bulk indexing, refresh interval, alias swaps for reindexing; tantivy was used here as a stand-in
Sharded storagePostgreSQL with Citus or application routing by hash of product id; Vitess for MySQL
GatewaysEnvoy or NGINX at the edge terminating TLS; gateways in Go, Node or Rust speaking SSE or WebSocket; Redis for interest sets
Load and canary testingk6 or a custom client that ramps the connect rate, not only the connection count
ObservabilityOpenTelemetry and Prometheus: slot bytes, consumer lag by age, new connections per second, handshake CPU
Paymentsa payment provider or aggregator offering virtual accounts, cards with 3-D Secure and e-wallets behind one API; signed webhooks and a status endpoint; a daily settlement report for reconciliation
Orders and cartsPostgreSQL sharded by buyer for carts and by order group for orders; a partial index on unpaid orders
Webhook receivingan HTTPS endpoint that checks an HMAC-SHA256 signature over the raw body and the timestamp, stores the event in a PostgreSQL table with a unique key, and answers 200; workers claim with SKIP LOCKED
Schedulinga worker or scheduler for expiry and reminders (see the announcement scheduler), claiming rows with SKIP LOCKED
Shipping and promoscarrier rate APIs behind a cache of zone rates; a promo service that is a pure function of cart, buyer and time
Live read modelRedis hashes or strings per product, updated by a Lua script that applies only newer versions; Kafka with a log-compacted topic as the feed; Debezium reading the owning services' databases
Stock gatea Redis Lua script in front of the Inventory DB for hot items — a gate to refuse early, never the authority
The sagastate in the Order DB with a transactional outbox, or a workflow engine such as Temporal or AWS Step Functions; an Idempotency-Key on every call
Worked Example AY — Channels, Live Delivery and Search

Design a Slack-Like Channel Messaging System

WebSocket vs SSE vs polling · ordering and retries · a 100,000-member channel · the reconnect storm and resume · a change stream (CDC + Kafka) · search that respects permissions · scaling the writes
Click to expand

A workspace chat product: members post in channels, see new messages live, scroll back through history, get unread counts and mentions, are notified when they are away, and search what they are allowed to see. It holds the same family of problems as the marketplace example but the chat version is harder in ways that matter: the connection must carry both directions; every member must see a channel in one order; a retry must not duplicate a message; a channel can have 100,000 members; and when a deploy drops 2 million WebSocket connections, clients must catch up on what they missed without hammering the database. Every measurement below came from one small machine (one core, 4 GB): PostgreSQL 16 for the send path, unread counts, history and the consumer rules; tantivy standing in for OpenSearch; and, for the handshake and storm arithmetic, the numbers from the earlier example. Kafka, Debezium and OpenSearch themselves were not run, and the text says which numbers are measured, assumed or extrapolated.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Members post messages in channels — public, private and direct — and edit or delete their own.
  • Members see new messages in open channels immediately, and can scroll back through history.
  • Each channel shows an unread count and mentions; reading it clears them on every device.
  • Members who are away are notified of mentions and direct messages.
  • Members search messages in the channels they can access.
  • Members see who is online and who is typing.
Non-functional
  • A message reaches online members within about 500 ms, and every member sees a channel's messages in the same order.
  • A send that is retried after a network failure appears exactly once.
  • 2 million concurrent connections, channels of up to 100,000 members, and 30,000 messages a second at peak.
  • Search is fresh within seconds and never returns a message the searcher may not see.
  • A gateway deploy neither becomes an outage nor loses a message.

A channel is a log. The live push, the unread count, the search index and the notification are all readers of that log that keep their own position — which is why one slow reader never delays a send, and why a lost push can always be repaired.

2
Core Entities
  • Channel — (channel_id, workspace_id, last_seq) — the counter is the ordering.
  • Message — (channel_id, seq, message_id, client_msg_id, author, body, version, deleted) — an edit is a new version, a delete a tombstone.
  • Membership — (channel_id, user_id, last_read_seq) — the read cursor; unread is last_seq minus this.
  • Mention — (channel_id, seq, user_id) — only for the members actually mentioned.
  • Change event — the log record for a message change — channel, seq, version.
  • Connection and interest — which gateway holds which member, and which channels each is viewing — soft state in Redis, with presence.

Presence and typing are ephemeral: they live in Redis with a short TTL and never reach the database or the change stream.

3
API

What the clients say over the WebSocket, and call over HTTP:

send {channel, client_msg_id, text} → ack {seq} · push {channel, seq, message}
view {channels} · typing {channel} · resume {channel → last seq}
GET /channels/{id}/history?before=seq → a page of messages
POST /channels/{id}/read {seq} · GET /unread
GET /search?q=… → hits the member may see

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. Maya types in #general, a channel of 100,000 members; her app makes a client_msg_id and sends it over her socket.
  2. The message service takes the next seq for #general, stores the message, and acknowledges: "seq 600,001".
  3. The change stream carries it, keyed by channel; the router finds the 40 gateways with members viewing #general and sends each one message.
  4. The gateways push it to the members who are viewing; every app checks the seq — no gap — and appends it. The others just update a badge.
  5. The indexer adds it to search; the notifier tells the members who were mentioned and are away.
  6. Later a gateway deploy drops sockets in waves; each app reconnects, sends its last seq per open channel, and fills any gap from the gateway's recent-message buffer.
5
High-Level Design

One log per channel. A message service assigns each message the next sequence number of its channel inside the storing transaction, so order is a number and a retry is recognised by its client id. The database's log feeds a Kafka stream keyed by channel; consumers — the live fan-out, search, notifications — read it at their own positions. Live delivery goes over WebSockets through gateways using interest routing, is best-effort, and is repaired by the sequence check; unread state is a cursor per member, so posting touches no member rows; search filters by visibility inside the query and re-checks the hits.

6
Deep Dives

Eight below: (a) WebSocket, SSE plus POST, or polling for chat, (b) sending: order, retries and a busy channel, (c) one message to a channel of 100,000 members, (d) the reconnect storm, and resume that works for chat, (e) the change stream for messages, (f) search that never shows a message you may not see, (g) history, storage and hot channels, and (h) presence, typing and what fails — then the edge cases.

Members hold a WebSocket to a gateway; the message service stores each message with the channel's next seq; the database log feeds Kafka keyed by channel; a router pushes to the gateways with viewers, an indexer feeds search, a notifier reaches members who are away; history, unread state and search are read through an API. The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them.
Illustration — from a member's keystroke to everyone's screen, step by step
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
1a member's app makes a client_msg_id and sends the message over its WebSocket to its gatewayGatewaysthe id is what makes a retry safe
2the message service looks the id up, takes the channel's next seq (or a batch of them) and stores the message in one transactionMessage serviceorder is a number; batching lifts the hot-channel limit

The numbers match the ones on the diagram above. The reconnect storm (deep dive d) is what a gateway deploy does to steps 1, 6 and 9 at once.

One message
  1. The app makes a client_msg_id and sends; a retry carries the same id.
  2. The message service stores it with the next seq and acknowledges.
  3. The log carries it to the router, the indexer and the notifier, each at its own pace.
  4. Viewers get it within a fraction of a second; everyone else's badge moves; search has it in seconds.
One gateway deploy
  1. The old gateways drain a few percent of their clients at a time.
  2. Each app waits a random moment, reconnects, and sends its map of channel → last seq.
  3. The gateway answers short gaps from memory and points long gaps at the latest page.
  4. Nobody loses a message, and the database never sees the whole workspace ask at once.
Key deep dive — WebSocket, SSE plus POST, or polling for chat
NFRA message reaches online members within about 500 msNFR2 million connections
Thought process
  1. Chat is the case where the transport question really has two answers. A price feed is one-way, so SSE fits (see the marketplace example). A chat connection carries sends, acknowledgements, typing indicators, presence heartbeats and pushes — both directions, all the time. That is what WebSocket is for: one full-duplex connection per client, with every channel multiplexed over it.
  2. SSE plus POST is a real alternative: receive over an SSE stream, send with an HTTP POST. It passes through proxies without an upgrade and reconnects by itself. But look at what the built-in resume gives you: Last-Event-ID is one value, and a chat client has dozens of channels with independent sequences. On reconnect it has to send a map — channel to last seen sequence — whichever transport it uses, so you write the resume protocol either way, and the main advantage of SSE disappears.
  3. The other costs point the same way. Typing indicators and presence are small, frequent messages, cheap as WebSocket frames and expensive as separate HTTP requests. Every send needs an acknowledgement carrying the assigned sequence number, which is natural as a reply on the same socket. And a sender who loses the connection mid-send must be able to retry safely — the next dive.
  4. What WebSocket costs you: a load balancer that understands the upgrade (or plain layer-4), idle-timeout and ping/pong handling, and reconnect, resume and backpressure written by you. Holding the connections is affordable — 39.9 KB per idle TLS connection measured in the marketplace example, about 77 GB for 2 million across the fleet. What hurts is connections arriving, which is the reconnect-storm dive below.
  5. Polling is the fallback for networks that break persistent connections, not a design: 2 million clients asking every 5 seconds is 400,000 requests a second, nearly all answering "nothing new". Long polling — ask, and the server holds the request until there is something — is the usual fallback below WebSocket.
  6. The choice, in one line: WebSocket for the main chat connection, long polling as the fallback, and SSE where the feed really is one-way — a notification badge, a status page, a live read-only view.
Illustration — what chat needs from the transport
NeedWebSocketSSE + POSTLong polling
send a message, and get its sequence backa frame and a reply on the same socketan HTTP POST and its responsean HTTP POST and its response
receive pushespushed on the socketpushed on the streama held request answered, then asked again
typing and presence, many small messagescheap frameseach one an HTTP requestexpensive
reconnect and resumeyou write it: a map of channel → last seqreconnect is built in, but Last-Event-ID is a single value — you still write the mapyou write it
through proxies and load balancersneeds the upgrade to passplain HTTPplain HTTP
best forthe main chat connectiona one-way live view, a badgethe fallback

SSE's automatic reconnect and Last-Event-ID are from the browser specification; the WebSocket API has neither. Connection memory is the figure measured in the earlier example.

Key deep dive — sending: order, retries and a busy channel
NFREvery member sees a channel in the same orderNFRA retried send appears onceNFR30,000 messages a second
Thought process
  1. Order is a number, not a clock. Each channel has a counter, and a message takes the next value — its seq — inside the same transaction that stores it. Clients order by seq; timestamps are for display, because two servers' clocks can disagree. In the test, 8 workers posted 4,000 messages to one channel at 2,411 a second: the sequence ran 1 to 4,000 with 0 gaps, and no author's own messages ever arrived out of order.
  2. A retry must not become a second message. The client makes a client_msg_id before its first attempt and sends the same one every time; a unique key on (channel_id, client_msg_id) recognises it. The tempting one-statement version — bump the counter and insert with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING — stores the message once but moves the counter every time: with 200 messages each sent three times at once, it left 394 holes (highest seq 594 for 200 messages). Holes are not harmless: a client that sees seq 5 then 9 cannot tell a missing message from a gap, so it fetches history needlessly.
  3. The fix is to look the retry up first, then take the number, and let a concurrent duplicate fail on the unique key so its transaction — counter bump and all — rolls back. The same test then stored 200 messages with seq 1 to 200 and 0 gaps, at the price of 286 internal retries across 600 sends.
  4. The counter row is the cost of ordering: one channel's sends serialise on it. One busy channel took 2,411 messages a second against 4,838 spread over 1,000 channels — the same machine, the same workers. The remedy is batching per channel: collect the messages that arrive for a channel in the same few milliseconds, take one range of numbers, and insert them together. One channel then ran at 1,749 a second one by one, 12,579 in batches of 10 and 32,492 in batches of 100, gap-free throughout.
  5. Shard by channel_id (a hash), so a channel's counter and messages live together and its order is a property of one shard — not by workspace, which puts every channel of a huge workspace on one shard. Cross-channel questions (the unread badge, search) then need their own read models, which is what the rest of the design is.
  6. Two other designs are worth a sentence. Log first: write to Kafka keyed by channel and let a writer persist in order — the order is free, but the acknowledgement now waits on Kafka and the database lags. Database first (this design) makes the acknowledgement mean "stored", and lets the change stream be derived. Say which you chose and why.
Illustration — the send, and the version that leaves holes
-- one message: look up the retry first, then take the next number, then store
SELECT seq FROM messages WHERE channel_id = $1 AND client_msg_id = $2;      -- found: it's a retry, return that seq
UPDATE channels SET last_seq = last_seq + 1 WHERE channel_id = $1 RETURNING last_seq;
INSERT INTO messages (channel_id, seq, client_msg_id, author_id, body) VALUES ($1, <seq>, $2, $3, $4);
--   a concurrent retry hits the unique key, the transaction rolls back, and its number goes with it

-- the tempting one-statement version leaves holes in the sequence: the counter moves even when the insert doesn't
WITH bump AS (UPDATE channels SET last_seq = last_seq + 1 WHERE channel_id = $1 RETURNING last_seq)
INSERT INTO messages (channel_id, seq, client_msg_id, author_id, body)
SELECT $1, last_seq, $2, $3, $4 FROM bump
ON CONFLICT (channel_id, client_msg_id) DO NOTHING;

-- batching: one number-range per channel per few milliseconds
UPDATE channels SET last_seq = last_seq + $n WHERE channel_id = $1 RETURNING last_seq;   -- then insert seq = last - n + 1 .. last

Key deep dive — one message to a channel of 100,000 members
NFROnline members see it within about 500 msNFRA 100,000-member channel does not melt the system
Thought process
  1. A message in a big channel triggers two different fan-outs, and they must not be built the same way. One is live delivery to the members who are online right now. The other is unread state for everyone, online or not.
  2. Live delivery uses interest routing. Each gateway keeps a map from channel to its local sockets, and registers in Redis which channels its clients are viewing. The router reads the change stream, looks up the gateways with viewers, and sends each one message; the gateway writes to its own sockets. If 30,000 of a channel's 100,000 members are online across 40 gateways, that is 40 messages between router and gateways and about 750 local writes each — not 30,000 hops.
  3. Go one step further with two tiers of interest. A member who is viewing the channel needs the full message. A member who is only in the channel needs to know that something arrived, for the badge. The second is a tiny hint — "channel X is now at seq N" — which can be coalesced to a few a second per gateway. If 10% of the online members are actually viewing the channel, that is about 3,000 message pushes plus a trickle of hints, instead of 30,000 full messages.
  4. Unread state must not be a row per member per message. Keep one cursor per member per channel — last_read_seq — and compute unread as the channel's last_seq minus the cursor. Measured, one message to a 100,000-member channel wrote 2 rows in 0.49 ms with cursors, against 100,000 rows in 200 ms with a row per member — about 408 times the time, and a table that grows by 100,000 rows per message. Posting doesn't touch a single member row.
  5. The read side is cheap too. A member's badge across their 208 channels was one join and one subtraction: 1.035 ms (2,350 unread in total). Reading a channel is one row: 0.065 ms; marking all 208 channels read: 1.916 ms. Because the cursor belongs to the member, not to a device, reading on the phone clears it on the laptop.
  6. Mentions are the exception that needs real rows. "You were mentioned" and "unread in a muted channel" don't fall out of a subtraction, so keep a small table of mentions only for the members actually mentioned. An @channel in a 100,000-member channel then means up to 100,000 mention rows and up to tens of thousands of notifications, so it is treated as a rare, permissioned, rate-limited action, and its notifications go through the notification system with per-person limits.
  7. In a distributed database the badge's join needs each channel's last_seq, which lives on the channel's shard while the cursors are sharded by member. Either scatter-gather across shards, or send the latest seq with the live hint and keep a cached copy — the measured single-node join is the floor, not the promise.
Illustration — the cursor design, and what it replaces
CREATE TABLE channel_members (
  channel_id    bigint NOT NULL,
  user_id       bigint NOT NULL,
  last_read_seq bigint NOT NULL,                   -- the cursor: everything at or below this is read
  PRIMARY KEY (channel_id, user_id));
CREATE INDEX members_by_user ON channel_members (user_id, channel_id);

-- the unread badge for every channel a person is in: subtraction, no counting
SELECT c.channel_id, c.last_seq - m.last_read_seq AS unread
FROM channel_members m JOIN channels c USING (channel_id)
WHERE m.user_id = $1;

-- reading a channel: one row, whatever the channel's size
UPDATE channel_members SET last_read_seq = $seq WHERE channel_id = $1 AND user_id = $2;
Illustration — what one message to 100,000 members costs

One message into a channel with 100,000 members, time to write the unread state (measured).

a row per member100,000 rows · 200 ms
a cursor per member2 rows · 0.49 ms

about 408 times faster, and nothing grows with the size of the channel

PostgreSQL 16, one core. The row-per-member figure is a single INSERT … SELECT inside a transaction that was rolled back, so it excludes the commit and the index growth on disk — the real gap is wider. The 30,000-online and 3,000-viewing figures are assumptions.
