Key deep dive — the reconnect storm, and resume that works for chat
NFRA deploy must not become an outageNFRNo message is lost across a reconnect
Thought process
  1. This is the scenario the question is built on: 2 million healthy WebSocket connections, a deploy drops them, and almost every client reconnects at once. The full arithmetic is in the marketplace example — a full TLS handshake cost 0.56 ms of server CPU there, a fleet of 320 cores can accept about 89,887 connections a second, so reconnecting 2 million clients takes at least 22.2 seconds even perfectly spread. The lesson there: drain in waves, jitter the first reconnect, refuse early, make a reconnect cheap. Draining over five minutes took the peak from 2,000,496 attempts a second to 6,996 and each client's time offline to a median of 0.3 s.
  2. Chat adds a cost that a price feed doesn't have: resume. A reconnecting client must catch up on what it missed, and if every one of 2 million clients asks the database at once, the storm moves from the gateways to the database.
  3. Keep resume cheap with sequence numbers. On reconnect the client sends a map — each open channel and the last seq it saw. The server compares it with each channel's current last_seq (0.138 ms for 200 channels) and answers only where there is a difference. A client with 20 open channels and about 30 missed messages in each: 0.349 ms and 600 rows. If all 2 million clients did that against the database it would be 698 CPU-seconds (2,000,000 × 0.349 ms) — on top of the handshakes.
  4. So most resumes should never reach the database. Each gateway keeps a ring buffer of the last few hundred messages per active channel in memory and answers short gaps from it; only long gaps go to the read replicas, and even then the client fetches just the latest page and pages back lazily as the user scrolls, rather than replaying everything.
  5. Delivery is at-most-once, repair at-least-once. A push may be lost — a gateway restarts, a socket dies. The client repairs it: every message carries its channel's seq, and a client that receives seq 9 after 5 knows 6–8 are missing and fetches them. That makes the live path allowed to be best-effort, which is why it can be fast, and it makes gap-repair rate a metric worth watching: a spike means pushes are being lost.
  6. Deploy the gateways in waves and start with a canary; alert on the connect rate and the reconnect ratio rather than on concurrent connections. And every reconnect re-registers interest in Redis, so a gateway that dies takes only its own entries with it — they expire on their own.
Illustration — what chat adds to the reconnect cost
Cost per reconnecting clientWhere it landsKeeping it small
a TLS handshakegateway CPU — 0.56 ms measured (ECDSA)terminate TLS at the edge; ECDSA certificates
authenticate and register interestgateway CPU and Redisa cheap token check; batch the Redis writes
resume: compare the client's seq mapdatabase — 0.138 ms for 200 channelsanswer from the gateway's ring buffer where the gap is short
resume: fetch what was misseddatabase — 0.349 ms for 20 channels × 30 messagesonly the latest page; the rest on scroll
everyone at onceall of the above × 2,000,000 in secondsdrain in waves; jitter the first reconnect; refuse early

The handshake and storm numbers come from the earlier example; the resume numbers are measured on this example's 2,999,520-message table, warm cache.

Illustration — what a reconnecting client does
StepWhat happens
1wait the server-suggested time plus its own random jitter
2connect, authenticate, and send the map: channel → last seq seen, plus the channels being viewed
3the gateway registers interest, then compares each channel's last_seq with the map
4short gaps are replayed from the ring buffer; long gaps get the latest page and a "load earlier" marker
5from now on every push carries its seq; a jump means a gap, and the client repairs it
Key deep dive — the change stream for messages: edits, deletes and the log
NFRSearch, notifications and analytics all stay currentNFRA deleted message stays deleted
Thought process
  1. The message table's own log becomes the stream: a Debezium connector reads the write-ahead log and publishes to Kafka keyed by channel_id, so a channel's changes stay in commit order in one partition. The search indexer, the notification service and any analytics consumer each read it at their own pace. The mechanics of the slot, the column list and idempotent consumers are measured in the marketplace example; here is what messages add.
  2. Messages are not append-only. They are edited and deleted, and both arrive as later events. An edit is version 2, 3…; a delete is a tombstone — a version with a deleted flag, not the absence of a row. Consumers apply a change only if its version is newer than what they hold.
  3. That rule matters more than it looks. Tested: 5,000 messages, a third of them deleted, with 29,041 deliveries (duplicates included) in random order. The version-guarded tombstone consumer ended with 0 wrong rows. The tempting version — a delete that removes the row, and unguarded upserts for edits — ended with 3,506 wrong rows: 1,244 of 1,667 deleted messages came back to life when a late edit re-created them, and 2,262 live messages showed an old edit. A deleted message reappearing in search is a privacy incident, not a glitch.
  4. The stream's size follows the body. A message row is small next to a product page but it is all body — a column list can't drop it. What the stream costs is WAL: with a stalled connector the slot pinned 24.7, 79.3 and 156.5 MB of WAL after 100,000, 300,000 and 600,000 updates in the earlier test, so alert on the slot's retained bytes and cap it deliberately.
  5. Watch the latency. Reading the log adds a hop — the WAL, the connector, Kafka — to anything that consumes the stream. For search and notifications, seconds are fine. For live delivery, which has a 500 ms budget, that hop is a real cost, and it is not measured here. The practical answer: publish live messages straight from the message service after commit, and let the change stream feed everything else. It is safe because a lost live push is repaired by the seq gap check — the very thing that makes the live path allowed to be best-effort.
Illustration — the consumer rule that keeps deletes deleted
-- one row per message in the search state; an edit is version 2, 3…; a delete is a version with deleted = true
INSERT INTO search_state (message_id, body, version, deleted) VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4)
ON CONFLICT (message_id) DO UPDATE
   SET body = excluded.body, version = excluded.version, deleted = excluded.deleted
 WHERE excluded.version > search_state.version;          -- a late edit can never undo a delete

-- the tempting version: DELETE FROM search_state WHERE message_id = $1  (and unguarded upserts for edits)
Illustration — what the edits-and-deletes test measured
ConsumerWrong rows of 5,000Detail
version-guarded, delete as a tombstone0every message ended at its highest version; deleted ones stayed deleted
delete removes the row, edits unguarded3,5061,244 of 1,667 deleted messages reappeared · 2,262 live messages showed an old edit

29,041 deliveries of about 16,700 distinct changes, in random order. Kafka and Debezium were not run: this is the consumer's rule, tested on PostgreSQL, with the connector's behaviour taken from the earlier example.

Key deep dive — search that never shows a message you may not see
NFRSearch fresh within secondsNFRNo message the searcher may not see
Thought process
  1. Search is a copy of the messages, built from the change stream, with the fields it needs: the text, the channel, whether the channel is public, the author, the time. It lags by seconds. The new problem in chat is permissions: a result must be filtered by which channels the searcher can see, and that set changes whenever someone joins or leaves a private channel — so it can't be baked into each document.
  2. Tested on 400,000 messages across 5,000 channels, 10% of them private, using tantivy as a stand-in for OpenSearch. A text query with no permission filter took a median of 0.04 ms. The same query restricted to the 200 channels a member belongs to took 6.62 ms; to 2,000 channels, 6.35 ms (p95 14.64 ms); with a public flag plus 20 private channels, 4.86 ms. The permission filter, not the text match, is the cost — about 166 times the unfiltered query — because a filter can't skip ahead the way a ranked text query can.
  3. The design choices only moved it modestly (4.86–6.62 ms), but they still matter. Store a public flag on each document and keep the per-member filter to the few private channels — that was the cheapest here, and it keeps the filter small for a member of thousands of channels. Route each workspace to its own shard or index, so a query never scans another workspace's documents. And re-check the hits against the database before returning them: the index is a copy, and a member removed a second ago must not see a message because the copy was stale.
  4. Filtering after the search — take the top 200 hits, then drop the ones the member can't see — is faster and wrong: a member with narrow access can get an empty first page even though matches exist. Filter inside the query, verify at the end.
  5. Visibility changes are the expensive events. A channel flipping between public and private means updating the flag on every one of its documents; treat it as a bulk reindex of that channel, off the hot path. Deletes must reach the index quickly and reliably — the tombstone rule from the previous dive — because a deleted message that is still searchable is the worst failure this index can have.
  6. The rest is as in the marketplace example: index in bulk on a refresh cadence of a few seconds, shard by workspace, replicate for reads, and reindex by building a new index from a snapshot plus the stream and swapping an alias.
Illustration — the query, with visibility
QueryMedianp95
text only — no permission filter (unsafe)0.04 ms0.16 ms
text + a member of 200 channels6.62 ms7.02 ms
text + a member of 2,000 channels6.35 ms14.64 ms
text + public flag OR 20 private channels4.86 ms5.93 ms

400,000 messages, 5,000 channels, one core, tantivy in place of OpenSearch. The unfiltered figure is unrealistically fast because a ranked text query can stop early; the point is the size of the gap the filter opens, not the absolute times.

Illustration — what goes in the index
FieldWhy
message text, author, timewhat people search and sort by
channel_idthe shard and filter key
is_publiclets most searches skip the per-member list
version, deletedso an edit or a delete is applied once and in order
NOT the member list of a channelmembership changes constantly; look it up at query time and re-check the hits
Key deep dive — history, storage and hot channels
NFRScrolling back is instant at any depthNFRStorage that keeps growing
Thought process
  1. History is a range scan on the primary key (channel_id, seq), newest first, LIMIT 50. On 2,999,520 messages in 5,000 channels, one of them with 600,000 messages: the latest 50 of that channel took 0.022 ms; a page 300,000 messages deep took 0.029 ms; the latest 50 of a small channel 0.028 ms — all an index scan backwards. Depth costs nothing, so "load earlier" never needs OFFSET, only "before this seq".
  2. Storage is the part that keeps growing. This table cost 499.0 MB of heap, 90.2 MB for the primary key and 116.2 MB for the client-id unique index — about 247 bytes per message all in. At an assumed average of 3,000 messages a second that is about 64 GB a day. So plan retention on day one: recent months in the primary shards, older history moved to cheaper storage and read through the same API, deletes for compliance done as tombstones plus a purge of the body.
  3. The client-id unique index is 16% of that, and a retry happens within seconds, not months. Keep it only for a window — for example by partitioning and dropping it from older partitions, or by holding recent client ids in a small table with a TTL — the same trade the clock-in example made with its registry.
  4. Shard by a hash of channel_id: the primary key contains the channel, so partitioning and sharding by channel both work, and a channel's order lives in one place. A single channel can still be hot; its counter row limits it to what one row can take (deep dive b), which batching raises well above any human conversation. Very large organizations — a single workspace whose traffic dominates — belong in a cell of their own; see isolating the massive organizations.
  5. Order across channels is not defined and not needed. A thread is just messages with a parent seq in the same channel, so it inherits the channel's order; a thread's reply count is a counter like any other.
Illustration — history and resume queries
-- history: a range scan on the primary key (channel_id, seq); depth costs nothing
SELECT seq, author_id, body, created_at FROM messages
WHERE channel_id = $1 AND seq < $before ORDER BY seq DESC LIMIT 50;

-- resume: what did I miss in the channels I have open?
SELECT m.channel_id, m.seq, m.body
FROM unnest($1::bigint[], $2::bigint[]) AS t(ch, last_seen)            -- the client's map: channel -> last seq
JOIN LATERAL (SELECT * FROM messages x WHERE x.channel_id = t.ch AND x.seq > t.last_seen
              ORDER BY x.seq LIMIT 200) m ON true;
Illustration — what the history tests measured
QueryMedianPlan
latest 50 in the 600,000-message channel0.022 msindex scan backward on the primary key
a page 300,000 messages deep0.029 msthe same
latest 50 in a small channel0.028 msthe same
resume: 20 channels × 30 missed messages0.349 msa lateral join on the primary key
check the last seq of 200 channels0.138 msa lookup on the channel table

PostgreSQL 16, one machine, warm cache, 2,999,520 messages. The 64 GB-a-day figure is arithmetic on an assumed 3,000 messages a second and the measured bytes per message.

Key deep dive — presence, typing, and what fails
NFRPresence and typing never touch the databaseNFRKnow before the members do
Thought process
  1. Presence and typing indicators are ephemeral: they are true for seconds, worthless afterwards, and must never reach the database or the change stream. Keep them in Redis with a short TTL. A client refreshes its presence every 30 seconds — for 2 million clients that is about 66,700 small writes a second, so batch them per gateway (one refresh message per gateway per interval, not one per client) and let the TTL expire the rest.
  2. Fan-out for presence is the same interest idea: a client subscribes only to the people visible on screen — a few dozen — not to everyone in the workspace. A presence change then goes to the few dozen who can see it. Typing indicators are rate-limited to one per few seconds per person per channel and go only to members currently viewing that channel; in a 100,000-member channel that is a handful of people, not everybody.
  3. The failures worth a sentence each are in the table. The pattern to say aloud: because every consumer reads the channel log at its own position, a slow search index or a lagging notifier never delays a send, and a lost live push is repaired by the sequence check.
Illustration — what fails, and what the design does
FailureWhat happensThe design answer
a gateway dies, or is deployedits clients reconnectdrain in waves; jittered first reconnect; refuse early; resume from a seq map and the ring buffer
a push is losta member misses a message until they lookevery push carries the channel seq; a jump means a gap; the client fetches the missing range
a message shard is downsends to its channels fail; history from replicas still worksclients retry with the same client_msg_id; the message appears once when the shard returns
a hot channelits counter row limits sendsbatch per channel; the limit is far above a human conversation
Kafka or the connector stallssearch and notifications laglive delivery is unaffected; alert on the slot's retained bytes and consumer lag by age
the search index is downsearch is stale or unavailablesends and reads are unaffected; rebuild by alias swap
Redis (interest, presence) is lostpushes stop routing; presence resetsgateways re-register from their own connection tables within seconds; clients fall back to polling briefly
an @channel in a huge channela notification stormpermission and rate-limit it; coalesce; the notification system applies per-person limits
a member is removed from a private channel while onlinethey could still receive pushesremove their interest entry and close the channel on their socket; re-check search hits against membership
Illustration — what to measure, and when to be woken (illustrative thresholds)
LayerMeasureAlert when
sendsend-to-ack latency p99 · commit latency · sends retried · counter conflictsp99 above the promise; conflicts rising on one channel
live deliverycommitted-to-delivered latency p99 · gap-repair rate (clients fetching a missing range)p99 above 500 ms; a spike in gap repairs means pushes are being lost

Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • A message sent twice because the network dropped the ack — the same client_msg_id returns the same seq; the message appears once and the sequence has no hole.
  • An edit arrives after the delete it followed — the delete is a higher version, so the edit is ignored — in the database, the index and every consumer.
  • A member is removed from a private channel — their cursor row goes, their interest entry is removed, their socket leaves the channel, and search re-checks the hits against membership.
  • A 100,000-member workspace joins a new channel at once — 100,000 membership rows in batches, each batch repeatable; nothing per message is written for them.
  • Two devices, one member — the cursor is per member and channel, so reading on one clears the badge on the other.
  • Clock skew between servers — order is by seq, never by timestamp; timestamps are for display.
  • A huge paste or a flood of small messages — a body-size limit and a per-member rate limit at the gateway, before the message service.
  • The largest workspace dominates the platform — give it a cell of its own — its own gateways, shards and search — see isolating the massive organizations.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Every member sees a channel in the same orderA per-channel counter taken in the storing transaction: 8 workers, 4,000 messages, seq 1–4,000, 0 gaps.
A retried send appears onceclient_msg_id with a lookup-first send: 600 sends of 200 messages left 0 holes (the one-statement version left 394).
Big channels do not melt the systemInterest routing sends one message per gateway; unread state is a cursor: 2 rows and 0.49 ms per message instead of 100,000 rows and 200 ms.
A deploy is not an outageDrain in waves and jitter the first reconnect (peak 6,996 attempts a second, median 0.3 s offline, from the earlier example); resume from a seq map and a ring buffer keeps the database out of the storm.
Deleted messages stay deletedVersioned tombstones: 0 wrong rows of 5,000 against 3,506 for a plain delete.
Search never shows what you may not seeThe permission filter is inside the query (4.86–6.62 ms against 0.04 ms unfiltered) and the hits are re-checked against membership.
Scrolling back is instantA range scan on (channel_id, seq): 0.022–0.029 ms at any depth.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
WebSocket for the main connectionFull-duplex, cheap small frames and acknowledgements — in exchange for writing reconnect, resume and backpressure yourself, and needing a load balancer that understands the upgrade.
A counter row per channel for orderA gapless, comparable sequence — in exchange for serialising a channel's sends on one row, which batching lifts far above any conversation.
Unread as a cursorNo per-message write to members — in exchange for mentions needing their own small table and a distributed badge needing each channel's latest seq.
Best-effort live push, repaired by seq gapsA fast live path with no delivery guarantees to maintain — in exchange for the client having to detect and fill gaps.
CDC for everything except the live pushA faithful, ordered stream for search, notifications and analytics — in exchange for an extra hop of latency that the live path avoids by publishing directly.
Filtering search inside the queryNever an empty page for a member with narrow access, never a forbidden hit — in exchange for a filter that costs more than the text match itself.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Gatewaysa WebSocket server in Go, Node or Elixir behind a layer-4 or WebSocket-aware load balancer; TLS terminated at the edge with ECDSA certificates
Interest and presenceRedis with short TTLs: channel → gateways, presence, typing
Message storagePostgreSQL sharded by a hash of channel id (application routing, Citus or Vitess for MySQL); read replicas for history and resume
The change streamDebezium on the write-ahead log into Kafka, keyed by channel id; consumers idempotent by version
SearchOpenSearch or Elasticsearch, an index or shard per workspace, a public flag on each document
Notificationsthe notification system — with per-person limits, digests and quiet hours
Load testingk6 or a custom client that ramps the connect rate and includes the resume step
Worked Example AZ — Chunks, Sync and Streaming

Design a File Storage, Sync and Video Streaming Platform

chunks and hashes · resumable and parallel uploads · dedupe · delta sync · offline and conflicts · big downloads · video streaming
Click to expand

A Dropbox-style platform with video: people upload and download files of any size — one or thousands at a time — keep a folder in sync across devices that go offline and come back, and play videos that were uploaded as ordinary files. One idea carries almost all of it: a file is an ordered list of chunk hashes. Resumable uploads, dedupe, delta sync, versions and conflict detection each follow from it, and video reuses the same storage with a transcoding pipeline on top. Every measurement below came from one small machine (one core, 4 GB): NumPy for chunking, PostgreSQL 16 for the block index, versions, journal and conflicts, a simulation for upload resume, and ffmpeg for transcoding. The object store, the CDN and the notifier were not run; the text says which numbers are measured, simulated, assumed or arithmetic.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Upload and download files of any size, one or many at a time, resuming after any interruption.
  • Folders, rename, move, delete and version history.
  • Keep a folder in sync across devices, work offline, and catch up when back online.
  • Edit a large file and sync only what changed.
  • Play uploaded videos in a browser or app, starting quickly and adapting to bandwidth.
Non-functional
  • A 50 GB upload survives dropped connections and never re-sends finished chunks.
  • Editing a big file re-uploads only what changed; identical data is stored once.
  • Two devices editing the same file never lose an edit silently, and all devices converge.
  • The API never carries file bytes.
  • A new video is watchable within minutes; playback starts in a couple of seconds.
  • No chunk is lost, and unreferenced data is really deleted.

Read the requirements as one sentence: identify content by its hash and make every operation about hashes, not bytes. The rest is bookkeeping, and the bookkeeping is where a wrong choice loses data.

2
Core Entities
  • Namespace — a user's root or a shared folder — the unit of sharding and of the journal.
  • Node — (node_id, namespace, parent_id, name, is_dir, head_version) — the tree, by id and parent pointer.
  • Version — (node_id, version, size, chunk hashes) — a file is a list of hashes.
  • Block — (hash, size, refcount) — one row per unique chunk; the bytes live in the chunk store.
  • Journal entry — (namespace, seq, node, op, version) — the ordered history of a namespace.
  • Device — (device_id, cursor) — its place in the journal.
  • Video asset — the renditions, segments and manifest built from a committed video.

Chunk bytes are immutable and content-addressed: a chunk is never changed, only added or, when nothing references it, eventually deleted.

3
API

What the clients call:

POST /commit {node, base_version, chunks:[{hash,size}]} → the missing chunks with presigned URLs, or the new version, or a conflict
PUT <presigned url> → one chunk, straight to the chunk store
GET /changes?ns=…&cursor=… → journal entries and the new cursor
GET /files/{id}/versions/{v} → the chunk list and presigned GET URLs
POST /nodes/{id}/move {parent, name} · GET /videos/{id}/master.m3u8

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. Maya edits a 2 GB disk image on her laptop on a flight, offline. Her client notices the change and re-chunks only the modified file.
  2. Content-defined chunking finds that 3 of about 7,000 chunks changed; it queues one commit with the version it started from.
  3. Back online, the client pulls the journal first and sees nobody else touched the file, then proposes the commit: the server needs 3 chunks.
  4. She uploads 3 chunks straight to the store; the commit succeeds in one transaction and the journal advances.
  5. Her desktop at home is told the namespace advanced, pulls the journal, downloads 3 chunks and rebuilds the file.
  6. Later she uploads a video: the chunks arrive like any file, an event starts a transcoding job, and the lowest rendition is playable in seconds.
5
High-Level Design

Two stores and a protocol between them. Metadata — a tree of nodes, versions that are lists of chunk hashes, and a per-namespace journal — sits in a sharded transactional database; the bytes sit in a content-addressed chunk store. A device chunks and hashes, asks which chunks are missing, uploads only those directly to the store, and commits in one guarded transaction; other devices learn of it from a notifier and pull the journal from their cursor. Video reuses the same upload, then an event starts parallel transcoding into a bitrate ladder that is packaged as segments behind a CDN. A collector deletes chunks nothing references.

6
Deep Dives

Nine below: (a) chunks — the idea everything follows from, (b) resumable, parallel uploads and many files at once, (c) dedupe, (d) metadata, (e) sync: a journal, a cursor and working offline, (f) conflicts, (g) big downloads, many downloads and hot files, (h) video streaming, and (i) what fails and what to watch — then the edge cases.

Devices talk to a metadata API and upload chunks straight to a content-addressed chunk store; the database holds the tree, the versions (lists of chunk hashes), the block index and the journal; a notifier tells other devices to pull; a garbage collector removes unreferenced chunks. A committed video starts a queue-driven transcoding pipeline that writes segments to a media store behind a CDN. The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them.
Illustration — from an edit on one device to a screen on another, step by step
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
1the device watches its folder, splits changed files into content-defined chunks and hashes each oneDevice Adelta and dedupe start here
2it sends a commit proposal — file, base version, chunk hashes; the server answers with the missing chunks and presigned URLs, or with a conflictMetadata API11.621 ms to check 4,096 hashes
3it uploads only the missing chunks, in parallel, straight to the chunk store; any failure resumes by asking againChunk storethe API never touches the bytes
4it commits again: the server verifies every chunk exists, bumps the version only if the head is still the base, and appends to the journal — one transactionMetadata DBatomic; exactly one commit wins a conflict
5the notifier tells the user's other devices that the namespace advancedChange notifiera hint; devices also poll slowly
6Device B pulls the journal since its cursor, downloads only the chunks it lacks, and rebuilds the fileDevice B · chunk storededupe on the way down too
7when a video is committed, an event queues transcoding; workers split it into segments and encode the ladder in parallelQueue · transcodersnever inline
8the packager writes segments and manifests to the media store; the player fetches them through the CDN and adapts its bitrateMedia store · CDN · viewersmall immutable segments cache forever
9the garbage collector deletes chunks whose refcount has been zero past a grace periodGarbage collectora deleted file cannot delete a shared chunk

The numbers match the ones on the diagram above. Steps 1–6 are the file path; steps 7–8 are the video path, which starts from the same upload; step 9 keeps the store honest.

One edit, one device to another
  1. The client re-chunks the changed file and proposes a commit with its base version.
  2. The server names the few chunks it lacks; the device uploads just those, directly.
  3. One transaction bumps the version, updates refcounts and appends to the journal.
  4. The other device is told, pulls the journal, fetches only what it lacks.
Two devices, one file
  1. Both devices were offline and edited the same file from version 4.
  2. The first to reconnect commits and becomes version 5.
  3. The second's commit still says base 4, so the guarded update finds nothing and refuses.
  4. It commits its work as a conflicted copy, or merges it if it is text; nothing is lost.
Key deep dive — chunks: the idea everything else follows from
NFREditing a big file re-uploads only what changedNFRIdentical data is stored once
Thought process
  1. A file is an ordered list of chunk hashes. Everything in this design falls out of that one idea: upload only the chunks the store lacks; sync only the chunks that changed; store identical chunks once; make a new version cost only its difference; resume an interrupted transfer at a chunk boundary.
  2. The question is where to cut. Fixed-size chunks are simple and fast — but an insertion shifts every later byte, so every later chunk gets a new hash. Content-defined chunking cuts where a rolling hash of the last few bytes hits a pattern, so the boundaries follow the content and re-align just after an edit.
  3. Measured on a 32 MB file (cutting 256 KB fixed chunks against content-defined chunks averaging 290 KB, 65–1024 KB): inserting 100 bytes at the start changed 129 of 129 fixed chunks — 32.0 MB, 100% of the file — but 1 of 113 content-defined chunks, 0.08 MB. Inserting in the middle: 16.0 MB against 0.22 MB. Deleting 1 KB at the start: 32.0 MB against 0.08 MB. An in-place overwrite of 4 KB cost one chunk either way, and appending 1 MB cost 1.0 MB with fixed chunks and 1.51 MB with content-defined ones — the one case where content-defined is slightly worse.
  4. The price is CPU on the device. The content-defined chunker took about 2.0 s per 32 MB in NumPy on one core (roughly 15 MB/s; a native implementation is far faster, so read this as a relative cost, not a benchmark). A phone might use fixed chunks, or chunk only files that changed. Delta sync also helps only when a file is edited in place — documents, disk images, databases, text. A zip, an encrypted container or an edited video usually rewrites everything, and no chunking can help.
  5. Chunk size is a trade-off. Smaller chunks dedupe and delta better but multiply the metadata and the requests. In the test, the block index took 136 bytes per chunk in PostgreSQL (730 MB of table and 563 MB of primary key for 10,000,000 chunks), so a petabyte of unique data at a 4 MB average is about 250 million chunks and about 34 GB of index (arithmetic); at 256 KB it would be 16 times that. Products commonly settle on an average of a few MB, with a minimum and a maximum so no chunk is tiny or huge.
  6. Below the chunk there is a second level of delta — an rsync-style comparison inside a chunk that mostly matches — and it is rarely worth the complexity: re-sending one chunk of a few MB is cheap next to the machinery of a second delta layer.
Illustration — one edit, two ways of cutting

Bytes to upload after inserting 100 bytes at the start of a 32 MB file (measured).

fixed 256 KB chunks32.0 MB · 129 chunks
content-defined chunks0.08 MB · 1 chunk

a hundred bytes of new data should cost a hundred bytes of chunk, not the whole file

Random (incompressible) data, chunked in NumPy on one core; the content-defined chunker uses a 32-byte gear hash with a 64 KB minimum, a 1 MB maximum and about 256 KB expected.

Illustration — five kinds of edit
Edit to a 32 MB fileFixed chunks re-uploadedContent-defined re-uploaded
overwrite 4 KB in the middle0.25 MB (1 chunk)0.22 MB (1 chunk)

insert 100 bytes in the middle16.0 MB (half)0.22 MB (1 chunk)

A chunk counts as re-uploaded when its hash isn't in the previous version. The same result is why storing a second version costs about the size of its difference.

Key deep dive — resumable, parallel uploads of big files, and many files at once
NFRA 50 GB upload survives dropped connectionsNFRThe API never carries the bytes
Thought process
  1. The upload is four steps, and the bytes never touch the API. (1) The device chunks and hashes the file. (2) It sends a commit proposal — file, the version it started from, the chunk hashes — and the server answers with the chunks it doesn't have, each with a short-lived presigned URL. (3) The device uploads those chunks in parallel, straight to the chunk store. (4) It commits again, and the server checks that every chunk exists and bumps the version in one transaction.
  2. Resume is not a feature; it is the protocol. The state of an upload is "which chunks does the store have", so after a crash, a dropped connection or a closed laptop the device simply asks again and uploads only what is missing. The server holds no upload session. Looking up 4,096 hashes (a 16 GB file at 4 MB chunks) against a 10-million-chunk block index took 11.621 ms.
  3. Why it matters, by arithmetic checked with a simulation (100 Mbit/s, the connection drops on average every 10 minutes, 2 s to reconnect — assumptions): 1 GB takes 80 s ideally and 86 s as one request; 10 GB takes 800 s ideally and 1,676 s as one request (simulated: 1,802 s); 50 GB takes 4,000 s ideally and about 470,863 s — five and a half days — as one request, because it must stay connected for 67 minutes. With chunked resume it took 4,014–4,030 s at any chunk size from 4 to 64 MB.
  4. Chunk size therefore barely changes the total time; it changes the request count (12,500 chunks for 50 GB at 4 MB, 781 at 64 MB) and the work lost per drop. A few MB to about 16 MB is the usual range. Fill the pipe with several chunks in flight at once — a single TCP stream is limited by its window and the round-trip time — and cap the total so a device doesn't starve everything else.
  5. Many files at once is a scheduling problem. Keep one queue with a global limit (for example a few files with several chunks each), send small files first so 10,000 tiny files don't wait behind a 50 GB one, batch tiny files into one commit to avoid per-file overhead, and let the user pause, throttle or wait for Wi-Fi.
  6. A presigned URL should be scoped to one chunk and expire in minutes, with the object key derived from the hash so a client can't overwrite someone else's data; an object store that verifies a declared checksum rejects a corrupted chunk at the door. And a commit is idempotent: retried with the same base version and the same list, it returns the version it already created.
Illustration — the four steps
StepDeviceServer
1split the file into chunks, hash each—
2send a commit proposal: file, base version, chunk hasheslook the hashes up in the block index (11.621 ms for 4,096); reply with the missing ones and presigned URLs, or a conflict
3upload the missing chunks in parallel, directly to the store; on any failure ask step 2 againthe store checks each chunk's checksum
4commit againverify all chunks exist; bump the version only if it is still the base; append to the journal; one transaction
Illustration — upload time with and without resume (100 Mbit/s, a drop every 10 minutes)
FileIdealOne requestResumable, 4 MB chunks64 MB chunks
1 GB80 s86 s (simulated 84)80 s81 s
10 GB800 s1,676 s (simulated 1,802)803 s806 s
50 GB4,000 s470,863 s (formula)4,014 s4,030 s

One request restarts from zero on every drop: expected time is M × (e^(T/M) − 1), where M is the mean time between drops and T the upload time. Key deep dive — dedupe: store identical bytes once
NFRIdentical data is stored onceNFRA deleted file never deletes a shared chunk
Thought process
  1. Because a chunk's key is the hash of its content, the same bytes are the same object: deduplication is a lookup, not a job. It works inside a version history, across a user's files, and across users — the same installer, the same attachment.
  2. Inside a file's own history it is already measured: after inserting 100 bytes into the middle of a 32 MB file, the second version added one chunk, 0.22 MB — under 1% — instead of another 32 MB. Across users it is arithmetic: 1,000 accounts holding the same 100 MB file are 100 GB without dedupe and 100 MB with it. The real ratio depends on the data; measure it before promising it.
  3. Dedupe happens twice. On the client — hash first, ask which chunks are missing — it saves upload bandwidth; on the server it saves storage. The first is the missing-chunks query from the previous dive; the second is the fact that the chunk store never holds a hash twice.
  4. Sharing needs bookkeeping. The block index keeps a refcount per chunk: a commit adds one for every chunk of the new version, deleting a version removes them. When a count reaches zero the chunk is not deleted at once — a concurrent commit may be about to reference it, a finished upload may not be committed yet, and versions and the trash keep files alive. The collector waits a grace period, and a periodic mark-and-sweep recomputes the counts from the version lists to repair any drift. A bug here is the worst kind: deleting a live chunk loses data, so the collector must be conservative and auditable.
  5. The trap is privacy. If the server says "I already have this chunk, skip the upload", an attacker who knows a document's hash can learn whether anyone stores it, and confirm a leaked file. The defences: make the client prove it has the bytes before it gets a reference — the server challenges with a nonce and a keyed hash over random parts of the chunk — or dedupe only within an account or a team, or only for public content. It is a straight trade of storage saving against a side channel.
  6. Deletion and quotas follow from the same model. Charge users for logical bytes, not physical, or dedupe punishes whoever uploaded first. A legal erasure of one user's file must only drop their references; the chunk lives on while others use it. And per-user encryption keys, which some products want, defeat cross-user dedupe — another trade, and it should be a stated choice.
Illustration — what dedupes where
WhereWhat is savedExample
between versions of one filestorage and uploada 100-byte insert into 32 MB stored as 0.22 MB
between files of one userstorage and uploadcopies, backups, a folder duplicated
between usersstorage, and upload if the client asks firstthe same installer or attachment 1,000 times
on downloaddownload bandwidtha device that has 99% of a new version's chunks fetches 1%
Illustration — the block index, measured
MeasureResult
chunks in the index10,000,000
table · primary key730 MB · 563 MB (136 bytes per chunk)
a petabyte of unique data at a 4 MB average chunkabout 250 million chunks · about 34 GB of index (arithmetic)

PostgreSQL 16, one core, warm cache. Shard the index by a prefix of the hash. The privacy defence and the garbage-collection safeguards are reasoning, not run.

Key deep dive — metadata: a tree, versions and a journal, kept apart from the bytes
NFRMetadata operations stay fastNFRThe API never proxies a byte
Thought process
  1. Split bytes from metadata. The bytes live in the chunk store — object storage, erasure-coded, huge and cheap. The metadata — the folder tree, each file's versions, the sync journal — is small, transactional and sharded by namespace (a user's root or a shared folder). Metadata servers never carry file bytes.
  2. A version is an ordered list of chunk hashes, and there are two ways to store it: an array in one row, or one row per chunk. For a 16 GB file (4,096 chunks) the commit took 34.8 ms with an array and 38.8 ms with a row per chunk — the same, because both are dominated by adding the refcounts. The difference is size: 144 KB in one row against 2.82 MB across 4,096 rows with their index, about 19 times more. Keep the array; add a reverse index (chunk → files) only if something needs it.
  3. Store the tree as parent pointers, not paths. Moving a folder of 100,000 files changed 1 row in 0.59 ms with parent pointers, and 100,000 rows in 0.32 s when every file stored its full path — and that second figure excludes the commit, the locks and the readers waiting behind them. It scales with the folder's size, so a folder of 10 million files would be a minutes-long rewrite. A rename is also one journal entry, which is what sync needs.
  4. Identify nodes by an id, not a path. A rename or a move is then a change to one node, not a delete and a create, and the sync logic can tell "moved" from "deleted and re-added" — which is what stops a rename from being uploaded again.
  5. Shard by namespace. A user's whole tree lives in one shard, so a commit, a move and a journal append are single-shard transactions. A shared folder becomes its own namespace mounted into several users' trees. A namespace with a hundred thousand members, or one that dominates the platform, is the case for a cell of its own — see isolating the massive organizations.
  6. A very large file needs care: a 5 TiB file at 4 MiB chunks is 1,310,720 chunks, and its version row would be about 42 MB of hashes. Store it as a two-level manifest — a list of manifests, each a list of chunk hashes — like a small Merkle tree, so a change touches one leaf and the version row stays small.
Illustration — the tables, and the four statements that matter
CREATE TABLE blocks (hash bytea PRIMARY KEY, size int NOT NULL, refcount int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0);     -- the block index
CREATE TABLE nodes  (node_id bigint PRIMARY KEY, ns_id bigint NOT NULL, parent_id bigint, name text NOT NULL,
                     is_dir boolean NOT NULL, head_version int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, UNIQUE (ns_id, parent_id, name));
CREATE TABLE file_versions (node_id bigint NOT NULL, version int NOT NULL, size bigint NOT NULL,
                            chunk_hashes bytea[] NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (node_id, version));           -- a file is a list of hashes
CREATE TABLE journal (ns_id bigint NOT NULL, seq bigint NOT NULL, node_id bigint NOT NULL,
                      op text NOT NULL, version int NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (ns_id, seq));

-- 1. which of these chunks does the store not have yet?
SELECT h FROM unnest($1::bytea[]) h WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM blocks b WHERE b.hash = h);

-- 2. the commit: one transaction, guarded by the version the device started from
UPDATE nodes SET head_version = head_version + 1
WHERE node_id = $1 AND head_version = $2 RETURNING head_version;           -- no row back: a conflict
INSERT INTO file_versions VALUES ($1, <new version>, $size, $hashes);
UPDATE blocks SET refcount = refcount + 1 WHERE hash = ANY($hashes);
INSERT INTO journal VALUES ($ns, <next seq>, $1, 'put', <new version>);

-- 3. what changed since my cursor?
SELECT seq, node_id, op, version FROM journal WHERE ns_id = $1 AND seq > $cursor ORDER BY seq LIMIT 1000;

-- 4. moving a folder of any size is one row
UPDATE nodes SET parent_id = $new_parent WHERE node_id = $folder;
Illustration — what the metadata tests measured
TestResult
commit a 16 GB version: hash array in one row34.8 ms · 144 KB
the same with one row per chunk38.8 ms · 4,096 rows · 2.82 MB with index
move a folder of 100,000 files: parent pointer0.59 ms · 1 row

PostgreSQL 16, one core. Commit timings exclude the network. The two-level manifest is reasoning.

Key deep dive — sync: a journal, a cursor, and working offline
NFRDevices convergeNFROffline work is never lost
Thought process
  1. Each namespace has an ordered journal: entries of (seq, node, op, version), numbered by a per-namespace counter (the same counter-row idea as the channel sequence in the Slack-style example). A device stores one number — its cursor, the last seq it applied — and asks one question: "what changed since my cursor?". Measured in a namespace of 1,000,000 entries, fetching 1,000 changes from the start took 0.255 ms, from the middle 0.221 ms, and finding that nothing was new took 0.005 ms. That last figure is why a notifier that re-checks constantly is affordable.
  2. Notification is a hint, never the data. The notifier tells a device "namespace N is now at seq X" over SSE or a long poll (the trade-offs are in the marketplace example and the Slack-style example); the device then pulls the journal itself. A lost hint is harmless because devices also poll slowly. A backgrounded phone uses the operating system's push instead.
  3. The device's loop has four parts. Detect local changes: watch the folder for events, and on start rescan by size and modified time, hashing only what looks changed. Compare with a local database of what was last synced. Push local changes as commits carrying their base versions. Pull remote changes from the journal and apply them. A device ignores journal entries that are its own commits coming back.
  4. Offline is just a long gap between two runs of the loop. Changes queue in the local database. On reconnect the device pulls first — learning what happened while it was away — and then pushes its commits with their old base versions. Anything changed on both sides is a conflict, handled in the next dive; nothing is overwritten to "make it work".
  5. A journal can't grow forever. Keep entries for a retention window and snapshot beyond it. A device whose cursor is older than the horizon can't catch up from the journal and does a full reconcile — list the tree, compare hashes — which is the rare, expensive path a laptop that was in a drawer for a year should take.
  6. Two refinements are worth naming. Selective sync and placeholders: the tree syncs, but the bytes download only when a file is opened — the chunk protocol makes that natural. Batching: a folder of 10,000 files commits as a few batches, not 10,000 round trips.
Illustration — one sync round on a device
StepWhat happens
1a folder event, or a rescan by size and modified time, finds candidate changes; hash only those
2compare with the local database: last synced version and hash per node
3pull: GET /changes?cursor=…; apply remote changes; download only missing chunks
4push: commit local changes with their base versions; a refused commit is a conflict
5store the new cursor and the new local state
Illustration — what the journal measured
QueryTime
1,000 changes from the start of a 1,000,000-entry namespace0.255 ms
1,000 changes from the middle0.221 ms
"anything new?" with nothing new0.005 ms

PostgreSQL 16, one core, warm cache, a primary key of (namespace, seq).

Key deep dive — conflicts: two devices, one file, no lost edit
NFRNo edit is lost silentlyNFRDevices converge on one tree
Thought process
  1. A conflict is two devices committing changes to the same file from the same base version. With a guarded commit — UPDATE … WHERE head_version = $base — exactly one wins and the other is told. Tested on 200 files with two devices committing at the same instant: guarded, 200 commits were accepted, 200 conflicts were detected, and no edit was lost; with an unguarded "last write wins" update, 400 commits were accepted, 0 conflicts were detected and 200 edits were silently overwritten.
  2. Never overwrite silently. The default for the loser is keep both: commit its version as a new file next to the winner, named like report (Ravi's conflicted copy 2026-09-30).docx, and tell the user. For mergeable types — text, code — a three-way merge is possible because the base version is available: it is just a chunk list you still hold. For binary files, keep both.
  3. Other conflicts have their own rules. Edit against delete: keep the edit — resurrect the file — because losing work is worse than an extra file. Rename against edit: no conflict, since both act on the same node id; apply both. Two renames of one node: the later journal entry wins and the other name is kept as a conflicted copy. Two devices creating the same path: a conflicted copy. A move that would create a cycle — A moves X into Y while B moves Y into X: the server rejects the second.
  4. Order by version, not by time. Clocks disagree, offline devices' clocks disagree more, and "the newest modified time wins" quietly discards the wrong edit. The server's per-file version and journal order are the only ordering that means anything.
  5. This is for files as blobs. Documents edited live by several people at once — Google Docs — need operational transforms or CRDTs; see the collaborative editing example. A file synced by a desktop client is the coarser, offline-friendly model, and the two can coexist: a document type can opt into live merging.
Illustration — two devices, the same base version, 200 files
CommitAcceptedConflicts detectedEdits lost
guarded: head must equal the base200 of 4002000
unguarded: last write wins400 of 4000200

Two threads per file, released together, against PostgreSQL 16: every guarded pair produced exactly one winner and one detected conflict.

Illustration — what to do with each kind of conflict
ConflictRule
edit and edit, same baseone wins; the other becomes a conflicted copy, or is three-way merged if it is text
edit and deletekeep the edit — resurrect the file
rename and editno conflict: same node id, apply both
rename and renamethe later journal entry wins; keep the other name as a copy
two new files at one patha conflicted copy for the second
moves that would form a cyclereject the second
case-only difference on a case-insensitive disktreat as a name collision and make a copy
Key deep dive — big downloads, many downloads, and hot files
NFRA big download survives interruptionsNFRPopular files do not melt the store
Thought process
  1. A download is the upload run backwards. The API resolves the version to its chunk list and returns short-lived presigned GET URLs; the device fetches the chunks directly from the store or a CDN, several in parallel, using Range requests where a chunk is large. It keeps the set of chunks it already has, so an interrupted download resumes by re-requesting only what is missing — and it verifies each chunk's hash on arrival, which gives integrity checking for free.
  2. Dedupe applies on the way down too. A device that already holds 99% of a new version's chunks — the previous version — downloads 1%. That is why a synced file that changed by a paragraph costs the same to receive as to send.
  3. Many downloads use the same scheduler as uploads: one queue, a global limit, priorities (the file the user just opened first), and throttling. A whole folder is best handled by syncing it. If a browser must download a folder as one archive, stream a zip: the server reads chunks in order and writes entries as it goes, without holding the archive — but a streamed zip can't resume, which is one more reason to offer sync for large folders.
  4. Here content addressing pays a bonus. A chunk is immutable: its bytes can never change without its hash changing. So chunks can be cached at a CDN forever, with no invalidation logic at all; a popular shared file — a public link, a release — is served from the edge, and only the long tail reaches the origin. Egress is usually the biggest cost in this system, and this is what tames it.
  5. Visibility lives in the metadata, not in the store. Every download resolves the current version and its permissions at request time, and presigned URLs last minutes, so revoking a share link takes effect almost immediately even for files already in the CDN — because the URL, not the chunk, is what is protected.
Illustration — upload and download, side by side
UploadDownload
what the API returnswhich chunks are missing, and presigned PUT URLsthe chunk list of a version, and presigned GET URLs
what makes it resumablethe store already has the finished chunksthe device already has the finished chunks
what makes it cheapdedupe: only missing chunks traveldedupe: only chunks the device lacks travel
integritythe store verifies the declared checksumthe device verifies each chunk's hash
many at onceone queue, a global limit, small files firstthe same
caching—immutable chunks cache at the CDN indefinitely
Key deep dive — video: transcode in parallel, package as segments, stream from the edge
NFRVideo starts fast and adapts to bandwidthNFRA new upload becomes watchable in minutes
Thought process
  1. A video is a file with a second life. It uploads like any large file — chunked, resumable, deduplicated — and when the commit lands an event starts a pipeline. Transcoding is never inline: it is heavy, slow and bursty, so it runs from a queue on a separate fleet.
  2. The pipeline: probe the file; split it into keyframe-aligned segments; encode every segment into every rendition of a bitrate ladder in parallel; package the result as HLS or DASH — short playback segments plus a manifest that lists the renditions — into a media store behind a CDN. The player fetches the manifest, starts on a low or middle rendition, and switches rendition segment by segment according to the throughput it measures.
  3. What it costs, measured with ffmpeg 7 and libx264 at the veryfast preset on one shared core, from a synthetic 720p source: encoding ran at 1.61× real time for 720p, 2.47× for 480p, 3.0× for 360p and 3.83× for 240p. That is 37.2, 24.3, 20.1 and 15.6 CPU-seconds per minute of video, or 97.2 CPU-seconds per minute for the four-rung ladder. A ladder that tops out at 720p is a floor: 1080p and 4K cost several times more.
  4. So one hour of video is 97.2 × 60 = 5,832 CPU-seconds — 97 minutes on one core. Encoded whole, the uploader waits an hour and a half. Split into 10-second segments it is 360 segments × 4 renditions = 1,440 independent tasks; on 100 workers that is about 58 seconds if perfectly balanced, plus queueing. At an assumed 100,000 hours of video uploaded a day, the average load is about 6,750 cores busy around the clock, and the peak needs a queue and an SLA rather than a fixed fleet — spot instances suit this work.
  5. Segment length has a cost. Encoding a 2-second piece took 0.56 s per second of video, 4 s took 0.48, 10 s took 0.44 and 20 s took 0.4 — short tasks pay start-up and keyframe overhead, up to about 40% more. So encode in longer, keyframe-aligned pieces (10–20 s) and cut the playback segments (2–6 s) at packaging time, which is a copy, not a re-encode: 0.02 s for 20 seconds of 480p video in the test.
  6. Make it watchable early. Encode the lowest renditions first and publish the manifest as soon as one rendition is complete, then add the higher ones as they finish: the video plays in seconds at low quality and improves. The master is kept, so a better ladder can be produced later without asking for another upload.
  7. Storage and delivery: at these target bitrates (2,511, 1,207, 704 and 303 kbit/s) the four renditions came to 11.27 MB per 20 seconds — about 1.98 GB per hour of video, 1.88× the top rendition alone. Segments are small and immutable, so they cache at the CDN indefinitely; viewing is heavily skewed to a few popular videos, so the head is served from the edge and the long tail from the origin. Start-up time is the manifest plus the first segment, so keep the first segment small.
Illustration — the pipeline, and what each stage needs
StageWhat happensWhy
eventcommit of a video triggers a job on a queuenever inline; absorbs bursts
proberead duration, codec, resolution, keyframeschoose the ladder; reject broken files
splitcut at keyframes into 10–20 s piecesindependent tasks, parallel and retryable
encodeeach piece × each rendition, on a worker fleetthe CPU cost — measured below
packagecut 2–6 s playback segments and write manifests (a copy)cheap; lets the player switch often
publishwrite to the media store; lowest rendition firstplayable within seconds; better later
deliverthe player fetches the manifest and segments via the CDNimmutable segments cache forever

Key deep dive — what fails, and what to watch
NFRNothing is lostNFRKnow before users do
Thought process
  1. The single most dangerous failure is silent: a bug in the garbage collector deleting a chunk that is still referenced. It is why the collector waits a grace period, why counts are recomputed by a separate sweep, why the store is versioned or soft-deleting, and why nothing is physically deleted without a second check.
  2. The others are ordinary and have ordinary answers: an interrupted upload resumes by chunk; a commit that finds a chunk missing tells the device to upload it; a duplicate commit returns the version it made; a metadata shard outage pauses sync while downloads with URLs already issued continue; a lost notifier hint is repaired by slow polling; bit rot is caught by hashes on upload, on download and by a periodic scrub.
Illustration — what fails, and what the design does
FailureWhat happensThe design answer
the connection drops mid-uploadthe device has some chunks storedask which chunks are missing; upload only those — no session to lose
a commit finds a chunk missingthe commit is refusedthe device uploads it and commits again; the version never appears half-built
a commit is retried after it succeededa possible duplicate versionthe same base and list return the version already created
the garbage collector is wronga live chunk could be deleteda grace period, a separate mark-and-sweep, soft delete, and an audit before any physical delete
a chunk is corrupteda wrong file could be servedhash checked on upload and download; periodic scrub; repair from another copy
a metadata shard is downsync and new commits pausedownloads with issued URLs continue; devices retry with backoff
the notifier is downdevices are not told at oncethey poll slowly and catch up from the journal
a video will not transcodeone job failsa retry limit, a dead-letter queue, an alert; other videos are unaffected
a device's clock is wrongtimestamps disagreeordering uses server versions and the journal, never modified time
Illustration — what to measure, and when to be woken (illustrative thresholds)
LayerMeasureAlert when
uploadsuccess rate · chunks re-sent as a share of chunks · commit refusals for missing chunksre-send share climbing — the network or the store is unhealthy
synctime from a commit to applied on another device (p99) · journal catch-up latencyp99 above the promise
conflictsconflict rate per thousand commits · conflicted copies createda jump after a client release
garbage collectionchunks pending deletion · refcount mismatches found by the sweepany mismatch — the target is zero
storagededupe ratio · bytes per user (logical and physical) · egressegress growing faster than users
videoage of the oldest transcode job · time until first watchable · failures · CDN hit ratio · start-up time and rebuffering (client-side)first-watchable above the promise; hit ratio falling
Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • A file changes while it is being uploaded — re-check size and modified time after chunking; changed regions are re-chunked, and a commit against a stale base is refused.
  • Ten million tiny files — per-file overhead dominates: batch commits, keep very small files inline in metadata or pack them, and batch journal entries.
  • A 5 TiB single file — a version row of about 42 MB of hashes: use a two-level manifest so a change touches one leaf.
  • A shared folder of 100,000 members — it is one namespace mounted many times; the journal fan-out is a read, so members pull; the largest ones get a cell — see isolating the massive organizations.
  • Deleting a user's data on request — drop only their references; a chunk stays while others use it — which is also why per-user encryption and cross-user dedupe cannot both be absolute.
  • Two files whose names differ only by case — on a case-insensitive filesystem that is a name collision; make a conflicted copy.
  • Malware or a takedown — scan asynchronously and quarantine by version; never block the upload path; a takedown removes the reference, and the garbage collector removes the bytes later.
  • A device that was offline for a year — its cursor is older than the journal horizon: it does a full reconcile of hashes rather than replaying a journal that no longer exists.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
A 50 GB upload survives dropsResume by chunk: about 4,014 s at any chunk size against about 470,863 s as one request under the same drop rate.
Editing a big file re-uploads only what changedContent-defined chunks: a 100-byte insert re-uploaded 0.08 MB of 32 MB; fixed chunks re-uploaded all of it.
Identical data is stored onceA content-addressed block index (136 bytes per chunk), refcounts and a grace period; a second version cost 0.22 MB.
No edit is lost silentlyA guarded commit: 200 accepted and 200 conflicts detected for 200 simultaneous pairs, against 200 edits lost without it.
Sync is fast and offline-safeA journal and a cursor: 0.255 ms to fetch 1,000 changes, 0.005 ms to learn there is nothing new; offline commits carry their base versions.
Video is watchable in minutesSegments encoded in parallel: 5,832 CPU-seconds an hour becomes about 58 s on 100 workers; the lowest rendition is published first.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Content-defined chunks instead of fixedEdits anywhere cost only their difference — in exchange for CPU on the device and slightly worse appends.
Cross-user dedupeLarge storage savings — in exchange for an existence side channel that needs a proof of possession, and for conflict with per-user encryption.
A hash array per version, not a row per chunk19 times less metadata — in exchange for a separate reverse index if you ever need chunk → files.
Keep both on conflictNo edit is ever lost — in exchange for conflicted copies the user has to reconcile.
Parent pointers for the treeMoves and renames are one row — in exchange for resolving a path by walking the tree (cache it).
Encode in long pieces, package in short onesLess encoding overhead — in exchange for a little more latency before the first rendition is ready.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Chunk storeobject storage — S3, GCS or a self-run store with erasure coding — keyed by chunk hash, with presigned URLs and checksum verification
MetadataPostgreSQL or MySQL sharded by namespace (application routing, Citus or Vitess)
Chunking and hashinga content-defined chunker such as FastCDC-style gear hashing and SHA-256, in a native library on the client
Change notificationSSE or long polling to desktop clients, platform push to mobile; a queue like Kafka behind the notifier
VideoFFmpeg workers on a queue (spot instances), HLS or DASH packaging, a CDN in front of the media store
Collection and integritya refcount sweeper plus a periodic mark-and-sweep and a scrubber that re-hashes stored chunks
Load testingsimulated clients that drop connections at random, edit large files in place and reconnect after days offline
Worked Example BA — Subscription Membership — Pay Once a Cycle, Save on Every Order

Design a Subscription Membership (GrabUnlimited)

one workflow per member · renewals without a cron · idempotent charges and grants · benefit counters · checkout eligibility · savings ledger · trials
Click to expand

A membership like GrabUnlimited: pay Rp24.000 for 8 weeks (or 2 or 4 weeks), try it free for 2 weeks if you are new, and get discounts on Food, Car, Mart, Express and more — each benefit with a use count, city rules and a minimum order — plus a running total of everything you have saved. The design follows what Grab's engineers published about rebuilding GrabUnlimited: purchase and renewal as two flows, the zombie memberships and double awards their first design produced, and the move to one durable workflow per member. Everything else is filled in with stated design choices, using the app's own screens (plans, Benefits, Manage, the savings total) as the specification. Every number below was measured on one small machine with PostgreSQL 16 and Redis 7; Temporal, payment providers and Grab's services were not run, and the text says which numbers are measured, simulated or arithmetic.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Members subscribe to a 2-, 4- or 8-week plan with a stored payment method; new members can take a free trial first.
  • Memberships renew automatically at the end of each period until cancelled; a failed payment is retried for a while before the membership lapses.
  • Each period grants a set of benefits — per service, with use counts, minimum orders, eligible cities and merchants — shown on a Benefits screen.
  • At checkout in Food, Car, Mart and Express, the best eligible benefit is applied automatically and can be combined with other promos where allowed.
  • Members can cancel (benefits continue to the end of the period), change plan, change the payment method, and see a lifetime savings total.
  • The app shows membership status everywhere it matters: the profile badge, the Subscriptions tab, checkout.
  • Members are reminded before renewals and told about failed payments; every charge produces a receipt; support agents can fix, refund or grant goodwill, with an audit trail.
  • Plans, prices, benefits, currency and tax are configured per country.
Non-functional
  • A member is never charged twice for a period, and never ends up both cancelled and renewed.
  • Every paid period's benefits are granted exactly once, even when a service fails mid-step.
  • Renewals never spike the database or the payment service; each happens near the member's own renewal time.
  • A benefit is never used more times than granted, even under concurrent checkouts and retries.
  • The membership check at checkout fits in a few milliseconds and never blocks an order.
  • The savings total is exact: duplicated or out-of-order order events and refunds never distort it.
  • Scale (assumed for sizing): 10 million members, 30 million app opens and 6 million member orders a day — status reads in a few ms at p99, the checkout decision within ~50 ms, every renewal within an hour of its time.
  • A payment-provider outage delays renewals; it never lapses a member.

"Unlimited" is honest about its caps: 240 uses a cycle is generous, but a number is what lets the system — and finance — reason about it.

2
Core Entities
  • Plan — length in weeks, price, trial rules; versioned.
  • Membership — one per member: state, period end, plan, payment method, cancel requested.
  • Cycle — one paid (or trial) period: number, start, end, the charge, the benefit-template version.
  • Charge — idempotency key member:cycle, amount, outcome.
  • Benefit template — service, discount, minimum order, cities, merchant opt-in, stacking, uses per cycle; versioned.
  • Entitlement — one row per member, cycle and benefit: granted, remaining.
  • Benefit use — one row per order that used a benefit: reserved → used or released.
  • Savings ledger row — one per order with a member discount; refunded flag.
  • Trial claim — one per normalised identifier (phone, payment instrument, device).
  • Wallet link — the auto-debit token and consent for a wallet or card; unlinking it is a change the workflow hears about.
  • Membership event — an outbox row written with each state change: subscribed, renewed, past due, cancelled, lapsed, plan changed.
  • Receipt — one per successful charge, with the country's tax.

Two keys carry most of the correctness: member:cycle(:step) for everything the workflow does, and order id for everything checkout does.

3
API

For a database question, the "API" is the queries the schema must serve well:

POST /subscriptions {plan, payment_method} · POST /subscriptions/cancel · PUT /subscriptions/plan · PUT /subscriptions/payment-method
GET /subscriptions/me → state, renews on, plan, savings total · GET /subscriptions/me/benefits → lines with remaining uses
between services: POST /entitlements:eligible {order} · POST /entitlements:reserve {order_id} · confirm and release by order id and benefit
POST /webhooks/payments → the provider's signed settlement, signalled to the workflow · POST /admin/memberships/{id}/… → support actions, each written to the audit log

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. Maya taps her avatar, opens Subscriptions and picks the 8-week plan with OVO; as a new member she starts with the 2-week free trial.
  2. Her workflow starts under her member id. It grants the trial cycle's benefits as counters and records her state; her avatar now shows the badge.
  3. She orders lunch for Rp45rb from a restaurant with the plan label; checkout finds the Rp10rb delivery benefit (minimum Rp40rb, her city), reserves one use for the order, and the order goes through.
  4. The order completes; an order event confirms the use and adds the saving to her ledger. Her Benefits screen shows one fewer use.
  5. Two weeks later the trial ends and the workflow charges OVO Rp24.000 with the key member:cycle 2; it grants the new cycle and sleeps for 8 weeks.
  6. She cancels a week before the next renewal. The signal reaches the same workflow; there is no next charge, and her benefits continue until the period ends.
5
High-Level Design

One durable workflow per member owns the lifecycle: it charges through the payment service, grants each cycle's benefits as counters, records the state for reads, and sleeps until the next renewal; cancel and plan changes are signals to that same workflow, so nothing runs concurrently for one member. Checkout reads membership from a status cache and reserves a benefit use per order; order events confirm or release it and feed an exact savings ledger.

6
Deep Dives

Eleven below: (a) the membership as a long-running workflow, (b) renewing millions without a nightly cron, (c) charging the renewal, (d) benefits as vouchers or counters, (e) checkout eligibility, (f) the savings total, (g) trials and abuse, (h) plan changes, cancellation, add-ons and coming back, (i) whether it is enough to scale, (j) the components around the core, and (k) what fails and what to watch — then the edge cases.

High-level design, part 1 — the core. Steps 1–6 are the membership: subscribe, then one workflow per member charges, grants and records each cycle and sleeps until the next. Steps 7–8 are every order: checkout reserves a benefit use, and order events confirm or release it and feed the savings ledger.
Illustration — the membership and an order, step by step
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
1the member chooses a plan and a payment method and subscribesMember app · API gateway · Membership APIthe request is validated against the plan catalog
2the API starts the member's workflow, or signals it if one is running (cancel, plan change)Membership workflows (Temporal)workflow id = member id: one operation at a time
3the workflow charges the stored method for this cyclePayment service · OVO or a cardkey member:cycle — never charged twice
4it grants this cycle's benefits as countersEntitlement service · Entitlementsinsert keyed by member, cycle, benefit — safe to repeat
5it records the state; the status cache followsMembership DB · Redisreads never touch the workflow
6it sleeps until the next renewal; a cancel arrives as a signal to the same workflowdurable timerno cron, no scan
7at checkout, the order reserves one matching benefit useCheckout · Entitlement serviceconditional decrement, keyed by order and benefit
8order events confirm or release the use; the savings ledger records the discountKafka · Entitlement service · Savings writereach order handled once, whatever the delivery

Two keys carry the correctness: member:cycle:step for the workflow, and order id plus benefit for checkout.

High-level design, part 2 — around the core: the provider webhook that settles pending charges, wallet links for auto-debit, the trial and risk check, the support console with its audit log, membership events (outbox → Kafka) feeding the status cache, notifications, marketing and finance, and the daily reconciliation. Deep dive (j) walks through it.
One renewal
  1. The member's timer fires a little before the period ends.
  2. The charge goes out with the key member:cycle; a timeout is answered by the same key.
  3. The new cycle's counters are inserted; a retry inserts nothing new.
  4. The state is recorded, the cache follows, and the workflow sleeps again.
One order
  1. Checkout asks: member? which benefit fits?
  2. One use is reserved under the order id.
  3. The order completes: the use is confirmed and the saving recorded — once, however many times the event arrives.
Key deep dive — the membership is a long-running workflow
NFRA member is never both cancelled and renewedNFREvery step can be retried without doing it twice
Thought process
  1. A membership lives for years and turns over every 2, 4 or 8 weeks: subscribe, charge, grant the cycle's benefits, wait, renew — until the member cancels or a payment finally fails. Grab's engineers describe exactly this as two flows, purchase and renewal, over a state machine. The design that holds up is one durable workflow per member — Temporal, as Grab moved to — with the workflow id equal to the member id, each step an activity with retries and backoff, and a durable timer doing the waiting.
  2. The states and what each allows are in the diagram below. The workflow owns what happens next; the Membership DB row is a projection for reads, written by a step, because the app reads membership status far more often than it changes (the avatar badge on every app open, every checkout).
  3. The race that produces zombies. Grab described a member cancelling in the middle of an auto-renewal and ending up both cancelled and renewed, because the renewal outlived a five-minute Redis lock. Reproduced with a real Redis lock and PostgreSQL: with a 60 ms lock and 289 of 1,200 renewals slower than it, 280 members ended active after their cancel was accepted and 279 were charged after cancelling.
  4. Two fixes, the same idea: one operation at a time per member. With a workflow engine, cancel and renew run under the same workflow id, so one finishes before the other starts. Without one, claim the step with a conditional update before doing it, and record a cancel that arrives mid-renewal instead of letting it overwrite. Tested: 0 lost cancels; every race resolved to one of two consistent outcomes — 653 cancelled before any charge, 547 renewed and then set to cancel at the end of the period they had just paid for.
  5. Idempotency keys come from the step, not the attempt. Grab's old state handler generated a fresh key whenever it was re-queued, so a retry after a partial failure awarded the first benefits again. Tested: 8,000 renewals each awarding 3 benefit sets, with 25% of calls failing after they took effect. A new key per attempt produced 19,128 extra awards (9,896 member-benefit sets awarded more than once); a key built from member, cycle and step produced 0.
  6. Long-running workflows outlive many deploys. Start a fresh run each cycle ("continue as new") so the history stays short, and version changes to the workflow code so a member mid-cycle finishes on the logic they started with.
Illustration — the membership lifecycle
Illustration — the race, on a timeline: a timed lock against claiming the step
Illustration — the workflow, in outline
workflow Membership(member_id)                        -- workflow id = member id: one runs at a time
  cycle = 1
  loop:
    charge(member_id, cycle)        key "m42:c7:charge"     -- retried with backoff; the key never changes
    grant(member_id, cycle)         key "m42:c7:grant"      -- inserts this cycle's counters; safe to repeat
    publish_state(member_id, cycle) key "m42:c7:state"      -- the DB row and the status cache follow
    sleep until renews_on - 24h     (a durable timer; or a cancel signal wakes it)
    if cancel was signalled: wait for the period to end, mark Expired, stop
    cycle += 1                      -- continue-as-new each cycle keeps the history short
Illustration — the same guarantee in plain SQL
-- without a workflow engine: claim the step, then do it
UPDATE membership SET state = 'renewing'
WHERE member_id = $1 AND state = 'active' AND NOT cancel_requested
RETURNING period_end;                                 -- no row: cancelled first, or someone else is renewing

-- … charge and grant, with keys member:cycle:step …

UPDATE membership
SET state      = CASE WHEN cancel_requested THEN 'cancel_at_period_end' ELSE 'active' END,
    period_end = period_end + interval '56 days'
WHERE member_id = $1 AND state = 'renewing';

-- a cancel never overwrites a renewal in flight: it is recorded, and applied at the end of the period
UPDATE membership SET cancel_requested = true,
       state = CASE WHEN state = 'active' THEN 'cancel_at_period_end' ELSE state END
WHERE member_id = $1;

TestResult

the same, claiming the step first0 cancels lost · 653 cancelled first · 547 renewed, then cancel at period end
