Real Redis 7 and PostgreSQL 16 on one shared core; the lock TTL and payment delays are scaled down from minutes to milliseconds so the race shows up in seconds. Temporal itself was not run: the tests show the rule it enforces.

Key deep dive — renewing millions without a nightly cron
NFRRenewals never spike the databaseNFREvery renewal happens near the minute the member joined
Thought process
  1. Arithmetic first: 2,000,000 members on 8-week plans means about 35,787 renewals a day. Grab's original renewal was a daily cron that pulled every membership due that day from the database; it slowed as membership grew, batching didn't stop the surges, and the database was scaled vertically to cope.
  2. The query itself is not the problem: finding a day's renewals with an index took 17.864 ms on 2,000,000 rows. The problem is the burst it releases — every charge, every benefit grant and every notification for the day at once. Dispatching 35,787 renewals in ten minutes is 59.6 a second against the payment and reward services.
  3. Renew each membership at the minute it started, and the load follows how people signed up. With sign-ups clustered at lunch and in the evening, the busiest minute held 149 renewals — 2.5 a second, about 24× gentler than the cron burst. A per-minute claim over a partial index took 0.078 ms. With durable timers (Grab's choice) there is no scan at all: each workflow wakes itself.
  4. Charge a little before the period ends — Uber's membership terms, for example, allow charging up to 24 hours ahead — so a declined wallet has time to be retried before the member loses anything. Store renews_on in UTC and compute it from the plan's length in weeks, not calendar months.
  5. Two cautions with timers: thousands of members who joined in the same promo minute wake together, so add a few minutes of jitter; and rate-limit the payment activity per provider, so a provider outage turns into a queue of retries rather than a stampede when it recovers.
Illustration — renewals per hour, one day, two strategies
Illustration — three ways to trigger renewals
ApproachHowDatabase loadTrade-off
nightly cronone query at midnight, dispatch everythinga spike every nightsimple; the burst hits every dependency at once
per-minute claimclaim what is due this minute from a partial indexsmall and steadya scheduler to run; the index to maintain
a timer per membereach workflow sleeps until its own renewalnone for schedulingneeds a workflow engine; add jitter for promo spikes
Illustration — what the renewal test measured

Key deep dive — charging the renewal: wallets, retries and grace
NFRNever charged twiceNFRA temporary wallet problem does not end a membership
Thought process
  1. The member pays with a stored method — OVO in the screenshots — and every renewal charge carries an idempotency key of member:cycle. Because it is the same on every retry, a timeout followed by a retry can never charge twice; the payment service returns the first result. See the idempotent payments example.
  2. Treat the three outcomes differently. Succeeded: grant the cycle. Declined (insufficient wallet balance, a blocked card): move to Past due and retry on a schedule. Unknown (a timeout): never charge again with a new key — ask the payment service for the status of that key first.
  3. Past due with a grace window is a product decision worth stating: keep benefits on for a few days while retrying, show "top up OVO or change the payment method" in the app, and send reminders through the notification system. If the member saved another method and allowed it, fall back to it; Uber's published terms describe the same pattern. When the window closes, the membership lapses and the workflow ends.
  4. A free trial still needs a payment method, because its end is the first real charge — the first renewal is the conversion. The trial itself grants a normal cycle of benefits.
  5. Wallet charges can settle later. An auto-debit from a linked wallet or a card may come back as pending, with the real outcome delivered by the provider's webhook. The charge step then waits for a signal — the payment service verifies the webhook and signals the member's workflow — with a timeout after which it asks the provider for the status. Auto-debit needs a wallet link: a token and the member's consent, stored by the payment service. If the member unlinks OVO or removes the card, the next renewal can't be charged: prompt them before the renewal date, not after it fails.
  6. A provider outage is not the member's failure. When the payment provider itself is down, pause the past-due clock and retry when it recovers, instead of lapsing members who did nothing wrong. Separate declined (the member's problem) from unavailable (ours).
  7. Each successful charge produces a receipt with the tax each country requires, and finance recognises the fee over the period it pays for, not on the day it was charged. A card chargeback or wallet dispute ends the membership at once and is recorded against the member for risk checks.
  8. Cancelling stops the next charge; the current period is already paid, so benefits continue until it ends and nothing is refunded for it (the common rule, and what "cancel anytime" usually means). A plan change takes effect at the next renewal, which avoids prorating.
Illustration — a renewal charge: every outcome, and a declined renewal over time
Illustration — what each charge outcome does
OutcomeWhat the workflow doesThe member sees
succeededgrant this cycle; schedule the next renewalnothing — it just renews
declinedPast due: retry later (illustrative: +12 h, +24 h, +48 h after the first attempt); keep benefits during grace"Top up OVO or change the payment method"
unknown (timeout)query the status of the same key; retry only that keynothing yet
grace overLapsed: no benefits; the workflow ends"Your membership has ended — rejoin anytime"

The retry schedule and grace length are illustrative design choices; Grab's exact rules are in its Help Centre and were not publicly readable.

Key deep dive — benefits: vouchers or counters?
NFRGranting a cycle is one small writeNFRA benefit is never used more times than granted
Thought process
  1. The benefits screen lists 14 lines with a use count each — 40× for Mart, 8× for airtime, 240× for food and car, 12× and 8× for Express. That is 1,868 uses per member per 8-week cycle, so "unlimited" is really a generous, fair-use cap.
  2. As vouchers — one row per use, as a promo system often stores them — 1,000 members took 1,868,000 rows, 161.7 MB and 3.64 s to grant. That is about 1.87 billion rows and 158 GB per million members, every cycle.
  3. As counters — one row per member, benefit and cycle, holding granted and remaining — 100,000 members took 1,400,000 rows and 136.5 MB. That is 14 million rows and 1.33 GB per million members, about 119× less, and finding a member's remaining benefits took 0.01 ms. Granting is an insert keyed by (member, cycle, benefit), so a retried grant changes nothing.
  4. Using one is a conditional decrement. With 5 uses left and 64 checkouts racing, read-then-write granted 59; remaining = remaining − 1 WHERE remaining > 0 granted exactly 5.
  5. One order can use more than one benefit — a Mart delivery discount plus a partner deal, say — so a use is keyed by (order_id, benefit), not by the order alone. Keyed by the order alone, 500 orders that each used 2 benefits silently dropped 500 of them; keyed by order and benefit, all 1,000 were recorded. Each use also records who funds the discount — Grab, or a merchant or partner for exclusive deals — so finance can settle it.
  6. Benefits are data, not code: a template says which service, the discount, the minimum order, the cities, whether a merchant must opt in, and what it stacks with. Each cycle records the template version it was granted under, so a member keeps the terms they paid for when marketing changes the offer mid-cycle.
Illustration — one member's cycle as vouchers or as counters, and the last-uses race
Illustration — the entitlement tables and a safe use
CREATE TABLE entitlement (
  member_id bigint, cycle int, benefit text,          -- e.g. 'food_delivery_10k_min40k'
  template_version int NOT NULL,                       -- the terms the member paid for, frozen at grant
  granted   int NOT NULL,                              -- 240
  remaining int NOT NULL CHECK (remaining >= 0),
  PRIMARY KEY (member_id, cycle, benefit));            -- granting twice is harmless

CREATE TABLE benefit_use (                             -- one row per benefit an order used
  order_id bigint, benefit text, member_id bigint, cycle int,
  funded_by text NOT NULL,                             -- 'grab' or a partner: who pays for this discount
  state text NOT NULL,                                 -- reserved → used | released
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, benefit));                    -- an order may use more than one benefit

-- reserve at checkout (one transaction): the order id makes a retry harmless
INSERT INTO benefit_use VALUES ($order, $m, $c, $b, 'reserved') ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING 1;
UPDATE entitlement SET remaining = remaining - 1
WHERE member_id = $m AND cycle = $c AND benefit = $b AND remaining > 0 RETURNING remaining;
-- no row: none left → roll back and offer the next-best benefit
Illustration — vouchers against counters, measured
Vouchers (a row per use)Counters (a row per benefit)
rows per member per cycle1,86814
measured1,000 members: 1,868,000 rows, 161.7 MB, 3.64 s100,000 members: 1,400,000 rows, 136.5 MB, 2.8 s
per million members, per cycle1.87 billion rows · ~158 GB14 million rows · 1.33 GB
last 5 uses, 64 racing checkoutsread-then-write: 59 grantedconditional decrement: 5 granted

PostgreSQL 16; per-million figures are arithmetic from the measured rows. Benefit lines and counts are taken from the app's Benefits screen.

Key deep dive — checkout: which benefit fits this order, in milliseconds
NFRThe member benefit is decided inside the checkout's time budgetNFRA retried or cancelled order never uses a benefit twice
Thought process
  1. Every Food, Car, Mart and Express checkout asks one question: is this person a member, and which of their benefits fits this order? "Fits" is the template's rules: the service, the order's city (where it is delivered or picked up, not where the member lives), whether the merchant has opted in — the restaurant page shows the plan label — the minimum order, and the stacking rules. The app says the food discount combines with other promos and the car discount stacks with other discounts.
  2. Reserve, then confirm. At checkout the entitlement service reserves one use, keyed by the order id; when the order completes, an order event confirms it; when it is cancelled, the use is released. Each call can be retried: with 2,000 orders, 199 of them cancelled, and every reserve, confirm and release sent twice, the uses consumed were 1,801 for 1,801 completed orders — exact. This is the same reservation pattern as the stock holds in the marketplace example.
  3. The read path is tiny and hot. Membership status is cached in Redis, refreshed when the state changes, because the avatar badge and every checkout read it. A member's counters are at most a few dozen rows, so they can be read from the database or a replica directly.
  4. Advance bookings and orders that cross a boundary. A car booked tonight for next week reserves its use now, against the cycle current at reservation; the reservation lives until the ride completes or is cancelled. An order reserved while the member was active is honoured even if the membership ends before the order completes — the price shown at checkout is a promise.
  5. The client never sends a discount. The app shows what the server decided; the checkout service computes the price with the benefit, and only checkout services may call the entitlement service. A tampered request can't invent a benefit.
  6. When the entitlement service is slow or down, the checkout must not wait: give it a few tens of milliseconds, then place the order without the member discount and say so, rather than failing the order. Whether to credit the missed discount afterwards is a product choice; reconciliation can find those orders.
Illustration — one checkout, as a sequence
Illustration — one checkout, step by step
StepWhat happensTool
1is the buyer a member, and until when?Redis status cache, refreshed on state change
2which benefits match: service, city, merchant opt-in, minimum order, stackingbenefit templates · the member's counters
3reserve one use for this orderconditional decrement + a row keyed by order id
4show the discount; place the ordercheckout
5order completed → confirm · cancelled → releaseorder events (Kafka), each handled once per order

Key deep dive — "Total savings since 28 Dec 2022"
NFRThe savings number is exactNFRA refund removes its saving
Thought process
  1. The plan screen shows a lifetime total — Rp16.692.238 in the screenshot. It is the sum of the member discounts on every completed order, minus refunded ones, across years and services. It doesn't need to be instant, but it must be exact: an inflated number erodes trust, and finance may reconcile it.
  2. A running sum fed by order events breaks in two ways at once: events are delivered more than once, and a refund can arrive before the completion it cancels. Tested with 120,000 orders, 5% refunded and 219,074 events delivered with duplicates in random order: a running sum was wrong for 19,059 of 20,000 members; a ledger keyed by order id, where a refund flips a flag, was wrong for 0.
  3. Refunds are often partial — one item of a basket — so each refund is its own ledger entry with a negative amount, keyed by (order, entry). And reading years of rows on every screen open is wasteful, so keep a per-member running total updated in the same transaction, only when a ledger entry is actually inserted. Tested with 60,000 orders, full and partial refunds, 116,854 events delivered with duplicates in random order by 8 concurrent writers: 0 members wrong, the total read in 0.005 ms, at 4,949 events a second on one core.
  4. Summing the ledger instead took 0.015 ms with an index on member (it was 6.097 ms without). Over years of orders that sum keeps growing, which is why the screen reads the running total and the ledger is kept for audits and corrections.
Illustration — one order's events becoming one exact total
Illustration — the ledger
-- one entry per event that changes a saving: the completion, and each (partial) refund
CREATE TABLE savings_ledger (order_id bigint, entry text, member_id bigint, amount int,   -- refunds are negative
                             created_at timestamptz, PRIMARY KEY (order_id, entry));       -- partitioned by month
CREATE TABLE savings_total  (member_id bigint PRIMARY KEY, total bigint NOT NULL);

-- in one transaction, for every event (duplicates and any order are fine):
INSERT INTO savings_ledger VALUES ($order, $entry, $m, $amount, now()) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING 1;
-- only if a row was inserted:
INSERT INTO savings_total VALUES ($m, $amount)
ON CONFLICT (member_id) DO UPDATE SET total = savings_total.total + excluded.total;

SELECT total FROM savings_total WHERE member_id = $m;     -- the number on the screen, O(1)
Illustration — what the savings test measured
ApproachMembers with a wrong total
running sum of events19,059 of 20,000
ledger keyed by order id, refund as a flag0

219,074 events, duplicates and out-of-order refunds. PostgreSQL 16.

Key deep dive — trials and abuse
NFRA free trial is once per person, not once per accountNFRFair-use caps limit what an abuser can extract
Thought process
  1. "Free for new members" invites new accounts. Decide what counts as a person: a verified phone number, the payment instrument (a wallet account or a card fingerprint), and the device. Record each normalised identifier in a trial-claims table with a unique index, and grant a trial only when none of them has claimed one — two accounts racing for the same phone number resolve to one winner, the same pattern as unique emails in the multi-org identity example.
  2. Requiring a payment method for the trial does double duty: it's needed for the first charge, and it ties the trial to an instrument that is harder to multiply than accounts.
  3. The 240× caps are themselves an abuse control: they bound what one membership can extract. Watch for patterns that look like resale — one member's benefits used at many different delivery addresses, or orders placed and cancelled just to test reservations — and act on the membership, not the order.
Illustration — one trial per person, decided by unique identifiers

IdentifierNormalised asWhy

the rulea trial if none of them has claimed oneunique indexes decide races
Key deep dive — plan changes, cancellation, add-ons and coming back
NFREvery change has a defined effective timeNFRAdd-ons never outlive their rules
Thought process
  1. One live membership per member. A double tap on Subscribe, or two devices, must not create two memberships. With 2 simultaneous taps for each of 400 members, check-then-insert created 799 memberships; a unique index on the member over the live states created exactly 400. The subscribe request also carries an idempotency key, so a retry returns the first answer.
  2. Cancel is a signal to the member's workflow: no further charges, benefits until the end of the paid period, then Expired. Because it is a signal to the same workflow, a cancel in the middle of a renewal waits for that renewal (deep dive a).
  3. Undo a cancel. Subscribing while in Cancel at period end is a resume, not a new membership: clear the flag, keep the renewal date, charge nothing now.
  4. Change plan (2, 4 or 8 weeks) takes effect at the next renewal: the next charge uses the new price and length. Switching immediately would need prorating and partial refunds for little gain.
  5. Add-ons, such as a one-week holiday pack, are separate one-off purchases with their own counters and their own end date. Grab's terms make that pack available only to existing members and say it does not auto-renew, so check membership at purchase and never attach it to the renewal workflow.
  6. Coming back after Expired or Lapsed starts a new workflow with a new first charge — no second trial — and keeps the member's savings history, because the ledger is keyed by member, not by membership.
  7. Price changes and retired plans apply at each member's next renewal after a notice period; a retired plan moves its members to the closest plan at renewal, with notice. The price is read from the plan version, so a member mid-cycle is never repriced.
  8. Countries: plans, prices, currency, benefits and tax are per country, and a membership belongs to one. A member who moves keeps their membership until it ends; benefits apply only to orders in that country.
  9. Deleting an account or suspending it for fraud cancels the workflow at once and stops benefits; personal data is removed, but charges, receipts and the savings ledger keep the anonymised financial records the law requires.
  10. Changing the offer for everyone (new benefit lines, new counts) applies from each member's next cycle, because each cycle is granted from the template version current at that moment.
Illustration — changes on a membership's timeline
Illustration — when each change takes effect
ChangeEffectiveWhat the member keeps
cancelno next chargebenefits until the period ends
change planat the next renewalthe current plan until then
change payment methodthe next chargeeverything
add-on packat purchase, for its own lengththe add-on's own counters

Key deep dive — is it enough to scale? capacity, partitions and the hot paths
NFREvery component has a stated scale and a way to growNFRThe hot paths stay cheap at peak
Thought process
  1. Grab doesn't publish its member count, so the sizing below uses stated assumptions — 10 million members, 30 million member app opens and 6 million member orders a day, with peaks five to six times the average — and measured per-core numbers from this machine. The point is the shape: which path is hot, and what it costs per unit.
  2. The membership itself is not the scale problem. About 339,000 renewals a day is under 4 a second; spread by join time, the busiest minute is about 24 a second. Ten million open workflows with one timer each is the workflow engine's normal job, and continue-as-new each cycle keeps every history a few dozen events long.
  3. The hot paths are reads and checkouts. Status reads come from Redis — 139 bytes a member, about 1.29 GB for 10 million, and 19,542 reads a second from Python clients on one shared core (p99 2.021 ms, mostly client overhead). Reservations are a conditional decrement plus an insert: 4,058 a second on one PostgreSQL core against an assumed lunch peak of about 420.
  4. How each part grows. Entitlements and benefit uses are sharded by member id (hash), so one member's counters and reservations live on one shard and every checkout touches one shard; add shards for capacity or to limit the blast radius of an outage. Benefit uses and the savings ledger are partitioned by time and archived; the running total keeps reads O(1). The status cache is a Redis cluster with replicas, and the checkout falls back to the database (rate-limited) if it is unavailable. Kafka topics are partitioned by member for membership events and by order for order events, so each key is handled in order.
  5. What to protect at peak: rate-limit the payment step per provider, jitter promo-minute renewals, and keep the checkout's entitlement call inside its budget with a timeout — a slow entitlement shard costs a missed discount, never a failed order.
Illustration — headroom on the hot paths

Key deep dive — around the core: async payments, events, support, finance and reconciliation
NFREvery state change reaches the services that care, exactly onceNFREvery mismatch is found by a job, not by a member
Thought process
  1. The first diagram is the core loop. A production membership needs more around it, shown in the second diagram: the provider's webhook that settles a pending charge and signals the workflow; wallet links for auto-debit; a trial and risk check in front of subscribe; a support console whose every action is a signal to the same workflow and a line in an audit log.
  2. Membership events. Each state change writes an outbox row in the same transaction as the state, and a relay publishes it to Kafka — subscribed, renewed, past due, cancelled, lapsed, plan changed. The status cache, notifications ("renews in 3 days", "payment failed, top up OVO"), member-only marketing and finance consume it; none of them asks the workflow. See the notification schema for the outbox pattern.
  3. Finance and receipts. Each charge gets a receipt with the country's tax, revenue is recognised across the period it pays for, and each benefit use carries who funds it, so merchant- and partner-funded deals settle correctly.
  4. Reconciliation, daily. Compare the provider's settlement report with recorded charges, charges with cycles, and cycles with granted entitlements. Charged but not granted, granted but not charged, settled by the provider but unknown to us: each becomes a ticket — Grab's own incident list was exactly these.
  5. Moving existing members onto a new design (the subject of Grab's planned follow-up post) is done cohort by cohort at a cycle boundary: start each member's workflow at their next renewal, keep the old job off for that cohort, and compare states between the two systems before widening the rollout.
Illustration — the daily reconciliation, three ways
Illustration — the components around the core (see part 2 of the high-level design)
ComponentWhy it existsKeyed by
settlement webhook → Payment service → signalwallet and card charges can settle after the call returnsmember:cycle
wallet linksauto-debit needs a token and consent; unlinking must be heard before renewalmember · wallet
trial & risk check + trial claimsone free trial per person, not per accountphone · instrument · device

Key deep dive — what fails, and what to watch
NFRMembers never lose what they paid forNFRProblems show up in metrics before support tickets
Thought process
  1. Grab's own incident list is the best checklist: memberships stuck in a corrupted state, renewals that didn't happen or couldn't be retried, and members who paid but didn't receive their benefits. Each maps to a guarantee above — one operation at a time, step-level idempotency, retries with backoff — and each gets a metric.
Illustration — what still works when one part fails
Illustration — what fails, and what the design does
FailureWhat happensThe design answer
the payment service is down at renewalcharges failthe charge step retries with backoff and the same key; past due only after real declines
the reward/entitlement service is down after a chargepaid, but no benefits yetthe grant step retries on its own; the charge is never repeated
cancel during a renewala zombie: cancelled and renewedone workflow per member, or claim the step first
a worker crashes mid-stepthe step is half donethe step is retried with the same key
the checkout cannot reach entitlementsno member discount decided in timeplace the order without it, say so; reconcile later
duplicate or out-of-order order eventswrong counts and savingshandle per order id: reserve/confirm/release and the ledger are keyed by it
a promo minute: thousands joined at oncetheir renewals wake togetherjitter on timers; rate-limit the payment step
the payment provider is downevery renewal fails at oncepause the past-due clock; retry on recovery; never lapse for our outage
a settlement webhook is losta charge stays pendingtime out, ask the provider by key; the daily reconciliation catches the rest
the member unlinks OVO or removes the cardthe next renewal cannot be chargedan event prompts them before the renewal date
Redis (status cache) is downbadge and checkout lose their fast readfall back to the Membership DB, rate-limited; show the last known state
an entitlement shard is downmembers on it get no discount at checkoutorders still go through; reconcile missed discounts
Kafka consumers laguses confirm late; savings and notifications are behindalert on lag; everything is keyed, so catching up is safe
the workflow engine is unavailablerenewals and grants waitnothing is lost; timers fire on recovery; extend grace automatically
Illustration — what to measure (illustrative thresholds)
MeasureAlert when
renewal success rate, by payment methodit falls against its normal band
memberships in Renewing for more than a few minutesabove zero for long
charged but not granted (by cycle)any — the target is zero
cancel requests not reflected in stateany
past due → recovered vs lapsedrecovery rate drops
checkout entitlement latency p99 · timeoutsp99 above the checkout budget
reserved uses older than an hourgrowing — confirms or releases are missing

pending charges older than the settlement timeoutgrowing
reconciliation mismatches (charges ↔ cycles ↔ grants)any — the target is zero

members lapsed during a provider outageany — the clock should have paused
Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • Cancel during a renewal — one workflow: either the cancel lands first (no charge) or the renewal does (cancel at the end of the new period).
  • A charge times out — ask for the status of the same key; never retry with a new one.
  • Wallet balance too low — past due: retries during a grace window, benefits on, a prompt to top up or switch method.
  • Benefit used up mid-cycle — checkout offers the next eligible benefit, or none; the screen shows 0 remaining.
  • Order in another city — eligibility follows the order's city, so a benefit may not apply while travelling.
  • Merchant not opted in — no member delivery discount there; other promos still apply.
  • Order cancelled after the use was reserved — released by order id; the count comes back.
  • Refund after delivery — the ledger flag removes the saving; the benefit use stays consumed (a product choice).
  • Rejoining after lapsing — a new first charge, no trial; the savings history continues.
  • Double tap on Subscribe — one live membership per member (unique index) and an idempotency key on the request.
  • Subscribe while set to cancel at period end — a resume: the flag is cleared, nothing is charged now.
  • One order uses two benefits — two uses, keyed by order and benefit.
  • A car booked for next week — the use is reserved now, against the current cycle, and held until the ride.
  • The membership ends before a reserved order completes — the reservation is honoured — the checkout price was a promise.
  • A partial refund — a negative ledger entry for that part; the running total follows.
  • Charge pending at the provider — the workflow waits for the settlement webhook, then asks by key after a timeout.
  • Wallet unlinked or card removed — prompted before the renewal; otherwise past due at renewal.
  • Provider outage at renewal time — the past-due clock pauses; nobody lapses for our outage.
  • Price change or a retired plan — applies at the next renewal after notice; a member mid-cycle is never repriced.
  • Chargeback or dispute — the membership ends at once; recorded for risk checks.
  • Account deleted or suspended — workflow cancelled, benefits stop; anonymised financial records are kept.
  • Member moves country — the membership stays in its country until it ends; benefits apply to orders there only.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Never charged twicecharge key member:cycle; a retry returns the first result.
Never cancelled-and-renewedone operation at a time per member: 0 lost cancels against 280 with a 60 ms lock.
Benefits granted exactly oncekeys per step: 0 extra awards against 19,128 with a key per attempt.
No renewal stampederenewals at each member's own time: 2.5/s at the busiest minute against 59.6/s for a cron burst.
Never over-usedconditional decrement: 5 of 5 uses granted under a race (read-then-write: 59).
An exact savings totala ledger keyed by order id: 0 members wrong (a running sum: 19,059); with partial refunds and a running total, 0 wrong.
One live membership per membera unique index over live states: 400 memberships for 400 members double-tapping (check-then-insert: 799).
Every benefit an order uses is recordeduses keyed by order and benefit: 1,000 recorded (keyed by order alone: 500 dropped).
Enough headroom at peak4,058 reservations a second on one core against an assumed peak of ~420; status cache 1.29 GB for 10 million members.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
A workflow enginecorrect by construction for long-lived state — in exchange for a new system to run and a learning curve, as Grab described.
Renew at each member's timea flat load — in exchange for timers (or a per-minute scheduler) instead of one simple job.
Counters instead of vouchersabout 119× less storage and one write per benefit — in exchange for a promo system that understands counters.
Benefits during gracefewer lost members over a low wallet balance — in exchange for a few days of benefits that may never be paid for.
Plan changes at renewalno prorating — in exchange for the member waiting until the next period.
Never block checkoutorders always go through — in exchange for an occasional missed discount to reconcile.
Honour reservations after the membership endsthe checkout price is always kept — in exchange for a few discounts after the end date.
A running total beside the ledgerO(1) reads — in exchange for updating two rows in one transaction.
Shards by memberone shard per checkout and a small blast radius — in exchange for cross-member queries going through analytics.

Worked Example BB — Scheduled Bulk Notifications — 20 Million Messages on Two Dates

Design a Monthly Savings Summary (20M Notifications, Twice a Month)

accumulate as orders arrive · close windows at the cutoff · prepare a day early · release onto a queue in waves · idempotent at every step
Click to expand

Tell every user how much they saved with promotions — discounts, free delivery, cashback — on the 28th ("so far this month") and on the 3rd ("last month"), by push and by email. Ten million users, two dates, two channels: 20 million messages on each send day. The interesting part isn't sending; it's getting an exact number for every user at a cutoff while orders keep arriving, preparing millions of messages so a crash never duplicates one, and releasing them at a pace the providers accept. Every number below was measured on one small machine with PostgreSQL 16; provider quotas are stated assumptions, and the text says which is which.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Record every saving from an order — promo discount, waived delivery fee, cashback — and remove it when the order is refunded.
  • On the 28th, tell each user what they have saved so far this month; on the 3rd, what they saved last month.
  • Send by push and by email, respecting each user's channel preferences; users who saved nothing get a different message or none.
  • Send at 09:00 in the user's local time.
  • The push, the email and the savings page in the app show the same number.
Non-functional
  • 10 million users, 20 million messages on each send day, inside a morning window.
  • The number sent is exact as of the cutoff, and never changes after it is sent.
  • No user gets the same message twice from our side; a crash or a rerun never duplicates.
  • Nothing heavy runs on the order database or on the send morning.
  • Every provider stays inside its rate quota; a security alert is never delayed by the batch.
  • Every prepared message is accounted for: sent, skipped or failed.

The design question is timing, not throughput: when is a total final, and how far ahead can the work be done?

2
Core Entities
  • Ledger entry — (order_id, kind) · user · window · amount; refunds negative.
  • Window — per market: id, open/closed, closed_at; two per month.
  • Window total — (user, window) · total and breakdown by kind.
  • Run — one per send date: id, windows covered, status, chunks done.
  • Statement — (run, user) · frozen total and breakdown — what every channel shows.
  • Send job — run:user:channel · release_at · status · lease · claim token · provider id.
  • Preferences / contacts — channels on or off, push tokens, email address — from the notification system.

Three keys carry the correctness: (order, kind) for savings, the window for cutoffs, and run:user:channel for messages.

3
API

For a database question, the "API" is the queries the schema must serve well:

GET /me/savings/statements/{run} → the frozen statement the push and email linked to · GET /me/savings?period=… → the in-app page
internal: order-completed events (Kafka) · POST /runs/{run}/approve and /stop for operators · provider webhooks for bounces and dead tokens

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. All November, every completed order with a promo adds ledger entries for its user, into window 11a; refunds add negative entries.
  2. At 00:00 on the 27th, window 11a closes; new events go to 11b. That day, the run for the 28th prepares 10 million statements and about 14 million send jobs in 1,000 chunks.
  3. On the 28th at 09:00 local, senders release the jobs in waves; Nadia gets "So far in November you saved Rp86.000" by push and by email.
  4. At 00:00 on 1 December, window 11b closes; on the 2nd the run for the 3rd prepares statements from 11a + 11b.
  5. On the 3rd, Nadia gets "In November you saved Rp131.500". A refund for a November order on 1 December lands in December's window instead of changing a number she was already sent.
5
High-Level Design

Savings are accumulated as orders complete — a ledger keyed by order and kind, with totals per statement window. An orchestrator closes each window at the cutoff, prepares one frozen statement and one send job per user and channel the day before, and on the day a release scheduler moves the due jobs onto a queue per channel in time-zone waves; senders consume it, skip anything already sent, and stay inside each provider's quota — so nothing is sent twice.

6
Deep Dives

Nine below: (a) cron at send time vs accumulate-and-prepare, (b) capturing every saving exactly once, (c) windows and cutoffs, (d) preparing 20 million messages the day before, (e) release and send, (f) from the table to the sender — releasing due jobs and checking each one, (g) one statement for every channel, (h) sizing at 10 million users, and (i) what fails and what to watch — then the edge cases.

Three time scales: all month, savings accumulate (1–2); the day before, the window closes and every message is prepared (3–5); on the day, jobs are released onto a queue in waves, sent within each provider's quota, and the run is reconciled (6–8). The table below the steps shows how one user's numbers are built.
Illustration — from an order to a push, step by step
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
1an order completes; the order service writes its promo breakdown to the outbox, published to Kafka keyed by userOrder service · Kafkaone event per order, published with the order
2the savings writer adds ledger entries by order and kind, and adds them to the user's total for the window its completion time falls inSavings writer · Savings DBduplicates insert nothing; refunds are negative entries
3at 00:00 local on the 27th and the 1st, the orchestrator closes the window and opens the nextOrchestrator · windowsthe closed totals are final
4the day before sending, prepare workers walk 1,000 user chunks: closed totals + preferences → statements and send jobsPrepare workers · Preferencescheckpoint per chunk; keys run:user:channel
5statements and jobs are stored; a sample is checked and the run is approved — or stoppedStatements + send jobsa full day to fix anything
6on the day, the release scheduler moves due jobs onto a queue per channel at 09:00 local, in batches of 500 keysRelease scheduler · send queuesthe schedule stays in the table; the queue only delivers
7senders long-poll the queue, check each job against today's data (already sent? run approved? still opted in? token alive? in time?), call the providers for the rest, mark every outcome in one update and ackSenders · rate limiter · providersa redelivered batch never sends twice; nobody gets a message they turned off
8bounces and dead tokens update contacts; the run is reconciled: prepared = sent + skipped + failedFeedback + metricsevery message accounted for

Savings, windows and messages each have their own key, so every step can be retried and nothing is counted or sent twice.

Illustration — how one user's savings become "month to date" and "last month"
The day before
  1. The window closes at local midnight; its totals are final.
  2. 1,000 chunks become statements and send jobs, each chunk checkpointed.
  3. A sample is checked; the run is approved.
Send day
  1. Waves open at 09:00 in each time zone.
  2. Senders claim, call, mark — with a lease and a token.
  3. Prepared = sent + skipped + failed, or someone looks.
Key deep dive — cron at send time, a timer per user, or accumulate-and-prepare?
NFRNothing heavy happens on the send morningNFRThe number sent is exact as of the cutoff
Thought process
  1. The tempting design is one cron job at 09:00 on the 3rd: scan the month's orders, total each user's savings, and send. It is simple to describe and wrong in three ways.
  2. It can't be exact. Orders keep arriving while the job runs, so "the month" depends on when each user's row was read. Tested: reading a single running total 3 seconds after the cutoff gave 3,757 of 20,000 users a number that included orders from after the cutoff.
  3. It puts everything on one morning. Aggregating 8 million ledger rows for 1 million users took 5.8 s on one core — about 58 s for 10 million. Affordable once, but on the order database, on the busiest morning, and a crash at 80% starts again from zero.
  4. A durable timer per user (as in the subscription example) solves a different problem: renewals at each member's own time. Here everyone shares two dates, so 10 million workflows buy nothing a calendar-driven batch doesn't.
  5. So: accumulate, close, prepare, release. Savings are totalled continuously as orders complete; at the cutoff the window is closed, so the totals are final; the day before sending, a resumable job prepares one statement and one send job per user and channel; on the day, senders release them in waves. Reading the precomputed totals for 1 million users took 0.06 s.
Illustration — three ways to trigger the work
Key deep dive — capturing every saving, exactly once
NFREvery promo saving is counted onceNFRRefunds remove exactly their part
Thought process
  1. The order service already knows the promo breakdown when an order completes — discount, waived delivery fee, cashback. It writes that breakdown to its outbox in the same transaction as the order, and a relay publishes it to Kafka keyed by user_id. Savings are never recomputed later from prices: the breakdown on the order is the only source.
  2. The savings writer turns each event into ledger entries keyed by (order_id, kind). A duplicate event inserts nothing; a refund is its own entry, keyed by the refund id, with a negative amount, so a partial refund removes only its part. In the same transaction it adds the amount to the user's total for the window its completion time falls in.
  3. So the total is calculated as each order arrives, not at the end. Nadia's GrabMart order on 9 November carries delivery Rp10.000 and cashback Rp2.500; within milliseconds of completing, two ledger rows are written and her window total goes from Rp12.000 to Rp24.500. On the 28th nobody adds anything up — her number is already sitting in one row (table below).
  4. This is the savings-ledger pattern tested in the subscription example — duplicates and out-of-order refunds left 0 members wrong there — with one addition: totals are kept per window, not per lifetime, so each statement can be closed.
  5. Load is modest: about 100 million ledger rows a month is roughly 40 a second on average; ledger partitions are monthly and dropped after a year, since the statements keep the history that matters.
Illustration — one order becomes ledger entries and a window total
Illustration — Nadia's window totals, event by event
Completed atEventLedger rows writtenWindowWindow total after
Nov 3 · 12:10GrabFood orderdiscount +12.00011aRp12.000
Nov 9 · 19:02GrabMart orderdelivery +10.000, cashback +2.50011aRp24.500
Nov 15 · 13:40GrabFood orderdiscount +8.00011aRp32.500
Nov 20 · 10:05partial refund of the Nov 15 orderrefund −4.00011aRp28.500
Nov 26 · 23:50GrabCar ridediscount +15.00011aRp43.500
Nov 27 · 00:10GrabFood orderdelivery +6.00011bRp6.000
Nov 29 · 18:30GrabMart orderdiscount +9.00011bRp15.000
Dec 1 · 00:30refund of the Nov 29 orderrefund −9.00012a−Rp9.000

Each row is one transaction: insert the ledger rows (ignored if already there), then add their sum to the window of the order's completion time.

Illustration — the ledger and the window totals
CREATE TABLE savings_ledger (                 -- one row per order and kind of saving; refunds negative
  order_id bigint, entry text,                       -- 'discount' | 'delivery' | 'cashback' | 'refund:<id>'
  user_id bigint NOT NULL, window_id int NOT NULL,   -- the window OPEN when the event arrived
  amount int NOT NULL, arrived_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, entry))                     -- a duplicate event inserts nothing
  PARTITION BY RANGE (arrived_at);                   -- monthly partitions, dropped after a year

CREATE TABLE window_totals (user_id bigint, window_id int, total bigint NOT NULL,
  discount bigint, delivery bigint, cashback bigint, PRIMARY KEY (user_id, window_id));

-- per event, one transaction:
SELECT id FROM windows WHERE market = $m AND status = 'open' FOR SHARE;    -- no row: it just closed, retry
INSERT INTO savings_ledger … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING 1;
-- only if inserted:
INSERT INTO window_totals … ON CONFLICT (user_id, window_id) DO UPDATE SET total = window_totals.total + excluded.total;
Key deep dive — windows and cutoffs: what each send covers
NFRA sent number never changesNFREvery saving lands in exactly one statement
Thought process
  1. Each market's month has two windows by completion time: 11a from the 1st to the end of the 26th, and 11b from the 27th to the end of the month. The 28th's push says "so far this month" — window 11a. The 3rd's push says "last month" — 11a + 11b.
  2. At each cutoff the orchestrator closes the window — but only once the savings writer has processed every event completed before the cutoff (its watermark: every Kafka partition is past 00:00). It then locks the window row, marks it closed, and the next window is already open for orders after the cutoff. From that moment the closed window's totals are final.
  3. Tested with 8 writers and duplicate events running through the cutoff: the closed window's totals matched its ledger for 0 wrong users, and 0 rows were written into it after it closed; 6,955 later events went into the next window. A first version of the test had writers crash when the window closed under them — the retry is part of the design.
  4. Why completion time and a watermark. Events reach the writer seconds after the order completes, and some partitions lag more than others. Tested with 8 partitions lagging up to 2.74 s: choosing the window by arrival and closing it at 00:00 put 382 of 2,400 orders completed before the cutoff into the next window; choosing it by completion time and closing only after the watermark put 0 there, closing 3.11 s after midnight.
  5. A refund for a November order that arrives on 1 December lands in December's first window and lowers December's figure: statements are like bank statements, booked by when things happen to the account, so a sent number is never edited.
  6. Windows are per market, in its own time zone, so "the end of the month" is local midnight for every user.
Illustration — a lagging stream at the cutoff
Illustration — a month of windows, cutoffs and sends
Illustration — month to date and last month, built from closed windows
Illustration — closing a window
-- the cutoff, 00:00 local on the 27th and on the 1st, one transaction per market:
SELECT id FROM windows WHERE market = 'ID' AND id = '2026-11a' FOR UPDATE;  -- waits for writers in flight
UPDATE windows SET status = 'closed', closed_at = now() WHERE id = '2026-11a';
INSERT INTO windows (id, market, status) VALUES ('2026-11b', 'ID', 'open');
-- from here on, every event lands in 11b; 11a can never change again
Key deep dive — preparing 20 million messages the day before
NFRA crash in preparation never duplicates a messageNFRA bad run can be stopped before anything is sent
Thought process
  1. The orchestrator — Airflow, or a Temporal schedule — starts the run the day before: on the 27th for the 28th, on the 2nd for the 3rd. A run has an id ("2026-12-03"), and everything it creates carries it.
  2. Users are split into 1,000 chunks by a hash of user_id. Each chunk is one transaction: read the closed window totals, join preferences (push on? email on? a token, an address), skip users who saved nothing — or give them a nudge variant — and insert one statement per user and one send job per channel with the key run:user:channel. Then the chunk is recorded as done.
  3. Tested on 1 million users in 100 chunks, crashing 60% of the way: restarting from the beginning without keys created 840,394 duplicate jobs; with job keys and chunk checkpoints, the rerun created 0. Preparation took 20.7 s for 1 million users — about 3 minutes for 10 million on one core, and chunks run in parallel.
  4. Preparing a day early is the safety margin: a failed chunk is retried hours before anyone is waiting, a sample of statements is checked against the ledger, and an obviously wrong run (every total zero, say) is stopped before a single message goes out.
Illustration — chunks, checkpoints and a crash
Key deep dive — release and send: a job table for the record, a queue for delivery
NFREach user gets each message onceNFREvery provider stays inside its quota
Thought process
  1. Two things are needed on send day, and they want different tools. The record — every job, its key and its status, so a run can be stopped, re-driven and reconciled — belongs in a database table. Delivery — handing millions of jobs to many senders quickly — is what a queue does best.
  2. So the release scheduler reads due jobs from the table at 09:00 in each time zone (WIT, then WITA, then WIB, ramping up over minutes) and puts them on a queue per channel as batches of 500 job keys: about 28,000 queue messages for a 14-million-job send day, not 14 million. A plain delayed queue can't do this alone — SQS delays stop at 15 minutes, and Kafka has no per-message delay — which is why the schedule stays in the table.
  3. Senders consume the queue as one consumer group. For each batch they select the jobs not yet sent, call the provider through the per-provider rate limiter (the notification system's priority limiter, so a security alert still goes first), mark them sent in one update, and acknowledge the batch.
  4. Tested with Redis Streams on 680,520 push jobs and 16 senders: 55,784 jobs a second on one core, against 3,296 when senders claimed rows from the table with leases — about 17× faster, because there is no claim to write and the mark is one statement per batch. With 50 senders dying before the provider call and 16 dying after marking but before the ack, 66 batches were redelivered and 8,000 jobs were skipped as already sent: 0 sent twice, 0 never sent. Releasing every job into the queue took 0.9 s.
  5. The table-only version (claims with a lease and a token) also works — 0 sent twice in its test — and is fine at smaller scale. Its first version is a useful warning: a 2-second lease shorter than a batch, and no token, let two senders own the same jobs and deadlock.
  6. Which queue in production. SQS fits best: its visibility timeout is the lease, redelivery is automatic and a dead-letter queue holds batches that keep failing. Kafka works if it is already the backbone, but it has no per-message acknowledgement — a consumer commits its offset after finishing a batch, and a batch that keeps failing is moved to a retry topic so it doesn't block its partition. Redis Streams was only the stand-in for the tests; it keeps data in memory and can lose the last moment of writes on a failover.
  7. One window remains that no design closes: the provider accepts, then the sender dies before marking. The batch is redelivered and those jobs go again — a push collapses on the phone by its collapse id; an email may arrive twice. Small batches keep that window small.
Illustration — the hybrid: table for the record, queue for delivery
Illustration — a sender, in outline
loop:
  batch = queue.receive()                         # 500 job keys, from the release scheduler
  todo  = SELECT job_key FROM send_jobs WHERE job_key = ANY(batch) AND status <> 'sent'
  for job in todo: provider.send(job)             # through the per-provider rate limiter
  UPDATE send_jobs SET status = 'sent' WHERE job_key = ANY(todo) AND status <> 'sent'   -- one statement
  queue.ack(batch)
# no ack (the sender died) -> the queue redelivers the batch after it sits idle;
# jobs already marked sent are filtered out by the SELECT, so they are never sent twice
Illustration — the table-only alternative: claims with a lease and a token

Kept for comparison: correct, but about 17× slower on the same core, because every job is claimed and marked with row locks.

Key deep dive — from the table to the sender: who takes jobs out, and how each one is checked
NFRA job is released once and finished onceNFRNobody gets a message they turned off since preparation
Thought process
  1. Each job is one row in send_jobs, and every change to it is made by one named actor (first diagram). The release scheduler moves it from queued to released and puts it on the queue; a sender finishes it as sent or skipped with a reason; a sweeper rescues jobs left in released too long.
  2. Taking jobs out of the table. Every few seconds the release scheduler runs one query: jobs of this run that are still queued and whose release_at (09:00 in the user's time zone) has passed, 20,000 at a time, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so a second scheduler can run alongside without taking the same rows. It marks them released, then enqueues them as messages of 500 keys.
  3. Mark first, enqueue second — and sweep. If the scheduler dies between the two, its rows sit in released with nothing on the queue. The sweeper re-enqueues anything released more than 5 minutes ago and still unfinished; enqueuing a job twice is harmless because senders check first. Tested: a scheduler crash stranded 20,000 jobs, the sweeper re-enqueued all of them, and they were delivered; two schedulers ran at once without overlap.
  4. How senders get work: they pull, with a long poll. Senders are long-running and scaled up before 09:00. Each one asks the queue for a message and waits up to 20 seconds for one (SQS WaitTimeSeconds, a Kafka consumer's poll(), Redis XREADGROUP BLOCK); the moment the scheduler enqueues a wave, the waiting requests return. Only the scheduler watches the clock. A batch a dead sender never acknowledged comes back to another sender — SQS does this through the visibility timeout. Tested: 162 empty long polls while 12 senders waited for the waves.
  5. Checking each job before it goes. A job was prepared yesterday; today some users have switched push off, some tokens have been reported dead, an operator may have stopped the run, and a delayed job may be too late to be worth sending. So the sender runs one check query per batch against today's data and gives each job a verdict: send, or skip with a reason. Tested on 680,520 push jobs: 646,958 sent, 20,331 skipped as opted out, 13,231 as dead tokens — 0 pushes to anyone who had switched off, 0 sent twice, 0 unfinished. A sender that only checked "not yet sent" would have pushed to 20,331 people who had turned push off.
  6. One statement for every outcome, then the ack. After the provider calls, the sender writes sent and every skipped reason in one update with the keys sorted, then acknowledges the batch. An earlier version wrote them in separate statements and deadlocked with the sweeper. A stopped run gets neither a send nor an ack, so its batches return when the run is approved again.
Illustration — one row, three actors
Illustration — how a sender waits: a long poll
Illustration — checking one batch, job by job
Illustration — the release, the sweeper, the check and the mark
-- the release scheduler, every few seconds (two can run at once: SKIP LOCKED keeps them apart)
WITH due AS (SELECT job_key FROM send_jobs
             WHERE run_id = $run AND status = 'queued' AND release_at <= now()
             ORDER BY job_key LIMIT 20000 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
UPDATE send_jobs SET status = 'released', released_at = now()
FROM due WHERE send_jobs.job_key = due.job_key
RETURNING send_jobs.job_key;                       -- then: enqueue these keys, 500 per message

-- the sweeper, every minute: released long ago but never finished (the scheduler died before enqueuing)
WITH stuck AS (SELECT job_key FROM send_jobs
               WHERE status = 'released' AND released_at < now() - interval '5 minutes'
               ORDER BY job_key LIMIT 20000 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
UPDATE send_jobs SET released_at = now() FROM stuck WHERE send_jobs.job_key = stuck.job_key
RETURNING send_jobs.job_key;                       -- re-enqueue them; senders will skip anything already sent
-- the sender's check: one query per batch, against today's data
SELECT j.job_key,
       CASE WHEN j.status IN ('sent', 'skipped')        THEN 'already_done'
            WHEN r.status <> 'approved'                  THEN 'run_stopped'      -- send nothing, don't ack
            WHEN NOT p.push_on                           THEN 'opted_out'
            WHEN d.user_id IS NOT NULL                   THEN 'dead_token'
            WHEN now() > j.release_at + interval '3 hours' THEN 'too_late'
            ELSE 'send' END AS verdict
FROM send_jobs j JOIN runs r USING (run_id)
LEFT JOIN preferences p USING (user_id) LEFT JOIN dead_tokens d USING (user_id)
WHERE j.job_key = ANY($batch);

-- after the provider calls: every outcome in ONE statement, keys sorted
UPDATE send_jobs SET status      = CASE WHEN v.verdict = 'send' THEN 'sent' ELSE 'skipped' END,
                     skip_reason = NULLIF(v.verdict, 'send')
FROM unnest($keys, $verdicts) AS v(job_key, verdict)
WHERE send_jobs.job_key = v.job_key AND send_jobs.status NOT IN ('sent', 'skipped');
Illustration — a sender, in outline
while True:                                         # a sender: long-running, scaled up before 09:00
    batch = queue.receive(wait_seconds=20)          # long poll: returns the moment a message exists
    if not batch:
        batch = queue.reclaim_idle(older_than=60s)  # a batch a dead sender never acked (SQS does this itself)
        if not batch: continue
    verdicts = check(batch.keys)                    # the query above
    if 'run_stopped' in verdicts: continue          # no send, no ack: it comes back when the run resumes
    for job in verdicts.send: provider.send(job)    # through the per-provider rate limiter
    mark(verdicts)                                  # one sorted UPDATE: sent / skipped + reason
    queue.ack(batch)
Illustration — what the release-and-check test measured
MeasureResult
push jobs · time-zone waves · schedulers · senders680,520 · 3 · 2 at once · 12
scheduler crash between marking and enqueuing20,000 jobs stranded → 20,000 re-enqueued by the sweeper
sent · skipped opted out · skipped dead token646,958 · 20,331 · 13,231
sent twice · left unfinished · pushed to opted-out · pushed to dead tokens0 · 0 · 0 · 0
a sender checking only "not yet sent" would have pushed to20,331 opted-out users and 13,231 dead tokens

PostgreSQL 16 and Redis Streams on one shared core; the time-zone waves are compressed into seconds. 3% of users switched push off and 2% of tokens died after preparation.

Key deep dive — one statement, every channel
NFRThe push, the email and the app always agreeNFRMessages never expose more than they should
Thought process
  1. Each user's statement is one frozen row: the total and its breakdown for the run. The push text, the email and the in-app savings page all read that row — never the live totals — so they can't disagree, even if a refund arrives a minute after the push.
  2. Push is short with a deep link ("You saved Rp131.500 in November"); email is rendered per user from a template per language, with images on a CDN and an unsubscribe link; the in-app page shows the breakdown. Rendering happens at send time from the statement, so a template fix doesn't require re-preparing.
  3. A savings total isn't sensitive the way a salary is, but order details still stay out of lock-screen text. Users who saved nothing get a different message or none — a product choice made once, in the template rules.
Illustration — one frozen row feeds every channel
Key deep dive — is it enough at 10 million users?
NFREvery stage has headroomNFRThe send window holds with the providers' quotas
Thought process
  1. The heavy work is spread out: writes all month, preparation the day before, and only claims, provider calls and bookkeeping on the send day. The sizes below use measured per-core numbers and stated assumptions for provider quotas.
  2. Window totals are about 0.7 GB per window for 10 million users; preparation is minutes, not hours; and about 14 million jobs on a send day (after opt-outs and zero savers) are handed to senders through the queue at 55,784 jobs a second per core (measured) — well inside the window; the job table only takes one bulk update per batch.
  3. Keep the tables small. The send-jobs table gets about 14 million rows per run, so it is partitioned by run and a run's partition is dropped after the audit period; statements stay (they are small and are what users see), and ledger partitions are monthly.
  4. The real limits are the providers: at an assumed 10,000 pushes and 3,000 emails a second, a send day takes about 12 and 40 minutes. Email needs warm sending IPs and a second provider ready; push needs valid tokens, so dead ones are dropped as they are reported.
Illustration — one send day, sized
Key deep dive — what fails, and what to watch
NFRA failure delays a stage; it never duplicates a messageNFREvery prepared message is accounted for
Thought process
  1. Each stage has its own keys and its own retry, so failures stay local (matrix below). The orchestrator won't close a window while the savings writer lags — it waits for the lag to drain, so late-but-in-time events aren't pushed into the next window by an outage.
  2. The orchestrator itself can fail. Temporal keeps each workflow's history and resumes it on another worker; Airflow records task state and retries. Either way every step is idempotent — closing a closed window, preparing a done chunk, releasing a released job and sending a sent message all do nothing — so retrying a step, or rerunning the whole run, is safe.
  3. Reconcile every run: prepared = sent + skipped (opted out, no token) + failed. Anything else is a ticket. Watch writer lag, chunk failures, claim throughput, provider errors and bounce rates, and open and unsubscribe rates — a jump in unsubscribes after a send is a product signal, not an outage.
Illustration — what still works when one part fails
Illustration — what to watch
MeasureAlert when
savings-writer lag at the cutoffabove a few minutes: hold the close
chunks failed / retriedany failure not retried within an hour
jobs released vs sent per minutesent falls behind for 10+ minutes
provider errors and throttlingerror rate above a few percent
prepared − sent − skipped − failednot zero after the window
bounces and unsubscribes per runabove the usual band
Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • Refund after the cutoff — lands in the next window as an adjustment; a sent number never changes.
  • Order completed at 23:59:59 — its completion time decides; the window closes only after the writer is past the cutoff, so a lagging stream can't push it into the next window.
  • User saved nothing — a nudge variant or no message — decided by template rules.
  • Opted out of push, or no token — email only; counted as skipped for push.
  • Turned push off after preparation — the sender's check reads today's preferences: skipped as opted out.
  • The release scheduler dies after marking jobs released — the sweeper re-enqueues them after 5 minutes; senders skip anything already done.
  • Email bounces — the contact is marked invalid; the next run skips it.
  • User changes time zone — the job carries the time zone at preparation; good enough for a summary.
  • A promo funded by the merchant — still a saving for the user; the ledger can tag who funded it for finance.
  • The run is started twice — same run id, same keys: nothing new is created or sent.
  • A sender dies mid-batch — no ack: the queue redelivers the batch; jobs already marked sent are skipped.
  • The provider accepted, then the worker died — the job is retried: push collapses on the phone; email may repeat once.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Exact as of the cutoffclosed windows: 0 users wrong (a running total read 3 s later: 3,757).
Nothing heavy on the send morningtotals are precomputed: 0.06 s to read for 1M users vs 5.8 s to aggregate.
No duplicate preparationjob keys + checkpoints: 0 duplicates after a crash (without: 840,394).
No duplicate sends from our sidequeue + skip-if-sent: 0 sent twice, 0 never sent, 66 batches redelivered.
The right window despite stream lagcompletion time + a watermark close: 0 misplaced (by arrival: 382 of 2,400).
Nobody gets what they turned offchecked against today's data at send time: 0 pushes to the 20,331 users who switched off after preparation.
Fast enough on send day55,784 jobs a second per core through the queue (table claims: 3,296).
Inside provider quotasa per-provider rate limiter and time-zone waves.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Windows by arrival timeexact, final statements — in exchange for late refunds showing up in the next month.
Prepare a day earlya day to retry and inspect — in exchange for numbers frozen a day before the send.
A calendar batch, not per-user timerssimple and cheap for shared dates — in exchange for a big job twice a month that must be resumable.
A job table for the record, a queue for deliveryfast delivery and an exact record you can stop, re-drive and reconcile — in exchange for two systems to keep in step (the skip-if-sent check makes that safe).
Render at send timetemplate fixes need no re-preparation — in exchange for rendering work on the send day.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Eventsorder-completed events from an outbox, on Kafka, keyed by user
Savings DBPostgreSQL, sharded by user: ledger, windows, window totals, statements, send jobs
OrchestrationAirflow or a Temporal schedule: close, prepare (chunked, checkpointed), release
Send queueSQS, Kafka or Redis Streams: one queue per channel, batches of job keys, redelivery when not acked
Sendingpush via APNs/FCM, email via a primary and a warm secondary provider, through the notification system
Observabilityper-run reconciliation, writer lag, chunk status, provider errors, bounces and unsubscribes
Worked Example BC — Payroll — A Million Employees, Hundreds of Companies, Their Own Paydays

Design a Payroll Run: From Inputs to a Payslip

inputs collected all month · a run per pay group · lock, calculate, review, confirm · render before payday · a link, not an attachment
Click to expand

Calculate and pay a million employees across hundreds of companies and several countries, then give each a payslip — by email and in the app — on their company's payday. The question isn't how to run one big calculation; it's how to collect every input once, freeze the right ones at each company's own cutoff, let a person review before money moves, and have every payslip ready before anyone can see one. This is the upstream half of the payslip distribution example: AL starts where this one confirms. Numbers were measured on one small machine with PostgreSQL 16, reportlab and headless Chromium; tax and contribution rates are illustrative.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Collect everything that changes pay during the period: salary changes, overtime, unpaid leave, allowances, bonuses, reimbursements, loan deductions.
  • Run payroll per pay group on its own calendar: cutoff, payday, time zone, currency and rules.
  • Calculate gross to net for every employee, let payroll admins review and fix, then confirm.
  • Pay each employee through a bank file, and produce a payslip PDF for each.
  • On payday, notify employees by email and push; they open the payslip in the app.
Non-functional
  • A million employees across hundreds of companies and several countries.
  • Every input counts once, in exactly one period; locked periods never change.
  • The same inputs and rules always give the same pay, and every result can be explained years later.
  • No one is paid twice, and nobody sees another person's payslip.
  • Every payslip exists and is checked before payday; payday is never missed because of another company.

Payroll is a calendar problem before it is a computing problem: the hard parts are dates, frozen inputs and approvals.

2
Core Entities
  • Pay group — a set of employees paid together: company, calendar (cutoff, payday), time zone, currency, rules.
  • Input — one change to pay, keyed by its source id: employee, period, kind, quantity, effective date.
  • Period — one per pay group per cycle: open or locked.
  • Rules version — tax table, contribution rates and caps, with an effective date; never edited.
  • Payroll run — one per pay group per period: state, rules version, approvers.
  • Result — (run, employee): gross, deductions, tax, net — a draft until confirm.
  • Snapshot — the confirmed figures, inputs and rules version for each employee.
  • Payment — (run, employee) in the bank file.
  • Payslip — (run, employee, version): stored PDF, hash, template version.

Three keys carry the correctness: the input's source id, (run, employee) for results and payments, and (run, employee, version) for documents.

3
API

For a database question, the "API" is the queries the schema must serve well:

POST /pay-groups/{g}/runs (by the schedule) · GET /runs/{id}/checks · POST /runs/{id}/recalculate {employees} · POST /runs/{id}/confirm
GET /me/payslips · GET /payslips/{id}/download → a one-minute link after the ownership check
internal: input events (Kafka) · bank file submission and rejections

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. During November, Budi's salary, 6 hours of overtime, one unpaid day, an allowance and a taxi claim each arrive as an input and land in PT Example's open November period.
  2. At 23:59 on 20 November the period locks. Overtime approved on the 21st, and a raise back-dated to the 1st, land in December's run.
  3. The run calculates gross to net for every employee from the frozen inputs and rules 2026.1; Budi's net is Rp14.671.014.
  4. The payroll admin reviews the flagged employees, fixes two inputs (only they recalculate) and confirms.
  5. The bank file and every payslip PDF are produced from the confirmed snapshot; PDFs are stored privately.
  6. At 09:00 on the 25th the run is published; Budi gets an email and a push, opens the app, and sees his payslip.
5
High-Level Design

Inputs are collected all month into a ledger, each once, into the period open for the employee's pay group. Each pay group's calendar drives its own payroll run: lock the period, calculate gross to net from frozen inputs and a pinned rules version, review and confirm a snapshot, then pay and render every payslip from that snapshot before payday. At 09:00 local on payday the run is published, and email, push and the app all lead to the same stored document behind an ownership check.

6
Deep Dives

Nine below: (a) one cron vs a run per pay group, (b) collecting inputs all month, (c) the lock and the run's states, (d) calculating gross to net, (e) review and approval, (f) paying and rendering before payday, (g) payday delivery, (h) sizing for a million, and (i) what fails and what to watch — then the edge cases.

Four time scales: all month, inputs accumulate (1–2); at each pay group's cutoff the run locks, calculates and is reviewed and confirmed (3–5); between confirm and payday, the bank file and every payslip are produced from the frozen snapshot (6); on payday the run is published and employees reach their payslip through a link (7–8).
Illustration — from an input to a payslip, step by step
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
1inputs arrive all month from HR, clock-in, leave, expenses, bonuses and loans, published keyed by employeesources · Kafkaone event per change, as it happens
2the input writer stores each input once, in the period open for the employee's pay groupInput writer · Payroll DBa re-sent input is ignored
3at the pay group's cutoff, the orchestrator locks the period; later inputs go to the next runOrchestrator (a schedule per pay group)the run's inputs are frozen
4calculators compute gross to net per employee from the frozen inputs and a pinned rules version, as draftsCalculatorsre-runnable; same inputs, same pay
5HR reviews the checks, fixes inputs (only those employees recalculate), approves; confirm freezes a snapshotHR reviewwhat is paid is what was approved
6the bank file and the payslip PDFs are produced from the snapshot; PDFs are stored privately with their hashPayment · render workers · object storagedone days before payday
7at 09:00 local on payday the run is published; email and push carry a link to the appPublisher · notification systemno salary in an email
8the employee opens the app; the document API checks ownership and returns a one-minute link to the stored PDFDocument API · object storagenobody else's payslip, ever

Inputs, results and documents each have their own key, so every step can be retried without double-counting or double-paying.

Cutoff to confirm
  1. The period locks; inputs are frozen.
  2. Gross to net runs in chunks, as drafts.
  3. Flags are reviewed, a few inputs fixed, only they recalculate, and the run is confirmed.
Confirm to payday
  1. One bank file, keyed per employee.
  2. Every payslip rendered and stored with its hash.
  3. At 09:00 the run is published; a link, not an attachment.
Key deep dive — one cron for everyone, or a run per pay group?
NFREvery company is paid on its own datesNFROne company's problem never delays another's payday
Thought process
  1. The first idea is a cron job that, a few days before month end, calculates every employee's salary. It feels wrong because payroll isn't one job: each company — and each pay group inside it, such as monthly staff, a weekly crew, or staff in another country — has its own cutoff, payday, time zone, currency, tax rules and approvers.
  2. A single cron gets those dates wrong for most groups, calculates while inputs are still arriving, has no place for a human to review, and turns one company's bad data into everyone's delay.
  3. So each pay group has a pay calendar, and the orchestrator (a Temporal schedule or an Airflow DAG per group) starts one payroll run per period: lock, calculate, review, confirm, pay, render, publish. Each run is its own workflow with checkpoints; a thousand companies means a thousand small runs on their own dates, not one giant job.
  4. The scheduler still exists — but it only triggers steps for one pay group at a time. The data work is spread across the month (inputs) and across companies (runs).
Illustration — pay calendars, and why each gets its own run
Key deep dive — collecting inputs all month, once each
NFREvery input counts once, in exactly one periodNFRA late or back-dated change never edits a locked period
Thought process
  1. Salary isn't calculated from nothing on the cutoff day. Everything that changes pay arrives during the month as events: contract and salary changes from HR, overtime and attendance from clock-in (clock-in example), unpaid leave, expense reimbursements, bonuses, loan deductions.
  2. Each one is written once into an input ledger, keyed by the source's own id (the timesheet line, the expense claim), so a re-sent input is ignored. It lands in the period that is open for the employee's pay group when it arrives — the same mechanism as the statement windows in the savings summary example, tested there: a locked period can never change.
  3. Late inputs — overtime worked on the 20th but approved on the 21st — flow into the next run. Back-dated changes — a raise approved on the 23rd but effective from the 1st — are not applied to the locked month in place: the next run calculates the difference for the months already paid and pays it as a retro adjustment line.
  4. Budi's November below shows all three: inputs before the lock, an overtime entry after it, and a back-dated raise.
Illustration — Budi's inputs, the lock, a late input and a retro change
Illustration — the input ledger
CREATE TABLE input_ledger (
  input_key  text PRIMARY KEY,          -- from the source: 'timesheet:88123:line4', 'claim:5521'
  employee_id bigint NOT NULL, pay_group text NOT NULL,
  period     text NOT NULL,             -- the period OPEN for that pay group when it arrived
  kind       text NOT NULL,             -- base_change | overtime_hours | unpaid_days | allowance | bonus | reimbursement | loan
  qty        numeric NOT NULL, effective_date date, source text);

-- writer, per input (one transaction): the pay group's open period, then the row
SELECT period FROM pay_periods WHERE pay_group = $g AND status = 'open' FOR SHARE;  -- none: it just locked, retry
INSERT INTO input_ledger … ON CONFLICT (input_key) DO NOTHING;                        -- a re-sent input is ignored
Illustration — a back-dated raise, handled next month
-- December's run, for a raise effective 1 Nov that arrived after November was locked:
retro = calculate(November inputs, NEW contract, rules 2026.1)      -- a what-if, never published
      − November's confirmed result
-- paid as one "retro adjustment" line in December; November's payslip is never edited
Key deep dive — the lock, and the run as a state machine
NFRA run moves forward one checked step at a timeNFRConfirmed figures never change
Thought process
  1. At the pay group's cutoff, the orchestrator waits until each input feed reports it has delivered everything up to the cutoff (a feed that is late produces a late-input report rather than a silent gap), then locks the period in one transaction: writers waiting on it either finish first or land in the next period. From then on the run's inputs are frozen.
  2. The run then moves through states — open, locked, calculated, in review, confirmed, paid, published — each a workflow step with a checkpoint. A crash resumes at the step it was in.
  3. Before confirmed, anything can be recalculated as often as needed. After it, figures are frozen into a snapshot; a mistake found later becomes an off-cycle correction run that produces a new document version, as in the payslip distribution example.
Illustration — one payroll run, step by step
Key deep dive — calculating gross to net for a million employees
NFRThe same inputs always give the same payNFRA fix recalculates only the people it touches
Thought process
  1. Gross to net is a pure function: frozen inputs plus a pinned rules version (tax table, contribution rates and caps, effective dates) give earnings, deductions, tax and net. Budi's November is worked through below with illustrative rates.
  2. It is not a throughput problem. Measured on a million employees across 400 companies (the largest 200,000) with 2,043,267 inputs: one set-based statement took 22.9 s; one employee at a time from the application took 0.48 ms each — about 8 minutes on a local connection, more across a network. Either finishes long before payday.
  3. What matters is that it reads only frozen inputs and a pinned rules version, so it can be re-run safely during review and always gives the same answer: two runs on the same inputs were identical. And a fix touches only the employees it changes: correcting 1% of employees' inputs recalculated them in 0.69 s, against 23.8 s for everyone — with the same result as a full recalculation.
  4. How the run executes: the schedule triggers, workers do the chunks. The schedule only creates the run and splits it into chunks of employees in a run_chunks table. Workers claim a chunk with a lease and a token (SKIP LOCKED), calculate it in one statement that upserts by (run, employee), and mark it done in the same transaction; progress is simply done / total. A worker that dies mid-chunk leaves its lease to expire and another worker re-runs the chunk, overwriting the half it wrote with the same values. Tested: 1,000,000 employees in 1,000 chunks with 6 workers and 40 crashes after writing half a chunk — 39 chunks retried, 1,000,000 rows, 0 duplicates, identical to a clean run, in 37.3 s. No checkpoint in a separate store is needed.
  5. Results are written as drafts keyed by (run, employee), so a crashed chunk is simply run again. A new rules version is first run in shadow against last month's frozen inputs and compared with what was paid, so surprises show up before it is effective.
