Rules change by adding a new version with an effective date, never by editing the old one, so a run from March can be recalculated in December with March's rules.
Illustration — Budi's gross to net, and how it runs for a million
Illustration — the schedule starts the run; workers do the chunks
Illustration — the calculation as one statement
-- one set-based statement per chunk (or per run): frozen inputs + pinned rules → draft results
INSERT INTO results (run_id, employee_id, rules_version, gross, social, tax, net)
WITH agg AS (SELECT employee_id, sum(qty) FILTER (WHERE kind = 'overtime_hours') AS ot, …
             FROM input_ledger WHERE period = $period AND pay_group = $g GROUP BY employee_id),
     g   AS (SELECT e.employee_id, base + allowance + bonus + ot * base/173 * 1.5 - unpaid * base/21 AS gross, …
             FROM employees e LEFT JOIN agg USING (employee_id))
SELECT $run, employee_id, '2026.1', gross, social(gross), tax(gross, '2026.1'), gross - social - tax + reimbursement - loans
FROM g
ON CONFLICT (run_id, employee_id) DO UPDATE SET …;    -- re-runnable while the run is a draft

Rates and tax brackets in the test and the example are illustrative, not legal tables.

Key deep dive — review and approval before anyone is paid
NFROdd results are seen by a person before paydayNFRWhat is paid is exactly what was approved
Thought process
  1. Before confirming, the run is checked automatically: net pay that moved more than 20% from last month, zero or negative net pay, joiners and leavers, missing or changed bank accounts, and the total against last month. Over 1,000,000 employees the checks took 1.0 s and flagged 4,739 people for a look.
  2. The payroll admin reviews the flags and fixes inputs; only those employees recalculate. Large runs can require a second approver. Confirm is one conditional state change on the run row — allowed only when the run is in review, every chunk is done and no recalculation is pending — and a recalculation request is refused once the run is confirmed, so the two can never interleave. Confirm then copies each employee's figures, inputs and rules version into a frozen snapshot — and everything after it (payment, payslips) reads only that snapshot.
Illustration — checks, review and the confirm step
Key deep dive — paying, and rendering every payslip before payday
NFREach person is paid onceNFREvery payslip exists before anyone can see one
Thought process
  1. Paying exactly once. Each payment instruction carries the key run:employee as its idempotency key (or end-to-end id) at the bank, and the bank file has a unique id, so a resubmitted file or a retried API call can't pay twice. The bank's statement is matched back to the instructions before payday — paid, rejected, missing — and only the rejected ones are retried.
  2. Two jobs read the same snapshot. The bank file holds one payment per employee keyed by run and employee, so a resubmission can't pay twice; rejected accounts are retried on their own. Rendering produces one PDF per employee, stored privately under company/run/employee/version with its hash recorded.
  3. Rendering is cheaper than it looks. Measured: a simple PDF library took 1.0 ms a payslip; HTML to PDF in a headless browser took 10.2 ms and about 20.0 KB — roughly 2.8 CPU-hours and 19 GB for a million. Doing it in the days between confirm and payday means a failure is retried long before 09:00.
  4. Rendering the same figures twice gave different bytes — PDFs embed timestamps and ids — so the stored file and its hash are the record of what was issued. With the library's invariant mode the bytes were identical, which lets a document be verified by re-rendering it later.
  5. Many companies share a payday, so render jobs go into a lane per company taken in turns (the notification system's fairness), and the largest company can't delay a small one.
Illustration — the snapshot, the bank file and the rendered payslips
Key deep dive — payday: email, push and the app show one document
NFRNobody sees a payslip that isn't theirsNFRThe email, the push and the app always agree
Thought process
  1. At 09:00 local on payday the run is published — a status change, not a mass update (the payslip distribution example). The notification system sends an email and a push: "Your November payslip is ready", with a link into the app.
  2. Sending the payday emails uses the same mechanism as the savings summary example: the publisher releases the run's notification jobs onto a queue in batches; senders long-poll, check each job against today's data (already sent? still entitled? address valid?), send within the provider's quota, mark every outcome in one statement and acknowledge — so a crash or a redelivered batch never sends twice.
  3. The PDF is not attached by default. Emails are forwarded, synced and kept for years — a poor home for a salary — while a link works only after login and the ownership check. A company that must send attachments can opt into password-protected PDFs, with the password never in the same email.
  4. In the app, the document API checks that the document belongs to the employee and returns a link valid for about a minute to the stored file. Email, push and app all point at that one file — one version, one hash; a correction appears as a new version with the old one marked superseded.
Illustration — two ways in, one document
Key deep dive — is it enough for a million employees?
NFREvery step has headroomNFRThe biggest company can't slow the others
Thought process
  1. None of the steps is a throughput problem: inputs are about one a second on average, a 200,000-person run calculates in seconds, checks take about a second, and rendering a million payslips is a few CPU-hours spread over days.
  2. The scale problems are shared dates and uneven sizes. Many companies lock on the 20th and pay on the 25th, so runs are independent workflows and rendering is fair per company; the Payroll DB is sharded by company; and a company that is a fifth of all employees can get its own cell (isolating huge customers).
Illustration — sizing, with the measured numbers
Key deep dive — what fails, and what to watch
NFRA failure delays one step for one companyNFREvery employee in a run is accounted for
Thought process
  1. The orchestrator itself can fail. A durable workflow engine resumes the run on another worker from its last completed step, and every step is idempotent — locking a locked period, re-running a chunk, regenerating a rendered payslip, resubmitting a payment with the same key — so retrying any step, or the whole run, is safe.
  2. Each run is its own workflow, so a failure delays one step for one company (matrix below). The hard limit is the payday itself: the orchestrator alerts when a run is behind its calendar — not confirmed three days before payday, say — so people act while there is time.
  3. Reconcile every run: employees in the pay group = calculated = confirmed = paid + held = payslips published. Watch input lag at the cutoff, flagged-variance counts, approval waiting time, bank rejections, and render failures per company.
Illustration — what still works when one part fails
Illustration — what to watch
MeasureAlert when
inputs still arriving after the cutoffa large late-input batch for one pay group
run behind its calendarnot confirmed N days before payday
flagged employees per runfar above the usual band
bank rejectionsany — each one is a person not paid
payslips rendered vs employeesnot equal by the day before payday
employees in group vs paid vs publishednot reconciled after payday
Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • Overtime approved after the cutoff — lands in the next period; the next run pays it.
  • A raise back-dated into a paid month — the next run pays the difference as a retro line; the old payslip is untouched.
  • An input sent twice — the source id is the key: ignored.
  • Employee joins mid-month — pro-rated by the rules; flagged as a joiner in review.
  • Employee leaves — final pay in their last run; they can still see their payslips afterwards (AL).
  • Missing bank account — payment held for that person only; flagged before confirm.
  • A calculator dies mid-chunk — its lease expires; another worker re-runs the chunk; the upsert overwrites the half it wrote.
  • The bank file is submitted twice — same file id and per-payment idempotency keys: rejected as a duplicate, nobody is paid twice.
  • A mistake found after payday — an off-cycle correction run and a new payslip version.
  • Tax rules change mid-year — a new rules version with an effective date; old runs keep theirs.
  • Employee in two companies — two memberships, two pay groups, two payslips (AR).
  • Payday falls on a holiday — the pay calendar moves it; the run follows the calendar.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Inputs counted once, in one periodsource-id keys and the open-period rule (tested in BB: a closed window never changed).
Same inputs, same paytwo runs on frozen inputs were identical.
A fix touches only its people1% recalculated in 0.69 s, same result as everyone (23.8 s).
Reviewed before money movesautomatic checks over 1M employees in 1.0 s, then a person confirms.
Payslips ready before paydayrendering ≈ 2.8 CPU-hours for 1M, done in the days before.
Nobody else's payslipownership check and one-minute links (AL).
Safe to retry any chunk40 crashes mid-chunk: 1,000,000 rows, 0 duplicates, identical to a clean run.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
A run per pay groupcorrect dates and isolation — in exchange for many small workflows to operate instead of one job.
Lock at the cutoffa stable, reviewable run — in exchange for late inputs waiting a month.
Retro adjustments next runlocked months never change — in exchange for a correction appearing a month later.
Render aheadpayday is just a publish — in exchange for storing a PDF per person per month.
A link instead of an attachmentsalaries stay out of mailboxes — in exchange for a login to read a payslip.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Inputsevents from HR, clock-in, leave and expenses on Kafka; an input ledger in PostgreSQL, sharded by company
OrchestrationTemporal schedules or Airflow DAGs, one per pay group; one workflow per run
Calculationset-based SQL or a rules engine with versioned rule sets
DocumentsHTML → PDF (headless browser) or a PDF library; private object storage with hashes (AL)
Deliveryemail and push through the notification system; signed links from the document API
Worked Example AQ — The Database Question

Database Schema — HR Workflow: Organizations, Employees and Approvals

tables and constraints that can't be bypassed · hierarchies · indexes chosen from queries · approving safely under concurrency · snapshots and history
Click to expand

A common interview format includes one database question: design the schema for a small but real domain, choose its indexes, and show how a write stays correct when two people act at once. Here the domain is the core of any HR and workflow product — organizations, their departments and employees, and approval requests (expenses, leave) that pass through one or more approvers. The answer is judged less on the tables themselves than on the reasons: which rules the database enforces, which queries each index serves, and what happens when a request is withdrawn at the same moment it's approved.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Organizations have nested departments; employees belong to a department and report to a manager.
  • Employees submit approval requests — expenses, leave — that go through one or more approval steps.
  • Approvers see what's waiting for them; requesters see their own requests, newest first; admins see everything pending.
  • A request can be withdrawn while pending; every action is recorded.
Non-functional
  • The database itself prevents invalid data — including references across organizations.
  • The common screens stay fast with millions of requests.
  • Concurrent actions — two approvers, or an approval and a withdrawal — leave a consistent result.
  • History is complete and can't be rewritten.

State these out loud before drawing a table. In a database question, the interviewer is listening for which rules you put in the schema and which you leave to application code — and why.

2
Core Entities
  • organizations — the tenant; everything else belongs to exactly one.
  • departments — a tree, through parent_id.
  • employees — a person's membership in one organization, with a department and a manager (another employee).
  • approval_requests — what was asked, by whom, its status, and a version for optimistic checks.
  • approval_steps — who must decide, in what order, and what they decided.
  • approval_events — an append-only history of every action.
3
API

For a database question, the "API" is the set of queries the schema must serve well:
Q1 requests waiting for my approval
Q2 my requests, newest first, page by page
Q3 all pending requests in my organization (admins)
Q4 everyone in a department, including its sub-departments
W1 approve or reject a step · W2 withdraw a request

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. Ravi submits a $124.00 expense. A request row is inserted with status pending, and its approval steps — his manager, then finance — are written in the same transaction.
  2. His manager Nadia sees it through Q1, served by a small partial index of pending steps.
  3. Nadia approves: the request row is locked, her step is marked approved, the request moves to its next step, and an event is appended — all in one transaction.
  4. At the same moment Ravi clicks withdraw. His transaction waits for Nadia's lock, then sees the request has moved on, and applies only if the rules still allow it.
5
High-Level Design

A relational schema in PostgreSQL. Every table owned by an organization carries org_id, and references between them are composite foreign keys that include it, so no row can point into another organization. Indexes are chosen one by one from the queries above. Every write to a request locks the request row, so concurrent actions on it happen one at a time. History is appended, never updated.

6
Deep Dives

Five below: (a) tables and constraints, (b) hierarchies, (c) indexes from queries, (d) approving safely under concurrency, and (e) snapshots and history — then the edge cases.

Six tables. Organizations own departments and employees; departments and employees each point to themselves for the tree and the reporting line. A request has many steps and many events; steps point to the employees who must decide. PK is a primary key, FK a foreign key, UQ a unique constraint, IX a column that leads an important index.
A two-step approval
  1. Ravi's expense needs his manager, then finance.
  2. Nadia approves step 1; the request moves to step 2.
  3. Finance approves step 2; the request becomes approved.
  4. Four events record who did what, and when.
Approve and withdraw at the same instant
  1. Nadia's approval locks the request row first.
  2. Ravi's withdrawal waits for that lock.
  3. When it gets the lock, it reads the current status and decides against that — not against the status it saw before.
  4. One of them wins cleanly; the other gets a clear "no longer possible" message.
Key deep dive — tables and constraints that can't be bypassed
NFRThe database prevents invalid data
Thought process
  1. Every rule the database enforces is a rule no future code path can forget. Put a rule in the schema whenever it can be expressed there.
  2. Status values get a CHECK. Money is an integer in the smallest currency unit plus a currency code — never a float, as the migration example shows.
  3. Uniqueness is scoped by organization: two companies can both have employee number 1042.
  4. The subtle one: a plain foreign key from employees to departments lets an Org A employee point at an Org B department. Making the foreign key include org_id rules that out in the database itself — the tenant isolation example, enforced in the schema.
Illustration — the schema, with the rules it enforces
CREATE TABLE departments (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  org_id     uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES organizations(id),
  parent_id  uuid,
  name       text NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (org_id, id),                                        -- target for composite FKs
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, parent_id) REFERENCES departments (org_id, id)
);

CREATE TABLE employees (
  id               uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  org_id           uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES organizations(id),
  user_id          uuid NOT NULL,
  department_id    uuid,
  manager_id       uuid,
  employee_number  text NOT NULL,
  status           text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pre_hire','active','departed')),
  UNIQUE (org_id, employee_number),                           -- unique within a company
  UNIQUE (org_id, user_id),
  UNIQUE (org_id, id),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, department_id) REFERENCES departments (org_id, id),   -- same company
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, manager_id)    REFERENCES employees   (org_id, id)    -- same company
);

CREATE TABLE approval_requests (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  org_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  requester_id  uuid NOT NULL,
  type          text NOT NULL CHECK (type IN ('expense','leave')),
  status        text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending','approved','rejected','withdrawn')),
  current_step  int  NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  amount_minor  bigint CHECK (amount_minor >= 0),               -- $124.00 → 12400
  currency      char(3),
  version       int  NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (org_id, id),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, requester_id) REFERENCES employees (org_id, id)
);

CREATE TABLE approval_steps (
  org_id       uuid NOT NULL,
  request_id   uuid NOT NULL,
  step_no      int  NOT NULL,
  approver_id  uuid NOT NULL,
  decision     text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending' CHECK (decision IN ('pending','approved','rejected')),
  decided_at   timestamptz,
  PRIMARY KEY (request_id, step_no, approver_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, request_id)  REFERENCES approval_requests (org_id, id),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, approver_id) REFERENCES employees (org_id, id)
);

A composite foreign key needs a unique constraint on the columns it references, which is why each referenced table also declares UNIQUE (org_id, id). approval_events follows the same pattern and is shown in deep dive (e).

Key deep dive — hierarchies: departments and reporting lines
FRNested departmentsFREveryone in a department and below
Thought process
  1. Departments nest — Company, Sales, Sales Lisbon — and managers form a reporting line. Both are trees stored in one table that points to itself.
  2. The simplest model is a parent_id column. Asking "everyone in Sales, including sub-departments" then needs a recursive query that walks down the tree.
  3. Company trees are shallow — a handful of levels — so the recursive query is cheap, and moving a department is a single-row update.
  4. The rule the database can't express on its own: no department may end up inside itself. Before moving one, check that its new parent isn't one of its own descendants, inside the same transaction as the move.
Illustration — walking a tree, and refusing a cycle
-- Q4: everyone in Sales, including its sub-departments
WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
    SELECT id FROM departments WHERE org_id = $1 AND id = $2
  UNION ALL
    SELECT d.id FROM departments d JOIN sub ON d.parent_id = sub.id
    WHERE d.org_id = $1
)
SELECT e.* FROM employees e JOIN sub ON e.department_id = sub.id WHERE e.org_id = $1;

-- before moving department $1 under $2: would it end up inside itself?
WITH RECURSIVE below AS (
    SELECT id FROM departments WHERE id = $1
  UNION ALL
    SELECT d.id FROM departments d JOIN below b ON d.parent_id = b.id
)
SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM below WHERE id = $2) AS creates_cycle;
ModelSubtree queryMoving a branchFits
parent_id + recursive queryrecursive walkupdate one rowshallow trees that change — companies
materialized path (e.g. ltree)one indexed prefix matchrewrite every descendant's pathdeep trees, read far more than moved
closure tableone indexed lookuprewrite many ancestor rowsheavy "all ancestors" queries
Key deep dive — indexes, chosen from the queries
NFRCommon screens fast at millions of rows
Thought process
  1. Don't add indexes by guessing. Take each query from the list, and give it the index that lets the database go straight to its rows in the order it wants them.
  2. Column order matters: columns compared with = first, then the column you sort or range over. org_id is always among the first, because every query filters on it.
  3. A partial index covers only the rows a query cares about. Pending steps are a small fraction of all steps, so an index of just the pending ones stays small and fast however large history grows.
  4. For "my requests, newest first", page with a keyset — "after the last row I saw" — rather than OFFSET, which re-reads every skipped row. See the news feed example.
Illustration — each query, and the index that serves it
-- Q1  waiting for my approval: only pending steps are indexed
CREATE INDEX ON approval_steps (org_id, approver_id) WHERE decision = 'pending';

-- Q2  my requests, newest first, one page at a time
CREATE INDEX ON approval_requests (org_id, requester_id, created_at DESC, id DESC);

-- Q3  all pending requests in my organization
CREATE INDEX ON approval_requests (org_id, created_at DESC) WHERE status = 'pending';

-- Q4  the tree and reporting lines
CREATE INDEX ON departments (org_id, parent_id);
CREATE INDEX ON employees   (org_id, department_id);
CREATE INDEX ON employees   (org_id, manager_id);

-- Q2's next page: continue after the last row shown, never OFFSET
SELECT id, status, created_at FROM approval_requests
WHERE org_id = $1 AND requester_id = $2
  AND (created_at, id) < ($3, $4)          -- the last row of the previous page
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
QueryPlan PostgreSQL chose, with 200,000 requests
Q1index scan on the pending-steps partial index
Q2index scan — the (created_at, id) < (…) comparison is used as an index condition
Q3index scan on the pending-requests partial index
Q4sequential scan — correctly: the subtree held two-thirds of all employees, and reading most of a table is cheaper without an index

These plans come from running this schema on PostgreSQL 16 with 2,000 employees and 200,000 requests. Q4 is the lesson worth saying out loud: an index helps when a query needs a small part of a table; for most of a small table, a scan is the right answer.

Key deep dive — approving safely under concurrency
NFRConcurrent actions stay consistent
Thought process
  1. Three races to design for: the requester withdraws while the approver approves; two approvers in a parallel step act at once; one approver double-clicks.
  2. Every write to a request starts by locking that request's row with SELECT … FOR UPDATE. Actions on the same request then happen one after another, and each one sees the result of the one before — the "lock the parent" fix from the data correctness toolkit.
  3. Each change is also conditional on the state it expects: a step changes only if it's still pending, a request is withdrawn only if it's still pending. Zero rows changed means someone else got there first — and a double-click simply changes nothing.
  4. Rules that span rows are checked inside the same transaction, because no single-row constraint can express them: an approver may not approve their own request, and a step may only be approved when it is the request's current step — finance can't approve before the manager has.
Illustration — the approval as one function, and a race run for real
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION approve_step(p_org uuid, p_request uuid, p_step int, p_approver uuid)
RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
  v_status text;  v_requester uuid;  v_current int;
BEGIN
  SELECT status, requester_id, current_step INTO v_status, v_requester, v_current
    FROM approval_requests
   WHERE id = p_request AND org_id = p_org
     FOR UPDATE;                                  -- concurrent actions on this request wait here
  IF v_status IS DISTINCT FROM 'pending' THEN RETURN 'no longer pending'; END IF;
  IF v_requester = p_approver THEN RETURN 'cannot approve your own request'; END IF;
  IF p_step <> v_current THEN RETURN 'not this step''s turn yet'; END IF;

  UPDATE approval_steps SET decision = 'approved', decided_at = now()
   WHERE request_id = p_request AND step_no = p_step AND approver_id = p_approver
     AND decision = 'pending';
  IF NOT FOUND THEN RETURN 'already decided'; END IF;             -- e.g. a double-click

  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM approval_steps                     -- is this step now complete?
                  WHERE request_id = p_request AND step_no = p_step AND decision <> 'approved') THEN
    IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM approval_steps WHERE request_id = p_request AND step_no > p_step) THEN
      UPDATE approval_requests SET current_step = p_step + 1, version = version + 1
       WHERE id = p_request;                                       -- on to the next step
    ELSE
      UPDATE approval_requests SET status = 'approved', version = version + 1
       WHERE id = p_request;                                       -- that was the last step
    END IF;
  END IF;

  INSERT INTO approval_events (org_id, request_id, actor_id, action)
  VALUES (p_org, p_request, p_approver, 'approve step ' || p_step);
  RETURN 'approved step ' || p_step;
END $$;
  1. session 1

    the approver calls approve_step, which locks the request

  2. session 2

    the requester's withdrawal asks for the same lock — and waits about 1.5 s

  3. session 1

    approves; the request is approved, version 2; commits

  4. session 2

    gets the lock, reads approved, and its … AND status = 'pending' update changes 0 rows — "can no longer be withdrawn"

Why a function: the whole approval is one call — one round trip, one transaction — and named parameters can't be misnumbered the way $1, $2… can across separate statements. The timeline is the actual result of calling it while a withdrawal ran at the same moment, on PostgreSQL 16 with this schema; a repeated call then changed nothing, and a requester trying to approve their own request was refused. On a two-step request, finance approving step 2 first was refused; after the manager approved step 1 the request moved to step 2, and finance's approval then completed it.

Key deep dive — snapshots and history
NFRHistory complete and unchangeable
Thought process
  1. Who must approve a request could be worked out live, from the current manager and department. But if Ravi's manager changes mid-approval, a request would silently change hands.
  2. So the approval chain is written as step rows when the request is submitted — a snapshot of who was responsible at that time. If an approver leaves, the step is reassigned explicitly, and that reassignment is itself an event.
  3. Every action appends a row to approval_events, which is never updated or deleted. The current status is on the request for fast reads; the events say how it got there.
  4. Events grow forever, so they're partitioned by month — recent ones stay fast, old ones archive cleanly. See partitioning by time.
Illustration — the history of one request
CREATE TABLE approval_events (
  id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  org_id      uuid NOT NULL,
  request_id  uuid NOT NULL,
  actor_id    uuid NOT NULL,
  action      text NOT NULL,
  at          timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, request_id) REFERENCES approval_requests (org_id, id)
);
AtActorAction
09:12Ravisubmit — steps written: Nadia, then Finance
10:40Nadiaapprove step 1
14:05HR adminreassign step 2 — Finance approver on leave
15:30Mei (Finance)approve step 2 — request approved
Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • Human-readable request numbers — "EXP-2026-00042" per organization comes from a counter row updated with UPDATE … SET next_no = next_no + 1 … RETURNING. It's gapless and safe under concurrency, at the cost of requests in one organization taking numbers one at a time — fine at human rates.
  • Expense lines — amounts belong in their own table with proper types and constraints, not inside a JSON blob, so totals can be checked and summed by the database.
  • An employee moves department mid-approval — the snapshot of approvers doesn't change; the next request uses the new department.
  • Time — every timestamp is timestamptz, stored as an instant; "today" is computed in the organization's own time zone.
  • Deleting things — employees and requests change status rather than being deleted; history and foreign keys stay intact, and retention rules remove old data on schedule.
  • Many organizations in one database — org_id leading every index is also what makes row-level security and later sharding by organization straightforward, as in the tenant isolation example.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
The database prevents invalid dataCHECK constraints, uniqueness scoped by organization, and composite foreign keys that make cross-organization references impossible.
Common screens fast at scaleOne index per query, equality columns first, partial indexes for pending work, and keyset pagination — verified with the planner.
Concurrent actions stay consistentEvery write locks the request row first; every change is conditional on the state it expects.
History complete and unchangeableApprovers snapshotted at submission; append-only events, partitioned by month.
Trees handled correctlyparent_id with recursive queries, and a cycle check inside the move's transaction.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Composite foreign keys with org_idWider keys and an extra unique constraint per table, in exchange for cross-organization references being impossible.
Locking the request rowActions on one request wait for each other, in exchange for simple, correct behaviour — and requests are rarely contended.
Snapshot of approversReassignments must be explicit, in exchange for requests never silently changing hands.
parent_id over a closure tableSubtree reads need a recursive query, in exchange for moves being a single-row update.
Partial indexesQueries must repeat the index's condition to use it, in exchange for small, fast indexes on the rows that matter.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
DatabasePostgreSQL — composite foreign keys, partial indexes, recursive queries and row locks, all used above
Checking the planEXPLAIN (ANALYZE) on each query, with realistic data volumes
Trees at larger scalethe ltree extension for materialized paths
From Gopgx with sqlc — SQL written by hand and checked at compile time
Worked Example AR — The Database Question, Again

Database Schema — Multi-Organization Identity: Accounts, Memberships and Records

one person, many employers · constraints that hold across organizations · state on the relationship · indexes chosen from queries · races between removal, switching and invitations · isolation by construction
Click to expand

The second database question — after the HR approvals schema — on the domain from the multi-organization identity example: one person, many employers. The schema has to let one account belong to many organizations, keep every organization's data walled off from every other, and stay fast when one organization has 100,000 members or one person belongs to 300 of them. As before, the answer is judged on the reasons: which rules the database enforces, which query each index serves, and what happens when a removal and a sign-in land at the same instant. Every statement below was run on PostgreSQL 16.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • One account can belong to many organizations; each relationship has its own status and roles.
  • People without an email sign in with an organization code and a login ID that is unique within that organization.
  • Admins invite people by email; an invitation can be accepted once, only by the address it was sent to, before it expires.
  • A departed member keeps one narrow permission — their own documents — until a set date; a rehire reuses the same account.
  • Each membership links to the person's record in every product and outside system, explicitly.
  • Every change to status, roles or links is recorded.
Non-functional
  • The database itself prevents invalid data — including a login, link or event that points into another organization.
  • Sign-in and switching stay fast with millions of accounts, thousands of organizations and one organization of 100,000.
  • Concurrent actions — a removal while a switch, an invitation clicked twice — leave one consistent result.
  • One organization's data, load and mistakes stay inside it: isolation by construction first, then by policy.
  • History is complete and can't be rewritten.

Say the second one out loud: "sign-in stays fast" hides two different queries — one starts from a person, before any organization is chosen, and one starts from an organization. They want different indexes.

2
Core Entities
  • accounts — the person and their credentials. Global; the email is optional and unique when present.
  • organizations — the tenant; the org_code typed at login, its login policy (MFA, single sign-on), and the cell that serves it.
  • memberships — the relationship: status, roles and, for a departed member, the end date of their access. One per organization and account.
  • membership_periods — each stretch of membership; a rehire adds one.
  • org_logins — login IDs for people without email, unique inside one organization.
  • system_identities — the explicit link from a membership to its record in a product or outside system.
  • invitations — single-use, expiring, tied to an address.
  • identity_events — an append-only history.
3
API

For a database question, the "API" is the set of queries the schema must serve well:

Q1 organizations this account can enter — searchable, page by page
Q2 organization code + login ID → the account
Q3 members of my organization, by status — page by page (admins)
Q4 an outside system's ID → the person
Q5 email → the account
W1 switch organization · W2 depart a member · W3 accept an invitation · W4 link people from an import file

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. An admin of Org B invites ana@mail.com. An invitation row is written, tied to that address, valid for seven days.
  2. Ana already has an account. She accepts: one conditional update marks the invitation used, and in the same transaction her membership, an open period and a join event are written.
  3. She lists her organizations — Q1, read from an index led by her account — and picks Org B.
  4. The switch reads her membership with a share lock, checks the organization's policy, and a token naming Org B alone is issued.
  5. To find her payroll record, the product looks up her membership in system_identities — never her name or email.
  6. When Org B removes her, one transaction marks the membership departed with the single role own_documents, closes her period and appends an event.
5
High-Level Design

A relational schema in PostgreSQL with two kinds of table. Two are global — accounts and organizations. Everything else belongs to exactly one organization, carries org_id, and points at memberships through composite foreign keys that include it, so no row can reference another organization's member. Status and roles live on the membership, never on the account. Indexes come one by one from the queries. State changes are conditional updates, and the ones that must not race take a row lock. Row-level security is a second wall on the admin-facing tables, and the organization's cell decides where it lives. History is appended, never updated.

6
Deep Dives

Six below: (a) tables and constraints, (b) status, periods and rehire, (c) indexes from queries, (d) races: a removal against a switch, and an invitation clicked twice, (e) linking people to outside systems, and (f) many organizations in one database — then the edge cases.

Eight tables. Accounts and organizations are global; every other table belongs to one organization and carries org_id. A membership joins one account to one organization, and logins, periods, links and events all hang off it through keys that include the organization. PK is a primary key, FK a foreign key, UQ a unique constraint, IX a column that leads an important index.
Joining and switching
  1. Org B invites Ana's address.
  2. Ana accepts; one transaction marks the invitation used and creates her membership and period.
  3. She lists her organizations and picks Org B.
  4. The switch checks membership and policy, and issues a token naming Org B only.
A removal at the moment of switching
  1. Org B's admin removes Ana: the membership row is updated, not yet committed.
  2. Ana's switch asks for a share lock on the same row, and waits.
  3. The removal commits; the switch reads departed and grants only own_documents.
  4. Without the lock, it would have read the old row and issued her old roles.
Key deep dive — tables and constraints that can't be bypassed
NFRThe database prevents invalid dataNFRNever the wrong person's data
Thought process
  1. Identity mistakes are the expensive kind — one wrong row shows a stranger's salary — so every rule that can live in the schema should. A rule in the schema is one no future code path can forget.
  2. Two tables are global, and their uniqueness is global. An email belongs to one account, through a partial unique index, so people without an email don't collide on NULL. An org_code belongs to one organization. Emails are stored lower-case, enforced by a CHECK, so the index compares exactly what was typed.
  3. Everything else is unique inside one organization: login IDs, and IDs in outside systems. Two companies can both have the login carter01 and the payroll number 1042.
  4. The rules that need a composite key: a login must belong to an account that is a member of that organization, and an outside link must point at a membership of the same organization. Both are foreign keys that include org_id — which is why memberships declares UNIQUE (org_id, id) and UNIQUE (org_id, account_id). The tenant isolation example, enforced in the schema.
  5. Some rules from the identity design become CHECKs: a departed membership may hold only the role own_documents and must carry an end date; an invited one holds no roles yet; an organization that requires single sign-on must name its provider.
Illustration — the schema, with the rules it enforces
CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  email         text CHECK (email = lower(email) AND position('@' in email) > 1),
  password_hash text,
  mfa_enabled   boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  status        text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active' CHECK (status IN ('active','locked','closed')),
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
-- partial: people without an email never collide
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX accounts_email_uq ON accounts (email) WHERE email IS NOT NULL;

CREATE TABLE organizations (
  id           uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  org_code     text NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (org_code ~ '^[a-z0-9-]{3,32}$'),      -- typed at login
  name         text NOT NULL,
  require_mfa  boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  sso_required boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  sso_issuer   text,
  cell         text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'shared',                                   -- shared pool, or a cell
  CHECK (NOT sso_required OR sso_issuer IS NOT NULL)
);

CREATE TABLE memberships (
  id           uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  org_id       uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES organizations(id),
  account_id   uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),
  status       text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('invited','active','suspended','departed')),
  roles        text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  access_until date,
  version      int NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (org_id, account_id),                                                   -- one per person and org
  UNIQUE (org_id, id),                                                           -- target for composite FKs
  CHECK (status <> 'invited'  OR cardinality(roles) = 0),                        -- nothing accessible yet
  CHECK (status <> 'departed' OR (access_until IS NOT NULL AND roles <@ ARRAY['own_documents']))
);

CREATE TABLE org_logins (
  org_id     uuid NOT NULL,
  login_id   text NOT NULL CHECK (login_id = lower(login_id)),
  account_id uuid NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, login_id),                                                -- unique inside one org
  UNIQUE (org_id, account_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, account_id) REFERENCES memberships (org_id, account_id)   -- members of that org only
);

The remaining tables — periods, links, invitations and events — follow the same pattern and appear in the deep dives below. Note that memberships carries no password and accounts carries no status per organization: credentials live on one, the relationship on the other.

AttemptEnforced byResult

The full run tried 33 writes — every bad one was refused by the database itself, and every good one accepted. "Rejected" is the passing result. These are the checks from the constraints above, run on PostgreSQL 16.

Key deep dive — status, periods and rehire
FRDeparted, but retrieving own documentsFRRehired employee
Thought process
  1. Status belongs on the membership, not on the account — the rule from the identity design — so leaving one organization changes exactly one row, and the person's other memberships are untouched.
  2. Roles change with status. Departing replaces the roles with the single narrow role and stamps an end date, in one UPDATE; the CHECK on memberships guarantees no code path can leave a departed member holding admin.
  3. Transitions are conditional updates. Departing changes a row only if it is active or suspended; a second click, or a second admin, matches nothing and gets "not an active member".
  4. A rehire does not create a second membership. The same row goes back to active, its version increases, and a new row is added to membership_periods. Last time's documents stay tied to last time's period. A partial unique index allows only one open period per membership.
Illustration — departing, as one function
CREATE TABLE membership_periods (
  id            bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  org_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  membership_id uuid NOT NULL,
  started_on    date NOT NULL,
  ended_on      date,
  CHECK (ended_on IS NULL OR ended_on >= started_on),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, membership_id) REFERENCES memberships (org_id, id)
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_open_period ON membership_periods (membership_id) WHERE ended_on IS NULL;

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION depart_member(p_org uuid, p_membership uuid, p_until date, p_actor uuid)
RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  UPDATE memberships SET status = 'departed', roles = ARRAY['own_documents'],
         access_until = p_until, version = version + 1
   WHERE id = p_membership AND org_id = p_org AND status IN ('active','suspended');
  IF NOT FOUND THEN RETURN 'not an active member'; END IF;
  UPDATE membership_periods SET ended_on = current_date
   WHERE membership_id = p_membership AND ended_on IS NULL;
  INSERT INTO identity_events (org_id, actor_id, membership_id, action, detail)
  VALUES (p_org, p_actor, p_membership, 'depart', jsonb_build_object('access_until', p_until));
  RETURN 'departed';
END $$;
ActionAllowed fromWhat changes
accept an invitationno membership, invited, or departedactive; roles from the invitation; a new open period; a join event
suspendactivesuspended; token exchange is refused
departactive, suspendeddeparted; roles become own_documents; end date set; the open period closes; a depart event
rehiredepartedthe same row: active again, version + 1, a new period

Run for real: departing returned departed; departing again returned not an active member; a token exchange for that organization then granted only own_documents. A rehire by a new invitation returned joined, and left one membership row at version 3 with two periods — the first closed, the second open.

Key deep dive — indexes, chosen from the queries
NFRFast at millions of accounts and one organization of 100,000
Thought process
  1. Take each query and give it the index that lets the database go straight to its rows. There are two shapes here, and they want different indexes.
  2. Organization-first queries — resolve a login, list members, follow an outside ID — lead their index with org_id, as in every multi-organization schema. Most of these are served by constraints that already exist: UNIQUE (org_code), the primary key (org_id, login_id), the primary key (org_id, system, external_id).
  3. Account-first is the exception. "Which organizations can this person enter?" is asked before any organization is chosen, so there is no org_id to lead with. Memberships gets an index led by account_id that also carries org_id and status, so the list can be read from the index alone. This is the one place the schema deliberately breaks its own rule.
  4. Add an index only where it changes the plan. An index on (org_id, status, id) looks redundant next to UNIQUE (org_id, id) — and for the active members, which are 96% of the rows, it is: the planner ignores it. For a selective status like suspended it matters: 0.07 ms with it, 0.62 ms without, because without it the database walks the organization's rows and discards the rest.
  5. Page with a keyset — "after the last row I saw" — not OFFSET, as in the news feed example.
Illustration — each query, and the index that serves it
-- Q1 organizations this account can enter — the one query that starts from a person
CREATE INDEX memberships_by_account ON memberships (account_id) INCLUDE (org_id, status);
SELECT o.id, o.name
FROM memberships m JOIN organizations o ON o.id = m.org_id
WHERE m.account_id = $1 AND m.status IN ('active','departed')
  AND lower(o.name) LIKE $2 || '%'                    -- the search box
ORDER BY lower(o.name), o.id LIMIT 20;

-- Q2 org code + login ID → account: served by UNIQUE (org_code) and PRIMARY KEY (org_id, login_id)
SELECT l.account_id FROM organizations o JOIN org_logins l ON l.org_id = o.id
WHERE o.org_code = $1 AND l.login_id = $2;

-- Q3 members of my organization: keyset paging, never OFFSET
CREATE INDEX memberships_by_org ON memberships (org_id, status, id);
SELECT id, account_id, status FROM memberships
WHERE org_id = $1 AND status = $2 AND id > $3 ORDER BY id LIMIT 50;

-- Q4 an outside ID → the person: served by PRIMARY KEY (org_id, system, external_id)
SELECT membership_id FROM system_identities WHERE org_id = $1 AND system = 'payroll' AND external_id = $2;

-- Q5 email → account: served by the partial unique index
SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE email = $1;
QueryPlan PostgreSQL chose, with 130,284 membershipsTime
Q1index scan on her 300 memberships — as an index-only scan of the account index joined by hash in one run, as a nested loop probing (org_id, account_id) in another — against a sequential scan of the 2,000-row organizations table, which is right when 20% of the names match "acme"0.9–2.6 ms
Q2index scan on the organization code, then on (org_id, login_id)0.03 ms
Q3 activeindex scan on (org_id, id); the extra index isn't used0.06 ms
Q3 suspendedindex scan on (org_id, status, id) — versus 0.62 ms without that index0.07 ms
Q4index scan on the primary key0.02 ms
Q5index scan on the partial email index0.02 ms

These plans come from running this schema on PostgreSQL 16 with 100,000 accounts, 2,000 organizations and 130,284 memberships — one organization of 20,000 people (576 of them suspended), and one accountant in 300 organizations. Q1 changed shape between runs because the planner works from statistics; both shapes read only her 300 entries. The accountant is the point: hundreds of organizations per person costs milliseconds, and never grows with the size of the platform.

Key deep dive — races: a removal against a switch, and an invitation clicked twice
NFRConcurrent actions stay consistentNFRRemoval takes effect
Thought process
  1. Two races matter. An admin removes someone at the moment they switch organizations; and an invitation is accepted more than once — a double-click, or two people holding the same link.
  2. The removal race is easy to miss. An ordinary read does not wait for an update that hasn't committed: it sees the old row, so the switch issues a token to someone whose removal is already in flight. The switch therefore reads the membership with FOR SHARE, which waits for any uncommitted change to that row, and then decides against the current status. (Tokens already issued are bounded by their short lifetime, as in the identity design.)
  3. The invitation is a single conditional update: it changes a row only where it is unused, unrevoked, unexpired and tied to this account's address. Concurrent callers queue on the row lock; the first wins, and each later one re-checks, matches nothing and is told the invitation is no longer valid.
  4. Rules that span rows live in the same transaction. Accepting must not consume an invitation for someone who is already an active member, so that case raises an error, which rolls the invitation update back — the invitation stays unused.
Illustration — a token exchange that waits for a removal
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION switch_org(p_account uuid, p_org uuid, p_via_sso boolean DEFAULT false)
RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE a accounts%ROWTYPE; o organizations%ROWTYPE; m memberships%ROWTYPE;
BEGIN
  SELECT * INTO a FROM accounts WHERE id = p_account;
  IF NOT FOUND OR a.status <> 'active' THEN RETURN 'deny: account not active'; END IF;
  SELECT * INTO o FROM organizations WHERE id = p_org;
  SELECT * INTO m FROM memberships WHERE account_id = p_account AND org_id = p_org
    FOR SHARE;                                    -- waits for a removal that is in flight
  IF NOT FOUND THEN RETURN 'deny: not a member'; END IF;
  IF m.status NOT IN ('active','departed') THEN RETURN 'deny: membership is ' || m.status; END IF;
  IF m.status = 'departed' AND m.access_until < current_date THEN RETURN 'deny: access period ended'; END IF;
  IF o.sso_required AND NOT p_via_sso THEN RETURN 'deny: organization requires single sign-on'; END IF;
  IF o.require_mfa AND NOT a.mfa_enabled THEN RETURN 'deny: organization requires MFA'; END IF;
  RETURN 'ok: roles ' || array_to_string(m.roles, ',');
END $$;
  1. session 1

    the admin's removal updates the membership and holds its transaction open for 1.5 s

  2. session 2

    0.3 s later, Ana's token exchange asks for a share lock on the same row — and waits about 1.2 s

  3. session 1

    commits: the membership is departed, roles own_documents

  4. session 2

    gets the lock, reads departed, and grants only own_documents

VariantResultWaited
read without a lockok: roles admin — a token for someone being removed0.00 s
read with FOR SHAREok: roles own_documents1.20 s

Both variants ran against the same in-flight removal, in two real sessions. The switch waits only as long as the removal's transaction stays open — 1.2 s here, because the test held it open for 1.5 s; a real removal commits in milliseconds. When no removal is in flight, the lock costs nothing.

Illustration — what the exchange decides, and a single-use invitation
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION accept_invitation(p_invitation uuid, p_account uuid)
RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE inv invitations%ROWTYPE; v_email text; v_member uuid;
BEGIN
  SELECT email INTO v_email FROM accounts WHERE id = p_account;
  UPDATE invitations SET accepted_by = p_account, accepted_at = now()
   WHERE id = p_invitation AND accepted_at IS NULL AND revoked_at IS NULL
     AND expires_at > now() AND email = v_email          -- single use, unexpired, tied to this address
  RETURNING * INTO inv;
  IF NOT FOUND THEN RETURN 'invitation not valid for this account'; END IF;
  INSERT INTO memberships (id, org_id, account_id, status, roles)
  VALUES (gen_random_uuid(), inv.org_id, p_account, 'active', inv.roles)
  ON CONFLICT (org_id, account_id) DO UPDATE
     SET status = 'active', roles = EXCLUDED.roles, access_until = NULL,
         version = memberships.version + 1
   WHERE memberships.status IN ('invited','departed')     -- a rehire, or an attach
  RETURNING id INTO v_member;
  IF v_member IS NULL THEN RAISE EXCEPTION 'already an active member'; END IF;   -- rolls the invitation back
  INSERT INTO membership_periods (org_id, membership_id, started_on)
  VALUES (inv.org_id, v_member, current_date);
  INSERT INTO identity_events (org_id, actor_id, membership_id, action)
  VALUES (inv.org_id, p_account, v_member, 'join');
  RETURN 'joined';
END $$;
AttemptResult
member of Org A, role adminok: roles admin
departed from Org C, without single sign-ondeny: organization requires single sign-on
departed from Org C, through single sign-onok: roles own_documents
an organization that requires MFA, account without itdeny: organization requires MFA
suspended memberdeny: membership is suspended
not a member at alldeny: not a member
the wrong account tries someone else's invitationinvitation not valid for this account
accept clicked three times at onceone joined, two not valid — 1 membership, 1 open period, 1 event
accept while already an active membererror already an active member; the invitation stays unused

Every line is a real result. Each denial names its reason — the interface can show "your organization requires single sign-on" instead of a bare refusal.

Key deep dive — linking people to outside systems: imports that report instead of guess
FRLinked to every product and outside systemNFRNever the wrong person's data
Thought process
  1. This is where the worst failure lives. A wrong link shows one person's data to another while every other layer looks correct, so a link is never inferred — it is set on purpose and the database refuses ambiguity.
  2. Two constraints do it. The primary key (org_id, system, external_id) says an outside ID is one person, inside one organization. UNIQUE (org_id, membership_id, system) says one person has one ID per system.
  3. Admins load links from files, so the import has to be as careful as a single insert. One statement classifies every row: people who don't exist in this organization drop out at the join; an ID repeated inside the file is not resolved by guessing which line is right; and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING catches IDs already taken and people already linked. The admin gets one outcome per row.
  4. Every link change is also appended to the event history — who linked which ID to which membership — because a wrong link is invisible to the person it affects.
Illustration — a six-row import file, and what happened to each row
WITH incoming AS (
  SELECT n, external_id, membership_id,
         count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY external_id)   AS same_id,       -- repeated inside the file?
         count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY membership_id) AS same_person
  FROM unnest($1::int[], $2::text[], $3::uuid[]) AS t(n, external_id, membership_id)),
ins AS (
  INSERT INTO system_identities (org_id, membership_id, system, external_id)
  SELECT $4, i.membership_id, 'payroll', i.external_id
  FROM incoming i JOIN memberships mm ON mm.org_id = $4 AND mm.id = i.membership_id   -- unknown people drop out here
  WHERE i.same_id = 1 AND i.same_person = 1                                            -- repeats in the file are never guessed at
  ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING                                                               -- ID already taken, or person already linked
  RETURNING external_id, membership_id)
SELECT i.n, i.external_id,
       CASE WHEN ins.external_id IS NOT NULL        THEN 'linked'
            WHEN mm.id IS NULL                      THEN 'unknown person'
            WHEN i.same_id > 1 OR i.same_person > 1 THEN 'repeated in the file'
            ELSE 'ID taken, or person already linked' END
FROM incoming i
LEFT JOIN memberships mm ON mm.org_id = $4 AND mm.id = i.membership_id
LEFT JOIN ins ON ins.external_id = i.external_id AND ins.membership_id = i.membership_id
ORDER BY i.n;
RowExternal IDOutcome
11042ID taken, or person already linked — payroll number 1042 already belonged to someone
22001linked
32002unknown person — no such membership in this organization
42003repeated in the file — not guessed at
52003repeated in the file — not guessed at
62004ID taken, or person already linked — that person already had a payroll ID

Only row 2 was written. The other five are reported back for a person to fix — none of them was silently skipped, and none was matched by name or email.

Key deep dive — many organizations in one database: isolation and scale
NFROne organization's data and load stay inside itNFRScales with the largest organization
Thought process
  1. Three walls, in order of strength. The first is by construction: org_id in every key and composite foreign keys, so a row can't point into another organization and an organization-first query only reads its own rows — Q3 on a 20,000-member organization takes 0.06 ms and never touches the other 1,999 organizations' rows.
  2. The second is by policy. Row-level security on the tables the admin console touches makes the database itself filter by organization, taken from a per-request setting. A query that forgot its WHERE org_id = … sees only its own organization's rows; with no setting it sees nothing; a write into another organization is rejected. Superusers always bypass it, and so does a table's owner unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set — so the application connects as its own role. The sign-in path, which must look across organizations for one account, doesn't use the policy: it runs functions such as switch_org under its own role.
  3. The third is by placement. organizations.cell says which database serves an organization — the shared pool, or a dedicated cell for the largest — the same routing as the high-level design in the multi-organization identity example. One caveat: accounts, and a slim directory of account → organization → cell that answers Q1, must stay global, because one person can belong to organizations in different cells. A membership that lives in a cell's database therefore cannot have a database-enforced foreign key to accounts — that one reference is checked by the application against the global table, while every other key in the cell stays enforced.
  4. Bulk work is what stresses a shared system. A 100,000-person directory import should run in batches — a thousand rows per transaction, say — so no lock is held for long, on a lane of its own per organization, as in the identity design. Events are partitioned by month, and next month's partition is created ahead of time.
  5. When one primary is no longer enough, the leading org_id in every key is what makes the next move straightforward: hash-partition the organization-scoped tables by org_id, keep accounts sharded by id, and serve Q1 from its own account-led index. That step wasn't run here — it's the reason the keys look the way they do.
Illustration — the second wall, run for real
-- the admin console connects as its own role, never as the owner
ALTER TABLE system_identities ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY org_wall ON system_identities TO admin_api
  USING      (org_id = nullif(current_setting('app.org_id', true), '')::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (org_id = nullif(current_setting('app.org_id', true), '')::uuid);

-- per request:  SELECT set_config('app.org_id', '<org from the token>', true);
-- a query that forgot its WHERE clause:
SELECT count(*) FROM system_identities;
Connected asSettingResult
admin_apiorganization A1 row — only A's
admin_apiorganization B1 row — only B's
admin_apinothing set0 rows — deny by default
admin_apiorganization A, inserting a row for Brejected new row violates row-level security policy
admin_apiorganization A, inserting a row for Aaccepted
the table's superuser owner—2 rows — it bypasses the policy, which is why the app never connects as it

The table held one row per organization, and the query is deliberately the careless one, with no WHERE clause.

Illustration — events: append-only, partitioned, created ahead
CREATE TABLE identity_events (
  id            bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
  org_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  at            timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  actor_id      uuid,
  membership_id uuid,
  action        text NOT NULL,
  detail        jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, at, id),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, membership_id) REFERENCES memberships (org_id, id)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (at);
CREATE TABLE identity_events_2026_09 PARTITION OF identity_events
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-09-01') TO ('2026-10-01');   -- created ahead of time, every month

CREATE FUNCTION events_are_append_only() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN RAISE EXCEPTION 'identity_events is append-only'; END $$;
CREATE TRIGGER no_rewrite BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE ON identity_events
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION events_are_append_only();

While testing this schema, an insert failed with no partition of relation "identity_events" found for row — the current month's partition hadn't been created. In production a scheduled job creates next month's partition ahead of time, and an alert fires if fewer than two future partitions exist. A trigger blocks UPDATE and DELETE; the stronger form is to also revoke those privileges from the application role.

Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • An accountant in hundreds of organizations — Q1 reads only her entries from the account-led index and pages through them; hundreds per person costs milliseconds, as measured above.
  • An invitation sent to the wrong address — it is tied to the address it was sent to, so another account trying it is told it isn't valid; it is also single-use and expires.
  • An expired invitation that was never revoked — the "one open invitation per organization and address" index can't include "not expired" (the current time isn't allowed in an index condition), so an expired one blocks a new invitation until it is revoked. A nightly job revokes expired invitations.
  • One person with two accounts — memberships are moved to the surviving account in one transaction. UNIQUE (org_id, account_id) refuses the merge if both accounts are already in the same organization: a person decides, nothing is silently overwritten.
  • A reassigned work email — the account's identity is its id, not its email; the unique index refuses to give an address to a second account until the first releases it, which surfaces the conflict instead of merging two people.
  • Deleting — accounts and memberships change status instead of being deleted, so history and foreign keys stay intact; retention rules remove old data on schedule.
  • A missing partition — inserts into the events table fail rather than land somewhere wrong; create partitions ahead of time and alert when few remain.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
The database prevents invalid dataCHECKs; uniqueness scoped globally for email and organization code, per organization for logins and outside IDs; composite foreign keys with org_id. 33 attempted violations, each handled as intended.
Status is per relationshipStatus and roles live on the membership; a CHECK limits a departed member to own_documents; a rehire reuses the row and adds a period.
Fast at millions of rowsOne index per query shape — account-led and covering for Q1, organization-led everywhere else; keyset paging. Every query measured between 0.02 and 2.6 ms.
Concurrent actions stay consistentThe switch reads with FOR SHARE; an invitation is a single conditional update; both shown with real races.
One organization can't reach or slow anotherorg_id in every key, composite foreign keys, row-level security on admin-facing tables, batched imports, and a cell for the largest.
History complete and unchangeableAppend-only events, partitioned by month; periods keep each stretch of a rehired member's history.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Composite foreign keys with org_idWider keys and an extra unique constraint per table, in exchange for no row ever pointing into another organization.
An account-led index, breaking "org_id first"One more index, and a query shape that does not follow the organization boundary, in exchange for a fast list of a person's organizations before any is chosen.
FOR SHARE on the switchA switch briefly waits for a removal that is mid-flight, in exchange for never issuing a token from a stale read.
Row-level security on admin tablesA session setting on every request and a separate database role, in exchange for a second wall behind the query.
One database for every organizationShared operations and simple cross-organization queries, in exchange for needing partitions or cells when the biggest customers grow — which leading keys with org_id keeps possible.
Cells for the largest organizationsAccounts and the account → organization directory stay global, and a cell's memberships lose their database-enforced link to accounts, in exchange for a big organization's data, load and imports living entirely in its own database.
Departed members keep their rowRows accumulate, in exchange for history and a rehire that reuses the same identity.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
DatabasePostgreSQL — composite foreign keys, partial and covering indexes, row-level security, declarative partitioning and row locks, all used above
