Worked Example AS — The Database Question, Once More

Database Schema — Notification System: Events, Deliveries and Inboxes

the event_id, made at the start · keys that keep a message from being sent twice · a claim two workers can't share · an inbox read from an index · organizations kept apart by the keys
Click to expand

The third database question, on the domain of the notification system: products report what happened, one service turns each event into a notification per person and channel, sends them, and keeps an in-app inbox. That example showed the three keys that stop duplicates in a few lines of SQL. This one is the whole schema, and it opens with a question the other example only answers in passing: where does the event_id come from? As before, the answer is judged on the reasons — which key sits where, which index serves which query, and what happens when the same event arrives twice. Every statement below was run on PostgreSQL 16.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Store each event once, however many times a product sends it.
  • Turn an event into one notification per person and one delivery per notification and channel — repeating the work adds nothing.
  • Let workers claim queued deliveries, one worker per delivery, and recover claims that were never finished.
  • Keep an in-app inbox per person per organization: newest first, with an unread count and mark-all-read.
  • Apply each person's preferences and quiet hours, except where a category can't be switched off — security alerts.
  • Record bounces so dead addresses stop being used.
  • Let a product ask what happened to its event.
Non-functional
  • The database itself prevents duplicates and invalid states, not careful code.
  • A 100,000-person organization's payday fans out in minutes: 100,000 notifications and 300,000 delivery rows for one event.
  • Claims, inbox pages and unread counts stay fast on the largest tables.
  • No organization's ids or load can affect another's.
  • The tables hold ids and status, never the content of a payslip — a message says "your payslip is ready", and no more.

Say the first one out loud: "no duplicates" is not a property of a queue, it is a property of keys. This example is about which key sits where — and who makes the first one.

2
Core Entities
  • categories — how each kind of event is treated: its priority lane, default channels, whether it can be opted out of. Global.
  • events — what a product reported, keyed by organization and the product's event_id.
  • notifications — one per event and person; its id is derived from them.
  • deliveries — one per notification and channel, from queued to sent or failed.
  • inbox_items — the in-app copy, per person and organization.
  • preferences — what a person chose: channels, and quiet hours. Only exceptions are stored.
  • contacts — email addresses and push tokens, per account, marked invalid when they bounce. Global.

Outside this database: the product's outbox where the event is born, and the attempt log in the NoSQL store.

3
API

For a database question, the "API" is the queries the schema must serve well:

Q1 store an event — a repeat stores nothing
Q2 fan out: notifications, deliveries and inbox items for a batch of people
Q3 claim a batch of queued deliveries · give back stuck claims
Q4 an inbox page, newest first · Q5 the unread count, and mark all read
Q6 preferences and contacts for a batch of recipients · Q7 mark a bounced address invalid
Q8 what happened to my event

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. Payroll marks a run published. In the same transaction it writes an outbox row, and the row's event_id is born there.
  2. The relay publishes it. It crashes before marking the row, and publishes the same row again — the same id.
  3. The intake inserts the event with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. The second copy returns no row, and nothing else happens.
  4. Fan-out writes a notification, three deliveries and an inbox item for each of the organization's 100,000 people, in batches, with derived ids.
  5. Workers claim queued deliveries by priority and organization; each claimed row is theirs alone.
  6. Ana opens her inbox: one index-only page, newest first, with the badge counted from a small partial index.
5
High-Level Design

A relational schema in PostgreSQL with two global tables — categories and contacts — and five organization-scoped ones that lead every key with org_id. The event's id is made by the product, at the start, and is the first key; the notification's id is derived from it and enforced by a CHECK; a delivery's key is the idempotency key. Rules that would otherwise live in code — security alerts can't be opted out, a delivery can't be sent without a provider id — are constraints. Each hot query has the index it needs: a partial index of queued deliveries for the claim, a covering index for the inbox, a partial index of unread items for the badge.

6
Deep Dives

Six below: (a) where the event_id comes from, (b) tables and constraints, (c) deliveries: the state machine and the claim, (d) the inbox, (e) preferences, quiet hours and contacts, and (f) many organizations in one database — then the edge cases.

Seven tables. Categories and contacts are global; every other table belongs to one organization and leads with org_id. An event has many notifications (one per person), a notification has many deliveries (one per channel) and one inbox item. Membership and account ids come from the identity service, so they are ids here rather than foreign keys. PK is a primary key, FK a foreign key, UQ a unique constraint, IX a column that leads an important index.
An event arrives twice
  1. The product's transaction writes the change and an outbox row; the row's event_id is made there.
  2. The relay publishes the row, crashes, and publishes it again.
  3. The intake inserts (org_id, event_id); the second copy conflicts and returns no row.
  4. Fan-out ran once, so each person has one notification.
Two workers, one queue
  1. Both ask for a batch of queued deliveries for the organization, security lane first.
  2. Each locks the rows it picks; rows the other holds are skipped.
  3. They get different rows: 4,000 claimed, none shared.
  4. A worker that dies leaves sending rows, and the sweeper gives them back.
Illustration — the product's outbox table: what's inside, and what it's for

An outbox is a table in the product's own database that holds the events the product still has to tell others about. It is written in the same transaction as the business change — so either both are saved or neither is: the product never has a change that nobody heard about, and never announces one that didn't happen. A separate relay reads the rows that are not published yet, sends them to the broker, and marks them published. If the relay crashes it simply sends again — and that is safe because every row already carries its own event_id, so the receiver can recognise a repeat.

ColumnWhat it holdsWhy it is there
event_idthe id of this event — a UUID made here, inside the business transactionthe id everything downstream dedupes on: made once, at the start, and reused on every retry
org_idwhose event it ispart of the receiver's key and of the topic's partition key, so one organization's events stay in order and can't be confused with another's
typewhat happened, for example payslip.publishedhow the receiver routes and classifies it
aggregate_idthe thing that changed — the run, the task, the announcementlets an id be derived from the fact, and lets a consumer fetch the thing
aggregate_versionwhich version of that thing this event describesmakes "the same fact emitted twice" recognisable, and orders changes to one thing
dataa small payload: ids and facts — never a payslip's figures or anyone's personal detailskeeps the event self-describing while the message stays small and safe to forward
created_atwhen the row was writtenthe order in which the relay publishes
published_atempty until the relay has sent the eventthe relay's to-do list: NULL means still to send

One row, as the relay sees it:

event_id           bfb28220-6d81…
org_id             041bdf64-8d1c…
type               payslip.published
aggregate_id       9f73a45a-e4de…
aggregate_version  1
data               {"run": "r-now"}
created_at         (the moment it was written, in the business transaction)
published_at       NULL          <- the relay has not sent it yet

The table, the index, and the relay's poll — tested on PostgreSQL 16:

CREATE TABLE product.outbox (                      -- in the PRODUCT's database, not the notification service's
  event_id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  org_id            uuid NOT NULL,
  type              text NOT NULL,
  aggregate_id      uuid NOT NULL,
  aggregate_version int  NOT NULL,
  data              jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  created_at        timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  published_at      timestamptz                        -- NULL = the relay has not sent it yet
);
CREATE INDEX outbox_unpublished ON product.outbox (created_at) WHERE published_at IS NULL;

-- the relay's poll: a batch of unpublished rows, oldest first; another relay's rows are skipped
SELECT event_id, org_id, type, aggregate_id, aggregate_version, data
FROM product.outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL
ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
-- ... publish them to the broker, then:
UPDATE product.outbox SET published_at = now() WHERE event_id = ANY($1);
MeasureResult
the table1,002,000 rows — 2,000 unpublished, the rest already published; 156.5 MB
the index of unpublished rows96 KB, against 21.5 MB for the same index over every row
the relay's poll0.114 ms — a LockRows over an index scan of outbox_unpublished
two relays polling at once1,600 rows taken, 1,600 distinct, 0 shared
retention: delete published rows older than 7 days697,608 rows in 70 batches of 10,000, 7.0 s

What it is not: it is not the queue the consumers read — Kafka or SQS is — and it is not an audit log: once a row is published and old enough it is deleted, in batches. Its whole job is to make "save the change" and "remember to tell everyone" one atomic step. One machine, one million rows: the plans and ratios are real, the absolute times are small.

Key deep dive — where the event_id comes from
NFRNo duplicate sendsNFRNothing lost
Thought process
  1. The event_id is made once, at the start: by the product, inside the same transaction as the business change, and stored in the outbox row next to it (the table is drawn in full just above). Everything after that carries the same id — the relay, Kafka, the intake, the fan-out. Any later step that made its own id would make a different one on every retry, and the intake could no longer recognise a repeat.
  2. Not the relay, and not the intake. The relay can crash after sending and before marking the row as published; the next pass sends the same row again. If the id were made at send time, the two sends would differ. In the test that gave 2 events and 10 notifications for one publish, where it should have been 1 and 5. The intake cannot make the id either: its whole job is to recognise repeats of what the product sent.
  3. There are two ways to make it. A random id (a UUID, a ULID) made in the transaction covers every retry of sending: two clicks on Publish plus a relay retry gave 1 event and 5 notifications. A derived id — a hash of the organization, the type, the thing that changed and its version — also covers the same fact being emitted twice, by a recovery job or a re-run batch: random ids gave 2 events and 10 notifications, derived ids 1 and 5. Derive when the same fact can come from more than one place, and make sure the version changes for a genuinely new occurrence — a password changed twice needs two ids.
  4. Guard the business action too, so the second click doesn't create a second event at all. Publishing is a conditional state change, ready → published; the second click changes 0 rows and writes no outbox row. In the test, 2 clicks wrote 1 outbox row.
  5. The key includes the organization: PRIMARY KEY (org_id, event_id). If event_id were the key on its own, an id that another organization had already used would count as a repeat — acknowledged and ignored, so a real event would vanish without a trace. With the bare key, organization B's event was refused; with (org_id, event_id), both were stored. The organization comes from the caller's token, not from the request body.
  6. The same idea reaches the next table. A notification's id is derived from the event id, the organization and the person, and a CHECK enforces it — id = md5(org:event:person)::uuid — so a random id can't be inserted, and a re-run finds the row it wrote before.
Illustration — from the product's transaction to the intake, tested on PostgreSQL 16
-- in the product's own database
CREATE TABLE product.outbox (
  event_id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),   -- made here, in the business transaction
  org_id            uuid NOT NULL,
  type              text NOT NULL,
  aggregate_id      uuid NOT NULL,
  aggregate_version int  NOT NULL,
  published_at      timestamptz);

-- the business change and its event: one statement, one transaction
WITH moved AS (UPDATE product.payslip_runs SET status = 'published', version = version + 1
               WHERE org_id = $1 AND id = $2 AND status = 'ready'      -- a second click changes nothing
               RETURNING id, version)
INSERT INTO product.outbox (org_id, type, aggregate_id, aggregate_version)
SELECT $1, 'payslip.published', id, version FROM moved;

-- or, when the same fact may be emitted from more than one place: derive the id
SELECT md5($org || ':payslip.published:' || $run || ':' || $version)::uuid;

-- in the notification service: the intake
INSERT INTO events (org_id, event_id, type, occurred_at)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4)
ON CONFLICT (org_id, event_id) DO NOTHING
RETURNING event_id;                                               -- no row back: a repeat
Illustration — where the id is made, and what each choice produced
ScenarioWhere the id is madeWhat happenedStored
Publish clicked twice; the relay crashed after sending, and sent againat the start, in the product's transaction — random1 outbox row; the second send was ignored1 event · 5 notifications
The relay crashed after sending, and sent againat send time — a new id on every attempttwo different ids reached the intake2 events · 10 notifications
A recovery job emitted the same fact againrandom, made at emissiontwo different ids2 events · 10 notifications
A recovery job emitted the same fact againderived from organization + type + run + versionthe second emission collapsed1 event · 5 notifications
Two organizations, the same id, a key without the organizationkey: event_idorganization B's insert returned no row — read as a repeat1 row for two events
Two organizations, the same id, a key with the organizationkey: (org_id, event_id)both stored2 events

Five people were told per event, so a correct run stores 1 event and 5 notifications. Every row here is a result of running the SQL, with the relay's crash simulated by sending the same outbox row twice.

Key deep dive — tables and constraints that can't be bypassed
NFRThe database prevents duplicates and invalid statesNFRNever the wrong organization's row
Thought process
  1. Two tables are global. Categories are the same for everyone. Contacts belong to a person, not to an organization: one email address, one account. Everything else is organization-scoped and leads with org_id.
  2. The keys, in the order the data flows. Events: (org_id, event_id), the dedupe key. Notifications: (org_id, id), with a unique constraint on (org_id, event_id, membership_id) — one notification per event and person — and the CHECK that the id is derived. Deliveries: (org_id, notification_id, channel), the idempotency key. Inbox items: (org_id, notification_id).
  3. Every parent link is a composite foreign key that includes org_id: a delivery can only point at a notification of its own organization, a notification only at an event of its own. The inbox item's link also includes the person, so an inbox item can't show one person another person's notification.
  4. Business rules become constraints. A security alert cannot be opted out: a CHECK on categories. A preference can only switch off what may be switched off — done without a trigger: preferences copies opt_out_ok from its category, a composite foreign key (category, opt_out_ok) ties the copy to the real value, and CHECK (enabled OR opt_out_ok) refuses to disable a non-optional category. A delivery that is sending must have a claim time; a sent email or push must have a provider id; quiet hours are all-or-nothing; email addresses are stored in lower case; an invalid contact must say when.
Illustration — the core tables, with the rules they enforce
CREATE TABLE events (
  org_id      uuid NOT NULL,
  event_id    uuid NOT NULL,                                             -- made by the product, at the start
  type        text NOT NULL REFERENCES categories(type),
  data        jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  occurred_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
  received_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, event_id)                                         -- the dedupe key, inside one organization
);

CREATE TABLE notifications (
  org_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  id            uuid NOT NULL,
  event_id      uuid NOT NULL,
  membership_id uuid NOT NULL,                                           -- from the identity service
  account_id    uuid NOT NULL,
  category      text NOT NULL REFERENCES categories(type),
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, id),
  UNIQUE (org_id, event_id, membership_id),                              -- one notification per event and person
  UNIQUE (org_id, id, membership_id),                                    -- target of the inbox's key
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, event_id) REFERENCES events (org_id, event_id),
  CHECK (id = md5(org_id::text || ':' || event_id::text || ':' ||
                  membership_id::text)::uuid)   -- derived, never random
);

CREATE TABLE deliveries (
  org_id          uuid NOT NULL,
  notification_id uuid NOT NULL,
  channel         text NOT NULL CHECK (channel IN ('in_app','push','email','chat')),
  priority        smallint NOT NULL CHECK (priority IN (0, 1, 2)),
  status          text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'queued' CHECK (status IN ('queued','sending','sent','failed')),
  attempts        int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (attempts >= 0),
  scheduled_for   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),                    -- quiet hours push it out
  claimed_at      timestamptz,
  provider        text,
  provider_msg_id text,
  last_error      text,
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, notification_id, channel),                        -- the idempotency key
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, notification_id) REFERENCES notifications (org_id, id),
  CHECK (status <> 'sending' OR claimed_at IS NOT NULL),
  CHECK (status <> 'sent' OR channel = 'in_app' OR provider_msg_id IS NOT NULL)
);

CREATE TABLE preferences (
  org_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  membership_id uuid NOT NULL,
  category      text NOT NULL,
  channel       text NOT NULL CHECK (channel IN ('in_app','push','email','chat')),
  enabled       boolean NOT NULL,
  opt_out_ok    boolean NOT NULL,                                        -- copied from the category
  quiet_start   time, quiet_end time, tz text,
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, membership_id, category, channel),
  FOREIGN KEY (category, opt_out_ok) REFERENCES categories (type, can_opt_out),
  CHECK (enabled OR opt_out_ok),                                         -- only what may be switched off can be
  CHECK ((quiet_start IS NULL) = (quiet_end IS NULL) AND (quiet_start IS NULL) = (tz IS NULL))
);
Illustration — 31 attempts against the running database
AttemptEnforced byResult

the same event_id in another organizationthe key includes org_idaccepted
a notification with a random idCHECK: id is derivedrejected
a notification in org A for an event that exists only in org Bcomposite foreign keyrejected foreign key violation

The full run tried 31 writes. "Rejected" is the passing result, and each rejection was checked against the specific constraint type it was meant to trigger.

Key deep dive — deliveries: the state machine and the claim
NFROne worker per deliveryNFRNothing stuck foreverNFRThe payday fan-out
Thought process
  1. A delivery moves queued → sending → sent, or to failed; a retry goes back to queued with a later scheduled_for, and quiet hours push that time into the future. The checks on the table keep it honest: nothing is sending without a claim time.
  2. The claim is one conditional statement: update the rows chosen by a subquery with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Two workers claiming at once get different rows. In the test, 2 workers each made 20 claims of 100 rows: 4,000 rows claimed, 4,000 distinct, 0 shared, at a median of 3.7 ms per claim.
  3. The claim gets its own index — on queued rows only: (org_id, priority, scheduled_for, notification_id) WHERE status = 'queued'. It reads the index in order, security lane first, with no sort: a LockRows over an index scan of deliveries_due, 0.497 ms, on 539,826 deliveries of which 19,970 were queued.
  4. That index churns. Every delivery enters it when it is created and leaves it when it is sent, so after the payday burst it was 22.08 MB for about 19,970 live entries; rebuilt, it was 1.31 MB, in 0.1 s. Plan for it: aggressive autovacuum on this table and a periodic REINDEX CONCURRENTLY.
  5. A worker that dies after claiming leaves a sending row. A small partial index on those rows lets a sweeper give them back: 30 rows requeued, from an index scan of 0.456 ms. The one window no schema can close is still there — the provider accepted the message and the worker died before recording it — and the channels limit the damage as the notification system describes.
  6. Fan-out is the same idea in reverse: insert with derived ids and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. One event for a 100,000-person organization, three channels each, in batches of 10,000 with one transaction per batch, wrote 100,000 notifications, 300,000 deliveries and 100,000 inbox items in 41.2 s. Running the whole fan-out again wrote 0 new rows, in 1.8 s — which is what makes a crash in the middle safe.
Illustration — the claim, and the fan-out that feeds it
UPDATE deliveries SET status = 'sending', claimed_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1
WHERE (org_id, notification_id, channel) IN (
  SELECT org_id, notification_id, channel FROM deliveries
  WHERE org_id = $1 AND status = 'queued' AND scheduled_for <= now()
  ORDER BY priority, scheduled_for, notification_id
  LIMIT 100
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)                       -- rows another worker holds are skipped
RETURNING notification_id, channel;

-- a worker that died: give its claims back
UPDATE deliveries SET status = 'queued', claimed_at = NULL
WHERE status = 'sending' AND claimed_at < now() - interval '10 minutes';
-- fan-out, one batch of 10,000 people: same statements, safe to run again
INSERT INTO notifications (org_id, id, event_id, membership_id, account_id, category)
SELECT m.org_id, md5(m.org_id::text || ':' || $ev || ':' || m.membership_id::text)::uuid,
       $ev, m.membership_id, m.account_id, 'payslip.published'
FROM recipients m WHERE ...
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;
INSERT INTO deliveries (org_id, notification_id, channel, priority) ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;
INSERT INTO inbox_items (org_id, notification_id, membership_id)     ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;
Illustration — the state machine
FromToByGuard
queuedsendinga worker's claimSKIP LOCKED; the claim time is set
sendingsentthe worker, after the provider acceptsWHERE status = 'sending'; a provider id for email and push
sendingqueuedthe sweeperthe claim is older than the timeout
sendingqueued, latera temporary failureattempts increase; scheduled_for moves out (backoff)
sendingfaileda permanent failurethe reason is kept in last_error

MeasureResult
two workers claiming at once4,000 rows claimed, 4,000 distinct, 0 shared; median 3.7 ms
the claim's planLockRows over Index Scan using deliveries_due on deliveries — 0.497 ms

Key deep dive — the inbox, read from an index
NFRA fast inbox and badge at the largest volume
Thought process
  1. An inbox page is newest first, and pages with a keyset — "after the last item I saw" — not OFFSET. The index (org_id, membership_id, created_at DESC, notification_id DESC) carries read_at too, so the page is an index-only scan. The person in the test had 5,001 items: the first page took 0.022 ms, and a page 2,500 items deep took 0.032 ms, both with heap fetches: 0.
  2. The badge is a count of unread items, from a partial index on read_at IS NULL. Only unread rows are in it, so it stays small however many items exist: 1,200 unread, counted in 0.172 ms by an index-only scan.
  3. Mark-all-read is one update over the same partial index: 1,200 rows in 9.3 ms. The cached badge in the notification system is cleared on every new item and every read, so the count that users see is never older than a few seconds.
  4. Every inbox query is organization-scoped, because a person in three organizations has three inboxes (see the inbox deep dive in the notification system). The organization is the first column of the index, so the query never touches another organization's rows.
  5. Inbox rows are cheap and numerous, so they need a retention rule — drop or archive items past a few months. Partitioning by time would make that a partition drop instead of a delete; it was not run here.
Illustration — the queries, and the plan PostgreSQL chose
-- the inbox: newest first, a keyset instead of OFFSET
SELECT notification_id, created_at, read_at FROM inbox_items
WHERE org_id = $1 AND membership_id = $2
  AND (created_at, notification_id) < ($3, $4)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, notification_id DESC LIMIT 20;

-- the badge: only unread rows are in this index
SELECT count(*) FROM inbox_items
WHERE org_id = $1 AND membership_id = $2 AND read_at IS NULL;

UPDATE inbox_items SET read_at = now()
WHERE org_id = $1 AND membership_id = $2 AND read_at IS NULL;
QueryPlanTime
inbox, first pageindex-only scan inbox_by_member, no sort0.022 ms
inbox, 2,500 items deepindex-only scan the same index; the keyset skips the rest0.032 ms
unread countindex-only scan inbox_unread — a partial index0.172 ms
mark all readone update over the partial index — 1,200 rows9.3 ms

Measured on 184,942 inbox items, one person holding 5,001 of them.

Key deep dive — preferences, quiet hours and contacts
NFRRespect people's choicesNFRBounces stop for good
Thought process
  1. Fan-out reads preferences for a batch of recipients: WHERE org_id = $1 AND membership_id = ANY($2). The primary key leads with those two columns, so a 1,000-person batch took 4.308 ms.
  2. Store only what differs from the default. No row means the category's default channels; a row is a choice. In the lab, 179,942 people had 178,966 preference rows, not four per person — most people never open the settings page.
  3. Quiet hours are a start, an end and a time zone on the preference, all or nothing. Fan-out turns them into scheduled_for for push and email — in-app is never delayed — and security alerts, priority 0, ignore them.
  4. Contacts belong to the account and are unique by (channel, address): an address is one person's. That unique index does double duty: it is also how a bounce finds its row. A 1,000-account batch lookup took 3.441 ms, and marking a bounced address invalid used the unique index and took 0.154 ms. An invalid contact needs a time, so the fan-out can see how long an address has been dead.
Illustration — the two lookups fan-out makes, and the feedback that keeps them clean
-- fan-out: preferences for a batch of recipients
SELECT membership_id, channel, enabled, quiet_start, quiet_end, tz FROM preferences
WHERE org_id = $1 AND membership_id = ANY($2) AND category = $3;

-- feedback: a hard bounce marks the address, whichever account owns it
UPDATE contacts SET status = 'invalid', invalid_at = now()
WHERE channel = 'email' AND address = $1;
QueryPlanTime
preferences for 1,000 recipientsbitmap scan on the primary key4.308 ms
contacts for 1,000 accountsbitmap scan on the primary key3.441 ms
mark a bounced address invalidindex scan on (channel, address)0.154 ms

These sit on the fan-out's path, so they are batched — one query for a thousand people — and never asked one person at a time.

Key deep dive — many organizations in one database
NFRNo organization's ids or load affect another'sNFRScales with the largest organization
Thought process
  1. Isolation comes first from the keys. org_id leads every primary key, so one organization's event ids can't suppress another's — the test above — and every organization-scoped query reads only its own rows. The claim, the inbox and the badge took 0.497, 0.022 and 0.172 ms on tables where one organization alone owned 300,000 of 539,826 deliveries.
  2. Because org_id is in every key, the big tables can be hash-partitioned by organization. In the test, 8 partitions kept the primary key enforced (a duplicate insert was refused), and a claim scanned 1 of 8 partitions in 0.127 ms.
  3. But hash partitioning spreads organizations, not one huge organization. The big organization's 300,000 deliveries all hashed to one partition, which held 329,673 of 539,826 rows — 61% of the table. When a single organization is that large, more partitions don't help: it needs a cell of its own (see isolating the massive organizations), or a second key to split it — the recipient, or time.
  4. Row-level security can be added as a second wall exactly as in the identity schema example, and the organization's cell decides where its rows live. Neither changes the tables.
  5. Deliveries are the highest-volume table, and the history is only useful for a while. Keeping about 90 days — the same window as the attempt log in the NoSQL store — is a retention job; partitioning by time would turn it into dropping a partition. That was not run here.
Illustration — hash-partitioning deliveries by organization, run for real
CREATE TABLE deliveries_hp (LIKE deliveries INCLUDING DEFAULTS) PARTITION BY HASH (org_id);
ALTER TABLE deliveries_hp ADD PRIMARY KEY (org_id, notification_id, channel);   -- allowed: org_id is in the key
-- eight partitions, modulus 8
MeasureResult
partitions8, by hash(org_id); 539,826 rows copied
a claim for one organization1 of 8 partitions scanned — 0.127 ms
the primary keystill enforced — a duplicate insert was refused
the biggest partition329,673 rows — the big organization; the other seven held 27,444 to 32,472 each

Partitioning by organization protects the many small organizations from each other. It does not shrink the largest one — that is the job of a cell.

Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • An event with 100,000 recipients — the fan-out runs in batches of 10,000, one transaction each, and every batch is safe to repeat, so a crash resumes instead of restarting.
  • A product retries with a changed payload but the same event_id — the first copy is kept and the change is ignored. A new fact needs a new id; with derived ids that means a new version.
  • A category that is retired — events point at categories, so it can't be deleted while events exist; mark it inactive instead, and stop accepting new events of that type.
  • A person in several organizations — notifications and inboxes are per membership, so each organization has its own; contacts are per account and shared.
  • The attempt log — every send attempt is high-volume history, kept 90 days, and belongs in the NoSQL store keyed by notification id, not in these tables; deliveries keep only the current state.
  • A preference for a departed membership — harmless and small; the retention job removes it with the rest.
  • A queue redelivers a job — the worker's claim finds the delivery already sending or sent and changes 0 rows, so the job is acknowledged and dropped.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
A repeated event is stored onceThe product makes the id at the start, in its transaction; the key is (org_id, event_id). Sent twice: 1 event, 5 notifications.
A re-run creates nothing newDerived notification ids and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING: re-running a 100,000-person fan-out added 0 rows.
One worker per deliveryThe claim uses FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED: two workers, 4,000 rows, none shared.
Nothing stuck foreverA partial index on sending rows lets a sweeper return old claims to the queue.
Fast on the largest tablesIndex-only inbox pages at 0.02–0.03 ms, the badge at 0.17 ms, a claim at 0.5 ms — with 540,000 deliveries.
Invalid states are impossible31 attempted violations, each refused by the constraint it was meant to trigger.
One organization can't affect anotherorg_id first in every key, composite foreign keys, and hash partitioning that prunes to one of eight partitions.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Derived ids instead of random onesA hash to compute and a version to maintain, in exchange for a re-emitted fact collapsing by itself; random ids cover retries of sending only.
A partial index on a churning stateVery fast claims, in exchange for index bloat that needs autovacuum and a periodic rebuild (22.08 MB became 1.31 MB).
Composite keys with org_id everywhereWider keys and more unique constraints, in exchange for no row ever pointing into another organization — and partitioning by organization for free.
A little deliberate duplicationPriority on deliveries, opt_out_ok on preferences, the person on inbox items: a copied value lets the database enforce a rule that would otherwise need a trigger.
Fan-out in batchesA batch is the unit of retry, in exchange for the whole event not being one transaction — which is fine because every batch is repeatable.
One database for every organizationShared operations, in exchange for needing a cell for the largest customer, which partitioning alone cannot fix.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
DatabasePostgreSQL — composite keys, CHECK constraints, partial and covering indexes, SKIP LOCKED, hash partitioning, all used above
Making event idsa UUID or ULID generated by the product in its transaction, or a hash of the business fact; UUIDv7 keeps ids roughly time-ordered
Outbox and relayan outbox table with a polling relay, or Debezium's outbox pattern into Kafka
QueuesSQS or Kafka carry the jobs; the delivery row remains the source of truth for whether it was handled
Maintenancepg_partman for partitions; autovacuum tuning and REINDEX CONCURRENTLY for the queued-rows index; pgx with sqlc for the queries
Worked Example AU — The Database Question, For Announcements

Database Schema — Announcement System: Audiences, Publishing and Read Receipts

a list only where there is a list · a lifecycle that publishes once · one job per announcement · a feed and badge from the right indexes · organizations kept apart by the keys
Click to expand

The fourth database question, on the domain of the announcement system: admins write an announcement, choose who it is for, and publish it now or at 09:00; employees see it in a feed; and the first open counts as a read. The interesting part of the schema is what it refuses: a second publish, a recipient list on an all-employees announcement, a script in a title. Every statement below was run on PostgreSQL 16.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Admins draft, schedule, publish and end announcements; ended ones can't be republished.
  • The audience is everyone, a selected list, or a list from a CSV.
  • Employees see the announcements meant for them, in their current organization.
  • Each recipient is notified in the app, and optionally by email and in chat.
  • Admins see how many recipients have read each one.
Non-functional
  • A scheduled announcement is published and notified exactly once, even if two schedulers run at once.
  • No one outside the audience ever sees it; nothing published vanishes while it is being read.
  • A 100,000-person organization is notified within minutes; the 9 a.m. rush doesn't slow the home screen.
  • Announcement text can't carry a script.
  • No organization's rows can reach another's.

The first requirement is a property of keys and one statement, not of a scheduler — this example is about which key sits where.

2
Core Entities
  • announcements — the lifecycle: status, audience type, publish and end times. Its audience type is part of a key.
  • announcement_recipients — the list, only for selected audiences.
  • publish_jobs — the announcement service's outbox: one row per announcement, ever.
  • deliveries — one per person and channel — the idempotency key.
  • read_receipts — one per person, written on the first open.
  • announcement_log — an append-only history of every change.

There are no global tables here: every table belongs to one organization.

3
API

For a database question, the "API" is the queries the schema must serve well:

Q1 create, edit, publish and end · Q2 the scheduler claims due announcements and enqueues their jobs
Q3 fan out a job into deliveries · Q4 the feed · Q5 the unread badge
Q6 record a read · Q7 the read count for an admin · Q8 who was it sent to

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. An admin drafts "Office closed on 14 March" and uploads a CSV of the Lisbon office; matched rows become recipients.
  2. She schedules it for Monday 09:00; the status becomes scheduled.
  3. At 09:00 two schedulers run; one statement flips the row to published and inserts its one job. The other finds nothing.
  4. A worker expands the job into a delivery per person and channel; a re-run adds nothing.
  5. Employees open the feed: newest first, from an index, with a badge counted from a small one.
  6. Each first open writes one receipt; the admin's count climbs.
5
High-Level Design

A relational schema in PostgreSQL where every table is organization-scoped and leads with org_id. The audience type is part of a key, so a recipient list can exist only for a selected audience. A trigger lists the legal status transitions; a job row with a primary key makes publishing happen once. Deliveries and receipts are keyed by person, so repeating work adds nothing. Each hot query has the index it needs — a partial index of published announcements for the feed, a person-led index of receipts for the feed and badge.

6
Deep Dives

Five below: (a) who exactly is the audience, (b) a lifecycle that publishes exactly once, (c) notifying everyone, once, (d) the feed, the badge and the read receipts, and (e) text that can't carry a script, a log that can't be rewritten, and many organizations — then the edge cases.

Six tables, all organization-scoped. An announcement has recipients (only if its audience is selected), one publish job, deliveries per person and channel, and read receipts per person; the log records every change without a foreign key. "member" is a membership id from the identity service. PK is a primary key, FK a foreign key, UQ a unique constraint, IX a column that leads an important index.
Publishing exactly once
  1. The scheduler picks the due rows with a lock that skips rows another scheduler holds.
  2. One statement flips them to published and inserts each one's job.
  3. The job's primary key allows one per announcement, whatever else goes wrong.
  4. A second scheduler, or an admin's publish-now, finds 0 rows and does nothing.
Opening it at 9 a.m.
  1. The feed walks the published announcements newest first.
  2. "Everyone" is a rule; "selected" is a lookup by the full key.
  3. The receipt insert ignores a repeat, so a fifth open is still one read.
  4. The badge is counted from an index that holds only unread rows.
Key deep dive — who exactly is the audience?
NFRNo one outside the audienceNFRA list only where there is a list
Thought process
  1. "All employees" is a rule, not a list: an all-employees announcement has no recipient rows, and the feed applies the rule when it is read, so someone who joins next week still sees the new expense policy. Only a selected audience has rows — those people, and only those.
  2. The schema enforces that, so no code has to remember it. A recipient row carries audience_type, a CHECK pins it to selected, and a composite foreign key (org_id, announcement_id, audience_type) points at the announcement's own row. A row for an all-employees announcement has nowhere to point. Tested: a recipient of an all-employees announcement was refused, a row claiming to be "all" was refused, and so was switching an announcement to "all" while it still had recipients — the admin must clear the list first. No trigger was needed.
  3. The primary key (org_id, announcement_id, membership_id) means a person appears once, and it is also what the feed uses to ask "am I a recipient?" — by the full key.
  4. The reverse question — "which announcements were sent to this person?" — is a different one, and the primary key can't answer it. Without an index it was a parallel sequential scan of 600,000 rows: 42.877 ms. With (org_id, membership_id, announcement_id) it was 0.043 ms — but that index is 38.9 MB, so add it only if the question exists: a "sent to me" view, an audit, or cleaning up when someone leaves. The feed itself doesn't need it.
  5. A CSV is checked before anything is saved: each employee number is matched to a membership, and unknown or duplicate rows are reported, not dropped. That statement is the same one as the import in the identity schema; nothing is written to the recipients table until the admin confirms.
Illustration — the announcement and its recipients
CREATE TABLE announcements (
  org_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  id            uuid NOT NULL,
  title         text NOT NULL CHECK (char_length(title) BETWEEN 1 AND 200 AND title !~ '[<>]'),
  body          text NOT NULL CHECK (char_length(body) BETWEEN 1 AND 10000 AND body !~* '<\s*/?\s*[a-z]'),   -- plain text, never markup
  status        text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'draft' CHECK (status IN ('draft','scheduled','published','ended')),
  audience_type text NOT NULL CHECK (audience_type IN ('all','selected')),
  publish_at    timestamptz,
  published_at  timestamptz,
  ended_at      timestamptz,
  author_id     uuid NOT NULL,                                                     -- a membership in the identity service
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, id),
  UNIQUE (org_id, id, audience_type),                                              -- target for the recipients' key
  CHECK (status <> 'scheduled' OR publish_at IS NOT NULL),
  CHECK ((status IN ('published','ended')) = (published_at IS NOT NULL)),
  CHECK ((status = 'ended') = (ended_at IS NOT NULL))
);

CREATE TABLE announcement_recipients (
  org_id          uuid NOT NULL,
  announcement_id uuid NOT NULL,
  membership_id   uuid NOT NULL,
  audience_type   text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'selected' CHECK (audience_type = 'selected'),
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, announcement_id, membership_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, announcement_id, audience_type) REFERENCES announcements (org_id, id, audience_type)   -- only for a selected audience
);

Each rule above is a line in these two tables. The recipient's key is what ties it to a selected announcement of the same organization.

Illustration — what the database refused
AttemptEnforced byResult
a recipient of an all-employees announcementcomposite foreign key with audience_typerejected foreign key violation
a recipient row that says its audience is "all"CHECK on the recipientrejected
switching to "all" while recipients existthe same foreign key, on updaterejected foreign key violation
the same recipient twiceprimary keyrejected unique violation
a recipient of a selected announcement—accepted
"who was this sent to?" with and without an index38.9 MB index42.877 ms → 0.043 ms

38 of 38 writes across the whole schema behaved as intended; each rejection was checked against the specific constraint type it was meant to trigger.

Key deep dive — a lifecycle that publishes exactly once
NFRPublished and notified exactly onceNFREnded can't be republishedNFRNothing vanishes while it is being read
Thought process
  1. The status has to agree with its timestamps, and CHECKs make sure it does: a scheduled announcement has a publish_at, a published or ended one has a published_at, and only an ended one has an ended_at. A row that says one thing and records another can't be written.
  2. Transitions are guarded by a small trigger that lists the only legal edges: draft → scheduled | published, scheduled → published | draft (cancelling a schedule), published → ended. Tested: ended back to published, published back to draft and a draft jumping straight to ended were all refused. The same trigger refuses deleting anything that is published, so a live announcement can't vanish while people are reading it; a draft or an ended one can go.
  3. Publishing exactly once is one statement. It picks the due rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, flips them to published, and inserts one row per announcement into publish_jobs, whose primary key allows exactly one job per announcement, ever. With 1,000 due announcements and two schedulers running side by side, 1,000 were published and enqueued, 1,000 distinct, 0 shared, in 0.05 s; a third run found 0.
  4. An admin's "publish now" can race the scheduler on the same announcement. The conditional update settles it: it changes the row only from draft, or from scheduled once due, so one caller gets 1 row and the other 0. In 30 trials with two threads, 30 had exactly one winner, and never two.
Illustration — the guard, and the one statement that notifies
CREATE FUNCTION announcement_guard() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  IF TG_OP = 'DELETE' THEN
    IF OLD.status NOT IN ('draft','ended') THEN RAISE EXCEPTION 'a % announcement cannot be deleted', OLD.status; END IF;
    RETURN OLD;
  END IF;
  IF NEW.status <> OLD.status AND NOT (
       (OLD.status = 'draft'     AND NEW.status IN ('scheduled','published')) OR
       (OLD.status = 'scheduled' AND NEW.status IN ('published','draft'))     OR
       (OLD.status = 'published' AND NEW.status = 'ended')) THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'an announcement cannot go from % to %', OLD.status, NEW.status;
  END IF;
  RETURN NEW;
END $$;
-- the scheduler: due rows are flipped and enqueued in ONE statement
WITH due AS (
  SELECT org_id, id FROM announcements
  WHERE status = 'scheduled' AND publish_at <= now()
  ORDER BY publish_at LIMIT 50
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED),                                   -- rows another scheduler holds are skipped
pub AS (
  UPDATE announcements a SET status = 'published', published_at = now()
  FROM due WHERE a.org_id = due.org_id AND a.id = due.id
  RETURNING a.org_id, a.id)
INSERT INTO publish_jobs (org_id, announcement_id)           -- PRIMARY KEY: one job per announcement, ever
SELECT org_id, id FROM pub;

-- an admin's "publish now": the same idea, for one row
UPDATE announcements SET status = 'published', published_at = now()
WHERE org_id = $1 AND id = $2
  AND (status = 'draft' OR (status = 'scheduled' AND publish_at <= now()));   -- 1 row: we won · 0 rows: someone else did
Illustration — the lifecycle, run for real
AttemptResult
ended back to publishedan announcement cannot go from ended to published
published back to draftan announcement cannot go from published to draft
draft straight to endedan announcement cannot go from draft to ended
delete a published announcementa published announcement cannot be deleted
delete a draft, or an ended oneaccepted
two schedulers, 1,000 due announcements1,000 published and enqueued · 0 shared · 0.05 s
a second job for the same announcementduplicate key value violates unique constraint "publish_jobs_pkey"
publish now vs the scheduler, 30 trialsexactly one winner every time
Key deep dive — notifying everyone, once
NFRAn organization notified within minutesNFRNo second send
Thought process
  1. Publishing writes one row — the job. A fan-out worker later expands it into one delivery per person and channel, in batches, so publishing itself stays instant however large the audience is. Because the delivery's key is (org_id, announcement_id, membership_id, channel), running a batch again adds nothing.
  2. Measured: one announcement to a 100,000-person organization on two channels wrote 200,000 delivery rows in 2.9 s, in batches of 10,000. Running the whole fan-out again wrote 0 new rows, in 0.7 s — which is what makes a crash in the middle safe.
  3. The table records state; it does not pace the sending. Email and chat limits are enforced per organization in the queue layer (see the announcement system), and the workers claim queued deliveries exactly as in the notification schema: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED over a partial index of queued rows.
  4. A chat channel post is one message for the whole channel, not one per person, so it is one row per announcement and target with the same kind of key — it isn't drawn here, to keep the diagram to what differs.
Illustration — the fan-out, and what a re-run does
-- fan-out, one batch of 10,000 people: safe to run again
INSERT INTO deliveries (org_id, announcement_id, membership_id, channel)
SELECT $org, $announcement, m.membership_id, ch
FROM recipients_of_this_batch m CROSS JOIN unnest('{in_app,email}'::text[]) ch
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;
MeasureResult
first fan-out200,000 rows in 2.9 s (100,000 people × in-app and email)
the same fan-out again0 new rows in 0.7 s
the same delivery inserted twicerejected unique violation
an email marked sent without a provider idrejected CHECK on deliveries

One machine, batches of 10,000 rows, no foreign-key fan-in from other tables: the absolute times are small, the shape is real.

Key deep dive — the feed, the badge and the read receipts
NFRThe 9 a.m. rush doesn't slow the home screenNFRRead counts for admins
Thought process
  1. A read receipt is written once per person: INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING stored the first open and ignored the second, at 0.031 ms. Opening an announcement five times records one read.
  2. The feed goes newest first through a partial index of published announcements, (org_id, published_at DESC, id DESC) WHERE status = 'published', and for each candidate asks "everyone, or am I on the list?" — by the full primary key of the recipients — and "did I read it?" from the receipts.
  3. The receipts need an index led by the person. The primary key is (org_id, announcement_id, membership_id), which is the wrong way round for "my receipts", so without help the planner scanned all 60,000 receipts. With receipts_by_member (3.9 MB) the feed went from 2.391 ms to 0.04 ms and the unread badge from 3.375 ms to 0.621 ms. That index is in the schema; the recipients one is not, because the feed never needs it.
  4. The admin's "read by 1,800 of 2,400" is a count of receipts for one announcement: 60,000 receipts counted in 7.388 ms, which is a sequential scan because the whole announcement's rows are wanted. Cached for a few seconds it is fine; at much larger volumes a counter row updated in batches would replace it (not run here).
  5. Only published announcements are in the feed, so an ended one disappears at once; and whether the person's membership is active is checked when the token is issued, not stored here, so pre-hire and departed employees see nothing whatever the audience says.
Illustration — the queries, and what each index did
-- Q4 the feed: newest first; 'all' is a rule, 'selected' is a lookup by the full key
SELECT a.id, a.title, a.published_at, (r.membership_id IS NOT NULL) AS read
FROM announcements a
LEFT JOIN read_receipts r ON r.org_id = a.org_id AND r.announcement_id = a.id AND r.membership_id = $2
WHERE a.org_id = $1 AND a.status = 'published'
  AND (a.audience_type = 'all'
       OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM announcement_recipients ar
                  WHERE ar.org_id = a.org_id AND ar.announcement_id = a.id AND ar.membership_id = $2))
ORDER BY a.published_at DESC, a.id DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Q6 the first open counts; every later one is ignored
INSERT INTO read_receipts (org_id, announcement_id, membership_id) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

-- Q8 "sent to me": the reverse question, which needs its own index
CREATE INDEX recipients_by_member ON announcement_recipients (org_id, membership_id, announcement_id);
QueryPrimary keys onlyWith the index it needs
the feed, first page2.391 ms0.04 ms · receipts_by_member
the unread badge (last 30 days)3.375 ms0.621 ms · receipts_by_member
"sent to me" — the reverse question42.877 ms0.043 ms · recipients_by_member, 38.9 MB
a receipt insert0.031 msthe primary key does the work
the read count of a 60,000-read announcement7.388 msa sequential scan is right here

Medians of repeated runs on 2,000 published announcements, 600,000 recipient rows and 60,000 receipts in a 100,000-person organization. A first single run of the feed had read 39 ms — a cold cache — which is why these are medians.

Key deep dive — text that can't carry a script, a log that can't be rewritten, and many organizations
NFRNo script injectionNFREvery change is loggedNFRNo organization's rows reach another's
Thought process
  1. Announcements are plain text. The title and body CHECKs refuse anything that looks like markup — an angle bracket followed by a letter — while plain text like "5 < 6" passes. That is defence in depth: the real defence is escaping at output, and the constraint means a script tag can't even be stored.
  2. The log is append-only, enforced by a trigger that refuses UPDATE and DELETE; every state change writes who did it, what and when. It has no foreign key to the announcement, on purpose, so it outlives a deleted draft.
  3. org_id leads every key, and every child points at its announcement through a key that includes it: a delivery or a receipt for another organization's announcement was refused by the foreign key. The big tables here — 600,000 recipients — are only ever reached through organization-scoped keys, and, as in the notification schema, that is also what would let them be hash-partitioned by organization.
  4. The very largest organizations are the exception to "one shared database" — see isolating the massive organizations for what a cell of their own contains.
Illustration — three walls, run for real
AttemptEnforced byResult
a title of <script>alert(1)</script>CHECK on the titlerejected
a body of 5 < 6 is still truethe same CHECKaccepted
rewriting a log entryappend-only triggerrejected
deleting a log entryappend-only triggerrejected
a delivery for another organization's announcementcomposite foreign keyrejected foreign key violation
a receipt for another organization's announcementcomposite foreign keyrejected foreign key violation
Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • A scheduled announcement whose author leaves — the author is an id, not a foreign key, so it keeps working; the log still names who scheduled it.
  • Editing text after publishing — allowed and logged, and it does not notify anyone again — only the publish transition creates a job.
  • An audience of one person twice in a CSV — the primary key refuses the second row; the upload report lists it before anything is saved.
  • "All employees" and a person who joins later — they see it, because the audience is a rule read at feed time; a selected list does not grow.
  • A publish job whose fan-out crashes halfway — the job stays open (fanned_out_at is empty) and the next worker resumes; every batch is repeatable.
  • Deleting an ended announcement — allowed, and it leaves the log; the recipients, receipts and deliveries would first need to be removed or archived.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Published and notified exactly onceOne statement flips and enqueues; the job's primary key allows one per announcement. Two schedulers, 1,000 due: 1,000 published, 0 shared; 30 of 30 manual-vs-scheduler races had one winner.
No one outside the audienceRecipients only for selected audiences (composite foreign key); "all" is a rule applied at read; membership status checked at token time.
Ended is final; nothing vanishesA trigger lists the legal transitions and refuses deleting a published announcement.
Notified within minutes100,000 people × 2 channels wrote 200,000 delivery rows in 2.9 s; a re-run added 0.
The 9 a.m. rush is cheapA feed page in 0.04 ms and the badge in 0.621 ms with a 3.9 MB index; a receipt insert in 0.031 ms.
No script injectionCHECKs refuse markup-shaped text; escaping at output remains the real defence.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
An index only where a query needs itThe receipts index (3.9 MB) is in; the recipients one (38.9 MB) is optional — it fixes a query the feed never asks.
A trigger for the lifecycleLegal transitions in one place, in exchange for a little logic in the database — worth it for a rule that must hold whoever writes the row.
"All employees" as a ruleNo 100,000-row list to write or to keep in step, in exchange for the audience count changing as people join.
A job row instead of notifying inside the publishPublishing stays instant and exactly-once, in exchange for a second step that must be repeatable — which the keys make so.
Plain-text CHECKsCheap defence in depth that can reject an odd but harmless title; escaping at output is still required.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
DatabasePostgreSQL — composite keys, CHECKs, triggers, partial indexes and SKIP LOCKED, all used above
Schedulinga scheduler that runs the due-announcements statement every few seconds on two or more instances — safe by construction
SendingSQS or Kafka for the jobs, per-organization limits in Redis; the delivery row stays the record
Sanitizingoutput escaping in the UI framework; DOMPurify only if formatting is ever allowed
Queries and maintenancepgx with sqlc; pg_partman if the receipts table is partitioned
Worked Example AV — The Database Question, For Clock-In

Database Schema — Employee Clock-In: Punches, Corrections and Timesheets

a punch that happens once, even across partitions · whose clock to trust · corrections, never edits · a timesheet built from two sources · an outside system that can be down
Click to expand

The fifth database question, on the domain of the clock-in service: a punch must be recorded exactly once, never edited, and turned into a timesheet. It opens with a tension that the high-level design doesn't show: the promise of "insert once by punch id" and the choice of "monthly partitions" pull against each other, and the schema is where that has to be resolved. Every statement below was run on PostgreSQL 16.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Clock in, out, and start and end breaks — from a phone, a browser or a shared terminal.
  • Phones keep working without signal and send their punches on reconnecting.
  • A mistake is fixed by a correction that a manager approves; the original stays on record.
  • Timesheets are built from punches plus approved corrections.
  • Companies that keep time in an outside system have punches forwarded there.
Non-functional
  • Never lose a punch, and never count one twice — including across a month boundary.
  • The recorded time is defensible: a phone's clock can be wrong or changed.
  • The shift-start spike is fast: "recorded" within a second.
  • An outside system being down never stops anyone clocking in.
  • Records are kept for years; no organization's rows reach another's.

"Never lose one, never count one twice" is two requirements pulling in opposite directions — retry to avoid losing, and retries are what create duplicates. Partitioning adds a third force, which is what this example is about.

2
Core Entities
  • terminals — shared terminals, per organization.
  • punch_ids — the registry: one row per punch, ever, that pins it to one moment.
  • punches — immutable, partitioned by month; a phone or terminal tap.
  • corrections — a new record that a manager approves; the punch it fixes is never edited.
  • timesheet_days — hours per person per day, built from punches plus approved corrections.
  • provider_links — who a person is in an outside attendance system.
  • provider_sync — one forward per punch and outside system.
  • outbox — the event for each punch, keyed by the punch.

There are no global tables here: every table belongs to one organization.

3
API

For a database question, the "API" is the queries the schema must serve well:

Q1 record a punch — exactly once · Q2 a person's recent punches, and whether a shift is open
Q3 request, approve or reject a correction · Q4 build a day's timesheets
Q5 queue and record a forward to an outside system · Q6 publish the outbox

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. Maya taps "clock in" at 08:58; the app makes punch_id p_4c1 and sends it.
  2. One function inserts the registry row, the punch at the server's time, and the outbox row — one transaction — and replies "recorded".
  3. The reply is lost; the app retries with the same id. The registry recognises it and nothing else happens.
  4. Consumers build the timesheet and queue a forward to the company's outside attendance system.
  5. That system is down; the forward waits in its own row, and Maya's screen says "pending".
  6. Next day she requests a correction for a forgotten clock-out; a manager approves; the timesheet is rebuilt.
5
High-Level Design

A relational schema in PostgreSQL where every table leads with org_id. A small registry table makes "one punch per id" a database fact even though punches are partitioned by month; punches are append-only, and corrections are new rows that someone else must approve. The write path is one function and three inserts. Timesheets are built by a window function from punches plus approved corrections, and forwards to outside systems are their own rows, off the write path.

6
Deep Dives

Six below: (a) a punch happens once, and the partition trap, (b) whose clock to trust, (c) corrections, never edits, (d) the thin write path and the timesheet build, (e) outside attendance systems and the outbox, and (f) many organizations in one database — then the edge cases.

Eight tables, all organization-scoped. The registry pins each punch to one moment, and the punches, the outbox, the forwards and the corrections all point at it. A punch belongs to one terminal or none. The timesheet is built from punches plus approved corrections. PK is a primary key, FK a foreign key, UQ a unique constraint, IX a column that leads an important index.
A retry after midnight
  1. The phone sends punch p_4c1 at 23:59:58; the registry records that moment.
  2. The reply is lost; the app retries at 00:00:03 with the same id.
  3. The registry finds p_4c1 and returns "duplicate" — the new time is never used.
  4. One punch, one outbox row, in the month where it was first received.
A forgotten clock-out
  1. The timesheet shows 213 minutes and an open shift.
  2. She requests a correction: a new row, with a reason.
  3. A different person approves it; the decision is final.
  4. The next build shows 494 minutes; the original punches never changed.
Key deep dive — a punch happens once, and the partition trap
NFRNever lose one, never count one twiceNFRRecords kept for years
Thought process
  1. The client makes the punch_id before its first attempt and sends the same one every time; the server inserts by that id and ignores repeats — as in the clock-in service. The obvious schema is a punches table with PRIMARY KEY (punch_id), partitioned by month so old years can be dropped cheaply.
  2. That combination has a trap. A partitioned table's primary key must contain the partition column, so the key becomes (org_id, punch_id, received_at) — and received_at is the server's time. A retry after midnight gets a new time, doesn't match, and is accepted. Tested: a punch first received at 23:59:58 and retried at 00:00:03 produced 2 rows for one punch. The design in the example promises "insert once", and the schema quietly didn't deliver it.
  3. The fix is a small registry: punch_ids, with PRIMARY KEY (org_id, punch_id) — one row per punch, ever — that also records the received_at. The punches table points at it with a composite foreign key that includes received_at, so a punch row can exist only at the registry's exact moment. A second row for the same punch at another time was refused by the foreign key.
  4. One function does the whole write: insert into the registry with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; if no row comes back it is a retry and nothing else happens; otherwise insert the punch, at the registry's time, and its outbox row, in the same transaction. Three copies of one punch sent at the same instant gave duplicate, duplicate, recorded — one punch row and one outbox row.
  5. It isn't free, and the numbers are honest: the registry cost 210 bytes per punch (201.7 MB for 1,009,000 punches, most of it its two indexes), about 58% on top of the punches table itself (345.8 MB). A cheaper variant drops the exact-moment pin and points punches at the registry by (org_id, punch_id) only, relying on the function for the rest; that gives up a database-enforced guarantee, and it was not run here. Because the foreign key ties each registry row to its punch, the registry lives as long as the punches do.
Illustration — the registry, and the one function that writes a punch
CREATE TABLE punch_ids (                                                   -- the registry: one row per punch
  org_id      uuid NOT NULL,
  punch_id    uuid NOT NULL,                                               -- made by the client
  received_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, punch_id),
  UNIQUE (org_id, punch_id, received_at)                                   -- pins a punch to one moment
);

CREATE TABLE punches ( ... 
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, punch_id, received_at),                     -- must contain the partition column
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, punch_id, received_at)
      REFERENCES punch_ids (org_id, punch_id, received_at),        -- ...so a punch has one moment
  CHECK (occurred_at <= received_at),
  CHECK (offline OR occurred_at = received_at),                    -- online: the server's clock
  CHECK (NOT offline OR device_time IS NOT NULL)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (received_at);
CREATE FUNCTION record_punch(p_org uuid, p_punch uuid, p_member uuid, p_type text, p_device_time timestamptz,
                             p_source text, p_terminal uuid, p_offline boolean, p_occurred timestamptz)
RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE v_at timestamptz;
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO punch_ids (org_id, punch_id) VALUES (p_org, p_punch)
  ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING received_at INTO v_at;
  IF v_at IS NULL THEN RETURN 'duplicate'; END IF;                              -- a retry: nothing else happens
  INSERT INTO punches (org_id, punch_id, membership_id, type, occurred_at, received_at, device_time, source, terminal_id, offline)
  VALUES (p_org, p_punch, p_member, p_type, CASE WHEN p_offline THEN p_occurred ELSE v_at END, v_at, p_device_time, p_source, p_terminal, p_offline);
  INSERT INTO outbox (org_id, punch_id) VALUES (p_org, p_punch);
  RETURN 'recorded';
END $$;
Illustration — the trap and the fix, run for real
CaseWhat happened
a partitioned key with the partition column, no registrypunch first received 23:59:58, retried 00:00:03 — accepted 2 rows for one punch
a second punch row for a registered punch, at another momentrejected foreign key violation
a punch that isn't in the registryrejected foreign key violation
the same registry entry twicerejected unique violation
three copies of one punch at the same instantduplicate, duplicate, recorded · 1 punch row · 1 outbox row
the registry's size210 bytes per punch · 201.7 MB for 1,009,000 punches

The trap is not specific to punches: any table partitioned on a column the client doesn't control can't enforce uniqueness of an id that is client-controlled without help. 32 of 32 writes across the whole schema behaved as intended.

Key deep dive — whose clock to trust
NFRA time the company can defendNFRWorks without signal
Thought process
  1. A phone's clock is under the user's control, so an online punch takes the server's time. The schema says so: CHECK (offline OR occurred_at = received_at) — an online punch whose time is anything but the moment the server heard about it is refused.
  2. An offline punch is the exception, and it has to show its work: it must carry a device_time (CHECK (NOT offline OR device_time IS NOT NULL)), and its time can never be in the future (CHECK (occurred_at <= received_at)). Whether an offline time is believable — the phone's uptime counter against the last sync — is a decision for the API, which sets the row's status to flagged for a manager when the two disagree.
  3. So the database guarantees the parts that can be guaranteed: online punches use the server's clock, offline ones explain themselves, nothing is from the future. The rest is a judgment that is recorded, not silently resolved.
Illustration — the clock rules, run for real
AttemptEnforced byResult
an online punch with a time other than the server'sCHECK on punchesrejected
an offline punch with no device timeCHECK on punchesrejected
a punch that claims to be from the futureCHECK on punchesrejected
an offline punch five minutes late, with its device time—accepted
a terminal punch without a terminal, or a phone punch with oneCHECK on punchesrejected
a terminal punch on another organization's terminalcomposite foreign keyrejected foreign key violation
Key deep dive — corrections, never edits
NFRFix mistakes with a manager's approvalNFRA history that stands up in a dispute
Thought process
  1. Punches are never edited. A trigger refuses UPDATE and DELETE on the punches table — with the message "request a correction" — and a row-level trigger on a partitioned table applies to every partition. Old years leave by dropping a whole partition, which is a different operation and doesn't touch the row rule.
  2. A correction is a new row: what should have happened, why, who asked. Three rules are in the table: a pending correction has no approver (CHECK ((status = 'pending') = …)), nobody can approve a correction that concerns them or that they asked for (decided_by <> requested_by AND decided_by <> membership_id), and once decided it is final (a small trigger). A missing punch is a correction with no punch_id; a wrong one names the punch it replaces.
  3. The timesheet is built from punches plus approved corrections, so nothing has to be rewritten. In the test, one employee's forgotten clock-out left 213 minutes and an open shift; after an approved correction the same build gave 494 minutes and a closed shift — and the day's 3 original punches were exactly as before.
Illustration — a correction, and the rule that makes it final
CREATE TABLE corrections (
  org_id         uuid NOT NULL,
  id             uuid NOT NULL,
  membership_id  uuid NOT NULL,                                            -- whose time is being fixed
  punch_id       uuid,                                                     -- the punch it fixes; NULL adds a missing one
  requested_type text NOT NULL CHECK (requested_type IN ('in','out','break_start','break_end')),
  requested_time timestamptz NOT NULL,
  reason         text NOT NULL CHECK (char_length(reason) >= 3),
  requested_by   uuid NOT NULL,
  requested_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  status         text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending' CHECK (status IN ('pending','approved','rejected')),
  decided_by     uuid,
  decided_at     timestamptz,
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, id),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, punch_id) REFERENCES punch_ids (org_id, punch_id),
  CHECK ((status = 'pending') = (decided_by IS NULL AND decided_at IS NULL)),
  CHECK (decided_by IS NULL OR (decided_by <> requested_by AND decided_by <> membership_id))   -- nobody approves their own
);

CREATE FUNCTION corrections_are_final() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  IF OLD.status <> 'pending' THEN RAISE EXCEPTION 'a decided correction is final'; END IF;
  RETURN NEW;
END $$;
CREATE TRIGGER final_once_decided BEFORE UPDATE ON corrections FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION corrections_are_final();
Illustration — the forgotten clock-out, run for real
StepTimesheet for that dayOriginal punches
before any correction213 minutes · open shift3, untouched
a correction is requested and approved by a manager— (the request itself is a new row)3, untouched
the timesheet is rebuilt494 minutes · shift closed3, untouched
AttemptResult
edit or delete a punchrejected punches are never edited or deleted — request a correction
the requester approving their own correctionrejected CHECK
changing a decision afterwardsrejected a decided correction is final
a reason of one characterrejected CHECK
Key deep dive — the thin write path and the timesheet build
NFRThe shift-start spike is fastNFRHours built from punches plus approved corrections
Thought process
  1. The write path is one function and three inserts (registry, punch, outbox) — nothing else waits for the reply. On one small machine record_punch did 2,026 punches a second on one connection (0.49 ms each) and 2,518 a second on four. The clock-in service puts the peak for a 100,000-person company at about 250 a second, so the write path has roughly ten times that on this machine; treat the ratio, not the absolute, as the point.
  2. The reads are indexed to match. A person's most recent punch — "do they have an open shift?" — took 0.015 ms and their last three days 0.021 ms, from an index led by organization and person, across both monthly partitions.
  3. The timesheet is built by a window function that pairs each in or break-end with the next break or out. For 50,000 people over 999,000 punches, building one day took 0.45 s for 50,000 employees, with 1,000 open shifts found (the 2% who never clocked out). Running the same build again took 0.62 s and left the table at 50,000 rows: the upsert is idempotent, and a guard stops an older build from overwriting a newer one.
Illustration — the build, and what it cost
-- the timesheet for one day: punches plus approved corrections, paired by a window function
WITH ev AS (
  SELECT membership_id, type, occurred_at FROM punches
   WHERE org_id = $1 AND occurred_at >= $2 AND occurred_at < $3
  UNION ALL
  SELECT membership_id, requested_type, requested_time FROM corrections
   WHERE org_id = $1 AND status = 'approved' AND requested_time >= $2 AND requested_time < $3),
seq AS (
  SELECT membership_id, type, occurred_at,
         lead(type) OVER w AS next_type, lead(occurred_at) OVER w AS next_at
  FROM ev WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY membership_id ORDER BY occurred_at))
INSERT INTO timesheet_days (org_id, membership_id, work_date, minutes, open_shift, built_at)
SELECT $1, membership_id, ($2)::date,
       coalesce(sum(extract(epoch FROM next_at - occurred_at) / 60)
                FILTER (WHERE type IN ('in','break_end') AND next_type IN ('break_start','out')), 0)::int,
       coalesce(bool_or(type IN ('in','break_end') AND next_type IS NULL), false),   -- no clock-out: an open shift
       now()
FROM seq GROUP BY membership_id
ON CONFLICT (org_id, membership_id, work_date) DO UPDATE
   SET minutes = excluded.minutes, open_shift = excluded.open_shift, built_at = excluded.built_at
   WHERE timesheet_days.built_at <= excluded.built_at;             -- a late, older build never overwrites a newer one
MeasureResult
a person's last punch0.015 ms — an index scan across the partitions
a person's last three days0.021 ms
building one day for 50,000 people0.45 s · 50,000 rows · 1,000 open shifts
building it again0.62 s · still 50,000 rows
recording punches, 1 connection2,026 a second · 0.49 ms each
recording punches, 4 connections2,518 a second

999,000 punches for 50,000 employees over five days, in a monthly-partitioned table, on one machine; the load skipped foreign-key checks for speed, and 0 punches were found without a registry row afterwards.

Key deep dive — outside attendance systems, and the outbox
NFRAn outside system down never stops a clock-inNFRNothing forwarded twice
Thought process
  1. Who a person is in an outside system is a link: provider_links has UNIQUE (org_id, provider, employee_code), so one code is one person in one system. Two people with the same code in the same system were refused; the same code in another system was accepted.
  2. Forwarding is one row per punch and outside system: provider_sync with PRIMARY KEY (org_id, punch_id, provider), so a forward can't be queued twice, and CHECK (status <> 'sent' OR external_ref IS NOT NULL) refuses to call a forward sent without the outside system's reference. Rows wait in a partial index of queued forwards, by provider, so one system's outage backs up only its own rows and never the write path.
  3. The outbox row is keyed by the punch itself: (org_id, punch_id). The event's id is the punch's id — the same idea as the event id in the notification schema, chosen at the start and never remade — so a relay that publishes twice sends the same id twice, and the consumers dedupe on it.
Illustration — links, forwards and the outbox
CREATE TABLE provider_links (
  org_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  membership_id uuid NOT NULL,
  provider      text NOT NULL,
  employee_code text NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, membership_id, provider),
  UNIQUE (org_id, provider, employee_code)
);

CREATE TABLE provider_sync (
  org_id          uuid NOT NULL,
  punch_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  provider        text NOT NULL,
  status          text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'queued' CHECK (status IN ('queued','sent','failed')),
  attempts        int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (attempts >= 0),
  external_ref    text,
  next_attempt_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  last_error      text,
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, punch_id, provider),                                -- one forward per punch and outside system
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, punch_id) REFERENCES punch_ids (org_id, punch_id),
  CHECK (status <> 'sent' OR external_ref IS NOT NULL)
);

CREATE TABLE outbox (
  org_id       uuid NOT NULL,
  punch_id     uuid NOT NULL,                                              -- the event's id is the punch's id
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  published_at timestamptz,
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, punch_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, punch_id) REFERENCES punch_ids (org_id, punch_id)
);
Key deep dive — many organizations in one database
NFRNo organization's rows reach another'sNFRScales with the largest company
Thought process
  1. org_id leads every key, and every child points at its parent through a key that includes it — a terminal punch on another organization's terminal was refused by the foreign key, and so was a correction for a punch that doesn't exist in that organization.
  2. That is also what lets the data be sharded. Sharding by a hash of org_id keeps an organization's punches, its registry, its outbox and its timesheets on the same shard, so the exactly-once write never has to look across shards; monthly partitions then live inside each shard. It wasn't run here — it is the reason the keys look the way they do.
  3. One very large company's 9:00 is a bigger problem than sharding by organization solves, because it all lands on one shard. That is what a cell of its own is for — see isolating the massive organizations.
Illustration — what keeps organizations apart here
AttemptEnforced byResult
a terminal punch on another organization's terminalcomposite foreign keyrejected
a correction for a punch that isn't in the organizationcomposite foreign keyrejected
the same employee code, another organizationthe key includes org_idaccepted
