the same punch id in two organizationsthe registry key includes org_idaccepted
Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • A phone that syncs three days late — its offline punches arrive with a device time and are recorded at the server's time of arrival; the registry still recognises any retry, however late.
  • Two genuine taps a second apart — each has its own punch id and both are kept; the timesheet treats two identical types seconds apart as one, without deleting either.
  • A month boundary in the middle of a retry — the registry, not the partitioned key, decides "already recorded" — the tested case above.
  • A manager who forgot to clock out — they can request a correction, but someone else must approve it.
  • An outside system that comes back after a day — its queued forwards drain in order from the partial index; punches never waited for it.
  • Years of retention — old months are dropped as whole partitions; the registry and corrections are kept as long as their punches are needed.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Never lost, never counted twiceA registry with an exact-moment foreign key: a retry after midnight, refused; 3 concurrent copies gave 1 recorded, 2 duplicates.
A time the company can defendOnline punches must use the server's clock; offline ones must carry their device time; nothing from the future.
A history that stands up in a disputePunches can't be edited or deleted; corrections are new rows, approved by someone else, and final once decided.
The shift-start spike is fastAbout 2,026–2,518 recorded punches a second on one small machine, against a ~250/s peak for a 100,000-person company.
Timesheets from punches plus correctionsOne day for 50,000 people in 0.45 s, rebuilt idempotently; a forgotten clock-out fixed from 213 to 494 minutes with the originals untouched.
An outside system down changes nothingForwards are their own rows, per punch and provider, off the write path.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
A registry beside the punches210 bytes per punch, about 58% on top of the punches table, in exchange for a database-enforced "exactly one punch per id" that survives partitioning.
Monthly partitions for retentionCheap deletion of old years, in exchange for a key that must contain the partition column — which is what made the registry necessary.
Corrections as rowsEvery change is visible and attributable, in exchange for the timesheet build having to combine two sources.
CHECKs for the clock rulesCheap guarantees for the parts that can be guaranteed; the believability of an offline time stays a recorded judgment, not a constraint.
The outbox keyed by the punchNo second id to invent and safe republishing, in exchange for one event per punch — fine here, where a punch is one fact.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
DatabasePostgreSQL — declarative partitioning, composite foreign keys, CHECKs, triggers, window functions, all used above
Partitions and retentionpg_partman for monthly partitions created ahead of time and dropped on schedule
Outbox and forwardinga polling relay, or Debezium's outbox pattern into Kafka; one queue per outside system
ShardingCitus or application routing by a hash of the organization, keeping an organization's tables together
Queriespgx with sqlc
Worked Example AW — The Database Question, For Payslips

Database Schema — Payslips and Tax Documents: Runs, Documents and Release

frozen at confirmation · never half a run · release as one row · the owner in every lookup · corrections as versions · kept for years, then deleted
Click to expand

The sixth database question, on the domain of the payslip and tax-document example: when payroll is confirmed, a document is produced for every employee, everything is checked before a chosen moment, and then all of it is released at once — to the right person only. The schema is where "never half a run" and "nobody else's payslip" stop being intentions. Every statement below was run on PostgreSQL 16.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • When payroll is confirmed, produce a document for every employee in the run.
  • Release them all at a chosen time and notify each employee.
  • Employees list and download their own documents.
  • A mistake is fixed by a corrected version; the original stays on record.
  • Departed employees can still retrieve their own documents for a set period.
Non-functional
  • No one can retrieve another person's document.
  • Nothing is visible until the whole run is generated and checked.
  • The payday rush is fast, however many open at once.
  • A document shows exactly what was issued, years later.
  • Documents are kept for the required period, encrypted, then deleted — unless a legal hold applies.

The fourth requirement quietly rules out the design most people start with — rendering the payslip from current data whenever someone opens it. Everything in this schema follows from that.

2
Core Entities
  • document_types — the keeping period per type. Global.
  • payroll_runs — one per organization and period; a status that can only move forward.
  • documents — one per employee per run and type; versions; a render state; a storage key under the organization's prefix.
  • snapshots — the frozen, encrypted figures, one per document.
  • legal_holds — stops an owner's documents being deleted.
  • document_views — an append-only access log.

Only document_types is global; every other table belongs to one organization.

3
API

For a database question, the "API" is the queries the schema must serve well:

Q1 confirm a run: documents and snapshots · Q2 a render worker claims a batch
Q3 mark the run ready · Q4 release it
Q5 my documents · Q6 the ownership check for a download
Q7 reissue a corrected version · Q8 delete what has expired

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. On the 20th, HR confirms the run for 100,000 employees: a document row and a frozen snapshot for each, all queued.
  2. Render workers claim batches of 500 and produce private PDFs; each finished document records its key, checksum and size.
  3. The run can become ready only when no document is left; the admin schedules the release.
  4. At 09:00 the run is published — one row — and every document becomes visible at once; each employee is notified once.
  5. Maya opens hers: the lookup includes her membership, so it is hers or it is a 404; she gets a 60-second link.
  6. A mistake is found: the document is reissued as version 2; version 1 stays, marked superseded.
5
High-Level Design

A relational schema in PostgreSQL where every table but one leads with org_id. A run's status can only move forward, and it can't become ready while any document isn't. Documents are created invisible and become visible through one row — their run being published — so release is instant. Every lookup includes the owner, files live under the organization's prefix, snapshots are frozen and encrypted, and corrections are new versions with exactly one current. Retention joins a small table of keeping periods and respects legal holds.

6
Deep Dives

Six below: (a) frozen at confirmation, (b) releasing everything at once, (c) nobody else's payslip, ever, (d) rendering 100,000 documents before payday, (e) corrections, versions and keeping documents for years, and (f) many organizations, one payday — then the edge cases.

Six tables. Document types are global; the rest belong to one organization. A run has many documents; each document has one snapshot and one type, and is viewed and held by membership. Only the current version of a document is visible by default. PK is a primary key, FK a foreign key, UQ a unique constraint, IX a column that leads an important index.
Releasing the run
  1. Every document is ready, so the run may become ready.
  2. The admin schedules the release; the schedule exists only on a ready run.
  3. At the due time one row changes: the run is published.
  4. Every document is visible at once, because visibility is a join to the run.
Someone else's document id
  1. A request names a document id and comes from a membership.
  2. The lookup includes the owner, and the run must be released.
  3. Someone else's id matches no row.
  4. The API answers 404 — the same as for an id that doesn't exist.
Key deep dive — frozen at confirmation, so it shows what was issued
NFRA document shows exactly what was issued, years laterNFREncrypted, kept, then deleted
Thought process
  1. The payslip and tax-document example rules out rendering a payslip from current data. The schema is what makes that concrete: confirming a run writes a snapshot for every document — the exact figures, encrypted, with a hash — and the document records the template_version it was rendered with. Years later, the same snapshot and the same template give the same page.
  2. A snapshot is frozen: a trigger refuses any UPDATE, and the primary key (org_id, doc_id) allows one snapshot per document. The figures are stored as data_enc with a key_id — encrypted with the organization's key by the application, so the database never holds them in the clear and deleting a key makes every copy unreadable.
  3. A snapshot points at its document with a composite foreign key that includes the organization, so it can't be attached to another organization's document. In the test: editing a snapshot, a second snapshot for one document, and a snapshot for another organization's document were all refused.
  4. Because a snapshot is one row per document, it is also the biggest table of the run: 100,000 snapshots for a 100,000-person payroll here. It is written once at confirmation and read only to render or re-render.
Illustration — the snapshot, and the trigger that freezes it
CREATE TABLE snapshots (
  org_id     uuid NOT NULL,
  doc_id     uuid NOT NULL,
  data_enc   bytea NOT NULL,                                               -- the frozen figures, encrypted with the organization's key
  key_id     text NOT NULL,
  hash       bytea NOT NULL,
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, doc_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, doc_id) REFERENCES documents (org_id, id)
);
CREATE FUNCTION snapshot_is_frozen() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN RAISE EXCEPTION 'a snapshot is frozen at confirmation'; END $$;
CREATE TRIGGER frozen BEFORE UPDATE ON snapshots FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION snapshot_is_frozen();
Illustration — what the database refused
AttemptEnforced byResult
editing a snapshota triggerrejected a snapshot is frozen at confirmation
a second snapshot for the same documentprimary keyrejected unique violation
a snapshot for a document of another organizationcomposite foreign keyrejected foreign key violation
a snapshot for a document of the same organization—accepted

38 of 38 writes across the whole schema behaved as intended; each rejection was checked against the specific constraint type it was meant to trigger.

Key deep dive — releasing everything at once
NFRNever half a runNFRRelease at a chosen time
Thought process
  1. A run moves draft → confirmed → generating → ready → published, and a trigger lists the only legal steps: a draft can't jump to published, and a published run can't go back. CHECKs keep the timestamps honest — a schedule (publish_at) can exist only on a ready or published run, a published run has a published_at.
  2. The rule that matters most is in the same trigger: a run can't become ready while any document isn't. With 100,000 documents still queued, the attempt was refused in 0.7 ms, because a small partial index holds only the not-ready documents. Once every document was ready, the run became ready in 30.3 ms. (Marking those 100,000 documents ready took 2.98 s — it is the rendering that takes the time, not the check.)
  3. Release is then one row. Documents are created invisible, and a document is visible when its run is published and publish_at has passed — a join, not a flag on every document. Publishing the run took 0.7 ms; flipping a flag on each of the run's 100,000 documents instead took 3.39 s (measured, then rolled back). Before the release the owner's own download check returned 0 rows; after, 1.
  4. Only one regular run per organization and period is allowed — a partial unique index on (org_id, period) WHERE kind = 'regular' — while off-cycle runs can repeat. Two regular runs for the same month were refused; an off-cycle one was accepted.
Illustration — the run, and the guard that keeps half a run from leaving
CREATE TABLE payroll_runs (
  org_id       uuid NOT NULL,
  id           uuid NOT NULL,
  period       text NOT NULL CHECK (period ~ '^[0-9]{4}-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])$'),
  kind         text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'regular' CHECK (kind IN ('regular','off_cycle')),
  status       text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'draft' CHECK (status IN ('draft','confirmed','generating','ready','published')),
  confirmed_at timestamptz,
  publish_at   timestamptz,
  published_at timestamptz,
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, id),
  CHECK (status = 'draft' OR confirmed_at IS NOT NULL),
  CHECK (publish_at IS NULL OR status IN ('ready','published')),           -- only a finished run can be scheduled
  CHECK ((status = 'published') = (published_at IS NOT NULL)),
  CHECK (status <> 'published' OR publish_at IS NOT NULL)
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_regular_run ON payroll_runs (org_id, period) WHERE kind = 'regular';
CREATE FUNCTION run_guard() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  IF NEW.status <> OLD.status THEN
    IF NOT ((OLD.status = 'draft'      AND NEW.status = 'confirmed')  OR
            (OLD.status = 'confirmed'  AND NEW.status = 'generating') OR
            (OLD.status = 'generating' AND NEW.status = 'ready')      OR
            (OLD.status = 'ready'      AND NEW.status = 'published')) THEN
      RAISE EXCEPTION 'a run cannot go from % to %', OLD.status, NEW.status;
    END IF;
    IF NEW.status = 'ready' AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM documents d WHERE d.org_id = NEW.org_id AND d.run_id = NEW.id AND d.render_state <> 'ready') THEN
      RAISE EXCEPTION 'a run is not ready while a document is not';
    END IF;
  END IF;
  RETURN NEW;
END $$;
Illustration — the release, run for real
StepResult
the run becomes ready while documents are queuedrejected in 0.7 ms · 100,000 not ready
the run becomes ready when every document isaccepted in 30.3 ms
publish the run — one row0.7 ms
flip a flag on every one of its documents instead3.39 s for 100,000 rows (rolled back)
a draft run going straight to publishedrejected a run cannot go from draft to published
a second regular run for the same periodrejected unique violation
an off-cycle run in the same periodaccepted
Key deep dive — nobody else's payslip, ever
NFRNo one retrieves another person's documentNFRA fast payday rush
Thought process
  1. The classic failure is a lookup by document id alone, which returns someone else's payslip because it checked the document exists but not who owns it. So the owner is in the lookup: WHERE id = $2 AND membership_id = $3. Someone else's id, or an unreleased run, returns no row — the same answer as a document that doesn't exist, so the API can say 404 for both.
  2. Tested on 610,000 documents: the owner's download check took 0.024 ms and returned one row after the release; the same document asked for by another person returned 0 rows. "My documents" — 7 rows across seven runs — took 0.044 ms from an index led by the owner.
  3. The file's location is constrained too: a document's storage_key must start with its organization's id (CHECK (storage_key LIKE org_id::text || '/%')). A key under another organization's prefix was refused, so a bug in the renderer can't file one company's payslips under another's path.
  4. Access is logged: document_views is append-only, refusing UPDATE and DELETE. The storage itself is private and served through short-lived signed links, which is outside the database; the schema's job is the ownership check that decides whether a link is issued.
Illustration — the ownership check, and the release rule it includes
-- the download check: the owner is IN the lookup, and the run must be released
SELECT d.storage_key
FROM documents d JOIN payroll_runs r ON r.org_id = d.org_id AND r.id = d.run_id
WHERE d.org_id = $1 AND d.id = $2 AND d.membership_id = $3          -- somebody else's id: no row, so a 404
  AND r.status = 'published' AND r.publish_at <= now();

-- my documents
SELECT d.id, r.period, d.type, d.version, d.status
FROM documents d JOIN payroll_runs r ON r.org_id = d.org_id AND r.id = d.run_id
WHERE d.org_id = $1 AND d.membership_id = $2 AND r.status = 'published' AND r.publish_at <= now()
ORDER BY r.period DESC, d.version DESC;

-- releasing a whole run is one row
UPDATE payroll_runs SET status = 'published', published_at = now() WHERE org_id = $1 AND id = $2;
Illustration — asking for a payslip
Who asksFor whatRows
the ownerbefore the run is released0
the ownerafter the release1
another personthe same document id, after the release0
MeasureResult
the download check0.024 ms — a primary-key lookup plus the run
my documents (7 rows)0.044 ms — an index led by the owner
a file under another organization's prefixrejected CHECK
rewriting an access log entryrejected append-only trigger

A person named Carter and another person named Carter are different memberships, so the owner match never confuses them — the link from the identity schema is what carries that.

Key deep dive — rendering 100,000 documents before payday
NFREverything generated and checked before the releaseNFRFailures visible, not hidden
Thought process
  1. Each document is its own row with a render state — queued → rendering → ready, or failed — so the render fleet needs no separate queue table. A worker claims a batch of queued documents with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, over a partial index of queued rows: 0.608 ms for the plan.
  2. Two workers claiming at once, 20 claims of 500 each, got 20,000 documents, 20,000 distinct, 0 shared. A claim that updates 500 rows took a median of 40.7 ms.
  3. The checks on the row say what "ready" means: a ready document must have a storage key, a checksum and a size, and a rendering one must have a claim time. A failed document stays visible — the admin sees "49,988 ready, 12 failed" because the not-ready partial index holds exactly the documents that block the run.
  4. The renderer works from the snapshot, not from live data, so a re-render after a fix produces the same figures; it only changes the template version, which the new row records.
Illustration — the claim, and what the render race did
-- a render worker claims a batch; another worker's rows are skipped
UPDATE documents SET render_state = 'rendering', claimed_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1
WHERE (org_id, id) IN (
  SELECT org_id, id FROM documents
  WHERE org_id = $1 AND run_id = $2 AND render_state = 'queued'
  ORDER BY id LIMIT 500
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
RETURNING id;
MeasureResult
the claim's planLockRows over Index Scan using documents_to_render on documents — 0.608 ms
two workers, 20 claims of 500 each20,000 claimed · 20,000 distinct · 0 shared · 0.86 s
a ready document without a checksumrejected CHECK
a rendering document without a claim timerejected CHECK

One machine, one organization's 100,000 documents: the plan and the disjoint claims are the result; the absolute times are small.

Key deep dive — corrections, versions and keeping documents for years
NFRCorrected versions, originals keptNFRKept for the required period, then deleted
Thought process
  1. A correction is a new version: the current row is marked superseded and a new one is inserted with the next version, in one function. Only the current version can be superseded, so reissuing a version that is already superseded returns nothing.
  2. A partial unique index — (org_id, run_id, membership_id, type) WHERE status = 'current' — allows exactly one current version of a payslip. Trying to insert a second current one was refused, which is why the function supersedes the old row first. Both versions keep their own snapshot and template version, so each still shows what it said the day it was issued.
  3. Retention is per document type: document_types.keep_years is a small global table, and a delete joins it. A legal hold stops a person's documents from being deleted: legal_holds rows with no release date. In the test, 10,000 expired documents, 100 of them held, deleted 9,900 in 0.42 s, and left the 100 held.
  4. Encryption completes it: because each snapshot names the key it was encrypted with, retiring an organization's key makes every copy unreadable — including in backups — which is how a company that leaves is truly removed.
Illustration — reissuing, and retention with legal holds
CREATE FUNCTION reissue_document(p_org uuid, p_doc uuid, p_template text) RETURNS uuid LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE d documents%ROWTYPE; v_new uuid := gen_random_uuid();
BEGIN
  UPDATE documents SET status = 'superseded', superseded_at = now()
   WHERE org_id = p_org AND id = p_doc AND status = 'current' RETURNING * INTO d;      -- only the current version can be replaced
  IF NOT FOUND THEN RETURN NULL; END IF;
  INSERT INTO documents (org_id, id, run_id, membership_id, type, version, template_version)
  VALUES (p_org, v_new, d.run_id, d.membership_id, d.type, d.version + 1, p_template);
  RETURN v_new;
END $$;
-- retention: expired documents go, unless their owner is under a legal hold
DELETE FROM documents d USING document_types t
WHERE t.type = d.type AND d.org_id = $1
  AND d.created_at < now() - make_interval(years => t.keep_years)
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM legal_holds h
                  WHERE h.org_id = d.org_id AND h.membership_id = d.membership_id AND h.released_at IS NULL);
Illustration — the versions and the holds, run for real
AttemptResult
reissue the current versionaccepted v2 created, v1 superseded and kept
reissue a version that is already supersededreturns nothing
a second current version of the same paysliprejected one_current_version
the same version number twicerejected unique violation
a legal hold released before it beganrejected CHECK
retention: 10,000 expired documents, 100 on hold9,900 deleted in 0.42 s; 100 kept
Key deep dive — many organizations, one payday
NFRNo organization's files or figures reach another'sNFRScales with the largest payroll
Thought process
  1. org_id leads every key, and every child points at its parent through a key that includes it: a document for another organization's run, a snapshot for another organization's document, and a file under another organization's prefix were all refused. The same period in two organizations is fine — the run's uniqueness is per organization.
  2. Because org_id is in every key, the big tables — documents and snapshots, hundreds of thousands of rows for one payroll — can be hash-partitioned by organization, as tested in the notification schema; and the same keys are what a cell of its own needs (see isolating the massive organizations). It was not run again here.
  3. A run for a very large organization is the whole platform's peak in miniature: 100,000 documents to render before one moment. That is exactly what the render claim, the not-ready guard and the one-row release are shaped for.
Illustration — what keeps organizations apart here
AttemptEnforced byResult
a document for a run of another organizationcomposite foreign keyrejected
a snapshot for another organization's documentcomposite foreign keyrejected
a file under another organization's prefixCHECK on the storage keyrejected
the same period in a second organizationthe run's unique index includes org_idaccepted
Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • A run with failed renders — it can't become ready; the admin sees which documents failed, fixes the cause, and re-queues them — the snapshot means the figures don't change.
  • A departed employee — their documents are still theirs by membership; how long they may retrieve them is decided where access is decided, not stored here.
  • A correction after retention has started — the new version starts its own keeping period; the superseded one follows its own.
  • A person in two organizations — one membership per organization, so each company's documents are kept apart by the owner match.
  • An off-cycle run — allowed alongside the regular run of the same period; only regular runs are unique.
  • The template changes after issue — old documents keep their template version and snapshot, so they still show what they showed.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
No one retrieves another person's documentThe owner is in the lookup: another person's request returned 0 rows, and an unreleased run returned 0 even for the owner. Files must sit under their organization's prefix.
Never half a runA trigger refuses "ready" while any document isn't: refused in 0.7 ms with 100,000 pending.
Release at a chosen timeOne row: 0.7 ms, against 3.39 s to flip 100,000 documents.
A document shows what was issuedA frozen, encrypted snapshot and a template version per document; both versions of a corrected payslip keep their own.
The payday rush is fastAn ownership check in 0.024 ms and "my documents" in 0.044 ms.
Kept for the required period, then deletedPer-type keeping periods and legal holds: 9,900 expired documents deleted, 100 held ones kept, in 0.42 s.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Visibility from the run, not from each documentOne-row release and a join at read time, in exchange for every "my documents" query joining to the run.
Snapshots for every documentA big, write-once table, in exchange for a document that always shows what it said on the day.
A trigger for the run's rulesThe ready check and legal transitions in one place, in exchange for logic in the database — worth it for a rule that must hold whoever writes the row.
Render state on the document rowNo separate queue table, in exchange for a partial index that churns during the run.
Organization prefix in the storage keyA cheap, constraint-level wall, in exchange for a key format that can never be reorganized without a migration.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
DatabasePostgreSQL — composite keys, partial unique indexes, CHECKs, triggers and SKIP LOCKED, all used above
Filesprivate object storage (S3 or similar) with short-lived signed links; a key per organization in KMS
Renderinga fleet of render workers reading the snapshot; Chromium or a PDF library
Encryptionenvelope encryption with a key per organization; crypto-shredding to retire one
Retentiona scheduled job running the retention statement; pg_partman if the documents table is partitioned
Before You Walk In

Interview Playbook — Facilitating the 60 Minutes

The interviewer is a tech lead and a product owner in one chair. That changes the job: you are not answering an exam question, you are running a 60-minute design meeting — agreeing what to build with the product owner, letting the tech lead challenge the design, and keeping the clock. The Framework above is what to produce at each step; this section is how to carry it: the clock, the behaviour, three questions to ask of every box — scale, failure, metrics — and what to say when the conversation leaves the script.

The one-sentence model

You facilitate; they steer. You own the agenda, the pace and the decisions. They own the scope and the challenge. Facilitating is not talking more — it is making it easy for two busy people to agree with you, or to disagree usefully.

A · The 60 minutes at a glance

Eight blocks, one hard stop. The blocks are a plan, not a script — if the interviewer wants to go straight to a deep dive at minute 20, go, and say out loud what you are skipping. Colours show who is leading each block: you set the frame and the wrap, the product-owner hat decides scope, the tech-lead hat drives the challenge.

The 60 minutes. The numbered circles match the rows below the bar; the yellow ticks are the checkpoints — each one is a single, specific question to the interviewer. Requirements, numbers, entities and API together take about a quarter of the time; deep dives get the biggest block.
Three rules of the clock
RuleWhy
Deep dives get the biggest block — 20 of the 60 minutesThat is where the interview is decided. Everything before it exists to make it possible, which is the same rule the Interview-Day Checklist gives: requirements + API ≈ 25%.
The failure · scale · metrics sweep is protectedIf you are behind, shorten a deep dive. Never skip the sweep: it is the six minutes that show you have run a system, not only drawn one.
Checkpoint at every boundary — at least four timesScope (minute 9), the API (17), the first design and the choice of deep dives (30), the recap (56). Each is one question — "is this the scope you want before I draw?" — never a bare "does that make sense?".

Published guidance on the format agrees on the shape: a couple of minutes to frame, five to ten on requirements, ten to fifteen on the high-level design, fifteen to twenty on deep dives, and five to ten on bottlenecks and failure. For a 45-minute round keep the order and scale every block to three quarters.

B · Two hats in one chair

The person across from you is usually a product owner and a tech lead in one seat, and they will switch without warning. Each hat wants different things from you, asks different questions back, and needs the answer in different words.

HatWhat they care aboutAsk themThey will probeAnswer in terms of
Product ownerwho the users are · the outcome that matters · what the first release contains · what can wait · what a late, duplicated or wrong result costs a user
  • "Who uses this, and what does success look like?"
  • "Which matters more here — X or Y?"
  • "Is it OK if this arrives 30 seconds late? twice? never?"
  • "First release, or the end state?"
scope creep ("can it also…?") · priorities · the user-visible effect of your trade-offswhat the user sees: "it may arrive late, but never twice"
Tech leadscale · correctness · failure · operability · cost · fit with the team
  • "What does the team already run?"
  • "Any hard constraints — cloud, compliance, a latency budget?"
  • "How much scale for now, and how much for later?"
"why this database?" · "what happens when X fails?" · "how would you roll it out?" · "how do you know it works?"a decision, its cost, and the metric that would tell you it was wrong

When they switch hats, name it: "As a product owner you might want X; as a tech lead you would worry about Y — I'll design for Y and flag X." It shows you heard both, and it turns a challenge into a decision you make together.

C · How to facilitate — nine behaviours

Facilitating is not talking more. It is making it easy for two busy people to agree with you, or to disagree usefully. Nine behaviours do most of the work:

BehaviourWhat it sounds likeWhy it works
1 · Own the agenda"I'll take about seven minutes on requirements, then a first design, then two deep dives. Tell me if you want a different mix."They can redirect in the first minute instead of the thirtieth.
2 · Offer a default, ask for a veto"I'll assume 10 million users and a peak of five times the average — say so if that's off."Cheaper for the product owner than answering from a blank; shows judgement.
3 · Ask product questions, not trivia"What happens to the user if this arrives late?" — not "how many users do you have?"A product question surfaces the non-functional requirement; a number alone doesn't.
4 · Make it visibleKeep the requirements, the numbers, the decisions and a parking lot in a corner of the board.Nobody has to remember, and "I'll come back to that" becomes a promise you can keep.
5 · Decide, then price the decision"I'd use a queue here, because payday is spiky. The cost is added delay and duplicates, so consumers must be idempotent."A list of options reads as a survey; a priced decision reads as an engineer.
6 · Checkpoint with a specific question"Is this the scope you want before I draw?" · "Which of these two would you like deeper?""Does that make sense?" invites a nod. A specific question invites a steer.
7 · Invite the attackAfter the first design: "Where would you poke first?"You get the tech lead's real concern on the table — and it becomes your deep dive.
8 · Say what you don't know"I don't remember the exact number; I'll assume about N and I'd confirm it by measuring."Honest, and it comes with a way forward. Bluffing is the one thing they can't recover from.
9 · Recover out loud"I got that wrong: the fan-out is per person, not per event. That changes the number to…"A visible correction builds more trust than a design that was never wrong.

D · Three questions for every box: scale, failure, metrics

Junior answers draw boxes. Senior answers question them. For every box and arrow — not only at the end — ask the same three things, out loud, before the interviewer does. That is what the sweep in minute 50 collects; the habit is what makes it fast.

The three questions. Scale finds what breaks first, failure finds what the user sees when it does, and measure finds how you would know.
1 · Scale — climb the ladder only as far as the number requires

The drill has five questions: what grows (users, data, requests, fan-out)? Where is the hot spot (a key, a tenant, a partition)? What is the partition key, and why? What breaks first at 10× — and at 100×? What is the cheapest lever? Climb in order — one node, a bigger node, replicas, a cache, a queue, a partition, a cell — and name the cost at each step. The Scale Ladder has the full ladder.

SymptomLeverThe cost you must sayOn this page
Reads dominatea cache in front · read replicas · a CDN for static contentstale data · invalidation · a cold startCaching Playbook
Writes outgrow one nodepartition or shard by a key that spreads the load and keeps related rows togetherhot keys · cross-shard queries · re-shardingData Stores & Partitioning
Spiky traffic — payday, 09:00a queue to smooth the spike · autoscale ahead of the known peakadded delay · queue lag to watchPayslips · Notifications
One heavy tenantper-tenant limits · fair turns · a dedicated cell for the largestmore to run · a migration to planIsolating massive orgs · Multi-tenant limits
A slow downstreamasynchronous work · a rate limit · backpressure · a dead-letter queuethe user waits longerWebhooks
One event fans out to many peoplefan-out in batches · precompute on write, or compute on readstorage against latency · every batch must be repeatableNotification schema
A hot key — a celebrity, a viral itemsplit the key with a suffix · a small local cache in frontcomplexity · a slightly stale copyCaching Playbook
Data grows foreverretention · time partitions · tiering to cheaper storageslower restores · legal holdsPayslip schema
Users are far awayregional replicas · a CDN · multi-regionconsistency · costDisaster Recovery
Everyone retries at onceexponential backoff with jitter · a retry budgetslower recoveryResilient Front Door
Out loud — scale, with a number from this system"A million employees, ten percent opening a payslip in the first five minutes: 100,000 opens over 300 seconds — about 333 a second. That's light for an ownership check and a signed link, so payday is not a serving problem. It's a generation problem: 100,000 documents that must be ready before 09:00. That's where I'd spend the deep dive." The move: turn a scary number into the one place the design must work hard.
2 · Failure — for every arrow: down, slow, duplicated, out of order, wrong?

Ask the five words of every arrow, then answer four things: what the user sees meanwhile, whether it can retry safely, what the degraded mode is (stale, queued, partial — anything better than blank), and how far the damage spreads (one user, one tenant, everyone). Then say your pre-mortem: the three ways this system is most likely to fail in production.

FailureThe user seesThe design answerOn this page
A dependency is down or slowerrors, or a spinnertimeouts from a deadline · retries with backoff and jitter · a circuit breaker · a bulkhead · a fallback that is stale or queuedResilient Front Door
A request or message arrives twicea double charge · two emailsidempotency keys · a unique key on the work itself · safe retriesIdempotent Payments · Notifications
A change is saved but never announcedsomething happened that nobody was toldthe outbox: save the change and its event in one transaction, publish at least onceOutbox table
Overload, or a spikeslow pages · timeouts for everyonea queue to smooth · shed low-priority work first · backpressure · autoscale ahead of known peaksPriority lanes
One tenant floods the systemother companies slow downper-tenant limits · fair queues · a dedicated cell for the largestMulti-tenant limits · Isolation
A poison message keeps failingone queue stuck behind ita retry limit · a dead-letter queue · an alert on its sizeWebhooks
A hot cache key expiresa sudden database spikeTTL jitter · request coalescing · serve stale while refreshingCaching Playbook
A bad deploy or configerrors right after a releasea canary · feature flags · a fast rollback · config validated before it swaps inAPI Gateway
A zone or a region is lostan outage, or a slower servicereplicas across zones · a stated RPO and RTO · a failover you have rehearsedDisaster Recovery
A bug corrupts datawrong numbers, discovered laterappend-only history · backups you have actually restored · reconciliation jobsData Correctness · Audit Logging
Out loud — a pre-mortem, in twenty seconds"If this pages me at 3 a.m., I expect one of three things: · the email provider degrading — the dashboard shows send errors climbing; the system fails over to the second provider by itself · one company flooding a queue — its share of the queue jumps; per-company limits keep everyone else on time · a bad deploy — errors start at the release time; we roll back within minutes. For each, what the user sees is a delay, never a lost message."
3 · Measure — what tells me it is healthy, and what wakes me at 3 a.m.?

Start from the user, not the servers. Alert on symptoms (users are hurting) and keep causes on a dashboard; every alert needs an owner and a first step. Percentiles, not averages, and the age of the oldest item in a queue, not only its depth — a queue can be short and stuck. The thresholds below are illustrative: you would derive them from the promise (the SLO), not from a table.

LayerMeasureAlert when
What the user feels — the SLIsuccess rate and p95/p99 latency for each key journey — never the averagethe error budget is burning fast (an SLO burn-rate alert), not on one bad minute
Trafficrequests per second, in total and per tenanta sudden drop — an outage can look like quiet — or a spike
Errors5xx and 4xx counted separately · errors by dependency5xx above the SLO for a few minutes
SaturationCPU, memory, connections, threads, disk — whichever runs out firstit approaches the limit that would hurt, with time left to act
Queues and streamsdepth and the age of the oldest message · consumer lagthe oldest age exceeds what you promised users
Databasereplication lag · slow queries · lock waits · connection-pool use · disk growthlag above the staleness you allow · the pool nearly exhausted
Cachehit ratio · evictions · latencythe hit ratio falls — the database is about to take the load
Asynchronous workthe oldest unpublished outbox row · dead-letter queue sizeanything stuck past your delay budget · any dead-letter growth
Correctnessduplicates · reconciliation mismatchesabove zero, where zero is the promise
Business outcomewhat the product exists for: messages delivered in time, payslips opened, orders paidit falls below its normal band
Per tenantthe top-N share of each resourceone tenant above its share for days — a noisy neighbour
Costspend per tenant and per featuregrowth outpaces usage

See Observability & Alerting for how the metrics system itself is designed.

Example — the notification systemWhy this oneAlert (illustrative)
age of the oldest queued security notificationthe promise is "within seconds"over 10 s → page
age of the oldest unpublished outbox rowevents are safe, but nobody has been toldover 60 s → page
duplicate in-app deliveriesthe promise is exactly onceabove 0 → ticket
email provider error rateone provider failing must not stop emailover 5% for 5 minutes → fail over, ticket
one company's share of a queuea noisy neighbourover 40% for 10 minutes → alert, consider a cell

E · Minute by minute — what to do and what not to

The action items, phase by phase. Each row ends with a test you can apply to yourself: done when. If you cannot say it is done, do not move on — or say out loud that you are moving on with something still open.

WhenDoDon'tDone when
Before minute 0
  • have a blank canvas and a pen ready
  • know your skeleton: frame → requirements → numbers → API → design → deep dives → sweep → wrap
  • decide where on the board the requirements, numbers, decisions and parking lot go
  • take ten seconds of silence to breathe
  • arrive with one memorised architecture
  • bend the question to fit the example you studied last night
you know the first sentence you will say
0–2
Frame
  • restate the prompt in one sentence
  • propose the agenda with rough time boxes
  • ask: "does that work, or is there an area you want more depth on?"
  • start drawing
  • ask a run of questions without saying where you are heading
the interviewer has agreed to, or changed, the plan
2–9
Requirements
  • ask 3–5 questions in the product owner's language: users, outcome, priority, tolerance for late, duplicated or wrong
  • split into functional and non-functional; rank; draw the scope line; name what is out
  • put numbers on the top three non-functionals and say your assumptions
  • accept "whatever you think" without stating your assumption
  • ask questions whose answer would not change the design
  • list fifteen features
  • treat this as a formality
a top 3–5 feature list, three numbered non-functionals, an out-of-scope line — and a "yes"
9–12
Numbers
  • compute only what changes the design: peak requests per second, storage per year, fan-out, the hottest key or tenant
  • use round numbers and units; finish each with "so what" — one node or many? a queue or direct?
  • spend more than about three minutes
  • claim false precision
  • compute numbers you never use
3–4 numbers are on the board, each with a consequence
12–17
Entities + API
  • name 4–6 entities and 3–6 endpoints, each tied to a functional requirement
  • mention idempotency, pagination or auth only where they matter here
  • draw a full CRUD API for every entity
  • list every column
  • bikeshed REST against RPC
every requirement has an endpoint, and every endpoint has a requirement
17–30
High-level design
  • draw the simplest design that meets the functional requirements first
  • number the arrows and walk one write and one read
  • say why each datastore fits its access pattern
  • end with: "where would you like me to dig in?"
  • start with twelve boxes
  • name tools without a reason
  • split into microservices because it looks serious
  • draw in silence
one diagram exists, a request has been traced through it, and the deep dives are chosen
30–50
Deep dives
  • pick 2–3 from the riskiest non-functionals and the interviewer's interest
  • for each: the problem with a number → two options → your decision → its cost → the metric that says it works
  • time-box each to about 7–10 minutes; restate a follow-up before answering it
  • dive into something not tied to a requirement
  • list options without choosing
  • recite "add a cache" with no key, number or invalidation story
  • argue against a valid critique
each deep dive ended with a decision and its price
50–56
Failure · scale · metrics
  • say the three questions out loud
  • name the top 3 failure modes and the degraded mode
  • say what breaks first at 10×
  • list 4–6 metrics and 2 alerts; add a sentence on security or privacy if the data is sensitive
  • skip it because you are short of time
  • list every failure that could exist
  • say "we'd monitor everything"
you have named failures, a scale limit, and what would page you
56–60
Wrap
  • recap against the requirements in about 30 seconds
  • state the trade-offs and the decisions still open
  • say what you would build first, and what next
  • ask what they would have liked deeper
  • apologise
  • introduce a new component
  • criticise your own design
  • run past time
you finished on time, and the last word was theirs

F · When it goes off script — what to say

Interviews leave the script. These are the twelve moments that most often throw people, with the sentence to reach for.

SituationWhat to sayWhy it works
The prompt is one line"Before I design anything, can I check who it's for and what success looks like? Then I'll propose a scope, and you tell me if it's off."You set the process without stalling.
The product owner says "you decide""I'll assume X and Y. I'll say where those assumptions drive the design, so you can change them."Assumptions become visible instead of silent.
You don't remember a number or a fact"I don't remember the exact figure — I'll assume about N for now, and I'd confirm it by measuring."Honest, with a way forward.
They challenge a choice"Fair point. If that happens, my design breaks here. I can do A or B; I'd take A, because…"Restate, then concede or defend — with a reason either way.
They redirect you"Happy to go there. I'll park the caching and come back to it if there's time."You follow the steer and keep the thread.
Your mind goes blank"Let me think out loud: the riskiest requirement here is the latency target. What would break first?"Anchoring on a requirement restarts the reasoning.
You're behind on time"I'm conscious of time. I'd like to go straight to the queue design and cover the rest in a sentence."Shows judgement, and protects the sweep.
The requirements change mid-way"That changes the ordering guarantee. Here's what stays the same, and here's what moves…"An impact analysis, not a panic.
You realise you made a mistake"I want to correct something I said earlier: it's per person, not per event. That makes the number ten times larger."Trust is worth more than looking flawless.
The interviewer stays silent"Should I keep going in this direction, or is there something you'd rather I look at?"An active check-in beats guessing.
They ask about a technology you haven't run"I haven't run that in production. From first principles I'd expect it to behave like X, and here's what I'd check."Reasoning beats name-dropping.
Wrap-up"To recap against the requirements: … The trade-offs I'd flag: … Decisions I'd still want to settle: … What would you like me to go deeper on?"You end on structure, with the last word theirs.

G · The first ninety seconds, weak and strong

The same prompt, the first minutes, two ways. The design has not started in either — and one of them has already won the interview's most important argument: what is being built.

Weak — the first six minutesInterviewer: "Design a notification system." Candidate: "Okay. So there'll be clients, a load balancer, an API gateway, then microservices — a notification service, a user service, a template service — Kafka for the queue, Redis for caching, Cassandra for storage. Let me draw that." [twelve boxes, six minutes, no requirements] Interviewer: "Who are these notifications for?" Candidate: "Uh — users. Probably push and email. I'll add an SMS service too."
Strong — the first ninety secondsCandidate: "Let me restate it: a service our products use to tell people things — a payslip is ready, a task is assigned — and get it to them on the right channel. Can I take about five minutes on requirements, then a first design, then two deep dives? Where would you like depth?" Interviewer: "Sure. Reliability, I think." Candidate: "Then a few questions that would change the design. Who receives them — employees of companies using our products? Which channels? And what is the worst thing a person could experience — a late message, a duplicate, or a missing one?" Interviewer: "In-app, push and email. Missing is worst. Late is fine — except security alerts." Candidate: "So: never lose one; security alerts within seconds; duplicates minimised but not impossible. For scale I'll assume 2,000 companies, the largest at 100,000 people, and a payday that reaches all of them within minutes — say if that's off. Marketing campaigns and a template editor are out of scope today. Does that match?" Interviewer: "That's about right."

What changed: in ninety seconds the strong version has an agreed scope, a priority in user terms (missing is worst), a scale assumption the product owner can veto, and the deep dive the tech lead wants. Every later choice can now be checked against something the interviewer said.

H · At a glance — twenty lines for the night before

For the night before. If you remember nothing else, remember these twenty lines.

DoDon't
State the plan and the time boxes in the first two minutes.Don't draw before the scope is agreed.
Ask questions that would change the design — in the product owner's language.Don't ask ten questions in a row without saying where you are heading.
Write requirements, numbers and decisions where both of you can see them.Don't go silent for more than half a minute — think out loud, or say you are thinking.
Offer a default and ask for a veto.Don't list technologies; every box needs a reason tied to a requirement.
Draw the simplest design that works, number the arrows, walk a request through it.Don't present options without choosing one.
Choose, then price the choice: "X, because Y; the cost is Z."Don't say "add a cache" or "shard it" without the number, the key and the cost.
Give every scaling claim a number from this system.Don't defend against valid criticism — restate, concede or counter with a reason.
For every box: down, slow, duplicated, out of order, wrong?Don't spend more than about five minutes on estimates or schema details.
Name the metrics and the two alerts you would set.Don't skip failure and metrics because you are short of time — shorten a deep dive instead.
Finish with a recap tied to the requirements, and the open decisions.Don't end with an apology or a new component.

I · Action items — rehearse these this week

Rehearse these; do not just read them. Each takes an evening.

  1. Run three timed mocks on a hard 60-minute clock. Stop each at 60 and write down which block overran.
  2. Record the first seven minutes and count your checkpoints. Aim for at least four questions to the interviewer that are not "does that make sense?".
  3. Write your opener and your wrap-up and say each in under a minute until they are automatic.
  4. For five of the worked examples on this page, write the three sweeps in five lines each: what breaks at 10×, the top three failures, the two alerts.
  5. Learn ten round numbers (requests per day → per second, bytes per row, read latencies) from the Math Toolkit, and practise saying "so what" after each.
  6. Practise "I don't know, I'd assume, and I'd check" until it stops feeling like weakness.
  7. Ask a friend to push back on every decision, and answer each with: restate → concede or counter → reason.
  8. Grade the mock with the Interview-Day Checklist and fix the lowest row next time.
Before You Walk In

Interview-Day Checklist

A self-grading rubric — run your own mock interviews against this before the real one.

DimensionWhat good looks likeRed flag
ScopingExplicit FR/NFR split, a clear line on what's in and out.Jumping straight to architecture with no stated requirements.
Entities & API3–5 clean endpoints, mapped 1:1 to functional requirements.A full CRUD API for every entity "just in case."
Architecture walkthroughTraces an actual request through the diagram, once per use case.A static diagram presented with no data flow narrated.
Deep-dive rigorTies a specific NFR number to a specific bottleneck and fix.Generic scaling buzzwords with no connection to this system.
Trade-off articulationStates the cost of every choice, not just the benefit.Every decision presented as free / obviously correct.
CommunicationThinks out loud, checkpoints scope and direction with the interviewer.Long silent stretches, or an uninterrupted monologue.
Time managementRequirements + API ≈ 25% of time; deep dives get the largest share.20 minutes perfecting a schema, 5 minutes on deep dives.
AdaptabilityFollows the interviewer's steer into unplanned areas without losing the thread.Rigidly sticking to a memorized script regardless of where they lean in.
Blueprint — a personal reference framework for system design interview prep. Six steps, run the same way every time: Requirements → Core Entities → API/Interface → Data Flow (optional) → High-Level Design → Deep Dives.
